title: Slides
text:
One deck per day, published here in full so that participants can look back at what was on the screen and so that anyone considering the programme can see exactly what is taught rather than a description of it.
They are facilitator decks rather than handouts. Each one carries the argument of the day, the cues for the live demonstrations, the lab briefs and the timings, and every deck has speaker notes recording what should be said out loud at each point — and, just as importantly, what should not be said yet, since several sessions depend on the room reaching a conclusion before it is offered one.
They are also deliberately sparse, and that is worth explaining rather than apologising for. The detailed content lives on the session pages, where it can be read properly and returned to; a slide dense enough to be read is a slide that is being read instead of listened to. If a deck looks thin next to the session page it accompanies, it is working as intended.

title: Slides
text:
Using them
Each deck opens in a browser and needs nothing installed. A few keys are worth knowing before you present from one.
Speaker notes open with S. They are not a script. They are the four or five things that decide whether a session lands: what to say immediately before a reveal, what to resist warning the room about, and where to stop talking and hand over the keyboard.
Full screen is F. Overview is Esc or O. Arrow keys or the space bar advance.
Offline. Every deck is a single self-contained HTML file with its fonts and figures embedded in it. Download one, carry it on a USB stick, open it on a machine with no internet connection at all, and it behaves identically. That is not incidental polish — classroom wifi is not something worth betting a session on, in Ajah or anywhere else.

title: Slides
text:
Adapting them

The decks are source, not output
There is no binary file to wrestle with here. Each deck is a Quarto .qmd file of a few hundred lines of markdown, living in slides/. Edit the text, run one command, and you have a new deck in the same house style:
quarto render slides/day3.qmd
The theme lives in slides/tdbg-slides.scss — change the palette there and all five decks follow.
This matters if you intend to run any of the material internally, which several alumni have. Fork the repository, replace the FMCG examples with cases from your own sector, and keep the structure — the structure is where most of the pedagogy sits. The licence permits all of it: materials CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, code MIT.

title: Slides
section: What is deliberately not in the decks
text:
What is deliberately not in the decks
Three omissions are choices rather than gaps, and each one has a reason behind it.
The salt key and the gallery solutions. These are for facilitators, and not before Friday afternoon. They live in the repository’s facilitator/ directory and are deliberately not linked from anywhere a participant might click while sitting in the room with a laptop open.
Long code. Code that has to be read carefully belongs on the session page, where it can be copied, run and paused over. On a slide it can only be gestured at, and the room ends up watching somebody scroll.
Anything that would let a facilitator talk for more than four minutes. The decks are built to run out of material before the room runs out of patience, which is a constraint on the person presenting rather than on the content — and it is the four-minute rule applied to the teaching materials themselves.

title: Capstone · Defence
section: The panel, and the three rooms
text:
The panel, and the three rooms
Three external people, none of them faculty, none of them from this school:

a CFO or finance director, who will attack the value case;
an analytics or data leader, who will attack the method;
a risk, audit or compliance officer, who will attack the governance.

They are external for a reason worth naming. A faculty member who has watched you work all week knows what you meant, fills in the gaps involuntarily, and grades the effort as well as the output. Somebody who has never met you has only what you say in the room, which is exactly the condition you will be in on a Monday in six weeks’ time when you present this to your own executive committee.
From 15:30 the cohort splits into three parallel rooms, one panellist and one faculty member in each. Each room takes its share of the defences, nine minutes each, ninety minutes. You get one of the three, and which one is drawn at lunchtime — so prepare for all three lines of attack, not the one you would prefer.
That is the trade the timetable makes: you do not hear the other defences, and in exchange every single person delivers one. Hearing other people defend is instructive. Defending is transformative. We buy the second.
They have read your two-page brief in advance. They have not seen your slides and they do not want any.

What is being tested
Not whether your model is sophisticated. Nobody on the panel cares, and if the method is elegant they will take that as read and move on to something else.
What is being tested is whether you can stand behind a number in front of people who do not want to believe it — which is, when you strip away the tooling, the entire job this programme exists to teach.
Underneath that headline the panel is really looking for four things, and it helps to know what they are, because they are not what most people prepare for:
Do you know where your number is weakest? Every estimate rests on something that could be wrong. A panellist forms their view of you largely on whether you name that thing before they find it. Somebody who volunteers their weakest assumption is treated as a reliable narrator for the rest of the conversation; somebody who has to be led to it is not.
Can you separate what you measured from what you concluded? This is the whole of Friday morning, compressed into a habit. The panel is listening for the join between the evidence and the claim, and for whether the verb you used matches the design you ran.
Would the decision actually change? They are trying to work out whether a real person, with a name and a diary, does something different next month. A great deal of technically excellent work fails here, and it fails silently, because nobody in the room wants to ask the question that sounds naive.
Are you honest under pressure? The most informative ninety seconds of any defence is the one after a question you cannot answer. That is the part they will remember, and it is the part almost nobody rehearses.

title: Capstone · Defence
text:
Format







5 minutes
You present. No slides. You may hold your two-page brief and put one chart on the screen.


4 minutes
Questions. The panel will interrupt during your five minutes as well.


9 minutes
Total, per person. The room runs to a visible clock and it is not negotiable.



Three rooms in parallel, each hearing its share of the defences, 15:30 to 17:00.
The visible clock is not there to make the afternoon stressful. It is there because a hard stop is the only thing that reliably produces the compression this exercise is about — and because without it, one person’s overrun is taken out of somebody else’s defence, which would be unfair in a way that matters more than anybody’s comfort.

title: Capstone · Defence
section: The rubric — the same one published on Monday
text:
The rubric — the same one published on Monday








Dimension
Weight
What earns a high mark




Business impact
40%
A named recurring decision, a named decision-maker, value with a range and three ranked assumptions, and an honest statement of what happens if the assumptions are wrong


Analytical rigour
30%
Grain stated. Defects found and handled. Leakage checked. Uncertainty quantified. Evidence standard matched to the claim. Naive benchmark reported.


Communication
20%
Number and action in the first sentence. Interval with its driving assumption. One chart that makes the case. Survives interruption.


Feasibility and governance
10%
90-day plan whose first milestone needs nobody’s permission. Lawful basis. Model card. The displaced person named.



A capstone cannot pass on rigour alone. A technically immaculate analysis of a decision nobody makes scores 30 out of 100 here, and that weighting is deliberate: it is the actual distribution of value in the world outside this room.
It is worth reading the weighting the other way round as well, because it is the more encouraging direction. A modest, well-chosen analysis of a decision somebody genuinely makes every month — clearly explained, honestly caveated, with a first step that starts on Monday — can score very well indeed on 70% of the rubric without any technical ambition at all. If your week produced less modelling than you hoped, that is not the constraint on your mark.

title: Capstone · Defence
text:
The five minutes
Five minutes is not eight minutes with things left out. It is a different document, and the discipline of it is the point — a senior audience gives you about this long before they have formed their view anyway.
A structure that works, and you may use it:
0:00–0:30 — The number and the action. One sentence containing a figure, a verb and a date. Then stop talking for two seconds and let it land.
0:30–1:15 — The confidence. The interval, and the single assumption that drives its width. What it would cost to narrow it.
1:15–1:45 — The ask. Specific, addressed, dated. Including “nothing, this is for information” if that is the truth.
1:45–3:00 — The evidence. Where the data came from, its grain, what you found wrong with it and what you did about it. This is your credibility, and it is Tuesday’s work.
3:00–3:45 — The evidence standard. What kind of claim you are making and what would be needed for a stronger one. Concede this before you are asked.
3:45–4:15 — Governance and the 90 days. Lawful basis, human in the loop, the first milestone.
4:15–5:00 — What happens if you are wrong, and how you would find out.
Everything else you know is in the four minutes of questions, or in the appendix nobody opens. Cutting to this shape is the last exercise of the week and it is not an accident that it is the hardest.

title: Capstone · Defence
section: What a strong defence sounds like
text:
What a strong defence sounds like
Structures are easier to follow once you have heard one filled in, so here is the first ninety seconds of a defence built on the availability case. It is not the only good version, and your figures will be your own, but the shape of it is worth studying.

“Availability in Q1 was 96.9%, and closing the gap to 97.5% is worth ₦17.9m of gross profit a year. I am asking for approval by 30 October to change the reorder policy at three depots for one quarter, with the other nine as a comparison group, at no new spend.
My range is ₦8.1m to ₦32.5m. Almost the whole of that width is one judgement — how much stockout demand is genuinely lost rather than deferred to the following week. I have assumed a third; the range spans 15% to 60%. About two weeks of point-of-sale analysis would settle it, and I have not spent that yet because the decision does not turn on it.
The evidence is sell-out from the WMS, one row per depot per SKU per week, and I found problems in it that changed the answer. I will come to those. The claim I am making is associational, not causal: I know availability and lost sales move together, and I do not yet know that this policy closes the gap. That is exactly what the three-depot comparison is for.”

Notice what has happened in those ninety seconds. The panel has the number, the action and the date before they have formed any view of their own. They know how uncertain it is and precisely why. They have been told the data had problems, by the presenter, before anybody could find them. And the causal claim has been downgraded to what the evidence supports, with the stronger design offered as the ask — so the obvious method attack has been made by the presenter and answered in the same breath.
What that costs is nerve, not preparation. Every sentence in it is a sentence a nervous presenter would soften or leave until later.

The five questions the panel always asks
Have the answer ready. Every one of these has been the subject of a session this week.

“What is the grain of this table?” — 2.4
“Would you have known this at the time you needed to act?” — 3.5
“Is that real or nominal?” — 1.2
“How would you know if you were wrong?” — 5.2
“Who loses if this works?” — 1.1

The sixth, which is not always asked but should be: “which of these numbers did the assistant produce, and which did you check?”
None of the five is a trap. Each is a question a competent panellist asks because the answer tells them how far the rest of your analysis can be trusted, and each can be answered in one sentence if you have done the work. That is why they are worth rehearsing aloud: the difference between knowing the answer and being able to say it fluently under a clock is larger than it seems from a chair.

title: Capstone · Defence
section: Answering a question you cannot answer
text:
Answering a question you cannot answer
This is the moment people fear, so it is worth planning for rather than hoping to avoid. It will happen — the panel is deliberately drawn from three different disciplines, so at least one of them will ask about something outside where you spent your week.
There are three bad responses and one good one, and the bad ones are bad in instructive ways.
Bluffing fails worst and fails permanently. Somebody on that panel does this for a living, and a confident answer with a wrong shape is immediately recognisable to them. Worse, it retrospectively contaminates everything you said before it, because the panel now has to wonder which of your other confident answers was also constructed on the spot.
Capitulating — “you’re right, that probably invalidates it” — is the opposite failure and it is more common in this room, because it feels like honesty. Usually it gives away far more than the question actually demanded. A specific objection to one assumption does not invalidate an analysis, and conceding as though it did leaves the panel unable to tell which parts of your work were sound.
Deflecting into detail — answering a question you were not asked, at length, in the hope that the clock runs out — is the most common of the three and the most transparent. The panel will simply ask again, and you will have spent a minute of your four.
The response that works has four parts, and it can be delivered in about fifteen seconds:

Say plainly that you do not know. Not apologetically, and without a preamble. “I don’t know.”
Say what you do know that bears on it. The adjacent fact, the related check you did run, the boundary of what you established. This is what distinguishes not knowing from not having thought about it.
Say how you would find out, concretely enough that somebody could start. Which table, which comparison, roughly how long.
Say what would change if the answer went either way. This is the part almost nobody does, and it is the part that turns the exchange around, because it demonstrates that you understand how much rests on the open question.

Put together: “I don’t know what the effect on returns was — I didn’t have returns data at the depot grain. What I do know is that the margin figure I used is gross of returns, so if returns rose the ₦17.9m is overstated. I would check it against the credit notes file, which is about a day’s work. If returns rose by more than about a fifth, the case stops being worth doing, and I would want that answered before the pilot rather than after.”
That answer contains an admission of ignorance and it makes the presenter sound more reliable, not less. It is the same asymmetry as in 4.5: a person who marks the edge of their knowledge precisely is easier to trust inside it.
One practical note. “I’d have to check” is fine once. Twice in nine minutes and the panel quietly reclassifies the whole item as not yet ready, however good the work behind it — which is the reason for the rehearsal below, and for writing down the questions you hope nobody asks.

title: Capstone · Defence
text:
The rehearsal, 14:30
Before the panel arrives you get forty-five minutes in pairs — roughly twenty minutes each way — with a Sceptic from a table you have not worked with. They have the rubric and the five questions.
Their instruction: find the question the presenter is least prepared for, and ask it twice.
Asking twice is the important half. The first answer to an uncomfortable question is usually a deflection produced under surprise; the second is the real one. Panellists know this and do it instinctively, so it is much better to meet it here.
Their second instruction: give exactly one sentence of feedback afterwards. Not a list. The one thing that, if fixed, most improves the defence.
The single-sentence limit is deliberate too. A list of eight observations delivered forty-five minutes before a defence cannot be acted on and mostly produces anxiety. One sentence can be acted on, and being forced to choose makes the Sceptic decide what actually matters.

title: Capstone · Defence
section: The checklist before you stand up
text:
The checklist before you stand up


First sentence contains a number, a verb and a date.


The interval is stated, and the assumption that drives its width is named.


You can state the grain of every table you used.


Every feature in your model has passed the leakage question.


Every number is real or nominal, and you know which.


Your causal verbs match your evidence. You audited them.


You can name the evidence standard your claim rests on, and the stronger design you would run next.


Model card written. Lawful basis identified. Human review defined.


The 90-day plan’s first milestone needs nobody’s permission.


You have named the person whose judgement this displaces, and what you will do about them.


The brief regenerates from the pipeline. You have tested this today.


If two or three of those are not true an hour before you stand up, do not attempt to fix them all. Fix the first one, which costs a single sentence and carries a fifth of the communication mark, and then be candid about the rest when they come up. An unfinished item you name yourself costs very little. The same item found by a panellist costs a great deal more.

title: Capstone · Defence
section: After the defence, 17:00 — and we finish at 17:30
text:
After the defence, 17:00 — and we finish at 17:30
The failure logbook, consolidated. Every entry from every table, deduplicated into one page: the ways the copilot misled us this week. It is read aloud and sent to the cohort.
It is, reliably, the artefact people forward to their teams — and it is the honest summary of what this week was actually about. It travels because it is the one document that is useful to somebody who was not here.
The two envelopes. The number you wrote on Monday morning, with its interval. The number you wrote this morning, with its interval. Compare them, and note which changed more: the number, or the interval.
For most people it is the interval, and it will have got wider. That is worth sitting with for a moment, because the instinct is to read a wider interval as having gone backwards — five days of work and you are less sure than when you started. But the Monday interval was narrow because it was uninformed: it was drawn before you knew what the data did on the joins, before you knew which assumption the value case actually rested on, and before you had asked what evidence your verb required. The Friday interval is wider because it now includes the uncertainty that was always there and was invisible to you.
That is not a failure of the week. It is the week working. You now know more about what you do not know, which is the condition for every good decision you will make with data from here.
Certificates. Certificate of Completion this afternoon.
Certificate of Implementation at Day 90, to those who can show the number that moved — and, more importantly, how they know it moved because of what they did.

title: Governance you can actually run
section: Why this is on Friday and not in a compliance module
text:
Why this is on Friday and not in a compliance module
Governance has a reputation as the thing that happens to a project after the interesting work is finished, and that reputation is the reason it so often arrives too late to be useful. The practical case for putting it here, at the end of a week about building things, is simply this: governance is where analytics programmes get stopped, and being stopped in month seven is far more expensive than being slowed down in week one. In month seven you have a model, a team, a sponsor and a set of expectations, and unwinding any of them is costly. In week one you have a design document and a conversation.
There is a version of this session that reads out a statute, and it fails, because a list of sections is not something anybody can act on. The version that works organises the same material around three questions an executive genuinely faces, usually with somebody waiting for an answer:

May this data leave my network?
May this decision be made by a model?
Who is accountable when it is wrong?

Everything below is in service of being able to answer those three quickly and defensibly.

title: Governance you can actually run
section: The Nigerian frame, in the parts that bite
text:
The Nigerian frame, in the parts that bite
Two documents matter. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 is the primary law — the thing that creates the obligations. The NDPC’s General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID) 2025 — issued 20 March 2025, effective 19 September 2025 after a six-month transition — is the operational detail: what you file, when, and at what tier. If you read only one, read the Act; if you have to act, you will need both.
Here is what an analytics function actually runs into.
Lawful basis, chosen and documented before you process. The starting point of the whole regime is that processing personal data requires a reason recognised in law, and that you should know which one you are relying on before you begin rather than after somebody asks. There are six: consent, contract, legal obligation, legitimate interest, vital interest, and public interest. Two things are worth internalising. “We already had the data” is not one of them — lawful acquisition and lawful use are separate questions. And “the customer agreed to the terms in 2019” does not automatically cover what you are doing now, if what you are doing now is materially different from what those terms described. Building a churn model on transaction data collected to run an account is exactly the sort of case where that needs an answer rather than an assumption.
Data controllers and processors of major importance. If you process personal data at volume, or you operate in a sector the Commission designates — financial services, communications, health, and oil and gas among them — you are likely in scope. Being in scope brings concrete obligations: registering with the Commission, appointing a Data Protection Officer, and filing compliance audit returns. GAID tiers this classification rather than applying one flat threshold, and the tier you land in determines what you file and what it costs. That is why it is worth resisting the single headline number you will find in a summary article — this page included — and asking your DPO which tier your organisation actually sits in.
The audit cycle. A compliance audit and an annual return, with filing fees under GAID running from ₦100,000 to ₦1,000,000 depending on the tier, from the 2026 cycle. Confirm the current filing window with your DPO — it is a fixed date in the calendar rather than a rolling anniversary of when you registered.
Data protection impact assessment (s.28). Where processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, you must carry out a DPIA. In plain terms a DPIA is a written analysis done before the processing starts: what you intend to do, why it is necessary, what could go wrong for the people whose data it is, and what you have put in place to reduce that. And where the DPIA concludes the processing would be high risk, you must consult the Commission before you process.
This is the obligation an analytics function is most likely to trip and least likely to have heard of, and the reason is understandable — it sits in data protection law rather than anywhere an analytics team would naturally look. Systematic profiling of individuals is squarely within it, and a churn score, an attrition score and a credit propensity are all systematic profiling of individuals. So: a model card is good practice. A DPIA may be the law. They are different documents written for different readers, and doing the first does not discharge the second.
Breach notification: 72 hours from discovery to the NDPC. There is a subtlety here that is easy and expensive to miss. As drafted, the trigger for notifying the Commission is a breach likely to result in a risk to rights and freedoms; the higher high risk threshold is what obliges you to notify the affected data subjects. Those are two different bars, and the failure mode is not deviousness — it is an incident room under pressure collapsing them into one question, deciding the breach is not serious enough to tell customers about, and concluding from that that it need not be reported to the Commission either. Keep a breach register, with the two questions asked separately and both answers recorded.
Cross-border transfer requires an adequate level of protection, demonstrated through the recipient country’s law, binding corporate rules, standard contractual clauses or an approved certification — and under GAID, instruments such as binding corporate rules require the Commission’s approval. Absent adequacy, transfer is still permitted on explicit informed consent, or for contract performance, vital interests, legal claims or the data subject’s direct benefit. The practical reading is that a route almost always exists, but it has to be chosen and documented in advance rather than reconstructed afterwards.
Automated decision-making. Data subjects have protection against decisions made solely by automated means, together with a right to human review. The word doing the work is “solely”, which is why the quality of the human review matters so much — a point the model card section returns to.
Penalties. For an entity of major importance, up to ₦10 million or 2% of annual gross revenue, whichever is higher. For others, ₦2 million or 2%. Non-compliance with a Commission order can carry imprisonment of up to one year. The figures are worth knowing, though in practice the disruption of an investigation and the reputational cost tend to dwarf the fine.

The question that applies to everything you learned this week
When you paste customer text into a hosted AI assistant, that is a processing operation, and if the model is hosted outside Nigeria it is very likely a cross-border transfer of personal data.
It needs a lawful basis and a transfer mechanism, in advance, in writing.
That lands uncomfortably at the end of a week spent doing exactly this sort of thing, so it is worth being clear about what it does and does not mean. It is not a reason to abandon the techniques in 4.2. It is the reason the local-model option appeared in that session rather than being tucked into a compliance annex at the end of the course. A model running on your own machine, processing your own data, transfers nothing anywhere — there is no recipient, no border and no mechanism to arrange — and for most theme-classification work the accuracy gap between a local model and a hosted one is smaller than the gap between two conscientious human labellers reading the same reviews.
The practical rule for Monday: anonymised or synthetic data, or shapes and schemas rather than values, may go to a hosted assistant. Actual customer records go to a local model, or to an enterprise deployment your organisation has procured and assessed, or nowhere. Most of the work you want to do fits comfortably in the first category, once you are in the habit of asking which category you are in.

title: Governance you can actually run
section: The three questions, answered as a decision tree
text:
The three questions, answered as a decision tree
The tree below is not a substitute for the analysis above; it is a way of getting to the right conversation quickly, for the routine cases. Run it while the work is being scoped, so that the answer shapes the design rather than arriving to challenge it.





flowchart TD
  A{"Does the work touch<br/>personal data?"} -->|No| OK1["Hosted tools fine.<br/>Still log what you did."]
  A -->|Yes| B{"Can it be anonymised<br/>or synthesised for<br/>this task?"}
  B -->|Yes| OK2["Anonymise, then<br/>hosted tools fine.<br/>Document the method."]
  B -->|No| C{"Do we have an approved<br/>in-region or on-prem<br/>deployment?"}
  C -->|Yes| OK3["Use it.<br/>Record the lawful basis."]
  C -->|No| D["Local model only.<br/>Nothing leaves the machine."]
  E{"Is a decision about a<br/>person made solely<br/>by the model?"} --> F["Human review in the loop,<br/>documented, with a route<br/>to challenge"]
  style OK3 fill:#D6F0EA,stroke:#00695C
  style D fill:#F6EFE0,stroke:#8A6D2F,stroke-width:2px
  style F fill:#FBE9E5,stroke:#B3341E,stroke-width:2px


 Run this before the work starts, not after the model is built.

title: Governance you can actually run
text:
Wednesday’s model comes back
On Wednesday several tables built an attrition model on hr_attrition.csv, and commute_minutes was among the strongest predictors. Nothing about that is surprising — how far somebody travels to work is a real and reasonable influence on whether they stay.
But consider what else that column carries. Commute time is a close proxy for where somebody lives; where somebody lives, in Lagos as in most large cities, is a close proxy for income; and in many markets residential geography also tracks ethnicity or religion. So a model with no protected attribute anywhere in its inputs — and there is none anywhere in that file — can nonetheless sort people substantially along lines the law cares about, because it has been handed a variable that quietly encodes them.
This is not a trap laid for the unwary. It is the ordinary situation, because useful predictors are useful precisely by being correlated with a lot of things about a person’s life.

The sentence to take away from Friday
Removing protected attributes from a dataset does not remove discrimination from a model. It removes your ability to measure it.
That is worth reading twice, because the intuition runs the other way: dropping the sensitive column feels like the responsible act, and it is often done in good faith by people trying to do the right thing. What it actually achieves is to leave the proxies in place while destroying the only column you could have used to check whether the model was treating groups differently.
So “is this variable allowed?” turns out to be the wrong question. Four better ones:

What decision is this score attached to? A retention offer is a benefit — the worst outcome for somebody the model overlooks is that they do not get a call. A promotion or redundancy score is a detriment, and detriment decisions carry a far higher standard of evidence, documentation and review.
Who bears the cost of being wrong? If the institution bears it, an error is a business cost. If the individual bears it — the employee not shortlisted, the customer refused — the bar rises again, because they did not choose the exposure and cannot see it.
Can the affected person find out and contest it? If there is no route by which somebody learns a score was applied to them and no route by which they can challenge it, you do not have a governed model, however thorough the documentation.
Would you defend this in front of the person it was applied to? Not to a regulator — to the employee, in a room, in ordinary words. It is a more demanding test than the compliance one and a considerably more useful one, because it catches the cases that are technically permitted and obviously wrong.


The honest resolution for the HR case is usually this: use the model to identify teams and conditions where attrition risk is elevated — commute burden, long waits for promotion, excessive span of control — and act on those systemically, by changing the conditions. Do not attach a score to an individual employee’s file.
That trade costs less than people fear. Nearly all the value in an attrition model is in knowing where and why the risk concentrates, which is what tells you what to change. Almost all the exposure is in the individual score, which is the part that gets applied to a person, sits in a file, and is very hard to explain to them. Giving up the second while keeping the first is not a compromise so much as a better use of the model.

title: Governance you can actually run
text:
The model card
A model card is one page per model, written in language a non-specialist can read, that records what the model is for and what it is not for. It takes about twenty minutes if you kept the comments from 2.6, and it is the artefact that makes everything else — the DPIA, the audit return, the answer to a data subject — possible to assemble later.

Model card — the fields that matter


Name


Retail churn propensity, v1.2


Owner


Named individual, plus the business owner who acts on it


Purpose


Rank customers for the monthly retention call list. Not for pricing, credit or service tiering.


Decision


Top 600 by expected value at risk are contacted. Benefit decision, not detriment.


Training data


12,000 customers, Jan 2024 – Mar 2026, one row per customer at snapshot


Features


Listed. Each with a note on when it becomes available in the business process.


Excluded, and why


closure_form_started — post-outcome, leaks. branch_state — geographic proxy, no business justification for the ranking.


Performance


AUC 0.77 on held-out data. Top-decile lift 3.0x. Baseline churn 10.6%.


Performance by segment


By segment, age band and state. Report the worst group, not the average.


Known limitations


Not validated on customers with under 3 months tenure. Not tested since the November re-segmentation.


Human review


Retention lead reviews the list; any customer may be removed with a logged reason.


Monitoring


Monthly: score distribution drift, feature drift, realised churn among contacted vs holdout.


Retire by


Review date, after which it must be revalidated or switched off.


Two of those lines are the ones organisations reliably leave blank, and it is worth understanding why each matters.
“Not for” exists because models are reused. A churn propensity built to order a call list is a plausible-looking input to a pricing decision, a service-tier decision or a credit decision, and eighteen months later somebody who was not in the room when it was built will find it in the warehouse and use it for one of those. They will not be behaving badly; the model is right there and it appears to answer their question. The “Not for” line is the only thing standing between that person and a decision the model was never validated for.
“Retire by” exists because models decay quietly. The world the model learned moves — a re-segmentation, a new product, a change in how a channel is used — and nothing in the pipeline announces that the model has become less accurate. A date forces the question to be asked on a schedule rather than after an incident, and it makes switching a model off a routine administrative act rather than an admission that something went wrong.
The “Human review” line deserves the same scrutiny, because given the protection against decisions made solely by automated means, this is the field where you establish that the decision is not solely automated. It needs to describe what the reviewer actually does, what they see, and what proportion of cases they change. A reviewer who approves a list of 600 in four minutes has not reviewed anything, and writing the field honestly is the point at which that becomes visible.

title: Governance you can actually run
section: Your AI-use policy — one page, drafted this afternoon
text:
Your AI-use policy — one page, drafted this afternoon
The policy that works is not a forty-page document with a version history and no readers. It is one page, seven lines, specific to your function, written so that somebody joining next month could follow it without asking. Length is not thoroughness here; a policy nobody has read governs nothing.


What may go into a hosted assistant. Name the categories. Be concrete: “aggregated figures, schemas, anonymised extracts, public documents — yes. Customer records, employee records, unredacted contracts — no.”


What must stay local. And which tool people should use for it, installed and working.


Who decides the edge cases, and how long they take to respond. A policy with no fast route for exceptions gets routed around.


What gets logged. At minimum: what was used, on what data, for what decision.


Where a human must be in the loop, and what that human is actually expected to do. “Reviewed by a human” who rubber-stamps a list of 600 is not human review.


How somebody affected finds out and contests it.


When this policy is next reviewed. Put a date on it.


The second and third lines decide whether the policy survives contact with a deadline. If what must stay local has no working local tool behind it, the policy is asking people to choose between the rule and the work, and the work wins. If edge cases go into a queue with no stated response time, people stop raising them — not defiantly, but because they have something due on Thursday. Both are failures of provisioning rather than of character, which is good news, because provisioning is something you control.

Core lab · 20 minutes


Run the decision tree on your capstone, write down which branch you land on, and answer in writing: does it need a DPIA? If it scores individuals, probably yes — name who would sign it.


Write the model card for the model you built this week. Eight minutes, and the two fields that matter are Not for and Retire by. Include performance on its worst segment, not its average.


Draft the seven-line AI-use policy for your function.


Sceptic: find the line in their policy that their own team will route around, and say why.


The Sceptic’s task is the sharpest one on the list, and it is meant kindly. Every policy has a line that will be quietly bypassed, usually because it makes a common task slower without offering a faster compliant route. Finding it now, from a colleague, costs nothing. Finding it in an audit costs a great deal more.


Stretch
Write the fairness section of your model card properly: performance broken down by every group you can lawfully measure, with the worst group named explicitly rather than averaged into the headline.
Then answer, in writing, the question the panel may ask this afternoon: “if this model is 6 points less accurate for one group, what happens to the people in that group, and is that acceptable?”
There is no formula that answers that, and the absence is not a gap in the method. Whether a gap is acceptable depends on what the score is used for, what the alternative process would have done, and who carries the cost of the errors — three things that no metric contains and that the person accountable for the decision has to weigh. That is precisely why the question sits with the person in this room rather than with the model, and why being able to answer it in your own words is worth more than any amount of documentation.

title: Governance you can actually run
text:
Takeaways

Governance is where programmes get stopped. Do it in week one, not month seven.
Lawful basis before processing. 72 hours for a high-risk breach. Cross-border transfer needs a mechanism, in writing, in advance.
Pasting customer text into a hosted assistant is very likely a cross-border transfer. The local model is the practical answer.
Removing protected attributes removes your ability to measure discrimination, not the discrimination.
A model card is good practice; a DPIA may be a legal obligation, and profiling individuals is squarely inside it. They are different documents.
One model card per model. The fields nobody fills in are “Not for” and “Retire by”.
A one-page policy people follow beats a forty-page one they route around.


Sources
Read the primary sources. They are short, they are free, and every summary below is somebody’s paraphrase — including this page.

Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 — the Act itself. Sections 28 (DPIA), 39–40 (breach), 24–27 (lawful basis and data subject rights), 44–45 (cross-border transfer), 48 (penalties). Published by the National Assembly and by the NDPC at ndpc.gov.ng.
General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID) 2025 — issued by the NDPC on 20 March 2025, effective 19 September 2025. The operative detail on registration tiers, DPO requirements, audit filing and transfer instruments. Published at ndpc.gov.ng.

Secondary summaries, useful for orientation and not for compliance:

NDPA 2023 — a guide for businesses
Nigeria: NDPC issues GAID — key compliance insights (DLA Piper, June 2025)
KPMG Nigeria — review of the NDPA 2023

Confirm the current position with your own legal and data protection functions before acting. Nothing on this page is advice, and the thresholds move.

title: Experiments that settle arguments
section: An experiment is the cheapest way to end an argument
text:
An experiment is the cheapest way to end an argument
Picture a disagreement you have watched before. Two executives take different views on whether a change works — a new checkout flow, a new reorder rule, a new call script. Each has evidence, because both have looked at data that is genuinely consistent with their position. The disagreement runs for two quarters, occupies four meetings, and is eventually settled by whoever is more senior or more persistent. Nobody involved has behaved badly. There was simply no evidence available that could distinguish between the two views, so something other than evidence had to do the work.
An experiment is the alternative. Four weeks, half the users given the change and half not, and at the end a number that both parties agreed in advance would settle the question. That is not mainly a statistical device. It is a management device — a way of converting an argument that seniority would otherwise decide into one that a measurement decides — and that framing is far more persuasive inside a business than any amount of talk about p-values.

What randomisation actually buys
The intuition most people arrive with is that randomising makes the answer more precise. It does not. What randomisation buys is comparability, and the distinction is worth a minute.
Suppose you want to know whether a new checkout flow lifts conversion. Measuring conversion in the group that saw it is easy. The hard part is knowing what that same group would have done without it, which is a thing you can never observe. So you use a second group as a stand-in, and the entire question becomes: is the second group a fair stand-in for the first?
If you let people choose — early adopters get the new flow, everyone else keeps the old one — the answer is no, because the kind of person who opts in differs from the kind who does not, in ways you can list and in ways you cannot. Assign at random, though, and the two groups end up alike on everything: the characteristics you measured, the ones you did not measure, and the ones nobody has ever thought to name. Not identical, but differing only by the amount that chance produces, which is a quantity you can calculate.
That is the whole trick, and it is why no amount of statistical adjustment on historical data reproduces it. Adjustment can only correct for confounders you thought of and recorded. Randomisation handles the ones you did not, because it does not need to know what they are.
It is also why “we don’t have enough data to run a test” is usually a misdiagnosis offered in good faith. Volume is rarely the binding constraint; the binding constraint is that nobody arranged for a comparison group before the change went out. That is a decision, and it is usually free.

title: Experiments that settle arguments
section: Design before you run, not after
text:
Design before you run, not after
There are five decisions to make, and the reason they are all made in advance and written down is not bureaucratic. Each of them is a decision that becomes much harder to make honestly once you have seen the data, because by then you know which choice gives you the answer you were hoping for. Writing them down first is how you protect yourself from your own future enthusiasm.
1 · The unit. What, exactly, is being randomised — individual users, whole customers, depots, branches, days, territories? This one decision determines everything downstream. The mistake that catches careful people is randomising at one level and analysing at another: assigning the new policy to whole branches, then treating each customer as an independent observation. Customers in the same branch share a manager, a catchment and a stock position, so they are not independent, and counting them as though they were makes your sample look far larger than it is. Intervals come out too narrow and differences look significant when they are not. Randomise by branch, analyse by branch.
2 · The metric, defined before you look. One primary metric, written down in a sentence precise enough that somebody else could compute it. The temptation afterwards is to add a second, and a third, until one of them is significant — and because each new metric is another chance for noise to look like signal, this reliably produces findings that do not replicate. It is not dishonesty. It is what curiosity does when it is allowed to run after the result is in.
3 · The minimum effect worth detecting. Not “any effect”, which is not a design target because any effect can be made detectable given enough time. The right question is: what is the smallest improvement that would actually change the decision? If a 0.2 percentage point lift in conversion would not cover the cost of rolling the change out, a test built to detect 0.2 points is a test built to answer a question nobody will act on.
4 · The duration. Computed from the answer to 3, before you start. That calculation is the next section.
5 · The guardrails. The metrics that must not deteriorate even if the primary metric improves — complaints, refunds, margin, page load times, call handling time. Name two or three in advance and commit to what you would do if one moved the wrong way. A checkout change that lifts conversion and doubles refunds has not succeeded; it has moved the cost somewhere you were not looking.

title: Experiments that settle arguments
section: Power: how long, computed before you start
text:
Power: how long, computed before you start
Here is the plain version of the idea, before the technical name arrives. Any test can fail in two directions. It can tell you there is an effect when there is not — that is the error people worry about, and the 5% significance level is what keeps it rare. It can also tell you there is no effect when in fact there is one, simply because you did not gather enough observations for a real difference to stand out from the ordinary week-to-week noise. That second failure is the one that quietly kills good ideas, and it is entirely preventable, because you can work out in advance how many observations you need.
That number depends on three things, each behaving the way common sense suggests. The rarer the event you are measuring, the more of it you need to see. The smaller the difference you want to catch, the more you need — and this one bites hardest, because halving the effect you want to detect roughly quadruples the sample required. And the more certain you want to be of catching it, the more you need again. The chance of detecting a real effect of a given size is called the statistical power of the test, and the convention is to design for 80% — meaning that if the effect really is as large as you specified, you have an 80% chance of coming away able to say so.
library(pwr)

baseline <- 0.0442         # current conversion rate, from the control arm
mde      <- 0.10           # smallest relative lift worth detecting: 10%

h <- ES.h(baseline * (1 + mde), baseline)
pwr.2p.test(h = h, sig.level = 0.05, power = 0.80)
#> n = 35,501 per arm

# At 4,000 eligible checkout sessions a day, split 50/50:
35501 * 2 / 4000
#> 17.8 days
Read that arithmetic slowly, because it is the whole apparatus in four lines. The current conversion rate is 4.42%, so roughly one session in twenty-three ends in a purchase. You have decided that a 10% relative lift — taking 4.42% up to about 4.86% — is the smallest change worth rolling out for. To have an 80% chance of detecting a difference that size, you need 35,501 sessions in each arm, so 71,002 in total. If 4,000 sessions a day are eligible and they are split evenly between the two arms, 71,002 divided by 4,000 gives 17.8 days.
Eighteen days. That is a date you can put in an email before the test starts, which is the real prize here: the conversation about when you will have an answer happens now, in the calm, rather than in week three when somebody senior asks how it is going.
Notice too how sensitive the answer is to traffic. At 1,800 eligible sessions a day rather than 4,000, the same 71,002 observations take about thirty-nine days — nearly six weeks rather than under three. That is a materially different conversation with the product director, and it is much better to have it in the design meeting than in week five, when the only options left are to keep waiting or to declare a result you do not have.

The three ways power calculations get skipped, and what each costs
None of these is a sign of carelessness. Each is a reasonable-sounding sentence that gets said in a busy room, and each has a specific cost that is invisible at the time.
“We’ll just run it and see.” The difficulty is that you will look at the numbers as they accumulate, and you will stop when they look good — not out of bad faith, but because a favourable result feels like the moment the question has been answered. Every look is another opportunity for random fluctuation to cross the threshold, and with enough looks a treatment with no effect whatsoever will cross it surprisingly often. The fix is not to stop looking; it is to fix the stopping rule in advance, or to use a design built for repeated peeking.
“We ran it for a week, it wasn’t significant, so it doesn’t work.” This is the most expensive of the three, because it retires an idea that may well have been good. An underpowered test that finds nothing has not told you the effect is zero; it has told you the effect, if present, was smaller than this test could see. “Not significant” and “no effect” are different statements, and the distance between them is exactly the power calculation nobody did. A useful habit: whenever somebody reports a null result, ask what effect size the test was powered to detect.
“We need 15,000 per arm and we only have 3,000.” This is not a failure. It is genuinely useful information, and it arrived before anybody spent the money. You now have four real options: run for longer; choose a more sensitive metric, further up the funnel, where the numbers are bigger; make the change bolder so the effect you are hunting is larger; or accept a quasi-experimental design and the weaker claim that comes with it, which is the subject of 5.3. All four are legitimate. Running the underpowered test anyway and reporting whatever comes out is the only option that is not.

title: Experiments that settle arguments
section: The thirty-second check that comes before the result
text:
The thirty-second check that comes before the result
SELECT arm, COUNT(*) AS users, ROUND(AVG(converted), 4) AS conversion_rate
FROM 'data/ab_test_checkout.csv'
GROUP BY arm;
control     59,981    0.0442
treatment   55,989    0.0468
The rates are the part everybody reads first. Treatment converts at 4.68% against control’s 4.42%, and 0.0468 divided by 0.0442 is 1.057 — a relative lift of 5.7%. On a business doing serious volume through that checkout, 5.7% is a real amount of money, and somebody in the room is already drafting the rollout email.
Before reading on, it is worth covering the right-hand column and looking only at the counts.


Look at the arm sizes before you look at the rates


59,981 against 55,989. Under a 50/50 split those two numbers should differ only by chance, and it is worth working out how much chance would explain. The two arms together hold 115,970 users, so a fair split puts 57,985 in each. Control is 1,996 above that and treatment 1,996 below. The typical wobble you would expect from a fair coin tossed 115,970 times is the square root of 115,970 × 0.25, which is about 170 users. The observed gap is 1,996 — roughly twelve standard deviations from what randomisation predicts. A departure of three standard deviations already happens only about once in a few hundred experiments; twelve does not happen.
This is a sample ratio mismatch, usually shortened to SRM, and the plain meaning is simply this: the assignment mechanism did not deliver the split it promised, so something other than the coin decided who ended up where. Here it was an instrumentation fault — a tagging bug that quietly dropped about 11% of treated Android users, which is 6.7% of the treatment arm.
Once you have an SRM, nothing downstream is interpretable, and this is the part that is hard to accept when the headline result is favourable. The users who went missing are not a random subset; they are Android users, who differ from iOS and desktop users in device, in demographics and in how they shop. Removing them changes the composition of the treatment arm, so the comparison is no longer between two alike groups. The difference in conversion rates is now a mixture of whatever the change did and whatever Android users are like, and no adjustment untangles that, because you cannot condition on a population you no longer have.
# The check, as one line. Run it on every experiment before you look at the result.
n <- c(control = 59981, treatment = 55989)
chisq.test(n, p = c(0.5, 0.5))
#> X-squared = 137.4, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16
That test asks exactly the question above — how surprising are these two counts if the split really was 50/50 — and returns a probability so small that R stops printing digits.
The correct response is not to adjust, and not to caveat. It is to fix the instrumentation and re-run. Several large technology organisations treat an SRM as an automatic invalidation with no discretion attached, precisely because the temptation to explain it away is so strong when the result is one you like. Removing the discretion removes the temptation.
Thirty seconds. Before the result, every time.

title: Experiments that settle arguments
section: The average that hides the decision
text:
The average that hides the decision
Suppose the instrumentation has been fixed, the test re-run, and the result holds. There is one more thing to do before the rollout email, and it is to look at the result for the groups of customers you actually manage the business by.
library(tidyverse)
ab <- read_csv("data/ab_test_checkout.csv")

ab |>
  group_by(segment, arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), cr = mean(converted), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = c(n, cr)) |>
  mutate(rel_lift = cr_treatment / cr_control - 1)



Segment
Relative lift
95% interval
p




Mass
+11.4%
+3.8% to +19.5%
0.003


SME
+38.9%
+20.7% to +59.8%
<0.001


Affluent
−16.6%
−24.4% to −8.0%
<0.001


Overall
+5.7%
+0.3% to +11.4%
0.039






Positive on average. Negative where the money is.


Read the intervals rather than the point estimates, because the intervals are what tell you how much of this you can rely on. The overall lift of +5.7% carries an interval running from +0.3% to +11.4%: it clears zero, but only just, and a rollout justified on that alone would be resting on a result that is barely distinguishable from nothing. Each of the three segments, by contrast, is resolved far more sharply — and, crucially, they do not point the same way. Two are clearly positive and one is clearly negative, and none of the three intervals touches the others.
That is already awkward. It becomes a genuine decision the moment you convert it into money, because conversions and naira do not distribute the same way across these segments. Affluent is 29% of conversions and 50% of revenue — an average basket of ₦38,700 against Mass’s ₦14,800, something over two and a half times as much per conversion. So the segment the change hurts is the segment that contributes half the revenue.
Ship to everyone and you lift conversions in aggregate while damaging the half of the revenue base that pays for the most. Ship to Mass and SME only and you keep the gains and avoid the harm — a different decision, a better one, and one that is entirely invisible in the headline number. This is the most common way a well-run experiment produces a bad rollout, and notice that nothing went wrong technically: the test measured conversions because conversions are what the platform reports, and the step nobody owned was converting the answer into the currency the business is actually managed in.
And none of it is interpretable until the SRM is fixed, because the users the tagging bug dropped were Android users, and Android users are not spread evenly across these three segments. The segment table inherits the problem the arm counts revealed.

The rule, and the trap next to it
Look at the result by the two or three segments that matter commercially, and pre-register those segments before the test starts.
The second half of that sentence is what separates the analysis above from a trap that looks almost identical. If you slice a finished result twenty different ways, you will find a “significant” segment somewhere by chance alone — that is precisely what a 5% significance level means, one false positive in twenty by construction. Naming three segments in advance is analysis, because you committed to being wrong about them. Finding twenty afterwards and reporting the interesting one is fishing, and it will not survive replication.
Write the segments into the design document alongside the primary metric. It takes one line, it costs nothing, and it is the difference between a segment finding a sceptic will accept and one that evaporates the next time anybody looks.

title: Experiments that settle arguments
text:
Beyond the digital A/B test
Experiments have a reputation as a website thing, and that reputation costs organisations outside technology a great deal, because the logic transfers anywhere you have more than one of something and can decide at random which ones get the change first.

Depots and branches. Randomise the new reorder policy to three of twelve depots. Nine controls. This is exactly what the availability capstone should propose.
Regions and territories. Switch a pricing rule on in half the territories.
Time slices. Alternate weeks, when the population genuinely cannot be split. Weaker, because seasonality moves between weeks and because customers can carry an effect from one week into the next, but real and much better than nothing.
Customer lists. Hold out 10% of the retention call list. This is the single most valuable experiment most organisations are not running, and it is what tells you the third term in 3.5 — does the call actually work?
Staggered rollout. You were going to roll out in phases anyway, because you always are. Randomise the order of the phases rather than choosing it, and the comparison comes free.

That last one deserves emphasis, because of all the ideas here it has the lowest cost and the lowest uptake: any phased rollout can be an experiment if you randomise the order rather than choosing it. Phased rollouts are normally ordered by readiness, enthusiasm or politics, which is exactly what makes the early sites incomparable with the late ones. Drawing the order at random costs a conversation and gives you a clean comparison at every stage of the rollout you were doing anyway.

Core lab · 30 minutes


Run the SRM check on the checkout experiment. Report the p-value. Say what you would do next.


Compute the naive overall lift. Then the three pre-registered segments.


Write the recommendation given both findings. It is not “ship it” and it is not “kill it”.


Design the experiment for your capstone: unit, primary metric, minimum detectable effect, guardrails, pre-registered segments.


Compute the duration. Write the date the test would conclude.


Sceptic: name the way this experiment could be contaminated. Spillover, seasonality, another test running at the same time.


The third item is the one worth protecting if the clock beats you. Recommendations that are neither “ship it” nor “kill it” are harder to write and much more often correct, and the practice of writing one is what stops a mixed result being flattened into a single verdict on its way up the organisation.


Stretch
Design the retention call holdout for the banking case: hold back 10% of the model’s top-scored customers, do not call them, and measure the difference in what happens to them.
Then confront what it costs, because this is not a costless design and pretending otherwise is why the conversation usually fails. You are deliberately not calling customers you believe are at risk, in order to learn something. Write the two-paragraph justification you would give the Head of Retention: the number of customers involved, the value at stake, and what you would do if the holdout showed the calls were working — and if it showed they were not.
The argument that carries it is usually the last one. Without a holdout, nobody in the bank knows whether the retention programme works at all, which means nobody can defend its budget either. A holdout protects the programme as much as it tests it.
That conversation is the real skill here, more than the arithmetic. Almost every organisation has a long-running programme nobody has ever tested, and the reason is rarely that somebody refused. It is that the case for testing it was made once, badly, and never made again.

title: Experiments that settle arguments
text:
Takeaways

An experiment is a device for ending an argument cheaply. Use that framing.
Randomisation buys comparability on the confounders you never measured.
Five decisions in advance: unit, metric, minimum effect, duration, guardrails.
The SRM check comes before the result. Thirty seconds, every time. An SRM invalidates; it does not adjust.
Pre-register two or three commercially meaningful segments. Three named in advance is analysis; twenty found afterwards is fishing.
Any phased rollout can be an experiment if you randomise the order.

title: Lab 4 · The one-number brief
text:
Run of show







Time
What happens




0–25 min
Build. The brief, rendered from your pipeline. Two pages.


25–32 min
Cross-table swap. Exchange briefs with somebody from a table you have not worked with. Read in silence.


32–50 min
Defence rounds, corners in parallel.


50–60 min
Rewrite the opening sentence in light of what happened. Pin to the wall.



The defence rounds are the part that needs the facilitator’s attention, because the arithmetic of a full room does not work in the obvious way. A room this size cannot have everyone present to everyone in eighteen minutes; a lab that pretends otherwise quietly becomes a lab where four confident people present and everybody else watches them.
So the room splits into corners of six or seven, each with a facilitator or helper holding a timer. In each corner the slot is ninety seconds to present, sixty seconds of questions — two and a half minutes a person, so seven people take seventeen and a half minutes, which fits the eighteen the timetable allows with thirty seconds to spare. The timer is visible and it is not negotiable. Running over is not a small discourtesy in this format; it is the thing that removes somebody else’s turn, and learning to land inside the slot is one of the skills the lab exists to build.
Everybody presents. That is the whole design: this is the rehearsal for Friday, and a rehearsal you watched is not a rehearsal.

title: Lab 4 · The one-number brief
text:
The brief
Page 1 carries five things, in this order and no other. The order is not stylistic — it is the order from 4.5, built so that a reader who stops after any one item still has something they can act on.


The number and the action. One sentence containing a figure, a verb and a deadline.


The interval and the assumption that drives its width.


The ask. What you need, from whom, by when. Including “nothing, this is for information” if that is the truth.


What happens if we do nothing. Two lines.


One chart. The one that makes the case.


Page 2 carries the method, written in the order a sceptic attacks it. Writing it in that order rather than in the order you did the work is the single easiest way to look prepared, because every question the reader forms is answered on the next line.


Data: source, grain, period, row count.


What was excluded, and why. Including the defects you found and what you did about them.


The assumption most likely to be wrong, and what it would cost to test it.


How you will know afterwards whether it worked.


Reproduction: the command that regenerates this document.



The rule that is being enforced today
No number in the prose may be typed.
Every figure in every sentence is inline code. Your Sceptic’s first act on receiving your brief is to open the source and search it for digits appearing outside a code block.
If they find one, you change the underlying data, re-render, and show the document updating in front of them. If it does not update, the brief is not finished — not because a rule has been broken, but because you have just demonstrated that at least one number on the page is no longer connected to the data it came from.
This sounds pedantic on a Thursday afternoon. It is the entire difference between a document that stays true and a document that was true once, and the gap between those two opens silently, at whatever point somebody next refreshes the source.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: Lab 4 · The one-number brief
text:
The starter file
Read the file below twice. The first time, follow the prose and ignore the code; the second time, look at how each sentence in the prose is fed by a named value computed above it. Three of the comments in the setup block are worth reading carefully, because each marks a decision that has ended a value case before now.
---
title: "Availability: closing the gap to target"
subtitle: "Decision brief for the Supply Chain Steering Committee"
date: today
format:
  pdf:  {geometry: [margin=2.2cm], fontsize: 11pt}
  html: {embed-resources: true}
execute: {echo: false, warning: false}
---

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
weekly <- arrow::read_parquet("outputs/fmcg_weekly.parquet")

# The shipped file stops on 2026-03-30 -- Q2 is held back for the forecast
# market -- so the last complete quarter is Q1 2026. Filter on a period the
# data does not contain and every inline number below,
# renders as NaN. Which is the lesson, arriving the hard way.
q1      <- weekly |> filter(week_starting >= as.Date("2026-01-01"))
avail   <- 1 - mean(q1$stockout_flag)
target  <- 0.975
gap_pp  <- (target - avail) * 100

# The one assumption the whole range rests on: what share of a stockout is a
# genuinely lost sale rather than demand deferred to the following week.
# Every naming decision below is downstream of this vector, so a reader can
# change one line and see the brief move.
lost_sale_share <- c(low = 0.15, mid = 0.33, high = 0.60)

# ANNUALISE, and say so. q1 is one quarter -- 6,240 depot-SKU-weeks -- so the
# recovered weeks it implies are a quarter's worth. The sentence below claims a
# figure "a year", and a quarterly number wearing an annual label is the single
# most common error in a value case. Multiply by four, or change the sentence.
quarters_per_year <- 4
weeks_recovered <- nrow(q1) * (target - avail) * quarters_per_year
rev_per_week    <- mean(q1$revenue_ngn, na.rm = TRUE)
gross_margin    <- 0.34

value <- weeks_recovered * rev_per_week * gross_margin * lost_sale_share
value_mid  <- value[["mid"]]
value_low  <- value[["low"]]
value_high <- value[["high"]]

fmt <- \(x) paste0("₦", format(round(x / 1e6, 1), nsmall = 1), "m")

title: Lab 4 · The one-number brief
text:
The number
Network availability in Q1 2026 was r scales::percent(avail, 0.1) against a target of r scales::percent(target, 0.1) — a gap of r round(gap_pp, 1) points. Closing it is worth about r fmt(value_mid) of gross profit a year.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: Lab 4 · The one-number brief
text:
How confident
My 80% range is r fmt(value_low) to r fmt(value_high). Almost all of that width is one assumption: what share of a stockout is genuinely lost sale rather than demand deferred to the following week. I have assumed r scales::percent(lost_sale_share[["mid"]]), with a plausible range of r scales::percent(lost_sale_share[["low"]]) to r scales::percent(lost_sale_share[["high"]]). Two weeks of point-of-sale analysis would replace the assumption with a measurement.
Note what that means: the range is not the model’s uncertainty. It is one judgement of mine. Say that out loud, because the version of this sentence that does not say it is the one that gets you caught.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: Lab 4 · The one-number brief
text:
The ask
Approval to change the reorder policy at three depots for one quarter, with the remaining nine as a comparison group. No incremental spend. Decision required by 30 October so the change lands before the December peak.
Three things in that file repay a second look.
The headline figure is computed. The first sentence under the heading contains `r fmt(value_mid)` — a calculated figure, so that even the number a reader sees first cannot go stale. It is also a small piece of theatre worth performing in the defence: change one input, re-render, and the figure moves. Keep it out of the title: line: inline R in the front matter runs before any code chunk, so a helper defined later is not found and the render stops.
The whole value case hangs from one vector. lost_sale_share carries three numbers, and because the low, mid and high values flow through the same multiplication, the money moves in direct proportion to that one judgement. A reviewer who thinks a third is too generous does not need to argue with your pipeline; they change 0.33 to whatever they believe and read the new answer. That is a very different conversation from defending a single figure, and a much better one to be in.
The annualisation comment is the one that has caught people. The quarter in the file is 6,240 depot-SKU-weeks, and every recovered week the calculation implies is therefore a quarter’s worth. quarters_per_year <- 4 turns it into an annual figure. Leave that line out and the arithmetic is still correct — it is simply correct about a quarter while the sentence beside it says “a year”, which understates the case fourfold and is nearly impossible to spot from the output. A quarterly number wearing an annual label is not an exotic mistake; it is the most common error in a value case, and it survives review precisely because both halves look right on their own.
Then page 2, and one chart, and you are done.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: Lab 4 · The one-number brief
text:
The defence
Ninety seconds. You may not use slides. You may hold the brief.
Say the first sentence. Then stop and take questions. Stopping is the part people find hardest and it is the part being practised — the silence after a strong opening line is where your audience decides what they actually want to know, and filling it with the second paragraph you had prepared takes that choice away from them.

Reviewer’s brief
You have sixty seconds of questions after each ninety-second presentation, and a few minutes with the brief before it. Use the reading time to pick your line of attack rather than to be polite about the formatting. All four attack types from 4.5 are available:

Data. “Where did this number come from, and what is the grain?”
Method. “Is this causal? If not, what are you actually claiming?”
Relevance. “So what? Who does something differently on Monday?”
Authority. “That is not what [other function] reports. Why?”

Then the fifth, which is specific to this programme:

Reproduction. “Change one input in your pipeline and re-render this in front of me.”

Score each brief out of five on: does page 1 lead with the number and the action; is there an interval with a named driving assumption; is the ask specific with a date; is the evidence standard stated honestly; did the document regenerate.
Hand the score back with one sentence of what to fix. Not five sentences. One. Choosing which single thing to say is most of the value you provide — a list of five gets nodded at, and one sentence gets acted on before Friday.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: Lab 4 · The one-number brief
section: The common failures, so you can avoid them
text:
The common failures, so you can avoid them
None of these is a sign of weak analysis. Each is what a good analyst produces when the brief is written last, at speed, from the inside of the work rather than from the reader’s side of it.
The brief that buries the number. Three paragraphs of background before the finding, because that is the order in which you discovered it. Every reader stops at paragraph one, and paragraph one was about data sources.
The interval that is decoration. A range quoted with no account of what drives its width. A sceptic will ask, and “the model produced it” is not an answer — it tells them the range came out of something, not what would make it narrower.
The ask that is not an ask. “We recommend continued monitoring.” Nobody has to do anything, no date passes, no one is accountable, so nothing happens. If the honest position is that no decision is needed yet, say so explicitly — that is a real ask, and it is respected.
The evidence standard that is silently absent. No comparison group, no holdout, no before-and-after — and, crucially, no acknowledgement that this is so. On Monday that was acceptable, because nobody in the room had the vocabulary for it. It is Thursday, and tomorrow morning is entirely about it.
The chart that was chosen because it existed. One chart. The one that makes the case. If you cannot choose between two, that is useful information rather than a formatting problem: it usually means the case has not yet resolved into a single claim.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: Lab 4 · The one-number brief
text:
Before you leave today


Brief rendered from the pipeline, both pages. HTML is fine — a self-contained .html is the deliverable, and a working PDF toolchain is not something anybody should be fighting at 16:30 on a Thursday. Render to PDF later if the committee wants paper.


Searched for typed numbers in prose. None found.


Dashboard built, with the decision sentence and the quality badge on it.


Defended for ninety seconds against a table you had not worked with.


Opening sentence rewritten after the defence.


Failure logbook entry.


Capstone checkpoint signed: dashboard and memo exist.



Tomorrow morning
The panel on Friday afternoon will ask, of every brief: “how would you know if you were wrong?”
It is a fair question and it is not a trap. What it asks is whether there is any future observation that would tell you your recommendation had failed — and if the honest answer is that there is none, then the case cannot be evaluated after the fact, only defended before it.
If your answer today is “we would look at the trend”, spend twenty minutes tonight on 5.2 and 5.3 before you arrive. The difference between a case that gets funded and one that gets deferred is almost always the answer to that single question.
