title: One source, five outputs
text:
The problem, which everybody has
Picture the last few days of a month end. An analyst produces the numbers. Somebody types a selection of them into a deck for the executive committee. Somebody else types a smaller selection into a Word memo for the audit committee. A third person, working from the same underlying extract but a slightly earlier version of it, builds the dashboard. Then the CFO asks a good question late on the Thursday, one number is recomputed, and the corrected value is patched into the deck — because the deck is the thing being presented on Friday — and not into the other two.
There are now four documents in circulation and at least two of them are wrong. Nobody was careless. The transcription happened under time pressure, it happened in three different places, and there was never a moment at which anyone could have seen all four versions side by side. This is a structural property of copying numbers between documents rather than a property of the people doing the copying, which is why it recurs in organisations that are otherwise extremely well run.
The second half of the problem arrives later. In March somebody asks why the December figure was restated, and the honest answer is that nobody can reconstruct it, because the calculation lived in a spreadsheet cell that has since been overwritten by the January calculation. The number was right, or it was wrong, and there is now no way to establish which.
The fix has been well understood for thirty years and it is simpler than it sounds: the document contains the code that produces its own numbers. Prose and calculation live in the same file. Nothing is transcribed. When the data changes you re-render, and every number, chart and table in the document updates together — or the render fails loudly and tells you which line it could not compute, which is also a perfectly good outcome, because a document that refuses to build is one you cannot circulate by accident.
The technical name for this is literate programming, and the tool we will use for it is Quarto. You will meet the idea again under other names — R Markdown, Jupyter Book, notebooks — but the underlying move is always the same one: put the sentence and the sum in the same place, so they cannot drift apart.

What this actually buys you
Consistency. The number in the memo, the deck and the dashboard cannot disagree, because there is only one of it. Every appearance is the same computation rendered in a different place.
Speed at month end. The first month is slower, and it is worth saying that plainly rather than discovering it: you are building the machine as well as the report. Every month after that is a single command. Teams that adopt this typically take a 10-day close narrative down to under a day of analyst time, and the saving compounds because the reclaimed days go into analysis rather than into assembly.
Auditability. “Why did the December figure change?” acquires an answer: a commit, with a date, a name and a diff showing exactly which line of code moved and what it moved to.
Version control that means something. You can diff a document — see, line by line, what changed between one version and the next. You cannot meaningfully diff a spreadsheet, and you certainly cannot diff a slide.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: One source, five outputs
text:
The shape of the source
Everything lives in one file: the prose you want people to read, and the code that produces the numbers inside it. Read the example below for its shape rather than its syntax — the block at the top is configuration, the block in the middle is the calculation, and the part at the bottom is the report itself.
---
title: "Depot availability, Q1 2026"
author: "Supply Analytics"
date: today
format:
  html:  {toc: true}
  pdf:   {documentclass: scrreprt, geometry: [margin=1in]}
  docx:  {reference-doc: templates/lbs-report.docx}
  revealjs: {theme: [default, templates/lbs.scss]}
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
weekly <- arrow::read_parquet("outputs/fmcg_weekly.parquet")

# Q1 2026 is the last complete quarter in the shipped file, which stops on
# 2026-03-30. Q2 is deliberately held back for Wednesday's forecast market, so
# no participant-facing code may reference it -- filter on it and every number
# below renders as NaN, in the one session about documents that stay true.
q1 <- "2026-01-01"
availability <- 1 - mean(weekly$stockout_flag[weekly$week_starting >= q1])
worst <- weekly |>
  filter(week_starting >= q1) |>
  summarise(rate = mean(stockout_flag), .by = depot_name) |>
  slice_max(rate, n = 1)
```

## Summary

Network availability in Q1 was **`r scales::percent(availability, 0.1)`**, against a
target of 97.0%. The weakest depot was **`r worst$depot_name`** at
**`r scales::percent(1 - worst$rate, 0.1)`**.

```{r}
#| label: fig-availability
#| fig-cap: "Weekly availability by depot, Q1 2026. The target line is 97%."
# ... chart code ...
```
Two things in that example are doing the real work, and both are worth slowing down for.
Inline code. The construction `r scales::percent(availability, 0.1)` sits inside an ordinary English sentence and is replaced, at render time, by a computed number. Nobody typed 96.9% into that paragraph. The document works out the availability figure from the weekly table, formats it as a percentage to one decimal place, and drops the result into the sentence. Change the data and the sentence changes with it. Notice too that the same technique picks the name of the weakest depot: `r worst$depot_name`. Text can be computed as readily as arithmetic, which means an exception list, a ranking or a “the three depots below target were…” sentence can all maintain themselves.
One YAML block, five formats. The section between the two --- lines at the very top is the front matter — configuration for the whole document, written in a format called YAML. The format: key lists everything this one source can become. A single command, quarto render report.qmd, produces all of them, and none of them is a copy of any of the others; each is a fresh rendering of the same source.

The single highest-value habit in this session
Never type a number into prose.
Not once. Not “just this one, it will not change”. Every number in every sentence is inline code that computes it.
This is the discipline that makes the whole arrangement hold, and it is the first one to go under time pressure — usually at eleven o’clock at night, on the one figure that is genuinely awkward to compute, with an entirely reasonable intention to come back and fix it properly. It happens to careful people, and it happens for good reasons.
It is worth resisting anyway, because of what it costs later. The moment one number is typed, the document can disagree with itself, and it eventually will — most often three months later, in front of somebody senior, when the typed figure is the only one on the page that did not move. A useful safeguard: if a number is hard to compute inline, compute it in the setup block and give it a name. value_mid in a sentence is still code, and it is far easier to read than a nested expression.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: One source, five outputs
text:
Five outputs, one command
quarto render report.qmd                 # every format in the YAML
quarto render report.qmd --to pdf        # just the board PDF
quarto render report.qmd --to docx       # for the person who needs to track changes
quarto render report.qmd --to revealjs   # the deck
quarto render dashboard.qmd              # the screen
Each of those outputs has a different reader with a different habit, and the last column of the table below is the thing that most often gets overlooked when a team first tries this.



Output
Who it is for
The one thing to get right




HTML
The team, day to day
Self-contained, so it survives being emailed


PDF
The board pack
Page breaks, page numbers, a real title page


Word
Legal, compliance, anyone who tracks changes
Use a reference doc so it lands in house style


reveal.js
Presenting it
One idea per slide; the appendix carries the detail


Dashboard
The recurring decision
Session 4.3



On Word specifically, because it is where this proposal usually meets its first objection. Organisations that insist on Word are generally right to insist on it: their review process depends on tracked changes, comments and a named person signing off a specific version, and none of that works in a PDF. The reference-doc: setting exists for exactly this. You supply an ordinary Word document carrying your house styles — the heading fonts, the table borders, the margins your communications team has already decided on — and Quarto writes its content into that skeleton, so the generated file arrives already looking like everything else the organisation produces. It is a two-line change, it removes the most common corporate objection to reproducible reporting outright, and almost nobody knows it exists.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: One source, five outputs
section: Parameters — the same report, twelve times
text:
Parameters — the same report, twelve times
A parameter is a value you leave deliberately unfixed in the source, so that the same document can be rendered against different scopes. Declare them in the front matter:
params:
  depot: "DP01"
  quarter: "2026-Q1"
and override them at the command line:
quarto render report.qmd -P depot:DP05 -P quarter:2026-Q1 \
  --output depot-DP05-2026Q1.html
Everywhere the report refers to params$depot, it now means DP05, and every number, chart and exception list recomputes for that depot alone.
Wrap that in a loop over the twelve depot codes and one command produces twelve tailored reports, each with its own figures and its own exceptions. This is the point at which reproducible reporting stops being a tidiness virtue and becomes an obvious economic decision. Consider the arithmetic from the other direction: if assembling one depot report by hand takes a careful analyst half a day, twelve of them is six days of work, every quarter, before anybody has thought about what the numbers mean. The loop below is four lines and it runs while you make coffee.
depots <- c("DP01","DP02","DP03","DP04","DP05","DP06",
            "DP07","DP08","DP09","DP10","DP11","DP12")

walk(depots, \(d) quarto::quarto_render(
  "report.qmd", execute_params = list(depot = d, quarter = "2026-Q1"),
  output_file = glue::glue("depot-{d}-2026Q1.html")))
There is a second, quieter benefit. Because all twelve reports come from one source, a depot manager reading their own report and a regional director reading the roll-up are looking at the same definitions. The familiar situation where two managers arrive at a meeting with incompatible versions of their own availability figure simply cannot occur.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: One source, five outputs
section: Freezing, so it renders on someone else’s machine
text:
Freezing, so it renders on someone else’s machine
Some computations are slow — a model fit, a classification pass over every review in the file — and re-running them every time somebody rebuilds the site is both wasteful and a good way to make people stop rebuilding the site.
execute:
  freeze: auto     # re-run only when the source changes
freeze: auto tells Quarto to store the results of each code chunk and reuse them until the code that produced them changes. The document still renders from a single source; it simply does not repeat work it has already done.
For anything genuinely expensive, go one step further and take the computation out of the document altogether. Do it in a pipeline script that writes a small result file — a summary table of a few dozen rows rather than the whole raw extract — and have the document read that file. The document should be fast to render. This is not fastidiousness: if rendering your report takes twenty minutes, nobody will re-render it to check a change, and within two months somebody will start typing numbers again, for entirely understandable reasons.

The reproducibility standard, stated as a test
Can a colleague clone your folder onto a clean machine and produce your PDF?
That is the whole standard. It is the one every scientific journal, every regulator and every serious audit function is converging on, and it has the great merit of being testable in ten minutes rather than argued about in a policy document.
Three things usually break it. None of them is a sign of sloppy work — each is what happens when a script grows out of an interactive session, which is how nearly all analysis begins.

Absolute paths. /Users/bongo/Desktop/data.csv exists on exactly one machine in the world. Use paths relative to the project root, so that the folder is portable.
Packages installed interactively. The code works because you installed something six weeks ago and have forgotten. Record the dependencies — renv in R, a lockfile in Python — so the next person can install the same set.
A manual step. “Then I open it in Excel and fix the header.” If it is not in the script, it does not exist, because it will not happen when you are on leave.



Core lab · 30 minutes


Write a two-page report on your capstone. Every number inline code. No typed figures.


Render it to HTML and PDF. Confirm the numbers match.


Change one thing in the pipeline. Re-render. Confirm every number moved.


Add a parameter and render the report twice for two different scopes.


Render to reveal.js and see what your report looks like as slides.


Hand the folder to the next table and have them render it on their machine.


That last step fails for about half the room on the first attempt, and it is designed to. The failure is nearly always one of the three items in the box above, it takes a few minutes to diagnose with somebody else’s error message in front of you, and it is very much better to find it here than to find it when a colleague inherits the report in nine months.


Stretch
Add a conditional paragraph — prose that appears only when the data warrants it.
```{r}
#| output: asis
if (availability < 0.95) {
  cat("::: {.callout-warning}\n",
      "Availability fell below the 95% floor in ", sum(breaches), " depot-weeks. ",
      "The service-level commitment to key accounts is at risk.\n:::\n")
}
```
Read that in English: if availability is below the floor, write this warning into the document; otherwise write nothing. The output: asis line tells Quarto to treat what the code prints as markdown rather than as program output, which is what allows the code to generate a formatted callout rather than a line of console text.
The report now escalates on its own. It raises the warning when the number crosses the threshold, and stays quiet when it does not — so nobody has to remember to check, and nobody has to remember to take the warning out again next month.
This is the beginning of the difference between a report and a monitoring system, and it costs six lines.


Copilot check
Assistants are excellent at this task. Describe your analysis and ask for a Quarto document and you will get a well-structured file with sensible sections, a working front matter block and code that runs.
There is one thing to check, every time: did it hard-code any numbers into the prose?
It usually will, and confidently. It sees the value 96.9% in the output you pasted and writes “availability was 96.9%” as ordinary text, because that is overwhelmingly what such a sentence looked like in everything it has read. It is not a lapse in reasoning; it is a very good imitation of how these documents are normally written, which is precisely the habit this session is trying to replace.
So search the source for digits appearing in prose, and replace every one with inline code. Then add this to your standing prompt, so you do not have to remember it again:

Every number that appears in prose must be inline code that computes it from the data. Do not hard-code any figure anywhere in the document text.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: One source, five outputs
text:
Takeaways

The document contains the code that produces its own numbers. Nothing is typed.
One source, five outputs, one command.
Use a Word reference doc, and the corporate objection disappears.
Parameterise, and twelve tailored reports cost the same as one.
The standard: a colleague clones your folder onto a clean machine and gets your PDF.

title: LLM classification at scale
section: The shift, and the discipline it requires
text:
The shift, and the discipline it requires
Three years ago, classifying free text by theme meant assembling a labelled training set of several thousand examples, holding a taxonomy argument that ran for a month, and finding a data scientist with time to do it. The economics of that ruled the approach out for most questions, which is why so much free text was left uncounted.
Now you write the categories in a sentence, run the corpus through, and have a labelled table in an afternoon. It works, it costs very little, and — as 4.1 argued — it handles Pidgin, code-switching and misspellings far better than any lexicon. That last point is why this session exists rather than being an appendix to the previous one.
It is not uniformly good, and the honest account of where it is weak matters more than the enthusiasm. Sarcasm remains the standing weak point of automated sentiment: “wonderful, another failed transfer” is scored positive by a great many systems, including capable ones. Published benchmarks on Nigerian Pidgin and other African languages — NaijaSenti, AfriSenti — consistently show accuracy below English on the same task, which stands to reason given what these models were trained on. Neither is a reason to avoid the approach. Both are reasons to measure it separately for the languages in your corpus, rather than quoting one overall accuracy figure that averages a strong result on the English rows with a weaker one on the rest.
That leads to the danger this session is built around. The old approach was expensive, and its expense acted as an accidental quality gate: nobody assembled three thousand labelled examples without also thinking hard about what the categories meant. The new approach removes the cost, and with it the gate. It is now trivially easy to produce a confident-looking distribution of themes without ever finding out whether the classifier is any good.

The rule for this session
An LLM classifier is a measurement instrument. Every measurement instrument has to be calibrated against something.
A classifier converts something you cannot count into something you can, and like any instrument that does that, the conversion has a tolerance. Nobody signs off a laboratory result without its error bars; this is the same object.
If you have not hand-labelled two hundred rows and compared, you do not have an error rate. And if you do not have an error rate, you do not have a measurement — you have an opinion that was expensive to generate.
Two hundred rows takes about forty minutes. It is the difference between “sentiment improved by four points” being a finding and being noise.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: LLM classification at scale
section: What the model can and cannot be trusted to do
text:
What the model can and cannot be trusted to do
Before writing any code it is worth being precise about the shape of this tool, because its strengths and weaknesses are not quite where intuition puts them.
It is reliable at recognition. Given a review and a fixed list of categories, deciding which one the review is about is close to what these models do natively. It reads “transfer failed but they debited me” and returns billing for much the same reason a person would — in Pidgin, in English, and in a sentence that switches between the two halfway through. It is untroubled by misspellings, missing punctuation and the compressed register people use on a phone.
It is unreliable at anything requiring knowledge it was not given. It does not know your product names, your internal process boundaries, or that “the Tuesday run” means the replenishment cycle. If the distinction between two of your categories depends on institutional knowledge, the model cannot make it — and it will not tell you that it could not.
It is weakest where humans are also weak, but it fails differently. Sarcasm, irony and mixed sentiment are genuinely hard, and two careful human labellers will disagree on them too. The difference is that a human labeller says “I am not sure about this one”. The model does not.

The failure mode to design against is the confident wrong label
Consider what a classical lexicon does with a sentence it does not understand. It finds no scoring word, returns neutral or nothing, and the row shows up as unclassified. The gap is visible; you can count it, and its size tells you how far to trust the rest.
A language model given an enum of seven categories returns one of those seven for every row it is shown, whatever the row contains. There is no “I do not know” in the schema unless you put one there. A review it has misread therefore does not arrive marked as doubtful — it arrives as branch_service, in the same column, indistinguishable from the rows it got right. The errors are silent, and silent errors do not get investigated.
Two further properties make this worse than it first looks:

The errors are not random, so they do not average out. If the classifier is weaker on Pidgin than on English, every theme those customers disproportionately raise is understated — consistently, in the same direction, every quarter. Random error shrinks as the corpus grows. Systematic error does not shrink at all; a bigger corpus simply gives you a more precise estimate of the wrong number.
Nothing downstream can recover it. Once the label is in the table, every chart and trend built on top inherits it, and each step makes the number look more solid. By the time it reaches a slide it has acquired a decimal place and a comparison against last quarter.

None of this argues against using the tool. It argues for the one countermeasure that works: hold some rows out and check them by hand. No diagnostic computed from the model’s own output, and no self-assessment you can ask it for, substitutes for a sample somebody labelled independently.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: LLM classification at scale
text:
Classifying the corpus

R (mall — runs locally)R (ellmer — any provider)Python


mall applies a local language model to a data frame column, row by row. Nothing leaves the machine, which for confidential text is frequently the difference between doing the work and not doing it.
library(tidyverse)
library(mall)

# Point at a locally-running model. No data leaves this laptop.
llm_use("ollama", "llama3.2", seed = 42, .cache = "_llm_cache")

reviews <- read_csv("data/customer_reviews.csv")

labelled <- reviews |>
  llm_sentiment(review_text, options = c("positive", "neutral", "negative")) |>
  llm_classify(review_text,
               labels = c("billing", "app_reliability", "network_quality",
                          "branch_service", "delivery", "pricing", "other"),
               pred_name = "theme") |>
  llm_extract(review_text,
              labels = "the single product or service the customer is talking about",
              pred_name = "subject")

labelled |> count(theme, .sentiment) |> pivot_wider(names_from = .sentiment, values_from = n)


library(ellmer)

chat <- chat_anthropic(system_prompt = paste(
  "You classify customer reviews for a Nigerian bank.",
  "Reviews may be in English or Nigerian Pidgin.",
  "Return only the requested structured fields."
))

schema <- type_object(
  theme     = type_enum(values = c("billing", "app_reliability", "network_quality",
                                   "branch_service", "delivery", "pricing", "other")),
  sentiment = type_enum(values = c("positive", "neutral", "negative")),
  intent    = type_enum(values = c("complaint", "praise", "question",
                                   "churn_threat", "other")),
  severity  = type_integer(description = "1 = trivial, 5 = would leave over this")
)

classify_one <- function(txt) chat$chat_structured(txt, type = schema)

# Batch, cache, and retry. Do not run 5,000 rows in a naive loop.
labelled <- reviews |>
  mutate(result = map(review_text, possibly(classify_one, otherwise = NULL))) |>
  unnest_wider(result)


import pandas as pd, json, time, pathlib, anthropic
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
SCHEMA = {"theme": ["billing","app_reliability","network_quality","branch_service",
                    "delivery","pricing","other"],
          "sentiment": ["positive","neutral","negative"],
          "intent": ["complaint","praise","question","churn_threat","other"]}

PROMPT = (
    "Classify this customer review for a Nigerian bank. It may be in English or "
    "Nigerian Pidgin. Return ONLY JSON with keys theme, sentiment, intent, severity "
    "(1-5). Allowed values: " + json.dumps(SCHEMA) + "\n\nReview: "
)

MODEL = "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929"      # PIN the dated version, not the alias


def _extract_json(txt):
    """Models add prose. Take the JSON object and nothing else."""
    i, j = txt.find("{"), txt.rfind("}")
    if i == -1 or j == -1:
        raise ValueError(f"no JSON in response: {txt[:80]}")
    return json.loads(txt[i:j + 1])


def classify(text, tries=4):
    for k in range(tries):
        try:
            r = client.messages.create(
                model=MODEL, max_tokens=150, temperature=0,   # temperature=0
                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT + text}])
            return _extract_json(r.content[0].text)
        except Exception:
            if k == tries - 1:
                return {"theme": "other", "sentiment": "neutral",
                        "intent": "other", "error": True}
            time.sleep(2 ** k)                                 # backoff


reviews = pd.read_csv("data/customer_reviews.csv")
out, path = [], pathlib.Path("outputs/labels.jsonl")
done = {json.loads(l)["review_id"] for l in path.open()} if path.exists() else set()
with path.open("a") as fh, ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=6) as pool:
    todo = reviews[~reviews.review_id.isin(done)]              # resume, don't restart
    for rid, res in zip(todo.review_id, pool.map(classify, todo.review_text)):
        fh.write(json.dumps({"review_id": rid, **res}) + "\n")  # write incrementally



All three do the same thing — send each review to a model with a fixed list of permitted answers, and write the answer back as a column. They differ only in where the model runs and how much of the machinery you build yourself.

Four operational things that will bite you
Cache. You will re-run this — to fix a bug, to add a category, to answer a question somebody asked in a meeting. Without a cache you pay twice and, worse, you get slightly different answers the second time, and then you cannot reproduce your own chart. Cache on a hash of the input text, so identical text always yields the stored label.
Constrain the output. Use a schema or an enum — a list of permitted values the model must choose from. Ask for a free-text category instead and you will receive billing, Billing, billing issue and payment/billing as four distinct categories, and spend an hour reconciling them into one.
Pin the model version and set temperature to zero. “We used the model” is not a method. “We used model X, dated version Y, at temperature 0” is. When the number moves next quarter you need to be able to say whether the business changed or the instrument did — and an alias like claude-sonnet-4-5 points at different weights over time, which is exactly the ambiguity you are trying to remove. Temperature is the setting that controls how much randomness goes into the model’s choice of words; at zero it makes the most likely choice every time.
Note that not every API offers a seed parameter, and temperature 0 is not a guarantee of determinism. The cache is your reproducibility mechanism, not the seed: hash the input text, store the label, and never re-classify a row you have already classified.
Batch and retry. Five thousand sequential calls will take an hour and fail somewhere in the middle. Parallelise modestly, retry with backoff, and write results incrementally — the .jsonl file in the Python tab exists so that an interrupted run resumes rather than restarts.

title: LLM classification at scale
section: Validation — the forty minutes that make it real
text:
Validation — the forty minutes that make it real
This is the section that separates a measurement from an assertion, and it is the one most often skipped — usually because the results already look plausible and there is a meeting on Thursday.
The procedure has four steps. First, draw a random sample — two hundred rows, not twenty. There is arithmetic behind that number rather than tradition: if the classifier agrees with a human on roughly 88% of rows, two hundred rows will contain about 200 × 0.12 = 24 disagreements, which is enough to see a pattern in. Forty rows would yield about five, which tells you whether something is catastrophically wrong but not where the boundary problems are.
Second, label them by hand, blind. A human reads the review and assigns a category without seeing what the model said. This matters more than it sounds: shown the model’s answer first, a labeller agrees with it far more often than they otherwise would. The phenomenon is called anchoring, it is not a weakness of the individual, and the remedy is to strip the model’s column out of the file before anybody opens it.
Third, compare. Fourth — and this is the step that repays the effort — look at where the disagreements fall rather than only at how many there are.
set.seed(1)
gold <- labelled |>
  slice_sample(n = 200) |>
  select(review_id, review_text) |>
  mutate(human_theme = NA_character_, human_sentiment = NA_character_)

write_csv(gold, "outputs/validation_blank.csv")
# --- a human fills this in, without seeing the model's answer ---

gold <- read_csv("outputs/validation_filled.csv") |>
  left_join(labelled |> select(review_id, theme, .sentiment), by = "review_id")

# Overall agreement
gold |> summarise(theme_agreement     = mean(theme == human_theme),
                  sentiment_agreement = mean(.sentiment == human_sentiment))

# The confusion matrix is where the useful information is
gold |> count(human_theme, theme) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = theme, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
The first summarise() produces raw agreement — the share of rows on which model and human chose the same label. It is the obvious number to report, and it is not sufficient alone.
Do not report raw agreement without a floor to compare it against. With seven categories and the largest holding 21% of the corpus, a classifier that ignored the text entirely and guessed the majority class every time would score 21% while knowing nothing at all — and on a more concentrated corpus, where one theme holds half the rows, that floor is far higher.
Cohen’s kappa does that comparison for you. It asks how much of the agreement you observed is more than chance would have produced, expressed as a share of how much room for improvement there was: κ = (observed − chance) ÷ (1 − chance). A kappa of 0 means the classifier is doing no better than guessing; 1 means perfect agreement. It is one line:
irr::kappa2(gold[, c("human_theme", "theme")])
The arithmetic is worth following once. Suppose observed agreement comes out at 0.88 and the agreement chance alone would produce, given how the seven categories are distributed, comes out at 0.20. Then κ = (0.88 − 0.20) ÷ (1 − 0.20) = 0.68 ÷ 0.80 = 0.85 — the classifier captured 85% of the improvement available over guessing. Quoting that alongside the raw 88% tells a reviewer you understood the difference.
Then read the confusion matrix, not the headline number. A confusion matrix is a table with human labels down the side and model labels across the top, so each cell counts the rows where the human said one thing and the model said another. 88% agreement sounds fine; the matrix answers the more useful question of where the 12% went.
The typical pattern in this corpus is that billing and app_reliability get confused, because “the app debited me twice” is genuinely both — a payment failure that happened inside the app. That is not a model failure. It is a taxonomy failure: your two categories overlap, the model is being asked to choose between them on a review that satisfies both, and two human labellers would split on it as well. The fix is not a better model. Either merge the themes or add a rule to the prompt saying which wins when both apply — and say in the method note which you did.
Carry the distinction beyond this example. Disagreements scattered evenly across the matrix suggest the classifier is struggling. Disagreements piled into one or two cells suggest your categories are, and that is a problem you fix with a definition rather than with technology.

What to put in the paper

Themes were assigned by [model, dated version] at temperature 0 against a fixed seven-category taxonomy; labels were cached, and the cache is included with this analysis. A random sample of 200 reviews, stratified by language, was independently hand-labelled without sight of the model’s answer. Model and human agreed on 88% of theme assignments (Cohen’s κ ≈ 0.85) and 94% of sentiment. Disagreements concentrated on the billing / app-reliability boundary, where the review describes a payment failure inside the app; these two themes are therefore reported together. 8.6% of the corpus is in Nigerian Pidgin, where agreement is lower than in English; the sample contains too few Pidgin rows to state a separate error rate with confidence, and a stratified follow-up is planned.

Four sentences, and each does one job: the first makes the run reproducible, the second establishes that the check was independent, the third states the error rate and where it concentrates, and the fourth admits a limitation the reader could otherwise have found for themselves — which is the sentence that earns the other three their credibility.
It converts “the model said” into a measurement with a stated error, and it is the difference between a technical reviewer trusting your paper and quietly discounting it.

title: LLM classification at scale
section: Where it runs, and why that is a board-level question
text:
Where it runs, and why that is a board-level question
There are three places this work can happen, and the choice between them is a legal question before it is a technical one.











Where the data goes
Speed
Quality
Use when




Hosted model
Leaves your network, often the country
Fast
Best
The text is not personal or confidential


Local model
Nowhere
Slower
Good, and improving fast
Customer records, HR text, anything under the NDPA


Enterprise / in-region deployment
Your tenancy
Fast
Best
Your organisation has procured it and DPIA’d it



For 4,938 anonymised course reviews any of the three is fine, which is why you can run today’s lab without a conversation with anybody.
Real call-centre notes are a different matter. They contain names, account numbers and the details of individual complaints, and sending them to a model hosted outside the country is a cross-border personal data transfer under the NDPA 2023, which needs a lawful basis established before anybody runs the script rather than discovered afterwards. That is where a promising internal project most often stops, and it stops late, after the work has been done.
The practical answer that unblocks most teams is to run it locally. A local model on a decent laptop classifies a few thousand short texts in an hour or two, costs nothing per call, works without internet, and never raises the transfer question at all. It is somewhat less accurate — and for theme classification against a fixed taxonomy, the gap is usually smaller than the gap between two human labellers doing the same job. That is the comparison to make when somebody asks whether the local option is good enough: good enough compared to what?
We come back to this properly in 5.4.

Core lab · 30 minutes
A classification pass over 4,938 reviews has already been run and cached — it is data/customer_reviews_labelled.csv, with the model and temperature recorded in the file. A whole room classifying five thousand rows each, simultaneously, on conference wifi, is an hour of waiting and nothing else. The lab is about validation.


Classify fifty rows yourself so you have run the mechanics once: enum, schema, temperature zero, cache.


Join the cached labels to the corpus. Produce the theme-by-quarter volume table. That table is the deliverable, not the classifier.


Hand-label forty rows as a table, blind — do not look at the model’s answer first. Stratify: make sure some are Pidgin.


Compute agreement, and then Cohen’s kappa, and build the confusion matrix.


Report per-class recall, not just the overall rate. Find the class the classifier is worst on, and ask what it costs you to miss it.


Find the category boundary causing most of the disagreement. Fix the taxonomy or the prompt, and say which.


Write the four-sentence method paragraph.


Per-class recall, in the fifth item, is the share of rows genuinely belonging to a category that the classifier actually assigned to it. It matters because a small theme can be missed almost entirely without moving the overall agreement figure by more than a point or two: the headline number stays healthy while the theme quietly disappears from your chart.
The full 200-row validation set is homework, and the cohort’s combined labels are pooled overnight so Friday morning has a real gold standard to argue about.


Stretch
Two options, pick one.
A · Run it locally. Install a local model, run the same classification, and compare the two on your validation set. Report the accuracy gap and the time cost. This is the number your risk function will want, and almost nobody has measured it.
B · Severity, and the money. Ask the classifier to score severity 1–5 and to extract the specific product mentioned. Join to the customer table. Now compute the value at risk behind each theme — not how many people complained about billing, but how much annual contribution sits behind those complaints.
Option B turns a theme chart into a prioritised remediation budget, and it is the version that gets funded — a chart of complaint volumes invites a discussion about whether the complaints matter, while a ranked list of contribution at risk invites a decision about which to fix first.


Copilot check
The failure mode here is not the usual one. The assistant is not wrong and it is not hallucinating. It is agreeable, and agreeableness is much harder to notice.
Ask it to classify reviews into your seven categories and it will classify every single review into one of your seven categories — including the reviews that belong in none of them. Somebody typing “test” to see whether the form works. A review left for a different company. A three-word fragment that could mean anything. Each comes back with a confident label and no note explaining that the category was a poor fit, because the taxonomy you supplied is treated as complete on the strength of your having supplied it.
Two fixes, both cheap:

Always include an other and a not_applicable category, and monitor their share. The share is itself the instrument. A small and stable share is fine; a share that climbs from one quarter to the next is your early warning that reality has moved — a new product, a new failure, a new kind of customer — and your taxonomy has not. Without those categories the signal has nowhere to appear, and the change shows up instead as a quiet distortion spread across the seven you did define.
Ask it to flag its own uncertainty. Add a confidence field to the schema, then hand-review the low-confidence rows. Treat that figure as a rough sort rather than a probability — it is not calibrated and should not be reported — but as a way of choosing which rows deserve a human’s forty minutes it works well, because taxonomy problems live disproportionately in that group.

title: LLM classification at scale
text:
Takeaways

A classifier is a measurement instrument. Two hundred hand-labelled rows, or you have no error rate.
Read the confusion matrix. Disagreement clusters reveal taxonomy problems, not model problems.
Constrain the output, cache it, seed it, pin the model version.
Always have an other category and watch its share.
Where it runs is a legal question. There is a local option, and it is usually good enough.

title: Lab 3 · The forecast market
text:
How it runs
Each table gets one depot. There are twelve depots in the data, so the format supports up to twelve tables. Your table owns its depot for the next hour.
data/fmcg_sell_out.csv — the file you have had all week — ends on 30 March 2026. Q2 2026 is genuinely held out. It is not in your folder, it is not in the repository, and it is not in the reference build. It is on the facilitator’s machine and it goes on the projector at the end of this session. That matters more than it might sound: an exercise where the answer is somewhere in the room is a different exercise, because there is always a way to look it up.
You post two numbers. Total units for your depot, Q2 2026, expressed as an 80% interval — a low value and a high value that you believe have an eighty per cent chance of containing the truth between them. Alongside the two numbers goes one card carrying a single sentence: why you widened or narrowed the interval your model produced.
Then everybody bets. Each participant receives six chips and may place no more than three on any one entry. A chip is a bet that the true value falls inside that table’s interval.
The scoring is designed so that honesty pays, and it is worth understanding why before you post anything.
For the table that posted the interval, we use the standard interval score. Lower is better:
\[S = (u - \ell) \;+\; \tfrac{2}{0.2}(\ell - y)\,\mathbf{1}\{y < \ell\} \;+\; \tfrac{2}{0.2}(y - u)\,\mathbf{1}\{y > u\}\]
In English, and reading the three terms in turn: the first is the width of your interval, which you pay for whatever happens. The second and third are penalties that apply only if the truth lands below your low value or above your high value, and they are ten times heavier per unit of distance than the width charge. So you pay for being vague, and you pay a great deal more for being wrong.
That combination is what makes an honest 80% interval — rather than a very wide one or a very narrow one — the answer that minimises your expected score. It is what statisticians call a proper scoring rule, meaning that your best strategy under it is to state what you actually believe. The obvious alternative, paying a flat prize whenever the interval contains the truth, is not proper: it rewards betting on anything more likely than a coin flip, and it rewards the poster for making the interval as wide as they can get away with.
For the bettors, a chip inside pays two and a chip outside pays nothing. The chips are not there to measure anybody’s calibration — six chips is far too few for that. They are there to make people read each other’s reasoning cards, which is where the learning is.
Then the holdout goes on the projector. Depot by depot, slowly.

title: Lab 3 · The forecast market
section: Why this teaches what a lecture cannot
text:
Why this teaches what a lecture cannot
Because the incentives are right, and because everyone in the room discovers the same three things at the same moment and by experience rather than by being told.
One — asked for an 80% range, most people produce one that contains the truth about 45% of the time. This is one of the more robustly replicated findings in the judgement literature (Soll and Klayman, 2004, among others), and it holds across professions, seniority and numeracy. Two caveats belong with it, and they are themselves part of the lesson rather than qualifications to it.
It is partly a property of how you asked. Elicit a range — “give me your 80% interval” — and hit rates come out around 45%. Ask the same people the same question in two separate parts, a low value and then a high value, and hit rates rise substantially. Nothing about the forecaster’s knowledge changed; only the format of the question did. That is worth knowing about your own planning process, where almost every number is elicited in the format that performs worst.
It is not universal across professions. Weather forecasters are famously well calibrated on probability of precipitation, and so are expert bridge players. The common factor is not mathematical training — it is frequent, prompt, unambiguous feedback on outcomes. A forecaster finds out tomorrow whether it rained. That is exactly the mechanism this lab is trying to install in the space of an hour, and exactly what most corporate forecasting lacks: the budget variance arrives eleven months later, attributed to six causes, and nobody is any better calibrated afterwards.
Two — the width is the hard part. Everybody can produce a central estimate; it is what most people mean by “a forecast”. Almost nobody can produce a width they can defend, because a width requires you to reason about what you do not know rather than about what you do, and there is no habit of doing that.
Three — the tables that handled the structural break win. Four of the twelve depots are in the North and were re-segmented in November 2025, which means their history before that date describes a different territory from the one they cover now. A table that fitted a model across the break without noticing will post an interval centred far too high. It is the same lesson as 3.3, delivered by the room and by the projector rather than by a facilitator at a whiteboard — which is why it sticks.

The calibration point, stated properly
Being right and being well-calibrated are different virtues, and most organisations reward the first while quietly depending on the second.
A well-calibrated forecaster’s 80% intervals contain the truth 80% of the time. Read that carefully, because the implication is counter-intuitive: they are wrong one time in five, on purpose. If their intervals are never missed, the intervals are too wide, and somewhere downstream that width is being paid for in safety stock, contingency budget and capital held against a risk that was overstated.
Now consider an organisation whose “80%” is really 45%. It is surprised 55% of the time, having planned to be surprised 20% of the time — nearly three times as often as it budgeted for. Every buffer in the business is sized for the wrong frequency of surprise. That is not really a forecasting problem, and it will not be fixed by a better model. It is a risk problem, and it sits underneath every capital allocation decision the business makes.

title: Lab 3 · The forecast market
text:
Preparing your entry


Build the weekly series for your depot. Check where the file ends — that is the cut, and there is nothing after it.


Plot it. Look for the break, the seasonality, the trend, the outliers.


Fit at least four models including both naive benchmarks. Backtest on a 13-week holdout inside your training period.


Take the model interval — then adjust it. Ask: what does the model not know?


Write your low and your high on the card. Also write, in one sentence, the reason you widened or narrowed the model’s interval.


Sceptic: before it goes on the wall, state what would have to happen for the truth to land outside the interval. If you cannot think of anything, it is too narrow.


The fourth step is the one that distinguishes a forecast from a model output. A prediction interval reflects the variation the model has already seen in the fitted history. It cannot reflect a price change nobody has announced yet, a competitor’s launch, a fuel subsidy decision, or a depot that is about to be reorganised. Those live in your head, not in the data, and the adjustment you make for them is the professional judgement the exercise is trying to elicit.

Two things worth knowing before you bet
Q2 contains no December. Anyone who built an interval from an annual average has folded in a December lift that simply is not present in the quarter being forecast. Check the seasonal profile of your own series before you assume this does not apply to you.
Four depots are in the North — Abuja Central, Kano, Kaduna and Jos. If a table holding one of those has not mentioned November 2025 anywhere in their reasoning, they have not handled the break, and their central estimate is roughly a quarter too high. That is public information, not inside knowledge: the reasoning card is pinned on the wall next to their interval, and you are entitled to read it before you place a chip.
Reading other people’s reasoning before betting is not cheating. It is the entire skill of being on a committee — and noticing that a confident number rests on an assumption nobody stated is the same act whether it happens here or in a capital approval meeting.

title: Lab 3 · The forecast market
section: The debrief — fifteen minutes, and the real content
text:
The debrief — fifteen minutes, and the real content
Do not skip this to make up time. The betting is the memorable part; the debrief is where the lesson actually consolidates into something transferable.
Count the hits. Across all entries, what fraction of the 80% intervals contained the truth? Write it on the board.
Be honest about the arithmetic while you do. With twelve entries, 80% is 9.6 intervals, which is not a number of intervals anybody can post. Under perfect calibration you would expect somewhere between 7 and 12 hits, simply because twelve is a small sample. If the room gets 5, that is a genuine finding worth discussing. If it gets 9, that is calibration, and the honest thing is to say so rather than to manufacture a lesson from a number that does not support one. Modelling that honesty in front of the room is itself part of the teaching.
Find the widest correct interval and the narrowest correct interval. Ask both tables to explain their reasoning. Both were right; one of them was much more useful. The gap between them is what “calibration” means in practice, and it is easier to see in two real examples than in any definition.
Find the table that missed by the most. Ask what they would have needed to know. The answer is almost always a data answer — the break, the seasonality, a promotion nobody mentioned — rather than a modelling answer. That is the point, and it is worth letting the room reach it rather than announcing it.
Then the executive translation. Ask the room:

Where in your organisation does someone commit to a number without an interval, and what happens when they are wrong?

Budgets. Sales targets. Project timelines. Capital plans. Regulatory submissions. Every one of those is a forecast reported as a single point, and every one of them has a variance report attached whose function is to explain, after the fact, why the point was wrong. A stated interval would have converted most of that explanation into something that had already been disclosed in advance.

title: Lab 3 · The forecast market
text:
Bringing it home
The single highest-value change most organisations could make to their planning process is to require an interval on every submitted number, and to score people on calibration at the end of the year rather than on point accuracy.
It costs nothing. It requires no technology and no new system. It is deeply unpopular for about two quarters — because the first people to give honest intervals look less certain than their colleagues, which is a real professional cost to them — and then it becomes the thing everybody says they always wanted. Knowing that the unpopularity is temporary, and why it happens, is most of what it takes to see the change through.
Write down, before you leave this session, the one number in your organisation that is currently submitted as a point and should be submitted as a range — and who would have to agree to it.

title: Segmentation you can act on
section: The test a segmentation has to pass
text:
The test a segmentation has to pass
A segmentation earns its keep when you would do something different for each segment. That is the whole test, and it is worth applying before any code is written, because it is the only part of the exercise that cannot be recovered later.
It is a demanding test, and a great many carefully built corporate segmentations do not quite pass it. The usual shape is six groups with evocative names, a slide carrying six photographs of people holding phones, and — when you look at what happens next — a single treatment applied to all six. Nobody set out to produce that. It happens because naming and describing groups is intrinsically satisfying work, and deciding what to do about them involves a different set of people who were not in the room.
So write the sentence before you cluster anything:

“If a customer is in segment 3, we will ______ instead of ______, and we expect ______.”

Three blanks, and all three matter. The first says what changes; the second says what would otherwise have happened, which is what makes the change measurable; the third commits you to an expectation you can be wrong about in public.
If you cannot complete that sentence for every segment, what you have built is a description rather than a segmentation. Descriptions are genuinely useful — they help people think, they give a marketing team a shared vocabulary, and they are often the first step towards something actionable. They simply should not be priced, resourced or reported as though they were decisions.

title: Segmentation you can act on
section: Start with RFM. It is not a poor relation.
text:
Start with RFM. It is not a poor relation.
Before reaching for any machine learning, run recency, frequency, monetary — usually shortened to RFM. The idea is about as old as direct mail: sort your customers by how recently they bought, how often they buy, and how much they spend, and treat the resulting groups differently. It is roughly fifty years old, it takes one query, and in most businesses it explains the great majority of what a sophisticated clustering will eventually find.
-- RFM on the retail banking base, scored into deciles.
WITH base AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         tenure_months,
         txns_last_90d                       AS frequency,
         avg_balance_ngn                     AS monetary,
         digital_engagement_score            AS engagement
  FROM 'data/bank_customers.csv'
)
SELECT customer_id,
       NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY frequency)  AS f_score,
       NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY monetary)   AS m_score,
       NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY engagement) AS e_score
FROM base;
NTILE(5) is doing the work here: it sorts everybody on a column and cuts the sorted list into five equal-sized buckets, so a score of 5 means “top fifth on this measure”. Three scores of five levels each gives 125 possible combinations, which is far more than any organisation can act on.
The move that makes RFM useful is collapsing those 125 cells into the handful that carry a decision. High value and engaged — protect them. High value and disengaged — call them, because that combination is what leaving looks like early. Low value and engaged — grow them; the relationship is there and the balance is not. Low value and disengaged — serve them digitally and cheaply.
Four groups, four actions, four owners, one query.

Run RFM first, always
RFM gives you a baseline that any machine-learned segmentation then has to beat — in exactly the same way that the naive forecast in 3.3 gives you a baseline that a forecasting model has to beat. Without a baseline, “the clustering found four segments” is an unfalsifiable claim.
It matters commercially because clustering algorithms are very good at finding the largest source of variation in a table, and in customer data that is usually value. So if your k-means solution comes back with groups amounting to “high value”, “medium value” and “low value”, the honest reading is that three weeks of work has reproduced a NTILE — which happens more often than the case studies suggest, and is much better discovered on day one than at the steering committee in week six.

title: Segmentation you can act on
section: k-means, and the four things that go wrong
text:
k-means, and the four things that go wrong
k-means is the workhorse clustering method, and the intuition behind it is simpler than its reputation. You tell it how many groups you want — that is the k. It drops that many points at random into the space your customers occupy, assigns every customer to the nearest one, moves each point to the middle of the customers it just collected, and repeats until nothing moves.
Two consequences follow, and both matter later. The method has no opinion about whether k is a sensible number — ask for nine and you get nine. And everything depends on what “nearest” means, which depends entirely on the units your columns happen to be measured in.
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

bank <- read_csv("data/bank_customers.csv")

# 1. Choose variables that relate to the DECISION, not everything available.
seg_vars <- bank |>
  select(customer_id, tenure_months, products_held, avg_balance_ngn,
         digital_engagement_score, txns_last_90d, complaints_last_12m)

# 2. Balance is log-normal. Cluster the log, or balance dominates everything.
prep <- recipe(~ ., data = seg_vars) |>
  update_role(customer_id, new_role = "id") |>
  step_log(avg_balance_ngn, base = 10) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>     # 3. Scale. Non-negotiable.
  prep()

X <- bake(prep, new_data = NULL) |> select(-customer_id)

# 4. Try several k and look at the elbow - then ignore it and use judgement.
set.seed(42)
kfits <- tibble(k = 2:9) |>
  mutate(fit = map(k, ~ kmeans(X, centers = .x, nstart = 25)),
         wss = map_dbl(fit, ~ .x$tot.withinss))

ggplot(kfits, aes(k, wss)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Within-cluster sum of squares by k",
       subtitle = "There is rarely a clean elbow in real business data. Choose on grounds you can defend.")

final <- kmeans(X, centers = 4, nstart = 50)
bank$segment <- factor(final$cluster)
Two lines in that recipe are worth pausing on, because they are the ones most often left out. step_log() compresses a very skewed column so that the gap between ₦10m and ₦100m counts about the same as the gap between ₦100k and ₦1m. step_normalize() puts every column on a common scale by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation, so that a column measured in millions and a column measured in units contribute comparably. The nstart = 50 simply runs the whole procedure fifty times from different random starting points and keeps the best result, which protects you from an unlucky start.

The four things that go wrong, in order of frequency
None of these is an exotic failure. All four are what happens when a competent person runs a clustering the way the documentation example runs one.
1 · Not scaling. avg_balance_ngn runs to eight figures; products_held runs from 1 to 8. Distance is computed by adding up differences across columns, so before standardising, a ₦2m difference in balance swamps a difference of every single product a customer could hold. The arithmetic is not wrong; it is simply answering a question about balance and calling the answer a segmentation. This is the most common error of the four, and it is dangerous precisely because the output looks entirely plausible — you get tidy groups, they differ from one another, and nothing on screen indicates that only one column was consulted.
2 · Not transforming skewed variables. Balance in a retail bank is log-normal: most customers cluster near the bottom and a small number sit a very long way out. Cluster the raw column and a handful of private banking customers will each be far enough from everyone else to claim a cluster of their own. You then get four segments, three of which contain almost nobody, and a fourth containing the entire business.
3 · Throwing in every available variable. It feels thorough, and it is the natural instinct when the data is already in front of you. But branch_state encoded as a number invents an ordering that does not exist, an identifier adds pure noise, and anything that is a consequence of the segment rather than a characteristic of it quietly builds the answer into the question. Choose variables that relate to the decision you intend to make, and be able to say why each one is there.
4 · Believing the elbow. The elbow method plots how much unexplained variation remains as k increases, and looks for the bend where adding another group stops helping much. In textbook data there is a clear bend. In real business data the line declines smoothly and there is nothing that anybody would honestly call an elbow. The number of segments should be decided by how many different things your organisation can actually execute — which is usually three or four, occasionally five, and never nine. If marketing can run three campaigns a quarter, a nine-segment solution is a nine-segment solution in name only.

title: Segmentation you can act on
text:
Naming and sizing
A cluster number is not a segment. “Cluster 3” tells a marketing team nothing they can use, and it will not survive its first contact with a steering committee. The work that converts one into the other is profiling: describing each group in the language of the business, sizing it, and attaching a decision and a person to it.
profile <- bank |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(
    customers      = n(),
    share          = n() / nrow(bank),
    med_tenure     = median(tenure_months),
    med_balance    = median(avg_balance_ngn),
    med_products   = median(products_held),
    med_engagement = median(digital_engagement_score),
    churn_rate     = mean(churned_90d),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(med_balance))
Note that the summary uses median() rather than mean() for balance, tenure and products. In a distribution with a long tail, the mean is pulled upwards by a small number of very large customers and stops describing anybody in particular; the median tells you about the customer in the middle of the group, which is the customer the campaign will actually meet.
Then the table that goes in the deck. This is the deliverable; the chart beside it is supporting evidence.



The four segments the course data actually produces, with the action attached to each.

Read along one row and you will see what a segmentation deliverable contains: a name a human being would actually use, a size in both customers and share, the numbers that justify the action, the action itself, and the function that owns it. A table with those columns can be argued with, resourced and reviewed in six months. A table of cluster centroids cannot.
That table is generated by the same script that draws the figure above it, from the recipe printed above, and it is not typed by hand. There is a reason for that, and it is not tidiness — the failure it prevents is one that any careful team can walk into.
An earlier version of this page carried a hand-typed table under the same figure, and the two disagreed on every single cell. The chart said Anchors were 2,505 customers at 3.2% churn while the table said 2,977 at 3.8%. Both sets of numbers looked entirely plausible — same order of magnitude, same qualitative story, neither resembling a typing error. Nobody noticed for weeks, and there was no reason anybody should have: checking a figure against the sentence beside it is not a step that appears in anybody’s review process.
The instructive part is what happened next. The obvious repair was to regenerate the table from the figure, and that is what was done — which made the visible contradiction disappear and left the real one in place, because the figure was the artefact that had drifted. It had quietly been built on five features while this page’s recipe selects six, so the corrected table was now the honest output of a clustering that this page never asks for, and the redundancy box below became false as a result. It took a second reviewer, re-running the recipe from scratch rather than comparing the two artefacts to each other, to find it.
Two lessons come out of that, and the second is the expensive one. One source, and every number in the prose computed from it — which is the whole subject of 4.4. And: when two artefacts disagree, establish which one is wrong before you make them agree. Reconciling to whichever is more convenient to change is how an error gets promoted from visible to invisible, and an invisible error is a great deal more expensive than a contradiction somebody can see.

Read the table before you name anything
Three things in that table are worth more than the clustering that produced them, and all three are visible without any statistics at all.
Median balance runs from ₦261k to ₦1.69m — a factor of 6.5. In other words the typical customer in the top segment holds about six and a half times the balance of the typical customer in the bottom one. These segments genuinely differ on value, which means value-based names are earned rather than merely asserted. Check that before you name anything: a segment called “Premium” whose median balance turns out to be within a rounding error of “Mass” is how a segmentation loses a room, and it happens more often than the published case studies admit.
The highest-balance segment has the lowest churn — 3.8% against a 10.6% base. That is not really a surprise once you look at what sits underneath it. Tenure, products held and balance all move together, and each of them independently makes leaving less likely: a customer of eight years with four products and a salary account has a great deal of friction between them and the door. But the commercial consequence is worth stating plainly, because it runs against instinct: your most valuable segment is not your most at-risk one, and a retention budget aimed at “our best customers” would be aimed at the people least likely to leave.
Now read the churn column and the churner column against each other. They are not the same question and they do not give the same answer. “At risk” has the highest rate at 20.1% — one in five of them goes in ninety days. But “Dormant mass” produces the highest count, at 536 leavers against 423 — a lower rate applied to a larger segment. Rate answers where is the problem worst? Count answers where are the customers we are actually losing? A retention team with capacity for a fixed number of calls a month needs the second, weighted by what each departure is worth — which is precisely the ranking 3.5 builds this afternoon.
And the Dormant mass leaves quietly, because each departure takes ₦261k of balance with it rather than ₦1.69m — and there are a lot of them, at 29% of the base. Whether that matters at all is a commercial judgement about cost-to-serve rather than a statistical one: if those accounts cost more to maintain than they contribute, their departure is not a problem to be solved. That judgement is exactly what this table exists to provoke, and it is not one the clustering can make for you.


The fifth thing that goes wrong, and it is live in this dataset
digital_engagement_score and txns_last_90d correlate at 0.86. Read that as: customers who transact a lot score highly on digital engagement, almost without exception. The two columns have different names and different units, but they are two measurements of the same underlying thing — how active this customer is.
That is a problem specific to distance-based methods, and it takes a moment to see. Distance is computed by adding up the difference on every feature. Standardise all six columns and cluster on Euclidean distance, and engagement contributes twice — two of six features, a third of the total weight in the distance metric, for one concept. Complaints, tenure and products each get one share; activity gets two. Nothing in the output mentions this.
Look at what it does in practice. Measure how far apart the four clusters sit on each standardised feature — the range between the highest and lowest cluster centre — and you get:




Feature
Between-cluster range




complaints_last_12m
2.25


txns_last_90d
1.75


digital_engagement_score
1.73


avg_balance_ngn (log)
1.51


products_held
1.20


tenure_months
1.03



The two bolded rows are the same concept, sitting side by side. Together they come to 3.48, which outweighs complaints at 2.25 — and complaints is the single strongest genuine separator in the list. One idea is doing two features’ work, and it is quietly the most influential thing in the model. The segments you are about to name are shaped by that, and to that extent they are partly an artefact of how the feature list was assembled rather than a fact about the customers.
The check is cheap and takes about a minute: compute the correlation matrix of your features before you cluster, and look at it. Where two columns correlate above roughly 0.8, drop one of them or combine them into a single index. This kind of redundancy quietly reweighting the distance metric is at least as common as failing to scale, and considerably harder to see, because the output of a redundant clustering looks exactly like the output of a good one.

title: Segmentation you can act on
text:
Stability — the question nobody asks
Here is the question that decides whether any of this survives contact with next quarter. You are going to run a campaign against these segments in three months’ time. Will the segments still be there?
The concern is not philosophical. k-means will return k groups from any data you hand it, including data with no group structure at all — that is what the algorithm does. So a segmentation can be perfectly well fitted and still be a description of noise, and the only way to tell the two apart is to check whether the structure reappears when you look again.
The cheapest version of that check is to split your customer base in half at random, cluster each half independently, and ask whether the two halves found the same thing.
# Split the base in half at random, cluster each half separately,
# and see whether you get the same structure.
set.seed(7)
half <- sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), nrow(X), replace = TRUE)

fit_a <- kmeans(X[half, ],  centers = 4, nstart = 50)
fit_b <- kmeans(X[!half, ], centers = 4, nstart = 50)

# Cluster labels are ARBITRARY between fits. fit_a$centers and fit_b$centers
# are in unrelated row orders, so comparing them row by row is meaningless.
# Score both halves with ONE set of centres and compare the partitions.
assign_to <- function(centres, X) {
  apply(as.matrix(X), 1, \(row) which.min(colSums((t(centres) - row)^2)))
}

lab_a <- assign_to(fit_a$centers, X)          # everyone, by half A's centres
lab_b <- assign_to(fit_b$centers, X)          # everyone, by half B's centres

mclust::adjustedRandIndex(lab_a, lab_b)
# 1.0 = identical partitions. Above ~0.7 the structure is real.
# Below ~0.4 you have found noise, and the campaign will not replicate.
The comment in the middle of that block is the part people get wrong, so it is worth saying in prose as well. Cluster numbers mean nothing between two separate fits: what half A calls cluster 1 may be what half B calls cluster 3, because labels are assigned in whatever order the algorithm happened to converge. Comparing the two sets of centres row by row therefore compares two unrelated orderings. The way round it is to score everybody twice — once using half A’s centres, once using half B’s — and then ask how much the two groupings agree about which customers belong together. That agreement measure is the adjusted Rand index, and the adjustment in its name is for chance: two random groupings score around zero rather than around some misleadingly positive number.
If two random halves of your base produce materially different partitions, you have found structure in noise, and the campaign built on it will not replicate. The check takes about four minutes and almost nobody runs it — not through carelessness, but because by that point everybody has moved on to naming the groups, which is the more enjoyable part.
The second stability question is about time rather than sampling. Re-run the segmentation on data from six months ago and count how many customers land in a different segment. A high rate of movement is not a failure; it tells you your segmentation is measuring a state rather than a type, and the two are used differently. State-based segments need re-scoring monthly and belong in an operational system; type-based segments can be assigned once and left alone in the CRM.

Core lab · 30 minutes


Run RFM on the banking base. Collapse to four actionable groups. Write the action for each.


Now run k-means properly: variables chosen, balance logged, everything scaled.


Fit k from 2 to 9, look at the elbow, then choose k on execution grounds and defend it.


Profile, name and size your segments. Build the six-column table above.


Run the split-half stability check, then compare your k-means segments with your RFM groups. Did the model earn its keep?


That last comparison is the one to protect if you run short of time. It is entirely possible for the answer to be “no, the model did not earn its keep” — and finding that out in thirty minutes, with nothing at stake, is a considerably better outcome than finding it out after a quarter of campaign spend.


Stretch
Segment something other than customers. The technique is identical, the data is usually already available, and the applications are badly under-used:

SKUs by demand pattern — fast and steady, fast and spiky, slow and lumpy, dying. Each of those needs a different replenishment policy, and getting the classification right is usually worth more than any improvement to the forecast itself.
Suppliers by lead-time reliability and spend. Consolidate, dual-source, exit.
Depots by growth and margin. Invest, hold, fix, close.
Employees by flight risk and replacement cost — with a Friday conversation attached about whether you should, which 5.4 takes up properly.

Pick one from your own business and do it.
And, if you have ten minutes: refit the bank segmentation with txns_last_90d dropped, so that one concept carries one feature’s weight instead of two. Put the two profile tables side by side and compare them honestly.
Two things are worth noticing, and the first is not what the warning above would lead you to expect. The segment sizes move by a few hundred customers and the balance ordering survives intact — clustering is more robust to this kind of redundancy than the warning implies, which is precisely why the error is so easy to leave in place. If it produced obvious nonsense, somebody would have caught it.
What does rearrange is the tenure profile. The highest-balance group stops being the longest-tenured, and a mid-value segment overtakes it by about two and a half years. If you had named your segments on tenure, or written a paragraph in the deck about your best customers also being your oldest, you would now be rewriting those sentences.
That is the honest size of the effect: the redundancy critique rarely changes who is in which group, and it regularly changes the story you tell about them. Both halves of that sentence are worth carrying into your own work.


Copilot check
Ask an assistant to “segment my customers” and it will produce clean, well-structured k-means code, and it will usually get the mechanics right. The gaps are not in the code; they are in the judgements the code cannot make.
Three things to check every time:

Did it scale? Sometimes yes, often not, and it will not warn you either way. This is the single highest-value line to look for in generated clustering code.
Did it choose k with a silhouette score or an elbow, and present that as the answer? The statistically optimal k is not the commercially executable k. The assistant has no way of knowing how many distinct campaigns your marketing team can run in a quarter, and it will not think to ask.
Did it name the segments? It will cheerfully invent evocative names from the cluster centres — “The Aspirational Urbanite” — with complete confidence and no knowledge of your market. Names carry meaning inside an organisation, and they outlive the analysis that produced them. Write them yourself.

The prompt that works better does two things: it specifies the preparation, and it explicitly withholds the judgements.

Cluster this data. Requirements: log-transform the skewed monetary variables, standardise everything, fit k from 2 to 9, and report both the within-cluster sum of squares and a profile table of the segment medians for each k. Do not choose k for me and do not name the segments — I will do both. Then run a split-half stability check.

title: Segmentation you can act on
text:
Takeaways

The test: would you do something different for each segment? Write the sentence first.
Run RFM first. It is the benchmark the model must beat.
Scale, and transform skewed variables, or you have clustered one column.
Choose the number of segments by what your organisation can execute, not by the elbow.
Check split-half stability before anyone builds a campaign on it.
