title: Charts that survive a board room
text:
A chart is an argument
It is natural to think of a chart as a way of showing data — of putting the numbers on a page so that people can see them. That description is accurate and it is not very useful, because it does not help you choose between the dozen chart forms that would all show the same numbers perfectly well.
The more useful description is that a chart is an argument. It has a claim, and the visual form is the evidence offered for that claim. Once you think of it that way, the design question stops being “which chart looks best?” and becomes “which arrangement of these numbers makes the claim visible without the reader having to work?”
Most business charts that fail do not fail because they are ugly. They fail because the form does not match the claim. Somebody wanted to argue “the North is falling behind” and drew a chart that displayed “here are revenues by region” — a chart which contains the evidence, but which leaves the audience to construct the argument themselves, in their heads, during the four seconds the slide is up, while the presenter is already talking about something else. That is a great deal to ask of anybody, and the request is usually declined.
So the sequence is: write the claim as a sentence first, then choose the form. The table below is a starting point, not a rulebook — but it covers most of what a commercial pack contains.







The claim
The form




X is bigger than Y
Bar, sorted, one colour, difference annotated


X is changing over time
Line. Never a bar


X is changing faster than Y
Indexed line, both starting at 100


X is spread more widely than you think
Distribution: histogram, density, box, or the points themselves


X and Y move together
Scatter, with the point that breaks the pattern labelled


X is made up of these parts
Stacked bar if 2–3 parts; small multiples if more


X is uncertain by this much
Line with a shaded interval, or points with ranges


Most of X comes from a few Y
Pareto: sorted bars with a cumulative line



Two rows deserve a note. “Never a bar” for change over time is unusually absolute for this course, and the reason is that a bar encodes a quantity by its length from zero, which implies each period is a separate thing being compared, whereas a line encodes continuity and lets the eye read the slope — which is what “changing” means. And Pareto is simply a name worth knowing: sorted bars with a cumulative percentage line running across them, so that the reader can see at a glance how much of the total the first few categories between them account for.
The title of the chart should then be the claim itself. Not “Revenue by region”, which describes the contents, but “North Central has lost roughly a third of its volume since November.” This feels presumptuous the first few times you do it, because a title that states a conclusion is committing to something in a way that a descriptive title never has to. That commitment is the point. If you cannot write the sentence, the honest reading is not that the chart is fine and the title is hard — it is that you do not yet know what the chart is for.

title: Charts that survive a board room
section: The grammar of graphics, in one idea
text:
The grammar of graphics, in one idea
There is a genuinely useful piece of theory underneath all of this, and it takes about a minute to explain. Every statistical chart, however elaborate, is the same three decisions:

Data — which rows.
Aesthetics — which variable maps to position, colour, size, shape.
Geometry — what marks get drawn: points, lines, bars, areas.

That is the grammar of graphics, and it is the idea ggplot2 in R is built on, which is why its code reads the way it does. Change the geometry and hold everything else fixed and you have a different chart of the same data: the same rows, the same variable on the same axis, drawn as points rather than as bars.
The practical value is that “which chart should I use?” stops being a matter of taste and becomes a question with structure. You are not choosing from a gallery of chart types; you are deciding what maps to position — the encoding people read most accurately — and then deciding what marks to draw. Someone who has this idea can invent a chart form they have never seen, and, more usefully, can say precisely what is wrong with one they have been handed.
The code below draws the regional series from Tuesday’s output. Read it for its structure rather than its syntax: a data step, then a set of mappings, then geometry, then the labelling that carries the argument.

R (ggplot2)Python (matplotlib)


library(tidyverse)

weekly <- arrow::read_parquet("outputs/fmcg_weekly.parquet")

regional <- weekly |>
  group_by(region, week_starting) |>
  summarise(units = sum(units_sold), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(regional, aes(week_starting, units, colour = region)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2025-11-03"),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2025-11-10"), y = Inf, hjust = 0, vjust = 1.4,
           label = "Northern re-segmentation", size = 3.2, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2E3A6E", "#16549B", "#00AFEF",
                                 "#009F8B", "#C4A060")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "North Central has lost roughly a third of its weekly volume since November",
       subtitle = "Weekly units sold by region, Jan 2024 – Mar 2026",
       x = NULL, y = "Units per week", colour = NULL,
       caption = "Source: sell-out data, deduplicated. Stockout weeks counted as zero.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())


import pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

weekly = pd.read_parquet("outputs/fmcg_weekly.parquet")
regional = (weekly.groupby(["region", "week_starting"], as_index=False)
                  .units_sold.sum())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
palette = ["#2E3A6E", "#16549B", "#00AFEF", "#009F8B", "#C4A060"]
for (name, grp), colour in zip(regional.groupby("region"), palette):
    ax.plot(grp.week_starting, grp.units_sold, label=name, color=colour, lw=1.4)

ax.axvline(pd.Timestamp("2025-11-03"), ls="--", color="0.5")
ax.annotate("Northern re-segmentation", (pd.Timestamp("2025-11-10"), ax.get_ylim()[1]),
            va="top", fontsize=9, color="0.3")
ax.set_title("North Central has lost roughly a third of its weekly volume since November",
             loc="left", weight="bold")
ax.set_ylabel("Units per week"); ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=5)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)



Three details in those blocks carry more of the argument than the chart type does. The vertical dashed line and its annotation name the event, so that the reader is not left to infer why the line moved. The caption states how stockout weeks were treated, which is a modelling decision disclosed on the face of the chart rather than buried in an appendix. And the title makes the claim, so that a reader who sees only the slide still leaves with the finding.

title: Charts that survive a board room
section: The bar chart of group means, and what it conceals
text:
The bar chart of group means, and what it conceals
The most common chart in business is a set of bars showing the average of some quantity for each of several groups. It is popular for good reasons: it is easy to produce, easy to read, and it answers the question people usually ask, which is “which group is highest?”
The difficulty is that it shows one number per group and hides everything that produced the number. To see how much that matters, consider four datasets that all yield an identical set of bars.
In the first, the groups genuinely differ: every observation in one group really is higher than almost every observation in another. In the second, three of the groups are ordinary and one is held up by a handful of extreme values, so that its mean describes none of its members. In the third, the distributions overlap so heavily that the differences between the group averages are not differences you would act on. In the fourth, one group is bimodal — split into a high cluster and a low one, with the mean sitting in the empty space between them, describing a case that does not occur.
The bars are the same in all four. The decisions you would take are not.



Four means, equal to fifteen decimal places. Four completely different situations. Only one is a case where quoting the mean tells the reader anything true.


None of this makes the bar chart a bad chart. It makes it a chart that answers a narrower question than the one people typically bring to it. What to draw instead, in increasing order of information carried:

Points, jittered — if you have fewer than a few hundred observations, simply show them. Nudging each point sideways at random (“jitter”) stops them landing on top of one another.
Box plot — the median as a line, the middle half of the data as a box, the extremes as whiskers, and anything unusual as individual points. Compact, honest, and readable by anybody once you have explained it once.
Violin, or violin plus box — the actual shape of the distribution, mirrored around its axis, which is the only one of these forms that shows bimodality unambiguously.
Bars with intervals — if the audience expects bars, at least let the bars carry the uncertainty, so that overlapping ranges tell the reader when a difference is not solid.


The two-second rule
An audience gives a chart roughly two seconds before they either understand it or stop trying and listen to you instead. This is not impatience; it is what happens when a slide appears while somebody is already speaking. Design for two seconds and everything else follows.
In practice that means: sorted by size rather than alphabetically. Labelled directly on the series, rather than through a legend the reader has to match by colour. One colour, unless colour is carrying meaning. The claim in the title. And the two things you want compared placed physically next to each other, because a comparison across a page is a comparison the reader has to hold in memory.
There is one further point that is easy to miss and does more work than the rest combined: the quantity you want compared should be positioned along a common baseline. Human eyes judge the lengths of things starting from the same line very accurately, and judge angles, areas and colour intensities poorly — a finding from a long line of graphical perception experiments that has held up consistently. That single fact explains why sorted bars beat pie charts, why stacked bars stop working beyond two or three segments (only the bottom segment shares a baseline), and why “which of these is bigger?” should almost never be answered with a treemap.

title: Charts that survive a board room
text:
Colour, and doing it once
Pick a palette once, use it everywhere, and make sure a given category is the same colour in every chart in the pack. In a fifty-page board document, that consistency does more for comprehension than any individual chart improvement, because it lets a reader carry a meaning from page eleven to page thirty-four without re-reading a legend.
Three rules matter more than aesthetics.
Check it in greyscale. Somebody will print it, or project it through a tired bulb, and a palette that relies on hue alone collapses into a set of indistinguishable greys.
Do not encode meaning in red-versus-green alone. Red-green colour vision deficiency affects several per cent of men — around 8% in northern European populations and lower, roughly 2–6%, in most African studies. Either way, in a large cohort it is likely to be somebody in the room. The fix is not to abandon red and green but to make them redundant: carry the same meaning in position, shape or a written label as well, so that the chart still works when the colour does not.
Reserve one loud colour for the thing you are arguing about, and make everything else grey. A single highlighted series against a muted background is the highest-impact change available to most charts, and it costs one line of code. It also enforces the discipline from the start of this session, because you cannot highlight one series until you have decided which series the argument is about.
# The whole programme's palette, defined once.
tdbg_colours <- c(indigo = "#2E3A6E", blue = "#16549B", cyan = "#00AFEF",
                  teal   = "#009F8B", gold = "#C4A060", grey = "#B6BDCB")

# Highlight one series, mute the rest.
ggplot(regional, aes(week_starting, units, group = region,
                     colour = region == "North Central")) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#C4A060", `FALSE` = "#D5DAE3"),
                      guide = "none")
The trick in that second block is worth noting, because it is not obvious the first time you see it. Rather than mapping colour to region, which would give five colours, it maps colour to the test region == "North Central" — a column of TRUE and FALSE. Two values, two colours, and the chart now argues rather than displays.

title: Charts that survive a board room
section: The chart that did not land
text:
The chart that did not land
Most people who present regularly have a chart somewhere that did not do what they hoped: the room went quiet in the wrong way, or the questions came back about something other than the point. Bring one of those to this session. They are far more instructive than a chart that worked, and the reason it did not land is almost never carelessness — it is usually a mismatch between the claim and the form of exactly the kind this session is about.
The diagnosis is nearly always one of five things.

No claim. The title described the data instead of the finding, so the audience had to locate the argument themselves and different people located different ones.
Wrong comparison. You showed levels when the audience needed change, or change when they needed levels. Both charts are correct; only one answers the question in the room.
Too many series. Beyond about five lines, nobody reads any of them, including the one that mattered. Small multiples — the same small chart repeated once per category, on shared axes — solve this better than any amount of colour work.
Uncertainty hidden. You showed a point estimate, were asked “how sure are you?”, and had no visual answer, so the conversation moved to whether the number could be trusted rather than to what to do about it. 3.3 is largely about this.
Wrong denominator. A rate where an absolute was needed, or the reverse. “Churn is up two points” and “we lost 240 customers” are the same fact and land completely differently, and which one is right depends entirely on what the audience is being asked to decide.


Core lab · 30 minutes


Take three charts from a real pack of yours. Write the claim each one is making, as a sentence, before looking at it again.


For each, decide whether the form supports the claim. Rebuild the two that do not.


Rewrite every title as its claim.


Build one Pareto chart of your own data — the sorted bars plus the cumulative line. Find out what share of your revenue comes from your top decile.


Sceptic: for each rebuilt chart, state the opposite conclusion and see whether the chart rules it out. If it does not, the chart is not finished.


Do the first item from memory, before you open the file. Writing down what you believe the chart says and then discovering what it actually shows is a small, private and unusually efficient exercise, and it is the reason the instruction says “before looking at it again”.


Stretch
Build the small multiples version of the regional chart: one small panel per region, same axes throughout, sorted by size.
Then argue with your table about which is better — the five-line chart or the twelve small panels. There is a right answer, and it depends entirely on whether the claim is about comparison between regions or behaviour within each one. A single set of overlaid lines is excellent for comparison and poor for detail, because the lines obscure one another; small multiples are the reverse. Working out which claim you are making is the exercise, and the disagreement at the table is usually a disagreement about that rather than about charts.


Copilot check
Assistants write chart code well and make chart decisions badly, in a specific and predictable way: asked for “a chart of this data”, they produce whatever is most common in their training material, which is a bar chart of group means, with a legend, and a title that describes the data. That is a reasonable answer to an underspecified request, and the fix is to stop underspecifying.
Two prompts do most of it:

Here is my data and here is the single claim I want the chart to make: “[claim]”. Propose three chart forms that would support that claim, say what each one hides, and recommend one. Then write the code with the claim as the title and direct labels rather than a legend.

and, afterwards:

Look at this chart specification. What conclusion could a reader draw from it that the underlying data does not support?

The second is the Sceptic’s question, delegated, and it works surprisingly well. Critiquing a specific artefact is a far easier task than auditing an open situation, which is exactly why it is worth handing over — and why the judgement about what the chart is for stays with you.

title: Charts that survive a board room
text:
Takeaways

Write the claim as a sentence, then choose the form. The title is the claim.
Data, aesthetics, geometry. Three decisions, every chart.
A bar of means hides the four situations that would change your decision.
Compare along a common baseline. Sort. Label directly. One loud colour.
Design for two seconds.

title: Lab 2 · The pipeline that reruns
text:
What “pipeline” means here
The word carries a lot of freight, so it is worth narrowing it before we start. We do not mean an orchestration platform, a scheduler, or anything you would need to procure. For today, a pipeline is simply this: a script that a person who is not you can run from a clean machine and get your number.
That is a modest-sounding standard and a demanding one. Most analytical work in most organisations does not meet it, not through any lack of care but because nobody ever asked it to — the work was done once, under time pressure, for a meeting that has since happened. Meeting the standard deliberately is what turns a piece of analysis into an asset somebody can inherit.
Five properties make the difference, and it is worth understanding what each is protecting against.

It starts from the raw files, unmodified, in a folder nobody edits. If the inputs can change without anybody noticing, none of the other four properties can be relied on.
Every step is in the script. No manual step, and in particular no “then I opened it in Excel and fixed the header.” A single manual step is enough to make the whole thing unrepeatable, and it is always the step nobody wrote down.
It is idempotent. That word simply means running it twice produces the same result as running it once — nothing accumulates, nothing is appended to a file that was already there. Run it twice, get the same answer; run it on a clean machine, get the same answer.
It tests before it publishes. The contract from 2.5 runs inside the pipeline, so bad data stops the run rather than reaching the output.
It says what it did. Row counts at each step, printed as it goes. This is what lets you see a problem in the middle of the run rather than inferring it from a strange number at the end.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: Lab 2 · The pipeline that reruns
text:
The shape





flowchart LR
  RAW["<b>raw/</b><br/>never edited"] --> CLEAN["<b>clean</b><br/>types, dedupe,<br/>entity fixes"]
  CLEAN --> GATE{"<b>contract</b><br/>pass?"}
  GATE -->|fail| STOP["stop<br/>+ report"]
  GATE -->|pass| MODEL["<b>model</b><br/>join, derive,<br/>aggregate"]
  MODEL --> OUT["<b>outputs/</b><br/>analysis-ready<br/>+ quality report"]
  style RAW fill:#EEF3FA,stroke:#2E3A6E
  style GATE fill:#F6EFE0,stroke:#8A6D2F,stroke-width:2px
  style STOP fill:#FBE9E5,stroke:#B3341E
  style OUT fill:#D6F0EA,stroke:#00695C,stroke-width:2px


 Five stages. The gate is not optional. 



The diagram is worth reading as a sequence of five stages, because the ordering is the whole design. Raw files go in and are never edited. Cleaning happens next — types, deduplication, the entity fixes you found this afternoon — and produces a candidate table. That candidate then meets the gate, which is the quality contract, and only a table that passes goes on to be joined, derived and aggregated. Everything that emerges lands in outputs/, alongside the quality report that licensed it.
The gate sits where it does deliberately. Putting it after the modelling step would tell you that something was wrong only once you had a number in your hand and a temptation to keep it.

title: Lab 2 · The pipeline that reruns
text:
The reference implementation
Read this, then build your own. Do not copy it — the point of the lab is that you can explain every line, and an explanation is much harder to produce for code you have not typed.
Three versions follow, doing the same five stages in R, SQL and Python. Read whichever language you work in, then glance at one of the others: the structure is identical, which is the useful observation.

RSQLPython


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# TDBG pipeline: raw sell-out files -> one analysis-ready weekly table.
# Run:  Rscript pipeline.R
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(pointblank)

say <- function(step, tbl) message(sprintf("%-28s %8d rows", step, nrow(tbl)))

# --- 1. Read raw, types stated, nothing guessed ----------------------------
sales <- read_csv("data/fmcg_sell_out.csv",
                  col_types = cols(
                    week_starting  = col_date(),
                    depot_code     = col_character(),
                    sku            = col_character(),
                    units_sold     = col_double(),
                    unit_price_ngn = col_double(),
                    on_promotion   = col_integer(),
                    discount_pct   = col_double(),
                    stockout_flag  = col_integer(),
                    revenue_ngn    = col_double()))
say("raw sell-out", sales)

depots   <- read_csv("data/fmcg_depots.csv",   show_col_types = FALSE)
products <- read_csv("data/fmcg_products.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# --- 2. Clean -------------------------------------------------------------
# 2a. The ETL re-run left 214 duplicate grains. Grain is depot x sku x week.
sales <- sales |> distinct(week_starting, depot_code, sku, .keep_all = TRUE)
say("after dedupe", sales)

# 2b. Missing units on a stockout mean zero sold, not unknown. This is a
#     DECISION, recorded here so the next reader can disagree with it.
sales <- sales |>
  mutate(units_sold  = if_else(is.na(units_sold)  & stockout_flag == 1, 0, units_sold),
         revenue_ngn = if_else(is.na(revenue_ngn) & stockout_flag == 1, 0, revenue_ngn))

# 2c. The depot dimension has a rename inserted rather than applied. WHICH row
#     survives is a DECISION, and "the first one" would be an artefact of file
#     order. The rename is the newer, more specific name, so we keep the longer
#     one and record why. If your dimension has a valid-from date, use that
#     instead - it is the right answer and this file does not have one.
depots <- depots |>
  group_by(depot_code) |>
  slice_max(nchar(depot_name), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()
say("depot dimension", depots)

# --- 3. The gate ----------------------------------------------------------
agent <- create_agent(sales, tbl_name = "sell_out_clean",
                      label = "TDBG contract") |>
  rows_distinct(vars(week_starting, depot_code, sku)) |>
  col_vals_gte(units_sold, 0, na_pass = TRUE) |>   # na_pass: 2b decided what
                                                   # the remaining NAs mean
  col_vals_in_set(depot_code, set = depots$depot_code) |>
  col_vals_between(discount_pct, 0, 0.5) |>
  col_vals_expr(~ !(discount_pct > 0 & on_promotion == 0)) |>
  col_vals_not_null(revenue_ngn) |>
  interrogate()

export_report(agent, filename = "outputs/quality_report.html")

if (any(agent$validation_set$f_failed > 0, na.rm = TRUE)) {
  stop("Data contract failed. See outputs/quality_report.html")
}
message("contract passed")

# --- 4. Model -------------------------------------------------------------
weekly <- sales |>
  left_join(depots,   by = "depot_code", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  left_join(products, by = "sku",        relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  mutate(gross_profit_ngn = revenue_ngn - units_sold * unit_cost_ngn,
         year = lubridate::year(week_starting))
say("after joins", weekly)   # MUST equal the row count after dedupe

stopifnot(nrow(weekly) == nrow(sales))   # the two-line habit, as an assertion

# --- 5. Publish -----------------------------------------------------------
dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)
arrow::write_parquet(weekly, "outputs/fmcg_weekly.parquet")
write_csv(weekly, "outputs/fmcg_weekly.csv")
message("wrote outputs/fmcg_weekly.parquet  (", nrow(weekly), " rows)")
Three details in that script are worth pulling out, because they are the parts people tend to leave out when writing their own.
The say() helper at the top exists only to print a step name and a row count. It is four lines of no analytical value whatsoever, and it is what turns a silent script into one that narrates itself. When something goes wrong in three months, the run log tells you which stage it went wrong at.
Stating the column types explicitly in read_csv() rather than letting them be inferred looks like pedantry until the month a file arrives with an empty column, the guess changes, and everything downstream quietly behaves differently. Stated types make that a loud error on line one.
And the stopifnot() near the end is the two-line habit from 2.4 turned into something permanent. Counting rows by hand protects you on the day you remember to do it; an assertion in the script protects you on every future run, including the ones executed by somebody who has never heard of fan-out.


-- pipeline.sql   Run:  duckdb tdbg.duckdb < pipeline.sql

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE depot_dim AS
SELECT depot_code, MAX(depot_name) AS depot_name,
       ANY_VALUE(region) AS region, ANY_VALUE(state) AS state
FROM read_csv_auto('data/fmcg_depots.csv')
GROUP BY depot_code;                              -- one row per depot, always

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE sell_out_clean AS
SELECT DISTINCT ON (week_starting, depot_code, sku)   -- kills the 214
  week_starting, depot_code, sku,
  CASE WHEN units_sold  IS NULL AND stockout_flag = 1 THEN 0 ELSE units_sold  END AS units_sold,
  unit_price_ngn, on_promotion, discount_pct, stockout_flag,
  CASE WHEN revenue_ngn IS NULL AND stockout_flag = 1 THEN 0 ELSE revenue_ngn END AS revenue_ngn
FROM read_csv_auto('data/fmcg_sell_out.csv');

-- The gate. Any row returned here means stop.
SELECT 'grain not unique' AS breach, COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT (week_starting, depot_code, sku)) AS n
FROM sell_out_clean
UNION ALL SELECT 'orphan depot', COUNT(*) FROM sell_out_clean s
  LEFT JOIN depot_dim d USING (depot_code) WHERE d.depot_code IS NULL
UNION ALL SELECT 'negative units', COUNT(*) FROM sell_out_clean WHERE units_sold < 0;

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE fmcg_weekly AS
SELECT s.*, d.depot_name, d.region, d.state,
       p.category, p.pack_size, p.unit_cost_ngn,
       s.revenue_ngn - s.units_sold * p.unit_cost_ngn AS gross_profit_ngn
FROM sell_out_clean s
JOIN depot_dim d USING (depot_code)
JOIN read_csv_auto('data/fmcg_products.csv') p USING (sku);

-- The assertion: the join must not have changed the row count.
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sell_out_clean) AS before_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fmcg_weekly)    AS after_rows;

COPY fmcg_weekly TO 'outputs/fmcg_weekly.parquet' (FORMAT parquet);
The SQL version makes one thing more visible than the R version does: the depot dimension is rebuilt as a table that is unique by construction. Grouping by depot_code and taking one value of each attribute guarantees one row per depot, whatever arrives in the file next month. That is a different and stronger move than deleting the duplicate you happened to find today, and it is generally the right instinct — fix the shape rather than the instance.


# pipeline.py   Run:  python3 pipeline.py
import pandas as pd, pathlib, sys

def say(step, df): print(f"{step:<28}{len(df):>8,} rows")

raw = pathlib.Path("data")
out = pathlib.Path("outputs"); out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

sales = pd.read_csv(raw / "fmcg_sell_out.csv", parse_dates=["week_starting"],
                    dtype={"depot_code": "string", "sku": "string"})
say("raw sell-out", sales)

sales = sales.drop_duplicates(subset=["week_starting", "depot_code", "sku"])
say("after dedupe", sales)

hard = sales.stockout_flag.eq(1)
sales.loc[hard, ["units_sold", "revenue_ngn"]] = \
    sales.loc[hard, ["units_sold", "revenue_ngn"]].fillna(0)

# One depot_code has two rows under two names. WHICH ROW SURVIVES IS A DECISION,
# and it belongs in the code where a reviewer can see it and disagree with it --
# not in whatever order the file happened to arrive in. Sorting the name
# descending keeps the longer, later name ("Abuja Central (Wuse II)") over the
# stub it replaced. Say so out loud when you present this, because the version
# of this line without the comment is indistinguishable from an accident.
depots = (pd.read_csv(raw / "fmcg_depots.csv")
            .sort_values(["depot_code", "depot_name"], ascending=[True, False])
            .drop_duplicates("depot_code"))

breaches = {
    "grain not unique": len(sales) - len(sales[["week_starting","depot_code","sku"]].drop_duplicates()),
    "negative units":   int((sales.units_sold < 0).sum()),
    "orphan depot":     int((~sales.depot_code.isin(depots.depot_code)).sum()),
}
if any(breaches.values()):
    sys.exit(f"Data contract failed: {breaches}")
print("contract passed")

weekly = (sales
          .merge(depots, on="depot_code", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
          .merge(pd.read_csv(raw / "fmcg_products.csv"), on="sku",
                 how="left", validate="many_to_one"))
assert len(weekly) == len(sales), "join changed the row count"
say("after joins", weekly)

weekly.to_parquet(out / "fmcg_weekly.parquet", index=False)
print(f"wrote outputs/fmcg_weekly.parquet ({len(weekly):,} rows)")
The breaches dictionary here is the whole quality contract compressed into three lines and a conditional. It is much less elegant than the pointblank report in the R version and it does the essential job just as well: if any count is above zero, the script exits with a message naming what failed. If you are building your first pipeline this evening and the reporting library feels like one thing too many, start here — a contract that is enforced plainly beats a beautiful report that never runs.




The comment that matters most
# 2b. Missing units on a stockout mean zero sold, not unknown. This is a
#     DECISION, recorded here so the next reader can disagree with it.
That comment is worth more than the line of code beneath it, and it is worth being precise about why.
Every pipeline contains judgement calls: what a missing value means, which of two duplicates to keep, where to draw a period boundary, which entity is the survivor of a merge. The code necessarily records what you decided, because it has to do something. Only the comment records that a decision was made at all — and that is the piece a successor needs, because you cannot revisit a choice you did not know was a choice.
Read the line without its comment and it looks like housekeeping: some nulls being tidied away. Read it with the comment and it is a documented position that a reasonable colleague might take differently, with the reasoning available to them. The code is the same either way; only one version can be argued with.
Write the comment as you go rather than afterwards. On Friday, when you come to write the model card, you will find it is mostly a matter of collecting them.

title: Lab 2 · The pipeline that reruns
text:
The two-run test


Delete the entire outputs/ folder.


Run the pipeline from the command line — not from inside your editor, from a terminal in a fresh session.


Record the final row count and one headline number.


Delete outputs/ again. Run again. Compare.


Now hand your script to the pair at the next table and have them run it on their machine.


That last step is where most pipelines fail on the first Tuesday: an absolute path, a package that was installed interactively, a file that only exists on your desktop. All three are worth finding today rather than in March.

Stretch
Put the pipeline under version control and commit it.
git init
git add pipeline.R data/ outputs/quality_report.html
git commit -m "Pipeline v1: dedupe, entity fix, contract, weekly table"
Then change one decision — treat missing units as missing rather than as zero — commit again, and look at the diff. That diff is a record of a judgement call, with a date and a name attached to it.
This is what “auditable” means in practice, and it costs about ninety seconds. When the regulator, the auditor or your successor asks why the number changed in March, the answer is a commit.


Copilot check
Ask the assistant to write this whole pipeline for you. It will, and it will be structurally good — sensible order, reasonable naming, decent error handling.
Then check the three things it cannot know:

Which duplicate survives. It will keep the first row. Is that right? In the depot dimension the newer name is the correct survivor, and “first” is an artefact of file order.
What missing means. It will either drop nulls or fill them with zero, and it will not flag that it chose.
Whether the assertion should be fatal. It writes warnings where you need failures, because it does not know what the number is for.

Three decisions, none of them technical, all of them yours. This is the whole week in one lab.

text:
Before you leave today


Pipeline runs end to end from a terminal.


Quality report exported, with at least two failures found and fixed.


Row-count assertion in place around every join.


Grain statement written for every table you touched.


Two failure logbook entries submitted.


Capstone checkpoint signed off: your pipeline runs.

title: Joins that lie
section: Why we give this hour to something so unglamorous
text:
Why we give this hour to something so unglamorous
Sessions on modelling and on AI get the attention, and both matter. But if you audited a year of expensive analytical mistakes across a portfolio of real companies — the ones where a decision was taken on a number that was not true — very few would turn out to be statistical. The great majority are about joins, grains, definitions and calendars: four mechanical things that determine whether the rows going into a total are the rows that ought to be there.
These errors are hard to catch for a sympathetic reason. They do not produce anything that looks wrong. The output is well formatted, the magnitude is plausible, the ranking is sensible, and the totals foot. A reviewer reads a table like that the way any sensible person does — by checking whether the conclusion makes sense — and the conclusion does make sense, because it was computed correctly from the wrong number of rows.
It is worth saying plainly what an assistant can do for you here, because this is one of the few places in the week where the honest answer is “not much”. Ask it to write the join and it will write a correct join. The problem lives in the data rather than in the code, and the assistant has never seen your data. That gap — between code that is right and data that is not what the code assumes — is where the rest of this hour lives.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: Joins that lie
section: Do this now, before reading on
text:
Do this now, before reading on
The demonstration works far better if you run it yourself first, so resist the temptation to read ahead. Two queries. The first counts the rows in the fact table — the big transactional file of weekly sell-out. The second attaches the depot dimension, which is the small reference table holding each depot’s name, region and state, and totals revenue by region.
-- 1. How many rows in the fact table?
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv';

-- 2. Attach the depot dimension and total the revenue by region.
SELECT d.region,
       ROUND(SUM(s.revenue_ngn) / 1e9, 2) AS revenue_bn
FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv' s
JOIN 'data/fmcg_depots.csv'   d USING (depot_code)
GROUP BY d.region
ORDER BY revenue_bn DESC;
Write down the region ranking somewhere you can find it again. Note in particular which region comes second — we will come back to that.
Now run the same join a third time, and this time do not summarise anything. Simply count how many rows the join produced.
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv' s
JOIN 'data/fmcg_depots.csv'   d USING (depot_code);


What just happened


55,474 rows went in. 60,094 came out.
That is 4,620 rows that did not exist a moment ago, and no error message anywhere. The transferable part is the principle rather than the cause: a join to a dimension table should never increase the row count. A dimension exists to describe things — one row per depot, one row per product, one row per customer — so attaching it should add columns to the rows you already had, never rows.
The cause here is that fmcg_depots.csv contains thirteen rows for twelve depots. Somebody renamed Abuja Central to “Abuja Central (Wuse II)” and inserted the new name as a fresh row rather than updating the existing one — an entirely ordinary thing to do, since the old row has history attached and deleting it feels risky. But the key DP04 now appears twice, so every Abuja Central sell-out line found two matching dimension rows, and the join dutifully emitted one output row for each.
Here is what a board would see, in the order they would see it:




Rows
Abuja Central revenue
Region ranking




As shipped
55,474
₦4.51bn
North Central 4th


After the join
60,094
₦9.03bn
North Central 2nd



The revenue figure is the tell. Each Abuja Central row is counted exactly twice, so its revenue exactly doubles: ₦4.51bn becomes ₦9.03bn, the last digit differing only because each total is rounded independently. A figure that is precisely double a plausible one should send you looking for duplication first.
(“As shipped” is not the same as “correct”. The file still carries 214 duplicate grains from the ETL re-run, which is a second overstatement sitting underneath this one. Two separate defects, two separate corrections, and you have to do both — which is itself a useful lesson, because finding one problem creates a strong and misleading feeling that you have finished.)
Follow it through to the network total. That duplicated ₦4.51bn is a straight addition to a total that was previously right, and it lifts network revenue by 9.6%. Abuja Central overtakes both Lagos depots to become the largest single site in the network. If a colleague were assembling an expansion case for the North that month, this is the table they would have reached for, and it would have supported the case handsomely.
Notice what would not have saved you. Nothing about the query is wrong. Run it past a reviewer, a linter or an assistant and it passes all three. The only thing that catches it is counting the rows.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: Joins that lie
text:
Why it happens: fan-out
A join multiplies rows. That is not a defect; it is the entire mechanism. For every row on the left, the database looks for matching rows on the right and emits one output row per match. If there is exactly one match, the row count is preserved. If there are two, the row is emitted twice. The behaviour is the same in either case, and so is the absence of any warning.
The technical name for the second case is fan-out: one input row fanning out into several output rows. It is worth knowing the word, because it is what a data engineer will say when you ask them what went wrong, and because it names a family rather than an incident.








Left grain
Right grain
Result




One row per order line
One row per product
Safe — many-to-one


One row per order line
Two rows per product
Every line doubles — fan-out


One row per customer
Many rows per customer (addresses)
Customer count inflates


One row per day
One row per day per region
Days multiply by regions



Read that as a sequence rather than a list. The first row is the arrangement you intended: many facts, one description of each thing they refer to. The other three are what happens when the right-hand side turns out to hold more than one row per thing, whether you knew it or not. In practice the cause is almost always one of four:

A duplicate in the dimension — a rename, a merge of two systems, a re-load that appended instead of replacing. That is what has happened in today’s file.
A key that is not unique in the way you assumed. A customer_id that turns out to be unique per branch rather than per customer is the classic. Nothing in the column name tells you which it is.
A slowly-changing dimension without a date filter. Some dimensions deliberately keep history — one row per version of a customer’s address, each with valid-from and valid-to dates. Joined without a date condition, every version attaches to every transaction. The design is correct; the join was incomplete.
A join on something that was never a key. Joining on a name, or on a code that got retired and then reused five years later.

None of these is a sign of carelessness. Three of the four are the ordinary consequences of systems that have run for a long time and accumulated history, which is what useful systems do.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: Joins that lie
text:
The two-line habit
Here is the habit, and it is the highest-return four seconds in this programme: count the rows before the join, and count them again afterwards. If the number moved and you did not expect it to, stop and find out why before you look at any total. The third check — the one that would have caught today’s problem in advance — asks whether the key on the right-hand side is actually unique.

SQLRPython


-- Before
SELECT COUNT(*) AS before_rows FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv';

-- The check that should have been done first: is the key unique?
SELECT depot_code, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM 'data/fmcg_depots.csv'
GROUP BY depot_code
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
-- DP04 | 2      <- there it is

-- After
SELECT COUNT(*) AS after_rows
FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv' s
JOIN 'data/fmcg_depots.csv'   d USING (depot_code);
The middle query is the pattern worth memorising: group by the column that is supposed to be unique, count the rows in each group, keep only the groups with more than one. A genuinely unique key returns nothing at all. Anything that comes back is a fan-out waiting to happen.


library(tidyverse)

sales  <- read_csv("data/fmcg_sell_out.csv")
depots <- read_csv("data/fmcg_depots.csv")

# Is the key unique on the right-hand side?
depots |> count(depot_code) |> filter(n > 1)

# dplyr will warn you about this one if you let it
joined <- sales |>
  left_join(depots, by = "depot_code", relationship = "many-to-one")
# Error: Each row in `x` must match at most 1 row in `y`.

nrow(sales); nrow(joined)
relationship = "many-to-one" is a small argument with a large effect. It states your assumption — many fact rows, at most one dimension row each — and asks the software to enforce it, so a false assumption produces an error rather than a wrong answer. One phrase per join, and it is the most valuable argument in the tidyverse.


import pandas as pd

sales  = pd.read_csv("data/fmcg_sell_out.csv")
depots = pd.read_csv("data/fmcg_depots.csv")

# validate= raises instead of silently fanning out
joined = sales.merge(depots, on="depot_code", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
# MergeError: Merge keys are not unique in right dataset

print(len(sales), len(joined))
validate="many_to_one" does in pandas exactly what relationship= does in dplyr: it turns a silent duplication into a loud failure at the moment it happens, rather than a puzzling number three steps later.




The two questions, for people who will never write a join
You do not need to know what a join is, or to write a line of code, to prevent this happening in work you commission. You need two questions, and you can ask them of anybody presenting you a number:

“One row per what?” — asked of each table that went into the analysis.
“How many rows before the join, and how many after?”

If the answer to the second is “I don’t know”, the number is not ready yet, and saying so is not a criticism of the analyst — it is a request for one more query that takes four seconds. If the row count did change and nobody had predicted that it would, that is the moment to pause rather than to press on.
Ask these once in a meeting, pleasantly, and you will notice the quality of what you are shown afterwards change. Not because anybody was being careless, but because a check that somebody senior is known to ask about is a check that gets run.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: Joins that lie
section: The second one: when one entity arrives as two
text:
The second one: when one entity arrives as two
The first defect inflated a number. This one does the opposite: it hides something valuable by splitting it in half. Run the supplier scorecard.
SELECT supplier_id,
       COUNT(*)                                   AS orders,
       ROUND(AVG(on_time), 3)                     AS on_time_rate,
       ROUND(SUM(order_value_ngn) / 1e9, 2)       AS spend_bn
FROM 'data/supply_chain_pos.csv'
GROUP BY supplier_id
ORDER BY spend_bn DESC;
Nine rows come back. A category manager reading that table sees a fairly even spread of spend with nobody standing out, concludes there is no obvious consolidation opportunity, and moves on. That is a reasonable reading of the table in front of them.
Before opening the panel below, try the question the table cannot answer on its own: how many suppliers does this business actually have?


What nine IDs are really describing


SUP-CEDAR was renamed SUP-CEDAR-NG in March 2025, and both identifiers remain live in the file. The scorecard therefore shows one supplier as two mid-sized ones, at 6.6% and 7.4% of spend respectively.
Add those together and Cedar is 14.0% of spend — the third largest relationship this business has, behind Alpha at 18.6% and Bridge at 16.2%. That alone would change the shortlist for a consolidation conversation. The service figure changes the conversation altogether: Cedar delivers on time on 98.5% of orders, against a network average of 77.4%, and the next best supplier in the file manages 85.9%.
So Cedar is not merely good. It is, by a wide margin, the best supplier this business has, and it is being under-used. The scorecard conceals that not through any error of arithmetic but by presenting it as two unremarkable halves, neither large enough to draw the eye. The consolidation opportunity — worth several points of network service level — never reaches the meeting, and nobody involved does anything wrong.
The fix strips the -NG suffix, then groups by the cleaned identifier.
-- The fix, and the reason entity resolution is a commercial issue
SELECT regexp_replace(supplier_id, '-NG$', '') AS supplier,
       COUNT(*)                                AS orders,
       ROUND(AVG(on_time), 3)                  AS on_time_rate,
       ROUND(SUM(order_value_ngn) / 1e9, 2)    AS spend_bn
FROM 'data/supply_chain_pos.csv'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY spend_bn DESC;
Deciding that two identifiers refer to the same real-world thing is called entity resolution. It sounds like a technical speciality, and it is usually a commercial judgement: are these two account numbers one customer or two? Is this subsidiary the same counterparty as its parent, for the purposes of an exposure limit?
The question that finds it: how many distinct real-world things is this key supposed to represent? Somebody has to hold the count in their head — eight suppliers — and compare it with what the file says. That reconciliation is not something the assistant can do for you, because only one of you has ever met the suppliers.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: Joins that lie
section: Grain, stated once and for all
text:
Grain, stated once and for all
Both defects above are the same idea seen from two sides, so it is worth stating that idea carefully and giving it its proper name.

The grain of a table is what one row represents.

If you cannot say the grain in a single sentence — “one row per depot, per SKU, per week”, “one row per purchase order”, “one row per customer as at today” — then you cannot safely trust any total computed from it, because you do not know what you are adding up. Writing the grain at the top of a script takes ten seconds and is the most useful comment in most pipelines.
Two grain errors cost real money regularly and are rarely taught anywhere.
Mixed grain inside one table. A sales extract containing both line items and order-level freight rows. Both carry a value, both are called “revenue” in the source system, and summing the value column double-counts the freight. Extremely common in ERP extracts, and nobody’s mistake: the source system represents two legitimate things and the extract has flattened them into one shape.
Silent grain change over time. A table that held one row per day until March and one row per day per channel afterwards, because a field was added and the extract widened to match. Every year-on-year comparison spanning March is now wrong, and nothing in the file announces it. The cheapest way to detect it is to count rows per period and look at the sequence: a genuine business trend drifts, whereas a grain change steps.
-- The grain-change detector. Run it on any time series you inherit.
SELECT week_starting, COUNT(*) AS rows_this_week
FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
-- Look for step changes, not gradual drift.
Run that on any time series somebody hands you. It takes seconds, it needs no knowledge of the business, and a flat line with one sudden step in it tells you more about the file than an hour of reading its documentation would.

Core lab · 35 minutes


Reproduce the Abuja result. Present it to your table as a finding, with a straight face, before revealing it.


Find the duplicate. Quantify the damage in naira and in ranking.


Fix it two ways: deduplicate the dimension, and add the relationship / validate guard so it can never happen silently again.


Now the supplier scorecard. Nine IDs, eight suppliers. Find it and quantify the missed opportunity.


Run the grain-change detector on all four FMCG files.


Two entries in the failure logbook today. This session earns them.


The presentation step in the first item is not a joke. Watching a room accept a wrong number politely, including the people who would normally ask good questions, is the most efficient way to understand why these errors survive review in your own organisation.


Stretch · break another table’s result
Take a finished query from a table that has moved on, and find a way to make its answer wrong without touching the query at all — only the data underneath it. Add a duplicate row to a dimension. Introduce a renamed entity. Change one table’s grain halfway through the period.
Then hand it back, without comment, and see whether they catch it.
This is the most useful stretch exercise in the programme, and it is worth saying why. Every other exercise builds a procedure: run this check, ask this question. This one builds an adversarial instinct — the habit of asking how a correct-looking result could have come from incorrect data — and that is the part an assistant cannot supply, because it requires imagining a world other than the one described in the prompt.


Copilot check
Try this pair of prompts in sequence, because the contrast between the two answers is the lesson.
First ask: “Here is my join. What could make it produce more rows than it should?”
You will get an excellent, complete, textbook answer — duplicate keys, one-to-many relationships, missing date filters on slowly-changing dimensions, keys that are unique at a different level than assumed. Every item correct, and a genuinely useful checklist.
Then ask: “Does that happen with my data?”
It cannot know. A well-behaved assistant will say so; a less careful one will produce a confident-sounding guess that reads exactly like the first answer did. The distance between those two responses is roughly the job description of everybody in this room: the checklist is available to anyone, and the knowledge of which item on it applies today is not.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: Joins that lie
text:
Takeaways

Most expensive analytical errors are joins, grains, definitions and calendars — not statistics.
Count rows before and after every join. Four seconds.
Use relationship = "many-to-one" in R or validate= in pandas so silent fan-out becomes a loud error.
Ask how many real-world things a key is supposed to represent, then check.
“One row per what?” is the question. Ask it of every table, including the ones you are handed in a meeting.

title: The laptop warehouse
text:
The thing that actually changed
For about thirty years, the sentence “we need to analyse more data than Excel can hold” began a project. It meant a server, a licence, a database administrator, a conversation about who is allowed to see what, and four months before anybody looked at a number.
That is no longer the case, and the change happened quietly enough that many organisations have not adjusted to it. What exists now is an in-process analytical database — a database that runs inside whatever program you are already using rather than as a separate service you connect to. There is no server to install, no background process to keep running, and in most configurations no administrator rights required. It reads CSV, Excel and Parquet files where they already sit, and it handles row counts that would have needed a warehouse in 2019. The whole thing is a single file of a few tens of megabytes.
Two consequences follow, and both are commercial rather than technical.
It works when the internet does not. In Lagos that is a practical argument rather than a footnote. A five-day programme in Ajah cannot depend on a cloud notebook staying reachable, and neither can a finance team’s month-end close.
A number can now be verified by the person who is accountable for it. This is the one that changes the politics of analytics. Checking a number used to mean asking the team that produced it and waiting — which is a reasonable thing to do once and an awkward thing to do three times. It now means twenty minutes and a copy of the extract. That ends a certain number of arguments and, to be fair about it, starts a few others; on balance it is a good trade, because the arguments it starts are about the data rather than about who to believe.

What to tell your CIO
This does not replace your data warehouse, and it is worth being able to say why without hesitating. The warehouse is where definitions are agreed, where history is retained, where access is governed and where lineage is recorded. A laptop engine does none of those things, and it is not trying to.
What it replaces is the waiting: the two-week queue for an ad-hoc extract, the analyst who cannot begin until a table is provisioned, the executive who wanted to check one figure and gave up on the way.
Nor is it automatically a governance hole, provided it is set up sensibly. The data still comes from a governed extract, and the query runs where that extract already is. The real governance question is which extract left the building, and that question long predates this tooling — until recently it was being answered, informally, by people emailing spreadsheets to each other.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: The laptop warehouse
text:
Query files where they sit
There is no loading step and no CREATE TABLE. You point the engine at the file.

Command lineRPythonThe browser UI


# Start the engine in the folder containing the data
duckdb

# Then, at the prompt:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv';
-- 55474

SELECT * FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv' LIMIT 5;

-- Read every CSV in a folder as one table
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM 'data/*.csv';

-- Read an Excel file directly, sheet and all
INSTALL excel; LOAD excel;
SELECT * FROM read_xlsx('data/board_pack.xlsx', sheet = 'Sales');


library(duckdb)
library(DBI)

con <- dbConnect(duckdb())

dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT depot_code,
         SUM(revenue_ngn) AS revenue
  FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv'
  GROUP BY 1
  ORDER BY revenue DESC
")

# Or stay in the tidyverse and let it write the SQL for you
library(dplyr)
sales <- tbl(con, "read_csv_auto('data/fmcg_sell_out.csv')")

sales |>
  group_by(depot_code) |>
  summarise(revenue = sum(revenue_ngn, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(revenue)) |>
  collect()


import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()

con.sql("""
    SELECT depot_code, SUM(revenue_ngn) AS revenue
    FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv'
    GROUP BY 1
    ORDER BY revenue DESC
""").df()

# It reads pandas DataFrames in the same breath
import pandas as pd
depots = pd.read_csv("data/fmcg_depots.csv")
con.sql("SELECT * FROM depots WHERE region = 'North West'").df()


duckdb -ui
That command opens a local notebook in your browser — a list of tables, a query editor, results and charts. Despite appearances, nothing leaves your machine; the browser is being used as an interface to something running locally. For anybody who has never worked in a terminal this is comfortably the most approachable thing in the entire stack, and it is where a number of people in each cohort end up doing most of their week.

title: The laptop warehouse
section: Why it is fast, in one paragraph you can repeat
text:
Why it is fast, in one paragraph you can repeat
Spreadsheets and traditional transactional databases store data row by row: everything about one transaction sits together, which is exactly right when the job is to retrieve or update one transaction. Analytical questions almost never want one transaction. They want one column across a very large number of rows — total this revenue, average this lead time, count these customers.
A columnar engine stores each column together instead. Answering “sum this column” then reads only that column, ignoring everything else in the file, and reads it in a layout that lets the processor add several values in a single instruction. That is the entire trick, and it is why 55,474 rows come back instantly and why 61 million would too.
Parquet is the file format built on the same idea: the same data, stored column by column, compressed, and — importantly — with the type of each column recorded inside the file. Nothing has to be guessed on the way in. Convert once and every subsequent read is faster and safer, because no reader can decide on its own that your account numbers are integers and quietly remove the leading zeros.
-- Convert the working dataset once. Everything downstream reads this instead.
COPY (SELECT * FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv')
  TO 'data/fmcg_sell_out.parquet' (FORMAT parquet);

The CSV type-guessing trap
A CSV is a text file with commas in it. It carries no types at all: it cannot say that one column is a date and another is an identifier that happens to look like a number. Every reader therefore guesses, and different readers guess differently — which is why the same file can produce two different answers in two different tools without anybody making a mistake.
The classic casualty in Nigerian data is an account number or a phone number with a leading zero. 0803... becomes 803... the moment something decides the column is numeric, and the join to the customer table then fails for exactly those rows — silently, because a failed match does not raise an error, it simply produces no match.
Two defences, both cheap:
-- 1. Tell it, don't let it guess. (Illustrative file name -- the same fix
--    applies to any extract where an ID could be read as a number.)
SELECT * FROM read_csv('data/your_extract.csv',
                       columns = {'account_no': 'VARCHAR', 'balance': 'DOUBLE'});

-- 2. Or convert to Parquet once, with the types stated, and never guess again
The first is the fix for a file you are handed today; the second is the fix for a file you will be handed every month. In practice this bites far more often than anything statistical, and it is worth checking any identifier column the first time you meet it.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: The laptop warehouse
text:
The three-second habit
Every time you open a file you have not met before, run these three things before you run anything else. Together they answer “what is in here, how much of it, and what is missing”.
-- What is in it, and what did it guess the types were?
DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv';

-- How many rows, over what period, at what grain?
SELECT COUNT(*)                                   AS rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT (week_starting, depot_code, sku)) AS distinct_grain,
       MIN(week_starting)                         AS first_week,
       MAX(week_starting)                         AS last_week
FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv';

-- What is missing, column by column?
SUMMARIZE SELECT * FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv';
Take those in turn, because each answers a different question. DESCRIBE lists the columns with the types the reader decided on, which is where a misread identifier column shows itself. The middle query is the grain check from yesterday, expressed in SQL: COUNT(*) is how many rows there are, and COUNT(DISTINCT (...)) is how many distinct combinations of depot, SKU and week there are — and if the table really is one row per depot per SKU per week, those two numbers agree. The MIN and MAX tell you what period you are actually holding, which is the check that catches a partial year before it reaches a chart.
SUMMARIZE then returns count, distinct count, nulls, minimum, maximum and quartiles for every column in one command. For somebody meeting a dataset for the first time it is the single most useful thing in the engine, and it takes about four seconds to run.
Run it now on fmcg_sell_out.csv and look carefully at two things: rows against distinct_grain, and the null count on units_sold compared with the number of genuine zeroes. Work out what each pair implies before you open the box.


What those two numbers should have told you


55,474 rows, 55,260 distinct grains. There are 214 rows more than there are distinct depot–SKU–week combinations. The grain is supposed to be one row per depot per SKU per week, and on this evidence it is not — something has been loaded more than once. Note that nothing here is corrupt: every individual row looks entirely reasonable, which is why this survives a visual inspection.
789 nulls in units_sold, in a file where only 18 rows record a genuine zero. Those two counts sitting side by side tell you that “we sold none” and “we do not know what we sold” have been recorded the same way somewhere upstream. Every average computed from this column therefore excludes a set of weeks that were almost certainly the worst ones, which moves the answer in the more comfortable direction — the direction that is hardest to notice.
Neither of these appears in any summary anybody hands you, and both take four seconds to find. This is what “read the data before you analyse it” means in practice: not a general virtue, but two specific commands run in a specific order.



Core lab · 30 minutes


Open the engine in your data folder. Confirm you can query without loading anything.


Run DESCRIBE and SUMMARIZE on all four FMCG files. Write down the grain of each.


Find the row-count-versus-distinct-grain discrepancy. Quantify it.


Count the nulls in units_sold and compare to the count of genuine zeros.


Convert fmcg_sell_out.csv to Parquet. Compare file sizes and query times.


Disconnect from the wifi and run all of it again. It should not matter.


The last step is not a gimmick, and it is worth actually doing rather than believing. Once you have watched the whole thing work with the wifi off, you know something specific about what this tool requires — and that knowledge is what lets you promise a month-end process that does not depend on a connection.


Stretch
Take the largest CSV you are permitted to bring from your own organisation and run SUMMARIZE on it. Then go looking for three specific things:

one column whose type was guessed wrongly,
one column where “missing” and “zero” have been conflated,
one column containing a value that cannot possibly be true — a negative quantity, a date in 1900, a lead time of four hundred days.

Extracts that have passed through several systems tend to carry all three, so the exercise is not really whether you will find them. It is how long it takes you, and which of the three you would have shipped a number on top of.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: The laptop warehouse
text:
Takeaways

An analytical database now runs inside your laptop, reads files where they sit, and works offline.
It does not replace the warehouse. It replaces the waiting.
DESCRIBE, SUMMARIZE, row count versus distinct grain. Four seconds, every new file.
CSVs have no types. Convert to Parquet once, or state the types, before a leading zero costs you a join.

title: Lab 1 · The use-case charter
text:
Run of show







Time
What happens




0–5 min
Read the template. Do not start writing yet.


5–30 min
Draft. Driver writes, Sceptic stays quiet. Yes, really.


30–40 min
Attack. Sceptic takes the charter apart against the six questions below. Driver may not defend, only take notes.


40–52 min
Rewrite. Driver rewrites in response.


52–60 min
Pin to the wall board. Read three other charters. Leave one written objection on each.



Two of those rules tend to be resisted, so here is the reasoning behind them.
The silent Sceptic during drafting exists because co-writing is comfortable and convergent. When two people draft together, each softens the parts the other hesitates over, and the charter ends up expressing what both of them already believed when they walked in. A charter written by one person and then attacked by the other covers more ground, because the attack has something specific to push against.
The no-defending rule during the attack phase is there for a similar reason. Defending an idea out loud commits you to it — you hear yourself make the argument and it becomes harder to abandon ten minutes later. Taking notes in silence keeps the option of agreeing open. You will get your turn in the rewrite, which is where a defence belongs anyway.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Lab 1 · The use-case charter
text:
The template

Use-case charter
1 · The decision. Which recurring decision does this change? Who makes it? How often? What are their current options?

Depot managers set a reorder quantity every Tuesday for 40 SKUs. Today they order to a fixed four weeks of cover, adjusted by feel. With this, they order to a forecast with a 95% service-level target, and any SKU with stockout probability above 15% is flagged for expediting.

2 · The number. Which node on your KPI tree moves? State its definition in one sentence — the version that survives cross-examination. State where it sits today.

Availability, defined as the share of depot-SKU-weeks with no stockout event recorded in the WMS, excluding SKUs delisted during the week. Today: 96.5%.

3 · The value. One line of arithmetic. Three assumptions, ranked. A range, not a point.
4 · The data. Which three tables. What grain. Do they have history. Who owns access. What is the single thing most likely to be wrong with them.
5 · The evidence standard. How will you know afterwards whether it worked? A control group, a holdout, a before-and-after with a comparison group, or — stated honestly — nothing yet. Writing “nothing yet” on Monday is a perfectly good starting position; the week is partly about turning it into something better by Friday.
6 · The person whose judgement this displaces. Name them. What will they say? What would make them an ally rather than an obstacle?
7 · The 90-day plan. Three milestones. The first one is in a fortnight and does not need anybody’s permission.

Two notes on filling this in. Sections 1 and 2 are the ones people rush, and they are the ones the Friday panel returns to; a vague decision in section 1 makes every later section vague, because there is nothing concrete for the value or the evidence to attach to. Section 7 is the one people over-plan. The only milestone that really matters is the first, and the test of it is whether you could start on Monday without asking permission — if you could not, it is not a first milestone, it is a request.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Lab 1 · The use-case charter
section: The six questions your Sceptic will ask
text:
The six questions your Sceptic will ask
These are the same six the Friday panel asks. They are published now, deliberately: a rubric you see on Monday changes how you work all week, whereas a rubric you see on Friday only allocates marks.

What decision changes, and who makes it? If the honest answer is “it gives us visibility”, the case is worth a good deal less than a decision-improvement case, and pricing it accordingly on Monday is far more comfortable than being told so on Friday.
Would you have known this in time? Take each data item in section 4 and ask whether it was available at the moment the decision is made, or only afterwards. A field that is populated at month-end cannot inform a Tuesday order, however predictive it looks in a back-test.
What is the grain, and does the number survive a duplicate check?
Real or nominal? And if the metric is a rate, what is the denominator doing while the numerator moves?
How would you know if it worked? Section 5, pushed hard.
Who loses? Section 6. If nobody loses anything at all, then either the change is small enough not to matter or the person who loses has not been identified yet — and it is usually the second.


Sceptic’s instruction
Your job in the attack phase is not to be unpleasant, and a hostile tone will simply make your partner defensive and slow the work down. Your job is to find the one assumption that, if wrong, makes the whole charter worthless — and to state it plainly enough that it cannot be waved away.
You have ten minutes. Spend the first three reading and the remaining seven on the single weakest point. Resist the temptation to distribute your fire: a list of eight small objections is much easier to survive than one unanswerable question, which is precisely why lists of eight small objections are so often what gets produced. One good objection, held steadily, is the more generous thing to give a colleague.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Lab 1 · The use-case charter
text:
Using the assistant here
Two prompts earn their place in this lab, and the order matters.
First, to stress the framing:

Here is a draft analytics use-case charter. Do not improve the writing. Instead, act as a hostile reviewer with a finance background. Give me: the single strongest reason this will not deliver the value claimed; the data item most likely to be unavailable at decision time; and the stakeholder whose cooperation is assumed but not secured. Be specific and be brief.

Then, to widen the option set:

Same charter. Now give me three alternative framings of the same underlying opportunity that would be cheaper to test in the next two weeks. For each, tell me what evidence it would produce and what it would leave unanswered.

The second prompt is the one that tends to surprise people. A first draft almost always describes the most complete version of an idea rather than the most testable one — that is what happens when you write down what you have been imagining for months — and an assistant asked explicitly for cheaper alternatives is genuinely good at generating them. Two of the three will usually be unsuitable, and the third is often better than what you brought.
What it cannot do is choose between them, because choosing depends on section 6: who is affected, what they will say, and what you can carry politically this quarter. Those are facts about people you know and it does not.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Lab 1 · The use-case charter
text:
Before you leave today


Charter pinned to the wall board with your name on it.


One written objection left on three other charters.


Your table’s first failure logbook entry submitted.


The number you now believe, with an interval, written on the card and sealed.


The sealed card is worth doing properly. On Friday you will open it, and the interesting thing is rarely whether you were right — it is which direction you moved, and which of this week’s sessions moved you.

Tomorrow
You will need your three tables. If they are confidential — and for most people at least one of them will be — bring the shape instead of the data: column names, types, row counts, date range. That is enough for everything Tuesday asks of you, and it keeps the question of what left the building simple.
You can also do the entire Tuesday programme against the course datasets and apply the technique to your own data afterwards. Several people in every cohort choose that, and it often turns out to be the better use of the day, because the course data is built to teach and your own data is built to run a business.
If you intend to work with your own data on a laptop that your IT department controls, have a word with the floor technologist at the break today rather than tomorrow morning. Permissions take longer to arrange than anybody expects, and the break is free time.

title: What AI actually changed
text:
The claim, stated carefully
It is worth being exact about what has changed, because the loose version of the claim leads to bad decisions in both directions — over-buying and over-dismissing.
The claim is not “AI does analytics now”. That version is sold by vendors and it is false in a specific and important way, which we will come to.
The claim is: the cost of translating an intention into code has fallen by roughly two orders of magnitude, and the parts of the work that require knowing your business have not moved at all. Two orders of magnitude means a factor of about a hundred — work that occupied an afternoon now occupies a couple of minutes. That is not an incremental improvement in productivity; it is large enough to change which questions are worth asking at all, because a question you would previously have dropped for want of an afternoon is now worth a try.
It is also worth being precise about what the claim does not say. Assistants are no longer confined to producing text. Give one a code environment and it will plot a series, look at the plot, and tell you unprompted that there is a level shift in November. Several of the checks taught in this programme can already be delegated, and over the next two years more of them will be. Anybody who tells you the boundary is fixed is guessing.
What does not follow is that the judgement travels with the mechanics. An assistant will audit an artefact you hand it — a query, a chart, a paragraph — often very well. What it cannot audit is the question you handed it, because the question is about your business, your decision and the consequences you carry, and none of that is in front of it unless you put it there.
So the barrier to entry used to be translation into code, and that barrier has largely gone. What rations good analytical work now is judgement, plus how much of your actual situation you were willing to type out.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: What AI actually changed
text:
The division of labour








The work
Who does it now
Why




Writing a query from a description
Assistant
Syntax is a solved problem


Knowing the right question to ask
You
Requires knowing the business and the decision


Cleaning and reshaping data
Assistant
Pattern-matching, and it is good at it


Knowing the data is wrong
You
Requires knowing what the world looks like


Fitting a model
Assistant
Genuinely commoditised


Choosing what to model, and what “good” means
You
A commercial judgement wearing a technical costume


Drafting the memo
Assistant
Fast, competent, slightly bland


Deciding what the memo should conclude
You
Nobody else carries the consequence


Explaining a chart
Assistant
Reliable


Standing behind the chart on Friday afternoon
You
This is the entire job



Read the right-hand column downwards and a pattern emerges. Every row that stays with you depends on one of two things: knowledge of a specific business, or accountability for a specific outcome. Neither of those is in a model’s training data, and neither is likely to be, since both are properties of your organisation rather than of the world in general.
Notice, too, that the rows alternate rather than splitting into an easy half and a hard half. The assistant writes the query; you decide whether the query answers a question worth asking. It cleans the data; you notice that a number in it cannot be true. This is why “give the whole task to the machine” and “do the whole task yourself” both perform worse than the alternating pattern, and why the pair-working format this week has one person on the keyboard and one person asking what could be wrong.

The single sentence to take away
An assistant is an outstanding generator and a poor auditor of the question it was handed.
It will answer the question you asked, beautifully, whether or not that was the question worth asking and whether or not the data can support an answer at all. It will not stop you, because it has no stake in the outcome and no model of your business — not from any lack of ability, but because nothing in the exchange gave it either.
Every mechanic in this programme — the Sceptic role, the salted datasets, the failure logbook, the four-minute rule — exists to build a habit into the human side of that partnership, which is the side where the habit has to live.

title: What AI actually changed
text:
The four-minute rule
No demonstration in this programme runs for longer than four minutes before the room does it themselves.
This is not a stylistic preference; it is a deliberate fix for the way most AI training fails. The usual pattern is that everybody watches a fluent, impressive demonstration, agrees afterwards that it was impressive, and leaves able to do none of it. The demonstration is enjoyable precisely because it is frictionless — and the friction is where the learning was. Watching somebody type a prompt teaches you almost nothing about what to do when the answer comes back subtly wrong.
So: four minutes, then keys. If a faculty member overruns, the room is entitled to say so, and we would rather you did.
