title: Prompt patterns
text:
A great deal has been written about prompting, and a good deal of it is folklore that stopped being true two model generations ago. Magic words, elaborate personas and threats of consequences all had their moment; none of them survives contact with a current assistant on a real analytical task.
What has held up is less exciting and considerably more useful. An assistant’s value on an analytical task is roughly proportional to how much of the surrounding business context you were willing to type. The model is fluent in SQL, R and statistics; what it cannot know is your grain, your fiscal calendar, your definitions, or which of your columns is populated only after the event you are trying to predict. Nearly every prompt on this page is a different way of supplying one of those.

title: Prompt patterns
text:
The four foundations

1 · Give it the shape, not the data
Three lines of description that remove most hallucinated column names before they happen.

The table is fmcg_sell_out.csv. 55,474 rows, of which 55,260 are distinct on (week_starting, depot_code, sku) — the grain is intended to be one row per depot per SKU per week and there are 214 rows too many. Jan 2024 to Mar 2026. Columns: week_starting (date), depot_code (text), sku (text), units_sold (number, nullable — blank means a stockout, not zero), unit_price_ngn (number), on_promotion (0/1), discount_pct (number), stockout_flag (0/1), revenue_ngn (number, nullable).
Write DuckDB SQL to …

Why it works. Given no schema, the assistant has to infer a plausible one, and it will — confidently, and in a house style that looks entirely reasonable — then write code against columns you do not have. Given the schema, it writes code that runs the first time. This is the cheapest improvement available anywhere on this page, and it takes about ninety seconds to prepare once per table.
The two lines people leave out are the two that do the most work.
The grain sentence lets the assistant reason about whether an aggregation is safe. And note what this version does that the obvious version does not: it says the grain is intended, and that the file does not meet it. Writing “one row per depot per SKU per week” when the file has 214 duplicates would be handing the assistant your own wrong assumption and asking it to build on it — which is precisely the failure this programme exists to prevent, committed in the prompt.
The nullability semantics — “blank means a stockout, not zero” — decides whether every average it writes is right or wrong.


2 · Ask for the check, not just the answer

Write the query. Then write a second query that would detect if the first one is wrong — specifically checking the grain, unexpected row-count changes across joins, and whether any aggregation is silently dropping nulls.

Why it works. Assistants are markedly better at auditing a specific artefact than at auditing an open situation, in the same way that a colleague finds it easier to review a draft than to imagine one. Giving it something concrete to attack — a query it has just written — reliably surfaces problems that “is this right?” never will. The second query is also worth keeping: it becomes the first rule in your data contract on Tuesday afternoon.


3 · Make it argue against itself

Give me the three strongest reasons this result might be an artefact of the data rather than a fact about the business.

Why it works. “Is this right?” tends to return yes, because agreement is the conversational default and the model has no independent stake in the answer. Asking instead for the strongest available counter-argument returns a different class of response entirely: it reframes the task from assistance to critique, and critique is where an assistant is most useful to somebody who already knows the business. Read the three reasons it gives you, and notice which one you were hoping it would not mention.


4 · Refuse the first answer once, on principle

That is plausible. Now assume it is wrong. What would have to be true?

Why it works. Rather less because of what the assistant produces and rather more because of what the habit does to you. The first answer to any question arrives fluent, formatted and plausible, and the temptation to accept it is strongest precisely when you are short of time. Refusing it once, as a matter of routine rather than suspicion, installs a pause where one would not otherwise exist — and the pause is where most of the errors in this programme get caught.

title: Prompt patterns
text:
By session
The patterns below are used on the days indicated, and each links to the session where it is introduced and worked through properly. They are written out here in full so that you can copy them, adapt the bracketed parts to your own situation, and take them back to your desk without having to remember what was on the screen.

Framing a use case — 1.1

I am going to describe an analytics initiative. Do not tell me it is a good idea. Instead: (1) classify it as decision-improving, cycle-time, new-revenue or visibility; (2) name the specific recurring decision it changes, or say clearly that it does not change one; (3) name whose existing judgement it displaces; (4) give me the three assumptions that, if wrong, make it worthless. Be blunt.
The initiative is: …

The instruction not to evaluate the idea is the important part. Asked whether an initiative is a good one, an assistant will tell you it is, and the answer will read well. Asked to classify it and to name what it rests on, it becomes a useful thinking partner instead of an enthusiastic one.


Stressing a value case — 1.3

Here is a value hypothesis. Do not improve it. Instead: (1) identify every number that is an assumption rather than a measurement; (2) for each, say what evidence would replace it and roughly what that evidence costs to obtain; (3) tell me which single assumption, if wrong by a factor of two, changes the decision; (4) give me the strongest argument a sceptical CFO would make against the whole case.

Point (3) is the one that earns its keep. Most value cases have a single assumption carrying the entire argument, and finding out which one before the CFO does is worth the ten minutes this takes.


Auditable SQL — 2.1

Rewrite this query as a sequence of named CTEs, one per logical step, with a comment on each saying what it produces and what its grain is. Do not change the result.

“Do not change the result” matters: without it you will get a tidier query that also quietly answers a slightly different question. With it, you get the same answer in a form you can read aloud to somebody who has never seen SQL — which is the form in which errors become visible.


Data quality rules — 2.5

Here are the columns and types, and here is what one row represents. Propose twelve data quality rules as business rules that cannot be false — not type checks. For each: the rule in English, the SQL that counts violations, and a severity of fatal, warn or note.

Asking for rules as business statements rather than type checks is what makes the output worth reading. A type check tells you a column contains numbers; a business rule tells you that a receipt cannot precede the order it belongs to, and that is the sort of rule whose violation means something has genuinely gone wrong upstream.


Exploratory analysis — 3.1

What in this dataset would surprise a domain expert? Give me five specific things to check, as queries. Do not summarise the data — I want the checks.

Refusing the summary is deliberate. A summary of a dataset is comforting and rarely informative; a list of five specific things that would surprise somebody who knows the business is a morning’s work, and you can run each of them yourself in a few seconds.


Charts — 3.2

Here is my data and the single claim I want the chart to make: “[claim]”. Propose three chart forms that would support that claim, say what each one hides, and recommend one. Then write the code with the claim as the title and direct labels rather than a legend.

And afterwards:

Look at this chart specification. What conclusion could a reader draw from it that the underlying data does not support?



Forecasting — 3.3

Forecast this weekly series 13 weeks ahead. Requirements: fit NAIVE and SNAIVE benchmarks alongside ETS and ARIMA; evaluate with rolling-origin cross-validation on a 13-week horizon and report MASE; check for structural breaks and tell me if you find one; produce 80% intervals; and state in one sentence what the interval assumes.



Segmentation — 3.4

Cluster this data. Requirements: log-transform the skewed monetary variables, standardise everything, fit k from 2 to 9, report both the within-cluster sum of squares and a profile table of segment medians for each k. Do not choose k for me and do not name the segments — I will do both. Then run a split-half stability check.

Withholding the choice of k, and the naming of the segments, is not an act of self-denial. Choosing how many segments to run and what to call them is a commercial judgement about what your organisation can actually operate, and it is the one part of a segmentation that an assistant has no basis whatsoever for making.


Leakage detection — 3.5

Here are the columns in my training data, a one-line description of what each means, and when each is populated in the business process. Identify any feature that could only be known after the outcome occurred, or that is a proxy for a protected characteristic. Explain your reasoning for each flag.

The clause in bold is doing all the work here. Leakage is a question about when a value becomes known, and that information exists nowhere in the data itself — no amount of inspection will reveal that a field is populated by the retention team after the customer has already given notice. Supply the timing and the assistant is genuinely good at this; withhold it and there is nothing it can do but guess.


Classification taxonomy — 4.2

Classify each review into exactly one of these categories: [list]. Include other and not_applicable. Also return a confidence field from 1 to 5. Return only structured output matching this schema. Do not invent categories.

Forcing an other and a not_applicable category, and refusing new ones, is what turns a classification into a measurement. Without those two escape hatches the model will squeeze awkward rows into whichever category fits least badly, and you will never see it happen.


Dashboard scope — 4.3

I need a dashboard for exactly one decision: [decision]. The user is [role], at [moment], with [time available], choosing between [actions]. Give me the minimum set of numbers that discriminates between those actions — no more than four — and tell me what you deliberately left out and why.

The closing instruction is the useful half. What an assistant deliberately left out, and why, is a much better conversation than what it chose to include — and it is the conversation you will otherwise have with the dashboard’s first user, in front of an audience.


Reproducible documents — 4.4

Every number that appears in prose must be inline code that computes it from the data. Do not hard-code any figure anywhere in the document text.

This one belongs permanently in your system prompt or project instructions rather than being retyped each time. Left to themselves, assistants write numbers directly into prose as literal text — confidently, correctly at the moment of writing, and permanently thereafter. The document then looks reproducible while quietly carrying last month’s figures in its sentences, which is a worse position than not having automated it at all.


The hostile reviewer — 4.5

Here is a two-page analytical memo. Act as the CFO it is addressed to. You are sceptical, short of time, and you have been given optimistic analytics numbers before. Give me the five questions you would ask, in the order you would ask them, and tell me which one you think the author is least prepared for.

Asking which question the author is least prepared for is what makes this more than a checklist. It is also, in most cohorts, uncomfortably accurate.


Auditing your own verbs — 5.1

For each sentence in this paragraph, classify the claim as correlational, contributional or causal. For every causal claim, state what study design would be required to support it, and rewrite the sentence to match the evidence I actually have, which is: [describe your data].

Run your capstone memo through this the night before the defence. It takes a few minutes, and it usually finds one sentence whose verb is claiming rather more than the evidence behind it — which is the sentence the panel would otherwise have found for you.


Causal design — 5.3

Estimate the effect of an intervention on [date] on [group] using difference-in-differences against [comparison]. Requirements: first plot and assess pre-period parallel trends and tell me honestly whether the design is valid; then estimate with a confidence interval; then run a placebo test at a date thirteen weeks earlier; then list three things that could have changed at the same time as the intervention and how I would check each.

Notice the order of the requirements: assess the design first, and only then estimate. A prompt that asks for the estimate first will get one, and the assumption it depends on will be mentioned politely somewhere in the third paragraph, after you have already written the number down.

title: Prompt patterns
section: Three things that do not work
text:
Three things that do not work
These are worth listing because all three are widely recommended, and two of them were once good advice. If you are doing any of them, you are in respectable company and can stop without embarrassment.
“You are a world-class expert data scientist.” Role-play preambles genuinely helped with earlier models, which is why they are still passed around. On a current assistant they add tokens and very little else. Describing the task and the audience precisely does the work the persona was standing in for, and does it better, because it says something true about your situation rather than something flattering about the model’s.
Long unstructured context dumps. Pasting an entire messy schema, three email threads and a policy document tends to produce a worse answer than three well-chosen lines would have. Relevance beats volume: the useful information gets diluted, and the assistant has no way of knowing which paragraph you actually cared about.
Asking an open “how confident are you?” about a free-form answer. What comes back is a number that sounds like a probability and has nothing behind it, and — more to the point — nothing you could check even if you wanted to. It gives the exchange a reassuring quality that the underlying answer has not earned.
That is different from asking for a confidence field on a constrained classification, which is the pattern used in 4.2 and which works: on a fixed taxonomy with a validation set, self-reported confidence is imperfectly but usefully correlated with correctness, so routing the low-confidence rows to a human is a real saving. The difference is that in that case you have measured the calibration — which is the whole point of the 200-row validation set.
Rule of thumb: ask for confidence where you can check it, and ask what evidence would change the answer where you cannot.


The one that matters most
None of these patterns gives an assistant the ability to know things about your business that nobody has told it, and it is worth being blunt about that because the fluency of the output suggests otherwise.
It does not know that your fiscal year starts in April, that a negative quantity is a legitimate return in your ERP rather than a data error, that account numbers beginning 07 are dormant by convention, or that the Head of Supply Chain has history with the Kaduna depot and will read any analysis of it as an attack.
Each of those has cost somebody in a previous cohort an afternoon, and in every case the work was competent and the answer was wrong for a reason no amount of prompt engineering would have reached. The fix is not a cleverer prompt. The fix is you, spending two minutes typing the context that only you have.

title: How this programme works
text:
Executive programmes about AI and analytics share a characteristic failure mode, and it is worth naming at the start because everything on this page is a response to it. The room watches a series of fluent, impressive demonstrations. Everybody agrees that they were impressive. The week is enjoyable, the food is good, and then people return to work able to do very little differently.
What makes this so persistent is that the demonstrations are enjoyable because they are frictionless. The presenter has already met every obstacle and removed it. But the obstacles were not incidental to the learning — they were the learning. The moment where the query returns three times as many rows as you expected, and you have to work out why, is the moment where the understanding actually forms.
So four mechanics exist to put the friction back deliberately. They are not decoration, and they are not team-building. If you take nothing else from this page, take these four.

title: How this programme works
text:
1 · The four-minute rule
No demonstration runs longer than four minutes before the room does it.
Four minutes is roughly the point at which watching somebody else work stops being orientation and starts being entertainment. Up to that point you are building a mental model of what is about to happen. Past it, you are a spectator, and spectators do not retain much. So after four minutes: hands on keyboards.
This has consequences, and they are worth naming in advance because on Monday morning they will feel like faults rather than choices:

Sessions look less polished than a keynote. There is more fumbling, and more visible difficulty, because real work looks like that.
Faculty answer more questions they did not plan for, which is uncomfortable for them and useful for you.
Less material gets covered than a lecture format would cover.

All three are the price of the design, and all three are worth paying — the alternative is a smoother week that leaves less behind. If a faculty member overruns, the room is entitled to say so out loud. Please do; it is genuinely helpful rather than rude.

title: How this programme works
text:
2 · Driver and Sceptic
You work in pairs, and the roles swap every day, so that everybody spends half the week in each seat.
The Driver is on the keyboard. They talk to the assistant, run the code, and produce the result.
The Sceptic may not touch the keyboard. Their job is to produce an objection before the result is used — not afterwards, when it has already been written on the wall board and defending it has become a matter of pride.

The Sceptic’s standing questions

What is the grain of this table? One row per what?
How many rows before the join, and how many after?
What period are we comparing to what period, and are they the same length?
Real or nominal? And if real, deflated by what?
Would we have known this at the moment we needed to act?
What had to be true for a row to exist in this file?
If this result is this good, what is wrong with it?

Seven questions. Between them they catch a large share of what goes wrong in commercial analytics, and — this is the part worth noticing — not one of them requires you to be able to write a line of code. They are questions about meaning, not about syntax, which is why they travel so well back to your own desk.

The Sceptic role is not a game and it is not a politeness. It exists because of a specific and fairly recent asymmetry: an assistant is an outstanding generator of analysis and a poor auditor of the question it was handed. Ask it a well-posed question and you will get an excellent answer. Ask it a subtly wrong question and you will get an equally excellent answer to the wrong question, delivered with exactly the same confidence. Nothing in the tool closes that gap. Somebody in the room has to, and pairing is how the habit gets built rather than merely recommended.
By Wednesday most pairs report that the Sceptic seat is harder work than the Driver seat. That is the correct discovery, and it usually arrives as a surprise.

title: How this programme works
text:
3 · Salted data
The data room carries thirteen deliberate defects, and does not tell you where they are.
You are told the kinds of thing to expect — a join key that silently duplicates rows, a feature that leaks the answer, a structural break a forecast will ignore, a definition that contradicts finance, an entity recorded twice under two names, an extract with a filter on it — and nothing at all about which file holds which. You find that out on Friday afternoon, and not before.
That distinction is deliberate and it is the whole design. Knowing the taxonomy of defects is the transferable part: it is what turns the useless instruction “check the data” into a short list of specific questions you can put to any table anybody hands you, for the rest of your career. Knowing that row 4,812 of one particular CSV is duplicated is worth precisely nothing on Monday week.
The defects are not one per file, and some files are entirely clean. That is deliberate too, and it is the detail people find most surprising. A room that has been told everything is dirty will hunt until it finds something, and finding a defect in a clean file is a worse habit to leave with than missing one in a dirty file — it teaches you to distrust your own instrument. The discipline being built is to run the same handful of checks on everything and let the file tell you what it is.
The underlying reasoning is simple enough. Being wrong in a classroom costs you a moment of mild discomfort among peers who are about to be wrong themselves. Being wrong in a board paper costs considerably more, and it tends to cost it slowly and in public. The instinct that prevents the second is built by experiencing the first, in a setting designed for it.
Three things follow, and they are worth saying plainly before Monday:

You will present findings that turn out to be wrong. Everybody does, including faculty when we run these labs ourselves. It is the design working, not a reflection on you.
Nobody is corrected in the moment. Tables present, the room listens, and the reveal comes afterwards — because being interrupted mid-sentence teaches embarrassment rather than method.
The tables that catch the defects are not the clever ones. They are the ones with the habit. The habit is the deliverable.

title: How this programme works
text:
4 · The failure logbook
Every table keeps a running log with three columns: what the assistant produced, what was wrong with it, and the question that caught it.
Two entries a day is typical, and it is a low enough bar that nobody has to strain for material. On Friday afternoon every table’s entries are consolidated, deduplicated and read aloud as a single page — the ways the copilot misled us this week — and then sent to the whole cohort.
It costs an hour of facilitation. It is also, reliably, the artefact people forward to their own teams in the week afterwards, and it is the most honest summary available of what the week was actually about.

title: How this programme works
section: Two more things that shape the week
text:
Two more things that shape the week

The daily one number
Every morning at 09:00, each person writes down one number they now believe about their business, with an interval around it. Ten minutes, no discussion.
Monday’s is sealed in an envelope. Friday’s is written next to it and the two are compared.
For most people the number itself moves only a little, and the interval gets wider. That looks at first like going backwards, and it is not. It is the week working: you now know more about what you do not know, which is the precondition for every good decision made with data. A confident point estimate that turns out to be wrong is a much more expensive object than a range you understood the shape of.


Two-speed labs
Every lab has a Core that everybody finishes and a Stretch for those who move faster, so that nobody is either stranded or idle.
The Stretch task is nearly always some version of “break another table’s result”. That is deliberate on two counts. It turns the strongest people in the room into a teaching resource rather than leaving them bored, and adversarial skill — finding the flaw in a plausible argument — is precisely the thing an assistant cannot supply for you.
A floor technologist handles setup problems throughout the week, so that faculty never have to stop teaching to debug somebody’s installation.

title: How this programme works
text:
What is expected of you


A one-page problem charter, submitted ten days before Monday. It becomes your capstone, so choose something you actually want an answer to.


The twenty-minute data-triage diagnostic. It is not a test — it is how we stream the labs and pair people well. Nobody sees anybody’s score.


Attendance at the setup clinic if your laptop is managed by your IT department. It is much easier to solve a fortnight out than on Sunday night.


Willingness to be on the keyboard. You will not learn this by watching, and the schedule does not really give you the option.


Willingness to take the Sceptic seat, which for many people turns out to be the harder half of the pairing.

title: How this programme works
text:
What is not expected
You do not need to be able to code. You do not need statistics beyond what you already carry. You do not need to have used an AI assistant before, and several people each cohort have not.
What you do need is a willingness to be wrong in front of other people. That is a different sort of demand from a technical one, and for a room of senior people it is usually the real one. It is also, in our experience, much easier here than it sounds now — everybody in the room has agreed to the same terms, and the week is arranged so that being wrong early is the cheapest thing you can do.

On the origins of this format
The structure of these materials — a page per session, a hex badge in the corner, all of it published openly rather than locked inside a learning platform — comes from the open teaching movement in academic statistics, and particularly from university data-skills teams who concluded that giving their courses away made those courses better. Publishing forces a kind of honesty into teaching material that private slides never quite acquire.
The pedagogy has been rebuilt for a very different room: people with profit-and-loss responsibility, an assistant that writes code faster than they can read it, and a Friday afternoon panel that does not care how elegant the model is.
What survives unchanged from the original is the conviction that materials should be free, complete and permanent. This site stays up after the cohort ends, and every version of it is public.

title: Glossary
text:
This page is written for somebody who has to use a term in a meeting on Thursday, not pass an exam on it in June. Each entry starts with the idea in plain language, then attaches the proper name to it, then says why it matters commercially and where in the week you will meet it. That order is deliberate: a term you understand but cannot name is hard to look up afterwards, and a term you can name but do not understand is worse than useless, because it gives an argument the sound of authority without the substance.
Where a term is routinely misused — and several of the most important ones are — the misuse is named alongside the definition, because recognising the wrong version in somebody else’s report is at least half of the value.
You are not expected to read this page in one sitting. It is here to be consulted during the week and afterwards, and the twelve terms that matter most are also printed on a single page of the participant guide.

title: Glossary
text:
A
A/B test — An experiment in which the units you care about, whether customers, sessions or branches, are assigned at random to a control condition and one or more treatments, and you then compare what happened. The randomisation is doing all the work here: it is what makes the groups comparable on the hundreds of things you never thought to measure, which is why an A/B test can support a causal claim that no amount of clever observational analysis can. Everything else about the test — the statistics, the dashboard, the significance threshold — is secondary to whether the assignment was genuinely random and stayed that way. You will design and interrogate one on Friday morning in 5.2.
AUC — Area under the ROC curve: a single number between 0 and 1 summarising how well a model ranks positive cases above negative ones. 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect. It is a genuinely useful diagnostic for the person building the model and a poor way to talk to a board, because nobody can convert it into money — which is why the programme asks you to report lift instead. Treat an unexpectedly high AUC as a bug report until you have proved otherwise; on Wednesday afternoon you will meet a model that scores beautifully for reasons you would not want to explain to a regulator.
Analytics engineer — The person who builds the tables everybody else trusts: the pipelines, the data models and the tests that sit between a raw system extract and something an analyst can reason about. It is a relatively new job title for work that has always existed, and it is usually the right first hire for an organisation whose analysts spend most of their week cleaning rather than analysing. Organisations more often hire a data scientist first, then discover that a well-paid modeller is doing plumbing. The choice comes up on Friday afternoon in 5.5.

title: Glossary
text:
B
Backtest — Testing a forecast against periods the model has never seen, repeatedly, by rolling the training cut-off forward through history and re-forecasting from each position. It is the only forecast evidence that means anything, because a model that has already seen the answer will reproduce it: in-sample fit measures memory rather than skill. Practically, a backtest is the difference between “our model fits the last three years well” and “our model would have been useful in each of the last three years”, and only the second is a claim a planner can act on. See 3.3.
Bimodal — A distribution with two distinct humps rather than a single central lump. Almost always it means two populations have been mixed together and handed to you as one: two products, two channels, two customer types, two periods, or the same measure taken before and after a definition changed. The commercial significance is that every summary statistic computed on a bimodal distribution describes a typical case that does not exist, which is why Wednesday morning’s 3.1 asks you to plot the shape before you compute the average.

title: Glossary
text:
C
Cardinality — How many rows on one side of a relationship match a row on the other: one-to-one, many-to-one, one-to-many. The phrase to hold on to is that a join is a claim about cardinality — when you join two tables you are asserting, usually without noticing, that each row on one side meets exactly one row on the other. A large share of analytical accidents are that unstated claim turning out to be false, and Tuesday afternoon’s 2.4 is built around watching one happen.
Causal claim — The assertion that changing X changes Y, as distinct from the observation that X and Y move together. Supporting one properly requires an experiment or a carefully argued quasi-experimental design, and the gap between what most business analysis can support and what most business language claims is wide. Watch the verbs, in your own writing as much as anyone else’s: drives, causes, improves, boosts and leads to are all causal claims wearing ordinary clothes. See 5.1.
Confounder — Something that causes both the thing you changed and the thing you measured, so that the two look related when neither is moving the other. Seasonal demand is the classic commercial example: it lifts marketing spend and conversions at the same time, and a naive comparison then credits the campaign with the season. Confounders you have thought of can sometimes be adjusted for; the reason randomisation is worth so much is that it handles the ones you have not.
Confidence interval — A range that would contain the true underlying parameter a stated proportion of the time if you repeated the whole procedure many times. It is a statement about a quantity you are estimating — a conversion rate, an average basket, a treatment effect — rather than about any single future observation.
Either way — see prediction interval — an 80% interval promises to be wrong one time in five, on purpose. That is not a defect to be engineered away. An interval that is never wrong is simply too wide to inform a decision, and the daily one-number exercise is designed to make that trade-off something you feel rather than something you are told.
Contribution (SHAP value) — A precise answer to the question “how much did this feature move this particular prediction away from the model’s baseline?”, derived from cooperative game theory. It is genuinely useful and genuinely well defined, and it is not a causal driver: a SHAP chart tells you how the model is reasoning, not how the world works. The practical test is that a “top drivers” chart which reorders itself when you swap the model algorithm is describing your model, and boardrooms routinely read it as describing the business. Friday morning is largely about that distinction.
Correlation — X and Y move together, and knowing one tells you something useful about the other. That is sufficient for prediction, targeting and segmentation, all of which are valuable, and it is insufficient for deciding to change X in the hope that Y follows. Much of the commercial value of Friday morning lies in being able to say which of the three claims — correlation, contribution or cause — your evidence actually supports, out loud, before somebody else says it for you.
CTE — Common table expression: the WITH step AS (...) construction in SQL, which lets a query be written as a sequence of named steps rather than as subqueries nested inside one another. The difference is not cosmetic. A query written as named steps can be read aloud, audited one stage at a time, and stopped halfway to check a row count; a deeply nested query can only be trusted or distrusted whole. Since an assistant will happily write either, asking for CTEs is one of the cheapest ways to keep generated code reviewable. See 2.1.

title: Glossary
text:
D
Data contract — A written set of conditions that data must satisfy, expressed as business rules that cannot be false — receipts follow orders, percentages sum to 100, a customer cannot churn twice in the same month — checked automatically, with a pass or fail result rather than a discussion. The shift it represents is from data quality as an occasional clean-up project to data quality as something a machine asserts every time the pipeline runs. It is also the point at which “please check the data” becomes an instruction somebody can actually carry out. See 2.5.
Dimension — A table of things that exist: customers, products, depots, suppliers, dates. Dimensions tend to be short and wide, carrying many descriptive attributes for relatively few rows, and they should have exactly one row per thing. That last property is an assumption rather than a guarantee, and it is worth verifying on any dimension table before you join it to anything, because a dimension with an unnoticed extra row will quietly change every total downstream of it.
Difference-in-differences — Comparing the change in a treated group with the change in an untreated group over the same period, so that anything affecting both groups equally cancels out. It is the workhorse of causal analysis when you cannot randomise, and it rests entirely on parallel trends: the assumption that, absent the intervention, the two groups would have moved together. That assumption is not testable directly, but the pre-period is, so plot it and show it. See 5.3.
Drift — What happens when the world moves away from the data a model was trained on. Feature drift means the inputs change; score drift means the outputs change; concept drift means the relationship between them changes, which is the dangerous one because the model carries on producing confident, plausible, wrong numbers. The commercial answer is unglamorous: monitor monthly, agree in advance what a drift signal triggers, and give the model a retirement date. Governance on Friday treats all three as operational rather than theoretical concerns.

title: Glossary
text:
F
Fact table — A table of things that happen: sales, orders, calls, payments, shipments. Facts tend to be long and thin — many rows, few columns — carrying dates, quantities and keys that point into the dimensions. Most of the numbers your organisation reports are sums over a fact table, which is why knowing its grain is the precondition for trusting any of them.
Fan-out — What happens when a join multiplies rows because the “one” side of a many-to-one relationship turns out to have more than one matching row, so that every row on the other side is duplicated. It is the most common source of silently wrong totals in commercial analysis, and it is silent precisely because nothing errors: the query runs, the chart draws, and the number is simply larger than it should be. The defence is a habit rather than a technique — count the rows before every join and after it, and expect the answer in advance. Tuesday afternoon is built on it.

title: Glossary
text:
G
GAID 2025 — The Nigeria Data Protection Commission’s General Application and Implementation Directive, issued under the NDPA on 20 March 2025 and effective from 19 September 2025. Where the Act sets the principles, the Directive supplies the operational detail an organisation actually has to comply with: registration, audit filing, data protection officer requirements, and the instruments permitting cross-border transfer — which matters more than it sounds when the assistant processing your customer data runs on somebody else’s infrastructure abroad. See 5.4.
Grain — What one row of a table represents, stated in a sentence: “one row per depot per SKU per week.” If you cannot say it, you cannot trust any total computed from the table, because you do not know what you are adding up. It is the single most useful question a non-technical executive can ask in a data conversation, it requires no technical knowledge whatsoever to ask, and it is the first of the Sceptic’s seven standing questions for exactly that reason.

title: Glossary
text:
H
Holdout — Data, or people, deliberately withheld from a model or an intervention so that performance can be measured against something rather than asserted. A retention-call holdout — 10% of the target list, deliberately not called — feels like leaving money on the table and is the only way to learn whether the calls are worth making at all. The general principle is that an intervention with no untreated comparison group cannot be evaluated, only defended, and the cost of the holdout is almost always smaller than the cost of running an ineffective programme for another two years.

title: Glossary
text:
I
Idempotent — A property of a process: running it twice produces the same result as running it once. A pipeline that is not idempotent — one that appends rather than replaces, or that depends on what happened to be in a folder that morning — will eventually give two different answers to the same question, and nobody will be able to say which is right. This is why Tuesday’s lab asks you to run your pipeline twice and prove the answers match, which sounds trivial until the first time it does not.

title: Glossary
text:
L
Leakage — A feature that encodes information which would not have been available at the moment you would actually have acted. It is the most dangerous failure in applied modelling because it announces itself as success rather than as an error: the model scores brilliantly, everyone is pleased, and the review that might have caught it is skipped because the numbers look so good. The test is a single question about time — would I have known this in time? — and it needs no mathematics at all. See 3.5.
Lift — How much better a model’s top-scored group is than a random group of the same size. It is the honest translation of model performance into something a commercial audience can act on, because it maps directly onto a campaign: three times the base rate in the top decile is a sentence a board understands and can budget against, whereas an AUC of 0.77 is a sentence that ends the conversation. Report lift, keep AUC for the model review.

title: Glossary
text:
M
MASE — Mean absolute scaled error: your forecast’s error divided by the error a one-step seasonal-naive rule makes in the training data. That in-sample denominator is the part most people get wrong, and it matters, because it is what makes the measure comparable across series of wildly different sizes. Below 1 means your out-of-sample error beats the naive rule’s in-sample error, which is a demanding bar and not quite the same claim as “we beat naive on the holdout”. It is preferred here to MAPE, which is undefined at zero, explodes near zero, and penalises over- and under-forecasting asymmetrically — three properties that make it actively misleading on the intermittent demand series most businesses actually have.
Model card — One page per model, written in plain language: what it is for, what it is not for, the training data, the features, what was excluded and why, performance overall and on the worst-performing segment, known limitations, where a human reviews it, how it is monitored, and the date it retires. The two lines nobody fills in are “Not for” and “Retire by”, which are also the two that would have prevented most of the model failures anybody can name. You will write one on Friday and leave with it.

title: Glossary
text:
N
NDPA 2023 — The Nigeria Data Protection Act, the statute governing personal data processing in Nigeria. In outline: you need a lawful basis before you process; a breach must be notified to the Commission within 72 hours of discovery, with a higher threshold before affected data subjects must be told; a DPIA is required where processing is likely to be high risk, with prior consultation if the DPIA confirms it; cross-border transfers are conditional; data subjects have rights including protection against solely automated decisions; and penalties reach ₦10m or 2% of gross revenue for data controllers of major importance. Friday’s governance session works through what each of those means for an analytics function rather than for a legal department.
DPIA — Data protection impact assessment: a structured, written assessment of the risk a piece of processing creates for the people in the data, required under NDPA s.28 wherever processing is likely to result in a high risk to rights and freedoms. Systematic profiling of individuals usually is. The distinction worth carrying away is that a model card is good practice you adopt because it makes you better at your job, whereas a DPIA may simply be the law.
Nominal vs real — Nominal is the number as recorded; real is the same number adjusted for inflation so that periods can be compared. In a high-inflation economy this is not a technicality, because every nominal series is a currency story wearing a growth story’s clothes, and a business can report handsome growth while shipping fewer units than last year. Ask “real or nominal?” first and “deflated by what?” second — the fourth of the Sceptic’s seven questions, and the one that most often changes a headline.

title: Glossary
text:
P
Parquet — A columnar file format that stores column types inside the file itself. It is smaller and faster than CSV, and — more importantly for anyone who has lost a morning to it — nothing downstream has to guess whether your account numbers are integers and helpfully strip the leading zeros. Tuesday’s session on the laptop warehouse uses it as the format you move data around in once it has left the spreadsheet.
Placebo test — Re-running a causal analysis at a date when nothing happened, or on units that were never treated, to see whether your method finds an effect anyway. It should find nothing. If it does find something, your design is picking up a pre-existing divergence rather than the intervention, and you have learned that before presenting rather than afterwards. It is four lines of code and disproportionately persuasive in front of a sceptical audience, which is a rare combination.
Prediction interval — A range expected to contain a future observation, as opposed to a parameter. It is always wider than a confidence interval computed on the same data, because it has to carry both the uncertainty in the estimate and the natural variability of the thing itself. Every “80% interval” in this programme’s forecasting sessions is a prediction interval. Confusing the two is not an academic error: it is how a planner ends up setting a safety-stock level from a range that describes the average week rather than next week.
Power — The probability that a test detects an effect of a given size, assuming that effect is real. It is computed before the experiment starts, because its purpose is to tell you how large a sample and how long a run you need for the result to be worth having. An underpowered test that finds nothing has not told you the treatment does not work; it has told you nothing at all, at the cost of a quarter.
Propensity model — A model that scores the probability of an event: this customer churning, this invoice going unpaid, this lead converting. The point the programme keeps returning to is that probability is only one of three things you need before you act. The others are the value at stake if it happens and whether your intervention actually changes the outcome — and a targeting list ranked on probability alone will faithfully send your best retention agents to the customers who were always going to leave.

title: Glossary
text:
R
RFM — Recency, frequency, monetary: a segmentation approach roughly fifty years old that takes one query, needs no machine learning, and is understood immediately by the marketer who has to act on it. It earns its place here as the benchmark a clustered segmentation has to beat before it is worth the complexity — and on Wednesday afternoon you will find that benchmarks of this kind are considerably harder to beat than they look.
Right-skewed — A distribution in which most values are small and a few are very large. Revenue, order size, account balance, tenure and lead time all behave this way, which means this is the normal condition of commercial data rather than an exception. The consequence is practical: the mean sits above the median and misdescribes the typical case, so a plan built on an average lead time or an average basket is quietly planning for a customer who does not exist.

title: Glossary
text:
S
Salted dataset — A dataset containing a deliberate defect, planted so that participants get burned in a classroom rather than in a board paper. The data room carries thirteen such defects, spread unevenly across the files, with several files left deliberately clean — which is the detail that makes the exercise work, because a room told everything is dirty will hunt until it finds something whether or not anything is there. Which file holds which defect is not published before Friday afternoon.
Sample ratio mismatch (SRM) — When the arms of an experiment are not the sizes the randomisation should have produced — a 50/50 split that arrives as 52/48 on a large sample, for instance. It indicates that the assignment mechanism is broken somewhere, and the uncomfortable consequence is that it invalidates the result and cannot be adjusted away: if the groups were not formed as designed, you no longer know what they are comparable on. It takes thirty seconds to check and belongs before you look at the result, every time, because checking afterwards is checking with a motive.
Star schema — One fact table surrounded by the dimension tables it points at, arranged so the diagram looks like a star. It makes semantic models fast, and — more importantly for a commercial audience — it makes measures consistent, because “revenue” is defined once at the centre rather than reinvented in each report. Monday afternoon’s 1.5 introduces it without the jargon.
Structural break — A permanent shift in the level of a time series: a new competitor, a price change, a policy, a lost customer. A forecasting model fitted straight across one will produce persistent error in a single direction, and an interval far too wide, because it is trying to average two different worlds. It is found by plotting the series and looking, which is a recurring theme of Wednesday: several of the week’s most expensive mistakes are visible to the naked eye and invisible to a summary table.
Survivorship bias — Analysing a population that is defined by having already succeeded, and drawing conclusions about how to succeed. “More sales touchpoints win more deals” is the standard commercial example, when touchpoints are only recorded for opportunities that were already qualified. The question that catches it is the sixth of the seven: what had to be true for a row to exist in this file?
Synthetic control — A weighted combination of untreated units, built so that it tracks the treated unit closely in the period before the intervention, and then used as the counterfactual afterwards. It is the tool for the awkward case where you have one treated unit — one market, one depot, one country — and no natural comparison. Placebo tests are how the inference is made credible, since there is no conventional standard error to lean on. See 5.3.

title: Glossary
text:
W
Window function — SQL that computes something per group without collapsing the rows away, written as OVER (PARTITION BY ...). It is how you get shares of total, ranks, running totals, moving averages and period-on-period changes — which, between them, are most of what a commercial dashboard actually displays. It is also the piece of SQL an assistant writes well and most people never learn to write themselves, which makes it a good example of the week’s broader argument: you need to be able to read it and check it, not to produce it from memory.


The seven questions, in one place

What is the grain of this table?
How many rows before the join, and how many after?
What period am I comparing to what period, and are they the same length?
Real or nominal — and if real, deflated by what?
Would I have known this at the moment I needed to act?
What had to be true for a row to exist in this file?
If this result is this good, what is wrong with it?

None of them requires you to write code, which is the point: they are questions about meaning rather than about syntax, and they travel back to your own desk unchanged. Together they catch most of what goes wrong in commercial analytics, and you will be asked them, and asked to ask them, every day of the week.

title: Faculty
text: A five-day programme is only as good as the people standing in the room, and this page says who they are — the academic director, the lab faculty who spend most of the week on the floor beside you, the external panel who hear the Friday defences, and the School that awards the certificate.

title: Faculty
text:
Academic Director

Prof. Bongo Adi
Prof. Bongo Adi holds a full-time faculty position in the Economics and Business Intelligence department of Lagos Business School, Pan-Atlantic University. He is a development economist, data scientist, PPP and project finance expert, and management consultant who has worked in infrastructure, economic development and policy for more than twenty years.
His work spans econometric modelling, monitoring and evaluation of large multi-country development programmes, survey design and execution, randomised controlled trials, propensity score matching, multi-sectoral computable general equilibrium modelling, macroeconomic forecasting, and SME development and finance. He has led multi-state randomised control experiments in health, evaluations of conditional cash transfer programmes in education, and market sounding and willingness-to-pay studies for infrastructure PPPs.
He holds a PhD in Regional Science and Development Economics and an MSc in Economic Development and Policy Management from the University of Tsukuba, Japan, under the Joint Japan/World Bank Graduate Scholarship. He completed postdoctoral training in data mining at the National Agricultural Research Centre in Japan and is a recipient of a Japan Society for the Promotion of Science fellowship. He has consulted for the World Bank on project design, preparation and appraisal.
His current research interests include electricity market design, public-private partnerships, and the political economy of mega projects. He is a regular economist and business analyst on Channels TV, CNBC Africa and CNN, and writes the bongonomics column in BusinessDay.

Why the Academic Director’s background matters for this particular programme
Friday morning — correlation, contribution and cause, experiments and quasi-experimental design — is the hardest content of the week, and it is the part most executive analytics programmes leave out. That is an understandable choice: it is demanding to teach, it resists being made to look impressive on a slide, and a room can be sent home perfectly happy without it.
It is taught here, and taught properly, because the person who designed the programme has run randomised controlled trials at national scale and knows from experience what a causal claim costs to make honestly. That is also why the session is candid about how rarely a business can meet that standard, and about what an honest weaker claim sounds like when it cannot.

title: Faculty
text:
Lab faculty and floor staff
Most of the week is spent with people working rather than listening, and a room that is working needs help close at hand. The programme therefore runs at a ratio of one helper for every eight participants, which means a team of people circulating throughout the day, sized to the cohort. Alongside them is a technologist whose only job is to unblock setup problems, so that a faculty member never has to stop teaching in order to debug somebody’s installation — and so that nobody has to sit quietly with a broken laptop while the session moves on without them.

To be confirmed for this cohort
Lab faculty are named cohort by cohort and confirmed once the cohort closes, because the mix is chosen to suit the people who have actually enrolled. This page is updated at that point rather than carrying a placeholder description in the meantime.
If you are considering the programme and would like to know who will be teaching the labs, please just ask — execedsales@lbs.edu.ng — and you will be told the names rather than a description.

title: Faculty
text:
The capstone panel
Three practitioners from outside the School hear the Friday afternoon defences: a CFO or finance director, an analytics or data leader, and a risk, audit or compliance officer. Between them they cover the three angles from which any real proposal gets attacked — is the money real, is the analysis sound, and can we defend this if it goes wrong.
They are recruited for each cohort. None of them is faculty, none of them has seen your work before, and none of them has any stake in being kind to you. That is the point, and it is also why participants consistently rate the questions they ask as one of the most useful parts of the week.

title: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative
text:
Most of what your organisation knows about its customers has never been in a database. It sits in call-centre notes, WhatsApp threads, branch survey free-text, app store reviews, and the things relationship managers write in the box at the bottom of the form because there was nowhere else to put them.
Until quite recently, reading all of that at scale was economically impossible, so organisations counted the star ratings and set the words aside. That constraint has now genuinely lifted, and the first half of today is about what to do with the material it releases — together with the discipline that has to come with it, because “the model said the sentiment was positive” is a claim that requires evidence rather than a finding you can put in a board paper.
The second half of the day turns outward. Everything you have built since Tuesday is only worth what somebody does with it, and getting an answer out of your own head and into a form that changes a decision on Monday is a distinct skill from producing the answer. Today you practise it twice: once as a dashboard designed backwards from a decision, and once as a two-page brief that regenerates itself when the underlying data moves.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative
text:
What today is really arguing
One. Text is data, and treating it as such is now routine rather than exotic. Five thousand reviews become five themes with volumes attached to them, and a theme with a volume attached has stopped being an anecdote and started being a business case somebody can fund. → 4.1
Two. An LLM classifier is a measurement instrument, and every measurement instrument has to be calibrated against something you trust more than the instrument. Until you have hand-labelled a couple of hundred rows and compared, you do not know your error rate — and “it looked right on the ones I read” is not an error rate, however many you read. → 4.2
Three. A dashboard built to answer “how are we doing?” is a data dump with good typography. A dashboard is finished when you can name the decision it exists to support, the person who makes it, and what they do differently in each state the screen can be in. → 4.3
Four. The report, the deck, the dashboard and the appendix ought to be four outputs of a single source. When they are assembled separately they begin to disagree almost immediately, and the disagreement is always discovered by the one person you did not want to find it. → 4.4

The question to hold all day
customer_reviews.csv will give you a mean rating and a detractor share in about four seconds, and both figures will be arithmetically correct. That is the difficulty with them: nothing about a correct calculation tells you whether the rows underneath it are the rows you think they are.
So before you build anything on top of those numbers, ask the question the whole day turns on: who is in this extract, and who is not? Every extract is a query somebody ran at some point, on a system you cannot see, and that query had a WHERE clause in it. Sometimes the clause is harmless. Sometimes it quietly removes exactly the population whose absence would change your conclusion, and nobody involved intended any harm — the person who ran it was answering a different question that week.
The discipline is short enough to remember under pressure: ask for the extraction query, not the extract. People are almost always happy to send it, and the ten minutes it takes to read is the cheapest insurance in analytics.

title: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative
text:
What you leave today with
By this evening the analysis is finished and what remains is the argument. These four artefacts are what you will actually stand behind on Friday afternoon.

Artefacts on the wall board by 17:00

Five themes with volumes and trend, from free text you have never read in full.
A validation table for your classifier: 200 hand-labelled rows, agreement rate, and the two categories it confuses.
A decision dashboard, one screen, with the decision written at the top of it.
A two-page brief that regenerates itself when the data updates, with the number, the interval, the assumption and the ask.



The Sceptic’s brief for today

What filter was on this extract? Ask it of every dataset that arrives today, your own included — the files you produced yourself are the ones you are least likely to interrogate.
What is the error rate of this classifier, and on which categories? A classifier can be 90% accurate overall and hopeless on the one category the decision depends on, so ask for the breakdown rather than the headline.
What decision does this dashboard support, and what does its user do differently when the number goes red? If your partner cannot answer both halves in a sentence, what has been built is a data dump — which is a common and entirely fixable place to be at four o’clock on a Thursday.

title: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust
text:
Yesterday you wrote down a decision worth improving and put a value on improving it. Today the question becomes whether the numbers underneath that decision can be trusted, and it is the day the room stops taking them on faith.
You will work with SQL — or more precisely, an assistant will write SQL and you will read it, argue with it, and correct it. That is the skill this week is really teaching, and it is a different and much more portable skill than writing queries from memory. By the afternoon you will have built a pipeline that runs from raw files to a single tested, analysis-ready table, and you will run it twice to prove it gives the same answer both times, which sounds like a formality and is one of the more revealing things you will do all week.
Somewhere between eleven o’clock and lunch, in most cohorts, a table presents a finding with real conviction that turns out to be an artefact of a join rather than a fact about the business. That is a designed feature of the day rather than an accident of it. The exercises are built so that this kind of mistake happens here, cheaply, among peers who are about to make one of their own, because the instinct that catches it later is built by living through it once rather than by being warned about it.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust
text:
What today is really arguing
One. SQL is the lingua franca of every data platform your organisation is ever likely to buy, from the warehouse to the BI tool to whatever replaces them. What has changed is that reading it is now enough: you no longer have to compose a query from a blank page to be useful in a conversation about one. → 2.1
Two. The kind of query that used to require a data warehouse project now runs on the laptop in front of you, offline and for nothing. That sounds like a technical detail and is really a political one, because it changes what a senior person can verify personally rather than request and wait for — and a number somebody can check themselves is discussed differently. → 2.2
Three. A join is a claim about cardinality: an assertion, usually unspoken, about how many rows on one side match a row on the other. Most analytical disasters are not statistical failures at all. They are a join, a grain, a definition or a calendar, and all four are within reach of a non-technical reader who knows to ask. → 2.4
Four. Data quality is not a clean-up exercise that finishes. It is a set of business rules that cannot be false, written down once and checked automatically every time the pipeline runs — which turns “please check the data” into something a person can actually be asked to do. → 2.5

title: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust
text:
The capstone checkpoint
By 16:45 today your capstone pipeline should run end to end, even if what comes out of the far end is almost trivially simple. The reason for setting the bar there rather than higher is that everything later in the week sits on top of this: a pipeline that produces one correct row on Tuesday is worth considerably more than a sophisticated model on Thursday that nobody, including its author, can reproduce on Friday morning. Get the plumbing working while there is still time to fix it, and the rest of the week has somewhere to go.

title: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust
text:
What you leave today with
The artefacts below are the raw material for the rest of the week, and the third one in particular is worth reading twice before the lab starts.

Artefacts on the wall board by 17:00

A query you can read aloud and explain to somebody who has never seen SQL.
A pipeline script that goes from the raw files to one analysis-ready table.
A data quality report with at least five rules, and a written record of at least two failures you found on the raw table and fixed — because a suite that passed on its first run against untouched data has not been written honestly. The gate at the end of your pipeline should pass; the first version of it should not have.
The grain statement for every table you touched, in one sentence each.



The Sceptic’s brief for today
Two questions, asked every time, before any number leaves your table:

What is the grain of this table? One sentence, said out loud. If your partner cannot produce it, the number is not ready to leave — not because they have done anything wrong, but because neither of you yet knows what is being added up.
How many rows before the join, and how many after? Predict the answer first, then look. If the two figures differ and nobody expected them to, stop there and find out why before going any further; the explanation is usually quick and always worth having.

Roles swap from yesterday, so if you were on the keyboard on Monday you are the Sceptic today. Most people find this the harder of the two seats, which is a useful thing to discover on a Tuesday rather than in a board meeting.

title: The data room
text: This is the material you will work with all week. It is worth a few minutes before Monday, partly so that the files are familiar when a session starts, and partly because how this data room was built is itself one of the arguments the programme makes.

title: The data room
text:
The files

The workhorse — FMCG distribution
Three files that fit together: a large fact table of what was sold, and two smaller reference tables describing the products and the depots. This is the shape most commercial data arrives in, and it is used on all five days.


File


fmcg_sell_out.csv — 55,474 rows


Grain


One row per depot per SKU per week


Period


1 Jan 2024 – 30 Mar 2026


Story


A consumer goods distributor: 40 SKUs across 12 depots, Lagos to Kano. Sell-out units, realised price, promotion flags, stockouts, revenue in naira.


Used in


All five days. It is the file you will know best by Friday.




File


fmcg_products.csv — 40 rows


Grain


One row per SKU


Contains


Category, pack size, unit cost, list price, launch week




File


fmcg_depots.csv — 13 rows


Grain

Contains


Name, region, state, opening date




Financial services


File


bank_customers.csv — 12,000 rows


Grain

Story


A retail bank’s customer base with a 90-day churn outcome (10.6%). Tenure, segment, balance, digital engagement, transactions, complaints, salary domiciliation, NPS.


Used in


1.2 · 3.1 · 3.4 · 3.5 · 5.1


The “no history” note is worth pausing on, because it constrains what can honestly be asked of this file. A snapshot tells you what is true now; it cannot tell you what changed, which is a different question and a more common one.
