5.2




Macroeconomic context


File


ng_macro_monthly.csv — 90 rows


Grain


One row per month, Jan 2019 – Jun 2026


Contains


Headline and food inflation, USD/NGN, policy rate, composite PMI, Brent


Why it is here


To deflate nominal series. It is the difference between “we grew 43%” and what actually happened, and it is the fastest credibility win available in a Nigerian board room.


Read this


These are not the real figures. The series are modelled to behave like Nigeria’s — the right order of magnitude, the same broad turning points, the June 2023 float step — but every number is synthetic. Use it to learn the arithmetic; never quote it as a fact about the Nigerian economy. For the real series, go to the NBS CPI release and the CBN statistics portal.




The two workbooks, and the reference build
The next two files are spreadsheets rather than CSVs, and they are here because that is how a great deal of management information genuinely arrives: laid out for a human reader rather than for a machine, with the meaning carried partly by the formatting. Reading them is a skill in itself, and Tuesday spends a session on it.


File


board_pack.xlsx — 3 sheets, 480 rows


Story


A month-end board pack as it actually arrives: three sheets, two title rows above the header on each, a currency column stored as text.


Used in


2.2 · 2.3




File


regional_report.xlsx — 12 data rows


Story


A report laid out for reading rather than computing: title rows, a draft warning, merged region cells, months across the top, a total row in the middle, currency as text.


Used in


2.3




File


customer_reviews_labelled.csv — 4,938 rows


Grain


One row per review, joining to customer_reviews.csv on review_id


Story


The same corpus with theme, sentiment and intent already attached. Classifying five thousand reviews live, across a room full of laptops, on conference wifi, is not a thing that works — so 4.2 uses these cached labels for the volume analysis and has you hand-label a sample blind to check them.


Used in


4.2




File


outputs/fmcg_weekly.csv — 55,260 rows (also .parquet)


What it is


Not raw data. This is the reference build: the sell-out file deduplicated to its true grain, nulls resolved, joined to the depot and product dimensions — in other words, the output Tuesday’s lab produces.


Why it ships


So that a pipeline which did not finish on Tuesday does not cost you Wednesday. Point the day’s code at this file and carry on; fix your own pipeline in the evening. Nobody is marked down for it.


Used in


3.2 · 3.3 · 4.4 · 4.6 · 5.3


That last file deserves a word, because participants sometimes feel they ought not to use it. Please do. Tuesday’s lab is genuinely difficult, and a week in which one bad afternoon costs you the following three days would be a badly designed week. Using the reference build on Wednesday morning and repairing your own pipeline that evening is a perfectly respectable route through, and it is the route several people take every cohort.

title: The data room
section: What “today” is in this data room
text:
What “today” is in this data room
There are three different cut-off dates in this data room, on purpose, and it is worth saying so before somebody assumes it is a mistake.








File
Last date
Why




fmcg_sell_out.csv
30 Mar 2026
Q2 2026 is held back so that Wednesday’s forecast market is a real forecast rather than a lookup


customer_reviews.csv
24 Jun 2026
No holdout is needed; Thursday scores its classifier against a hand-labelled sample, not against the future


ng_macro_monthly.csv
Jun 2026
Deflators have to extend past the series they deflate, or the last quarter has nothing to divide by



Treat “today” as the end of March 2026 whenever you are working the FMCG case. The other two files run ahead of it because the exercises they serve are not time-travel exercises and do not need a holdout.
Real data rooms look exactly like this — different source systems with different cut-offs, none of them aligned to each other, and nobody who owns the whole picture. Which is why “what is the as-at date of this table, and does it match the one sitting next to it?” belongs in the four questions, and why a mismatch between two dates is one of the most common ways a comparison quietly stops meaning what it appears to mean.

title: The data room
text:
Getting them
Cloning the repository is the quickest route, and it brings the session material with it:
git clone https://github.com/bongoadi/turning-data-into-business-growth.git
cd turning-data-into-business-growth
duckdb -c "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv'"
If the row count that prints matches the figure listed for that file above, everything has arrived intact. Alternatively, download individual files from the links in the sections above — each file name is a direct download.

title: The data room
text:
Rebuilding them
Every file in this room is generated by one script, and you are welcome to run it:
python3 build/make_data.py
It needs numpy, pandas and openpyxl. The seed is 20261012.
Please leave the seed alone unless you are prepared to do the other three steps. Every number quoted anywhere in this course is computed from it, so changing it moves every planted defect and quietly falsifies several hundred figures across the session pages, the decks and the participant guide. This is not a warning about fragility so much as an example of the thing the programme keeps arguing: a reproducible artefact is only reproducible if you respect what it depends on. The full regenerate-and-reconcile workflow — including an honest account of the hour of manual checking it costs — is in data/README.md.

title: The data room
text:
The four questions
Before you compute anything from any of these files — or, for that matter, from any file that lands on your desk for the rest of your career:

Ten seconds, every dataset

What is the grain? One row per what?
What period am I comparing to what period, and are they the same length?
What is missing, and is missing the same as zero?
Real or nominal — and if real, deflated by what?

Four questions. They catch four of the thirteen defects planted here, and rather more than four in your own data, which is the real point of them. Run all four on every file, including the ones that turn out to be clean. Discovering that a file is clean is a genuine result, and the only way to get it is to have checked.

title: The data room
text:
For facilitators
Two documents live in the facilitator/ directory of the repository, and neither is linked from anywhere on this site:

the salt key — every defect, the proof query, the day it bites, the executive lesson underneath, and how to run the reveal;
the gallery solutions — the trap behind each of the twelve gallery briefs.

Please do not publish either to a cohort before Friday. Half the value of the week is the moment a table finds one of these on its own, in front of the room, and a defect that has been announced in advance teaches nothing — the participant never has to develop the instinct that would have found it.

title: After Friday — 30 / 60 / 90
text:
Most executive programmes end on Friday afternoon. Everyone returns to an inbox that has been filling up for five days, the charter goes into a drawer for a fortnight that becomes a quarter, and six months later the honest summary is that it was a good week. This is not a failure of will on anybody’s part; it is what happens when a piece of work has no next date attached to it.
Three commitments are built into the programme to prevent that, and between them they are the reason its value tends to be realised in December rather than in October. They are also deliberately modest in size — ninety minutes, forty-five minutes, and half a day — because commitments that require a clear diary do not survive one.

title: After Friday — 30 / 60 / 90
text:
Day 30 — the clinic
Live, online, 90 minutes. Wednesday 11 November 2026.
This is a clinic rather than a webinar, which means there is no presentation. You bring whatever is stuck, and we work on it together with the rest of the cohort listening in — which is useful in itself, because the problem blocking you is very often the one blocking three other people who had not yet worked out how to describe it.


Bring your pipeline, in whatever state it is in.


Bring the specific error message, the specific query, the specific blocked access request.


Bring the conversation with the person whose judgement your initiative displaces, if it has happened.


Three problems turn up reliably at Day 30, in roughly this order, and it is worth knowing in advance that they are normal rather than a sign that anything has gone wrong:

The data access that was promised and has not arrived. Almost always resolved by asking a different person for a smaller thing, and the clinic is a good place to work out which person and which smaller thing.
The pipeline that ran in the classroom and does not run at the office. Almost always an absolute path, a package that was installed interactively and never recorded, or a corporate proxy. All three are quick to fix once somebody has seen the error message.
The decision-maker who has not changed what they do. This is the substantial one, it is rarely about the analysis, and it is what the clinic is really for.

title: After Friday — 30 / 60 / 90
text:
Day 60 — the structured peer call
Forty-five minutes, with the peer you were assigned on Friday. Week of 14 December 2026.
This one has an agenda, and the agenda is the point. Peer calls arranged without one are scheduled with genuine enthusiasm in October and quietly abandoned by November, so this is a structured forty-five minutes with four questions and a clear division of time.

The Day 60 agenda
Ten minutes each, then twenty-five minutes on whichever of you is more stuck.

What is the number now, and what is the interval around it?
What did you say you would do in the first fortnight, and did you?
What is the single thing blocking you?
What would you need from the other person to unblock it — a contact, a review, a piece of code, or somebody senior to say the same thing you have been saying?

The fourth question is the one that produces most of the value. A peer from a different sector carries no history with your organisation and no stake in its internal politics, which means they can sometimes make an introduction, or say the thing you have been saying, in a way that lands differently. It costs them very little and it is frequently decisive.

title: After Friday — 30 / 60 / 90
text:
Day 90 — the cohort reconvenes
Half a day, on campus and online. Thursday 14 January 2027.
Everybody shows the number that moved — and, more importantly, explains how they know it moved because of what they did rather than because of everything else that happened in the same quarter.
Eight minutes each, against the same rubric as the Friday defence with one addition: the evidence standard is now enforced. In October, “we will compare before and after” was a perfectly acceptable plan. In January it is a finding, and the panel will ask what else changed over the same period — which is exactly the question Friday morning prepared you for.
The part of the session everybody remembers is not the successes. It is the twenty minutes at the end on what did not work, which is where the honest learning sits and which almost nobody schedules into a review of their own accord. It is protected time here for that reason.

title: After Friday — 30 / 60 / 90
text:
The Certificate of Implementation
Issued at Day 90 to participants who show the number that moved with evidence.

What it requires, and what remains open
The standard is: a number, a comparison, a statement of the design that produced the comparison, and an honest account of the alternative explanations you can and cannot rule out.
“Availability went from 96.4% to 97.6% at the three pilot depots, against 96.3% to 96.5% at the eight comparison depots over the same period. Difference-in-differences estimate 1.0 points, interval 0.3 to 1.7. I cannot rule out that the pilot depots got more attention because they were the pilot.”
That last sentence is why the certificate means something. Anybody can show a number that went up. Naming the alternative explanation you cannot rule out is the part that requires both the method and the confidence to say it out loud, and it is the habit the whole programme is trying to build.
Whether self-report is sufficient, and who verifies it, is an academic governance decision for the School rather than for the faculty running the week. The current standard is confirmed with each cohort at the Day 30 clinic.

title: After Friday — 30 / 60 / 90
text:
What stays available to you
Nothing here expires when the cohort does, and everything below is yours to use inside your own organisation.
This site. Permanently, and it is versioned in the open, so you can see what changed between cohorts. If a session is updated because something in the toolchain moved, you can read the diff.
The datasets. Yours to reuse for internal training. They are synthetic, so there is nothing to clear.
The failure logbook. Your cohort’s consolidated one-page list of the ways the copilot misled the room. It is the most forwarded artefact of the week, and it is licensed for you to send to your own team.
The repository. Fork it. Several alumni have adapted the labs for internal sessions inside their own organisations, which is explicitly encouraged by the licence — materials CC BY-NC-SA, code MIT.

The one thing to do in the first fortnight
The temptation, in the first fortnight, is to improve the model or to smarten up the dashboard. Both are more enjoyable than the following, and neither is the right first move.
Run the pipeline at your desk, on your own machine, on real data, once.
Whatever breaks when you do that is the actual gap between the classroom and your organisation, and finding it in week one is worth considerably more than any further analysis. Everything else in the 90-day plan sits on top of it, and — unlike almost anything else you might attempt — it is a milestone that requires nobody’s permission and nobody else’s calendar.


Questions: execedsales@lbs.edu.ng · +234 (0) 802 501 4624

title: Capstone brief and rubric
text:
The brief
Take one real decision in your own organisation, and leave the week with a defensible answer to it.
Not a demonstration of technique, and not a tour of everything you learned. A decision, with evidence behind it, that you would be willing to act on yourself and that somebody more senior could act on without having to redo your work.
Choosing well matters more than it might seem. A modest decision that somebody genuinely makes on a regular cadence will carry you further through this week than an ambitious one that nobody owns — and it will produce something you can actually use in November.

title: Capstone brief and rubric
text:
Seven deliverables
The deliverables are spread across the week rather than saved for the end, so that each day produces something concrete and Friday is an assembly rather than a scramble.


Problem charter. One page. Submitted ten days before Monday, revised on Monday afternoon in Lab 1. The decision, the number, the value, the data, the evidence standard, the person whose judgement it displaces, and the 90-day plan.


Pipeline. Raw files to one tested, analysis-ready table. Runs from a terminal on a clean machine. Passes its own data quality contract. Due Tuesday 16:45.


Analysis. A forecast, a segmentation, a propensity model, a text analysis, or an experiment design — whichever your decision actually needs. With uncertainty quantified and a naive benchmark reported. Due Wednesday 16:45.


Dashboard. One screen, built backwards from the decision, with the decision written on it and a data quality badge. Due Thursday 16:45.


Two-page brief. Generated from the pipeline. Every number inline code, nothing typed. Due Thursday 16:45.


Model card and lawful basis. One page. Due Friday 14:30.


The defence. Individual, not by table. Five minutes, four minutes of questions, Friday from 15:30.

title: Capstone brief and rubric
text:
The rubric









Dimension
Weight
High mark
Low mark




Business impact
40%
A named recurring decision, a named decision-maker, a value hypothesis with a range and three ranked assumptions, and an honest statement of what happens if the assumptions are wrong
“This gives the business visibility.” No owner, no cadence, no alternative action, a point estimate with no range


Analytical rigour
30%
Grain stated for every table. Defects found and handled. Leakage checked feature by feature. Uncertainty quantified. Evidence standard matched to the claim. Naive benchmark reported
Numbers with no provenance. A model with no benchmark. A causal verb with correlational evidence


Communication
20%
Number and action in the first sentence. Interval with its driving assumption named. One chart that makes the case. Survives interruption
Background for three paragraphs. Four charts, none decisive. “We recommend continued monitoring”


Feasibility and governance
10%
90-day plan whose first milestone needs nobody’s permission. Lawful basis identified. Model card written. The displaced person named and a plan for them
A roadmap requiring a platform purchase. No lawful basis. Nobody loses, apparently




The weighting is the message
A capstone cannot pass on rigour alone.
A technically immaculate analysis of a decision that nobody actually makes scores 30 out of 100 against this rubric. That is deliberate rather than harsh, and it is roughly the distribution of value in the world outside this room — impeccable work aimed at the wrong question is one of the more expensive things an analytics function can produce, precisely because it is so hard to criticise.
The reverse holds just as firmly. A compelling business case built on a number that does not survive a grain check scores 40. The panel will find the grain problem, because one of the three panellists is an analytics leader and it is the first thing they look for.
The weighting is not an argument that rigour matters less. It is an argument that the two have to arrive together, and that most rooms are much better at supplying one than the other.

title: Capstone brief and rubric
text:
The daily checkpoints
These exist for one reason: so that nobody arrives at Friday morning with nothing. Each one is small enough to hit on a difficult day.









By
Checkpoint




Monday
17:00
Charter on the wall board, attacked by your Sceptic, three written objections left on other people’s


Tuesday
16:45
The pipeline runs. End to end, from a terminal. Even if the output is trivial.


Wednesday
16:45
The model scores. With an interval, and a leakage check on every feature.


Thursday
16:45
The dashboard and the memo exist, both generated from the pipeline.


Friday
14:30
Model card and lawful basis — then straight into the rehearsal against a hostile reviewer from another table.


Friday
15:30
Defence.



Tuesday’s is the one people underestimate, so it is worth being explicit: a pipeline that produces one correct row on Tuesday afternoon is worth considerably more than a beautiful model on Thursday that nobody, including you, can reproduce. Get something running, however small, and improve it from there.

title: Capstone brief and rubric
text:
The defence is individual
Everybody presents. Not one person per table, not a nominated spokesperson — you.
From 15:30 the cohort splits into three parallel rooms, each with one external panellist and one faculty member. Each room hears its share of the defences: five minutes to present, four minutes of questions, nine minutes a person, ninety minutes a room. The cohort reconvenes at 17:00 and the week ends at 17:30 — half an hour later than Monday to Thursday, which is worth knowing before you book a flight.
Splitting the room is what makes an individual defence arithmetically possible at all. It costs you the experience of hearing the other defences, and buys you the experience of having given one yourself, which is the half that transfers. Standing up and being questioned about your own numbers is a different kind of learning from watching somebody else do it, and it is the reason the week ends this way.

title: Capstone brief and rubric
text:
The panel
Three external people, none of them faculty and none of them from this school: a CFO or finance director, an analytics or data leader, and a risk, audit or compliance officer — one in each room, rotating between rooms is not attempted.
They will have read your two-page brief in advance, and they do not want slides. What they want is the number, the action, and an honest account of how much weight it will bear.

The five questions, published in advance

“What is the grain of this table?”
“Would you have known this at the time you needed to act?”
“Is that real or nominal?”
“How would you know if you were wrong?”
“Who loses if this works?”

And a sixth, which is specific to this programme:

“Which of these numbers did the assistant produce, and which did you check?”

They are published because knowing them changes how you work all week, which is the entire point of publishing them. Knowing a question in advance does not soften it — try answering the fourth one honestly on Monday, and you will find it is still there on Friday.

title: Capstone brief and rubric
text:
The charter template
Copy this. One page, due ten days before Monday. Draft it in whatever form suits you; the headings are what matter.

Use-case charter
1 · The decision. Which recurring decision does this change? Who makes it? How often? What are their current options?
2 · The number. Which node on your KPI tree moves? Its exact definition, in a sentence that survives cross-examination. Where it sits today.
3 · The value. One line of arithmetic: volume × rate × improvement × unit economics. Three assumptions, ranked by leverage. A range, not a point.
4 · The data. Three tables. Their grain. Do they have history. Who owns access. The single thing most likely to be wrong with them.
5 · The evidence standard. How will you know afterwards whether it worked? Control group, holdout, comparison, or nothing. “Nothing” is an acceptable answer on Monday and an unacceptable one on Friday.
6 · The person whose judgement this displaces. Name them. What will they say? What would make them an ally?
7 · The 90-day plan. Three milestones. The first is within a fortnight and needs nobody’s permission.

If a field is hard to fill in, leave it blank rather than filling it with something plausible. A charter with two honest gaps is a much better starting point on Monday morning than one that reads smoothly and papers over the parts nobody has worked out yet — and Lab 1 exists precisely to work on those gaps.

title: Capstone brief and rubric
text:
Certification
Certificate of Completion — issued Friday afternoon to participants who meet the rubric threshold at the defence.
Certificate of Implementation — issued at Day 90, to participants who reconvene and show the number that moved, together with the evidence that it moved because of what they did.

A note on the second certificate
The two-tier credential turns the Day 90 session from a well-intentioned nice-to-have into something people actually attend, and it is a genuine differentiator for the programme.
It is also an academic governance matter rather than a marketing one. The verification standard — who confirms that the number moved, and whether self-report is sufficient — is set by the School rather than by the faculty running the week. The current standard is confirmed with each cohort at the Day 30 clinic, so you will know where you stand well before it matters.

title: Capstone brief and rubric
section: Working with your own data — or not
text:
Working with your own data — or not
Every deliverable on this page can be completed against the course datasets, and a meaningful minority of each cohort chooses to do exactly that. It is not a lesser path. The planted defects are the teaching material, and your own data, whatever its merits, does not have its problems arranged nearly so conveniently for a week of practice.
If you do use your own data, please read 5.4 before Monday rather than after, and prefer shape over content wherever the analysis allows it — column names, types, row counts and grain will carry you through most of the week without carrying any risk.

title: Day 1 — Strategy, value, and what AI actually changed
text:
Nobody opens a laptop today, and that is on purpose. The most expensive analytics failures do not happen in the code — they happen weeks earlier, when a capable team is pointed at a question that was well worth answering and that nobody was ever going to act on. The work that follows is excellent, the dashboard is admired, and nothing changes. Monday exists to make that outcome less likely for the project you are about to spend the week building.
So today is about framing: where analytics value actually comes from, how a P&L number decomposes into things somebody can change, how to put a defensible figure on a benefit before you have built anything, and what the arrival of capable AI assistants has genuinely altered about the division of labour between you and your analysts.
By five o’clock you will have written the problem you are here to solve as a use-case charter — the business decision it changes, the number that would have to move, what that movement is worth, the data it would take, and the person who would have to behave differently for any of it to count. The charter goes on the wall board and stays there all week; it is also your capstone, and everything from Tuesday to Friday is machinery built in service of it. Choosing something you genuinely care about is therefore worth a few minutes of thought this morning.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Day 1 — Strategy, value, and what AI actually changed
text:
What today is really arguing
Three claims run through the day. Each is put to the room as something to be tested rather than accepted, and by the afternoon you should be able to say whether you believe it of your own organisation.
One. Analytics creates commercial value in four distinguishable ways — improving recurring decisions, shortening cycle times, creating new revenue, and providing visibility. Most organisations invest heavily in the fourth while the first remains largely untouched, and the four-way split gives you a straightforward way to audit your own portfolio. → 1.1
Two. A KPI that nobody owns, or that two departments define differently, does not function as a KPI at all. It generates meetings in which the first twenty minutes are spent reconciling two versions of the same number. Writing the definition down, precisely enough that it survives cross-examination, is unglamorous work that pays for itself quickly. → 1.2
Three. AI did not make analysts obsolete. It made typing cheap, which moved the bottleneck along to judgement — deciding what is worth asking, and noticing when a fluent answer is answering the wrong question. That is now the binding constraint on most analytics functions, and it is a constraint that hiring more engineers does not relieve. → 1.4
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Day 1 — Strategy, value, and what AI actually changed
text:
What you leave today with
Four things, all of them made by you during the day rather than handed over at the end of it, and all four visible on the wall board where the rest of the cohort can read them.

Artefacts on the wall board by 17:00

A use-case charter, one page, signed by you and challenged by one other person.
A KPI tree for your business unit, with the definition of the top node written out in a sentence a lawyer could not wriggle out of.
A value hypothesis with its three most fragile assumptions circled.
One entry in the failure logbook.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Day 1 — Strategy, value, and what AI actually changed
text:
Reading, if you want it
None of this is required, and the day works perfectly well without it. These are the three sources people most often ask for afterwards, so they are listed here rather than in a bibliography nobody opens.


Davenport & Harris, Competing on Analytics — still the clearest statement of why analytics is an organisational capability rather than a technology purchase.
McKinsey, Breaking away: the secrets to scaling analytics — on why the gap between leaders and the rest widens rather than closes.
HBR’s 10 Must Reads on Data Strategy — read the pieces on defensive versus offensive data strategy before Tuesday.



The Sceptic’s brief for today
You are working in pairs from this morning onwards, and the roles swap each day. Whoever is not on the keyboard has a single job today: for every charter, KPI tree and value hypothesis produced at your table, find the assumption that would make the whole thing worthless if it turned out to be wrong — and say it out loud while there is still time to do something about it, rather than after the artefact has gone up on the wall and defending it has become a matter of pride.
This can feel unkind the first few times, and it is worth being clear that it is not. Every charter on that wall has a fragile assumption in it somewhere, including the ones written by faculty, because that is what a charter is: an argument built on things you do not yet know. Naming the weakest of them is a service to the person who wrote it, and it is precisely the work an assistant cannot do for you — it will happily improve an idea, and it will not tell you that the idea rests on something that is not true.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Day 3 — Seeing, forecasting, segmenting
text:
Tuesday left you with a table you have reason to trust. Wednesday is what you do with it, and it is both the densest day of the week and the one most likely to produce a result that is impressive and wrong at the same time — which is exactly why it sits in the middle, with two more days left to absorb what it teaches.
Four things happen today. You look at data properly, meaning at the thing itself rather than at a summary of it, which is a discipline more than a technique and one that most analytical work skips. You build a forecast and put an honest interval around it, and then defend the width of that interval to a room. You cut a customer base into segments that a marketer could actually run a campaign against, as opposed to segments that are statistically tidy and commercially inert. And you build a churn model that scores 0.98, and then work out why a number that good should worry you rather than please you.
That last discovery is the pivot of the week. Nothing in the tooling will flag it, the model will not complain, and the assistant will congratulate you — so the only thing standing between a beautiful result and an expensive one is a question somebody in the room thinks to ask.

title: Day 3 — Seeing, forecasting, segmenting
text:
What today is really arguing
One. Exploratory data analysis is not a warm-up lap before the real work begins. It is the work, and the question driving it is not “what is the average?” but “what is odd here?” — a question that has the useful property of being answerable by anyone willing to look at a distribution rather than a total. → 3.1
Two. A chart is an argument, and like any argument it can be lost on delivery. Most business charts lose theirs by showing a quantity when the audience needed a comparison, or a single point when the audience needed a range — and the fix is usually to decide what the chart is claiming before choosing what it draws. → 3.2
Three. A forecast without an interval is not really a forecast; it is a hope with a decimal place. And a forecast fitted straight across a structural break will be confidently wrong in one direction for as long as anybody keeps using it, which is why part of this session is spent looking for breaks rather than modelling through them. → 3.3
Four. Model quality that arrives suspiciously easily is the strongest evidence available that something has leaked into the features which would not have been known at the moment of acting. The check costs one question per column and no mathematics. → 3.5

title: Day 3 — Seeing, forecasting, segmenting
text:
The day



09:00


The daily one number, and the logbook




09:15


3.1 What is odd here? — distributions, missingness, the partial year, and the discipline of looking before summarising




10:15


Coffee




10:45


3.2 Charts that survive a board room — the grammar of graphics, and banning the bar chart that hides its own distribution




11:45


3.3 Forecasting with intervals — seasonality, trend, breaks, backtesting, and what an 80% interval actually promises




12:45


Lunch




13:45


3.4 Segmentation you can act on — RFM, k-means, and the translation from cluster to persona to campaign




14:45


3.5 Propensity and the leak — churn scoring, lift, thresholds, and the AUC that was too good




15:30


Break




15:45


Lab 3 · The forecast market — tables post quarter-ahead forecasts with intervals, everyone bets, the holdout is revealed live




16:45


Close — capstone checkpoint: your model scores




Why the forecast market is where it is
Three o’clock on Wednesday is the energy trough of any five-day programme, and by long convention it is also where the densest content of the week gets scheduled. Those two facts sit badly together, and the honest response to them is not a better set of slides.
So Wednesday afternoon becomes a market. Each table posts a quarter-ahead forecast for one depot with an 80% interval around it. Everyone then bets on which table is closest, which forces you to read somebody else’s interval and decide whether you believe it. Only after the bets are placed does the held-out quarter go up on the projector.
What follows is usually the loudest hour of the week, and it teaches calibration — the difference between being confident and being right — more effectively than three hours of explanation. It also demonstrates something people find genuinely surprising: the table that wins is rarely the one with the cleverest model, and is very often the one that was honest about how little it knew.

title: Day 3 — Seeing, forecasting, segmenting
text:
What you leave today with
Today produces more artefacts than any other day of the week, and each of them is something you would be able to defend in front of somebody who did not build it.

Artefacts on the wall board by 17:00

Three charts of your own data, each one making a single argument you can state in a sentence.
A forecast with an 80% interval, backtested, with the break handled explicitly.
A segmentation with each segment named, sized, and given one action.
A scored list — the customers, SKUs or suppliers you would act on first — and the reason you chose that threshold rather than a different one.
The leakage check for every feature in your model: would I have known this at the moment I needed to act?



The Sceptic’s brief for today
The best result at your table today is the one to attack hardest, which runs against every instinct you have. A weak result invites scrutiny and generally survives it; a striking one gets adopted, quoted and built upon before anybody has asked where it came from. Three questions, then, aimed squarely at whatever your table is most pleased with:

What period are we comparing to what period, and are they the same length? Unequal periods are the most common way a growth number turns out to be an artefact of the calendar.
If this model is this good, what does it know that I would not have known in time? Ask it of every feature, one at a time, and accept no answer that is not about timing.
What does the interval actually mean — and what would we do differently if the true value landed at the top of it rather than in the middle? If the answer is “nothing”, the interval is decoration.

title: Day 5 — Proof, governance and the capstone
text:
Four days of this week have been spent producing a number you believe. Friday is about what happens to that number when it meets somebody who would prefer it were different, and who is entitled to ask where it came from.
The morning carries the hardest intellectual content of the programme, and it is placed first for that reason. It is the difference between correlation, contribution and cause, and what you are actually entitled to claim on the strength of each — a distinction that sounds academic until you notice how much commercial language quietly assumes the strongest of the three. From there the day turns to governance, approached not as a compliance lecture but as the small set of practical decisions that determine whether an analytics function is allowed to keep operating: who signs off, who can stop a deployment, what gets written down, and on what legal basis the data is being processed at all.
The afternoon belongs to you. You defend your capstone to a panel made up of a CFO, an analytics leader and a risk officer, none of whom work here and none of whom have any reason to be kind. Most people find it considerably less alarming than it sounds by the time they have done Thursday’s rehearsal, and almost everyone reports afterwards that the questions were the most useful part of the week.

title: Day 5 — Proof, governance and the capstone
text:
What today is really arguing
One. A SHAP value is a contribution to a prediction — a precise statement about how a model reached one answer. It is not a causal driver, and the distance between those two sentences is, in practice, the distance between a good decision and an expensive one taken with great confidence. → 5.1
Two. An experiment is usually the cheapest available way to end an argument that would otherwise occupy two quarters and several committees. It is also fragile in one specific way, and the sample ratio check that detects that failure takes about thirty seconds and belongs before you look at the result. → 5.2
Three. In most commercial situations you cannot randomise, and pretending otherwise is not an option. There is a genuine toolkit for that case; it yields weaker claims than an experiment does; and saying so plainly, before anyone asks, is what makes the rest of your argument credible. → 5.3
Four. Governance that exists as a policy document is not governance. What functions is a model card somebody actually fills in, a log somebody actually reads, and a named person with the authority to stop a deployment — three things that fit on one page and take longer to agree than to write. → 5.4

title: Day 5 — Proof, governance and the capstone
text:
The day



09:00


The daily one number — and the sealed envelope from Monday is opened




09:15


5.1 Correlation, contribution, cause — three claims, three evidence standards, and the SHAP chart that gets misread in every boardroom




10:15


Coffee




10:45


5.2 Experiments that settle arguments — design, power, the SRM check, and the segment that moves the other way




11:45


5.3 When you cannot randomise — difference-in-differences, synthetic control, and how to state a weaker claim honestly




12:30


Lunch




13:15


5.4 Governance you can actually run — NDPA 2023, GAID 2025, cross-border transfer, model cards, local models, and your draft AI-use policy




14:00


5.5 The operating model — centralised, federated or hub-and-spoke; who you hire first; and how a pilot becomes a portfolio




14:30


Rehearsal against a hostile reviewer — another table’s Sceptic, twelve minutes each way, no mercy




15:15


Break, and the panel arrives




15:30


Capstone defences — three parallel rooms, one external panellist in each, every participant presents: five minutes, four minutes of questions




17:00


Reconvene. The failure logbook, consolidated and read aloud. The two envelopes. Certificates.




17:30


End




Wednesday’s best model comes back
On Wednesday, commute_minutes turned out to be one of the strongest predictors in the attrition model, and several tables will have kept it. That is a reasonable thing to have done: it is a legitimate operational variable, it is measured accurately, and it genuinely improves the model.
This afternoon the same model is put in front of a risk officer, and the question is no longer whether it is accurate. It is this: how far somebody travels is a proxy for where they live, which is in turn a proxy for income and often for ethnicity or religion — so what decision is this score attached to, and who bears the cost when it is wrong? Depending on the answer, the same model can be entirely defensible or something you would not want to explain in public.
It is worth stating the general principle plainly, because it is counter-intuitive and almost always arrived at backwards. Removing protected attributes from a dataset does not remove discrimination from a model. It removes your ability to measure it, and leaves the proxies in place. That is probably the most important sentence of the day, and the room earns it by having spent Wednesday building the model rather than by being told it on a slide.

title: Day 5 — Proof, governance and the capstone
section: What you leave the week with
text:
What you leave the week with
Everything below was built by you during the five days rather than handed over at the end, which is the only reason any of it is still useful in November.

The full set

A defended capstone: problem, pipeline, model, dashboard, memo, value case and a 90-day plan, argued in front of people with no stake in being kind to you.
A draft AI-use policy for your function, mapped to the NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025, including the cross-border transfer question.
A model card for the model you built.
The failure logbook — one page, the whole cohort’s, consolidated.
The number you now believe, next to the one you wrote down on Monday morning, with both intervals.

title: Day 5 — Proof, governance and the capstone
text:
What happens after today
Day 30, Day 60 and Day 90 are part of the programme rather than optional extras, and they are where most of its value is actually realised. The reasoning is simple enough: what you leave with on Friday is a well-argued plan, and a plan only becomes worth the week when it survives contact with your own systems, your own colleagues and your own calendar.
The Certificate of Completion is issued this afternoon. The Certificate of Implementation is issued at Day 90, to people who can show the number that moved and say honestly how they know it moved because of what they did.

title: The brief gallery
text:
Twelve self-contained briefs written against the course datasets. Each one poses a business question that somebody would genuinely have to answer, names the decision sitting behind it, and contains at least one thing that will mislead you if you take the data at face value.
Use them for: stretch work when you finish a lab early; practice in the weeks before the programme; internal training with your own team afterwards; or as capstone material if you would rather work with the course data than bring your own.
Every brief follows the same five-part shape, and it is worth knowing what each part is for before you start. The question is what somebody has actually asked you. The decision names who will act on your answer and how often, which is what separates an analysis from a curiosity. The files tell you where to look. What to check before you answer is a set of questions to put to the data rather than a list of findings — it points at the kind of thing that could be wrong without saying whether it is. And the standard describes what a good answer looks like, so that you can mark your own work honestly.
What the briefs deliberately do not give you is the method or the answer. Working out how to approach the question, and noticing what the data is quietly doing while you do it, is the whole exercise; a brief that named its own trap would be a reading comprehension test rather than a piece of analysis. If you get partway in and feel stuck, that is the normal condition of real analytical work, and the seven standing questions at the foot of this page are usually enough to get moving again.
Facilitators: the worked answers live in facilitator/gallery-solutions.md, which is not published to this site.

title: The brief gallery
text:
1 · Which depots should we close?

Retail · Strategy · Day 2–3
A network review has concluded that the depot estate is larger than the business needs, and the executive committee has asked for the two weakest sites. Closure decisions are close to irreversible, so the interesting part of this brief is not the ranking itself but what the ranking is measuring and what it leaves out.
Question. Two of the twelve depots are candidates for closure. Which two, and what would the network lose?
Decision. A capital decision made once, by the executive committee, with a two-year payback expectation.
Files. fmcg_sell_out.csv, fmcg_depots.csv, fmcg_products.csv
What to check before you answer. Is your ranking measuring what you think it is measuring — is the depot list itself clean, and is it revenue or gross profit you are ranking on? Then: has anything changed in the demand these depots serve during the period you are using, and would your answer survive being asked “is this a structural change or a performance problem?”
Standard. Gross profit, not revenue. Real, not nominal. Stated grain. Say what the closure does not capture — the accounts the depot serves that would be lost entirely.

title: The brief gallery
section: 2 · What is our real growth rate?
text:
2 · What is our real growth rate?

Finance · Economics · Day 1–2
A growth figure has already been written into a board pack, and your job is to say whether it means what the reader will assume it means. This is the brief that most often changes how people talk about their own numbers afterwards, because the same three considerations apply to almost every growth rate quoted in a high-inflation economy.
Question. The board pack says the business grew 43%. Is that true?
Decision. What the CEO says on the earnings call, and what the incentive plan is calibrated against.
Files. fmcg_sell_out.csv, ng_macro_monthly.csv
What to check before you answer. Three separate things could each move the 43% on their own. One is about how many rows there are. One is about how much of a year you are comparing. One is about the unit the number is denominated in. Find all three before you write anything down.
Standard. Produce four numbers: nominal revenue growth, volume growth, real revenue growth, and like-for-like growth excluding depots that opened or changed. Justify your choice of deflator on the chart.

title: The brief gallery
section: 3 · Which supplier gets the next tranche of volume?
text:
3 · Which supplier gets the next tranche of volume?

Supply chain · Procurement · Day 2
Procurement wants to consolidate volume with whoever performs best, which sounds like a straightforward ranking exercise. It becomes considerably more interesting once you ask what a supplier actually is in this file, and what a planner would have to commit to in order to rely on the performance you are about to report.
Question. ₦4.1bn of annual spend across what appears to be nine suppliers. Where should the next 15% go?
Decision. Category manager, quarterly, at contract renewal.
Files. supply_chain_pos.csv
What to check before you answer. Count the suppliers. Then look at the distribution of lead times rather than its mean — both the shape of it and whether every value in it is possible. Ask what a planner would actually order against.
Standard. Landed cost including the cost of lateness. Plan to a percentile of the lead time distribution, not the mean, and say which percentile and why.

title: The brief gallery
section: 4 · Who gets the retention call this month?
text:
4 · Who gets the retention call this month?

Banking · Marketing · Day 3
A retention team with fixed capacity has to choose who to call, which is the most common commercial use of a predictive model and the one where the modelling is the easy part. Two questions decide whether the list is any good: what exactly you are predicting, and whether you would have known each input at the moment the call had to be made.
Question. Capacity for 600 calls. Twelve thousand customers. Which 600?
Decision. Retention team lead, monthly.
Files. bank_customers.csv
What to check before you answer. Ask the leakage question of every column: would you have known this at the time you needed to act? And before any of that, ask what “churned” means here — there is more than one defensible definition in this file, and they do not agree.
Standard. Rank by probability × value × intervention effectiveness, not by probability. Say where your effectiveness estimate came from, and if you do not have one, say that too and propose the holdout that would give you one.

title: The brief gallery
section: 5 · Are we paying too much for promotions?
text:
5 · Are we paying too much for promotions?

FMCG · Trade marketing · Day 3
Promotional spend is one of the largest discretionary lines in a consumer business and one of the least well evidenced, because the weeks chosen for promotion are never chosen at random. This brief is a good rehearsal for the wider problem of measuring anything your own organisation decided when to do.
Question. 14% of depot-SKU-weeks are on promotion. Is the volume uplift worth the margin given away?
Decision. Trade marketing, monthly promotion calendar approval.
Files. fmcg_sell_out.csv, fmcg_products.csv
What to check before you answer. Is the average discount you computed weighted by anything? And when you measure uplift against the same SKU’s non-promoted weeks, ask yourself who chose which weeks were promoted — and whether that choice was random.
Standard. Weighted discount. Incremental volume, not total volume. State honestly that this is an observational estimate and design the experiment that would settle it.

title: The brief gallery
section: 6 · What are customers actually complaining about?
text:
6 · What are customers actually complaining about?

Customer experience · Day 4
A substantial remediation budget is waiting on an answer that has to come from free text rather than from a system of record. The analytical work is now quick; the judgement lies in knowing which customers are represented in the file you were sent, and in reading enough of the raw material yourself to trust what a classifier tells you about the rest.
Question. Five thousand free-text reviews across six channels. What are the top five themes, how big is each, and which is growing?
Decision. Where the ₦200m service remediation budget goes.
Files. customer_reviews.csv, bank_customers.csv
What to check before you answer. Ask where this extract came from and whether anything was filtered out on the way. Then read fifty reviews yourself before you classify five thousand: check that the language you are counting in is the language they are written in.
Standard. Themes with volumes and trend. A validation set with an agreement rate. The caveat about the filter, stated in the first paragraph rather than in a footnote.

title: The brief gallery
section: 7 · Should we ship the new checkout?
text:
7 · Should we ship the new checkout?

Digital · Product · Day 5
An experiment has finished, the headline is positive, and a product director would like to ship on Friday. This is the brief that teaches the two habits worth carrying into every experiment review: validate the randomisation before you look at the outcome, and check whether the average effect is hiding a segment moving in the opposite direction.
Question. Four-week experiment. Treatment converts 5.7% better. Ship it?
Decision. Product director, this week.
Files. ab_test_checkout.csv
What to check before you answer. Run the thirty-second check on the arm sizes before you look at any result. Then, before you ship, split the overall effect by segment and see whether every segment agrees with the headline.
Standard. SRM check before the result. Segment analysis on pre-registered segments. A recommendation that is neither “ship” nor “kill”.

title: The brief gallery
section: 8 · Where is attrition costing us most?
text:
8 · Where is attrition costing us most?

HR · Day 3 and Day 5
Attrition analysis is where the technical and the ethical arrive at the same time, which is why this brief spans two days. A model that predicts who will leave is easy to build and difficult to use well, and the second half of the exercise is about what you would be comfortable doing with the score once you have it.
Question. 18% annual attrition across 4,200 employees. Where should a fixed retention budget go?
Decision. CHRO with the executive committee, annually.
Files. hr_attrition.csv
What to check before you answer. Apply the leakage question to every column. Then apply a second question to whatever your strongest legitimate predictor turns out to be: what is it actually a proxy for, and would you be comfortable explaining that to the person it affects?
Standard. Attrition weighted by replacement cost, not raw attrition. Act on teams and conditions, not on individual scores — and be able to defend that choice to a risk officer.

title: The brief gallery
section: 9 · Which marketing channel deserves more money?
text:
9 · Which marketing channel deserves more money?

Marketing · Day 5
Every marketing team is asked this question annually, and it is almost always answered by dividing spend by conversions and ranking the result. The brief exists to show what that ranking assumes, and to give you a defensible way of saying what observational data can and cannot settle here without simply refusing to answer.
Question. Six channels, weekly spend and conversions. Where does the next ₦100m go?
Decision. CMO, annual budget, with a quarterly reallocation.
Files. marketing_spend.csv
What to check before you answer. Plot spend and conversions over time before you divide one by the other. Ask what else moves on the same calendar as both of them, and what that does to a naive cost-per-conversion ranking.
Standard. Show the confounder. Estimate diminishing returns. Then say plainly what observational data cannot tell you here, and design the geo holdout that would.

title: The brief gallery
section: 10 · Is the sales team’s activity model right?
text:
10 · Is the sales team’s activity model right?

B2B sales · Day 3
A senior stakeholder already holds a view and is asking you for support rather than for an answer, which is a situation everyone in the room will recognise. The analytical content is about which rows carry the data you need; the professional content is about how to report back when the honest answer is that this file cannot settle the question asked.
Question. Does more sales activity win more deals? The CRO believes it does and wants to raise the activity target.
Decision. Sales comp and activity targets for next year.
Files. b2b_funnel.csv
What to check before you answer. Look at how much of the activity column is populated, then look at what the populated rows have in common. Ask what that does to a correlation computed on the rows that survive.
Standard. Report what fraction of rows carry the data and what those rows have in common. Then answer the question that can be answered from this file, which is a different one.

title: The brief gallery
section: 11 · What should we hold in safety stock?
text:
11 · What should we hold in safety stock?

Operations · Day 3
Safety stock is a working-capital decision dressed as an arithmetic one, and the formula everybody uses is only as good as the demand variability and the lead time you feed it. Both inputs need a decision from you before the formula can be applied, and neither decision is visible in the output.
Question. Set the reorder point for the top 20 SKUs at the three largest depots, to hit a 95% service level.
Decision. Supply planner, weekly.
Files. fmcg_sell_out.csv, supply_chain_pos.csv
What to check before you answer. Look at how a week with no sales is recorded, and what that does to the variance you are about to feed into a safety stock formula. Then look at the shape of the lead time distribution and ask what planning to its mean commits you to.
Standard. Demand variability computed with the blanks handled explicitly. Lead time at a stated percentile. Say what a 95% service level costs in working capital.

title: The brief gallery
text:
12 · Build the one-page board view

Executive · Day 4
This is the hardest brief in the gallery and the one with the least code in it. Everything you have learned about grain, comparison, real versus nominal and data quality has to survive being compressed onto a single page for readers who will not ask you what any of it means — and the omissions matter more than the inclusions.
Question. The board gets 40 pages monthly. Replace it with one page.
Decision. What the board discusses, and what it stops discussing.
Files. Any and all.
What to check before you answer. Notice what you want to do to this page every time you look at it, and ask whether the person it is for would agree.
Standard. Six numbers maximum, each with a comparison. Every number real or nominal and labelled. One exception list. A quality badge. And a written note of what you deliberately left out and why — which is the hardest part and the part that gets marked.



How to use these well
Do not simply hand the brief to an assistant and read what comes back. You will get a fluent, well-organised answer that walks straight into whatever the brief was built around, and because it will look exactly like a good answer you will learn nothing from it.
Do use the assistant as your Driver while you take the Sceptic’s seat. Ask it for the analysis, then work the seven standing questions from How this programme works against what it produces, one at a time. That is the same division of labour the week is built on, and it is the one that transfers to your desk afterwards.
A useful way to keep score, if you want one: the exercise is not really the answer, it is how many turns of that conversation it takes you to find what the brief is hiding. Most people find it takes fewer each time, which is the skill becoming a habit.


On the format of this page
The gallery format — a set of self-contained briefs against open data, published for people to work through in their own time — is borrowed from the open teaching materials tradition in academic statistics, where “here are ten datasets and ten questions, go” turned out to be better pedagogy than ten more worked examples.
What is different here is that every brief carries a decision and a decision-maker, because a question without a decision behind it is a puzzle rather than a business problem.

title: Participant guide
text: The site you are reading is the reference: everything about the programme is on it, and it stays up. The participant guide is a different sort of object. It is a printed workbook you carry through the week, and most of its pages are ruled space rather than prose, because the exercises that make the week work — the daily one number, the charter, the failure logbook, the questions you hope nobody asks — only work when they are written down by hand and compared later.

title: Participant guide
text:
What is in it
The guide is arranged in the order you will need it rather than in the order it was written, so it can be worked through front to back across the five days.
The seven questions, on one page, designed to be torn out. Grain · rows before and after the join · which periods · real or nominal · would I have known this in time · what had to be true for a row to exist · if this is this good, what is wrong with it.
The daily one number, with five ruled rows and a Friday comparison. This is the spine of the week, and it only works if it is written down.
The use-case charter, laid out as seven fields with room to draft. Submitted ten days before Monday, revised in Lab 1, defended on Friday.
A spread per day — what today argues, the sessions with times, the capstone checkpoint, space for your Sceptic’s objection, lab notes, and a failure logbook table with four rows.
The capstone rubric, in full, with the five questions the panel always asks — and the sixth that it should. Published before the programme starts, because a rubric you see on Monday changes what you do and a rubric you see on Friday only allocates marks.
The defence page — the five-minute structure, and ruled space for the five questions you most hope nobody asks, with your answers.
Quick reference — twelve terms and four prompt patterns.
Day 30 / 60 / 90, with space to commit to what you will bring to each.

title: Participant guide
text:
The failure logbook

The most forwarded artefact of the week
Four ruled rows a day, twenty over the week, with three columns: what the assistant produced · what was wrong with it · the question that caught it. Two entries a day is typical, which is a low enough bar that nobody has to strain for material — and the third column is the one that turns an anecdote into something reusable.
On Friday afternoon every table’s entries are consolidated, deduplicated and read aloud as a single page — the ways the copilot misled us this week — and then sent to the whole cohort.
It costs an hour of facilitation and it is, reliably, the artefact people forward to their own teams in the following week. That is a better test of usefulness than any feedback form, and it is the most honest summary available of what the week was actually about.

title: Participant guide
text:
Rebuilding it
The guide is generated rather than hand-set, which matters mostly to anyone who wants to adapt it. One Python script writes the HTML, and headless Chromium prints that to PDF; there is no layout file to maintain and nothing to re-typeset when a session time changes.
python3 build/make_guide.py
Change the dates, the sessions, the claims or the rubric in build/make_guide.py and the whole workbook regenerates in the same house style. That is deliberately the same argument the programme makes about business reporting on Day 4 — one source, several outputs, nothing typed twice — applied to its own materials, on the principle that a course making that case ought to be willing to live by it.

Also available

The five facilitator decks — self-contained HTML, with speaker notes.
The data room — twelve datasets and two workbooks, downloadable individually.
The salt key and the gallery solutions — facilitators only, in the repository’s facilitator/ directory. Not linked from this site, and not released to a cohort before Friday afternoon.

title: Turning Data into Business Growth
text:
An AI assistant will write your query, fit your model and draft your memo in minutes, and it will do all three fluently. What it will not do is notice that the join quietly doubled your Abuja revenue, that the feature predicting churn at 98% accuracy is only knowable once the customer has already gone, or that the 43% growth in your deck is mostly the naira rather than the business.
Those three judgements are still yours. This is a week spent learning to make them well, with the machine sitting beside you rather than instead of you.



Dates12–16 October 2026


FormatIn person · 09:00–17:00, Friday to 17:30


VenueLBS Campus, Ajah, Lagos


CohortFour sector lenses


Fee₦950,000 + VAT


DirectorProf. Bongo Adi

title: Turning Data into Business Growth
text:
Who this is for
This programme was built for senior people who have to make consequential decisions on evidence somebody else produced. That includes general managers and P&L owners; directors and senior managers in strategy, finance, marketing, operations, supply chain, HR and risk; and analytics and technology leaders who would like the commercial side of the room to understand what they are being handed and why it is harder than it looks.
It is a genuinely mixed room, and we have designed for that rather than around it. Some participants arrive able to read a regression output; others arrive having never opened a terminal and slightly worried about it. Neither group is the guest of the other. The material is substantial enough that an analytics director will find new things in it, and explained generously enough that a marketing director is never quietly lost — which is harder to write than either extreme, and is the thing we care most about getting right.
You do not need to be able to write code, and nobody will ask you to memorise syntax. By Friday you will be able to read code, which is the skill that actually transfers to your desk. You will also, along the way, have produced a great deal of it with an assistant, in front of colleagues who are encouraged to argue with your results.

What you leave with
Six things, all of them yours, all of them built during the week rather than handed over at the end of it.

A use-case portfolio for your own business — sized, sequenced, with the value hypothesis written down and the assumptions it rests on made visible rather than buried.
A working pipeline that runs again tomorrow and gives the same answer: from raw file to a tested, analysis-ready table, built by you and explainable by you line by line.
A forecast with an interval on it, and a considered answer to the question that always follows — “how confident are you, and what would change your mind?”
A decision dashboard and a two-page executive brief, both generated from the same source, both of which regenerate themselves when the data updates.
A draft AI-use policy for your function, mapped to the NDPA 2023 and the NDPC’s GAID 2025, including the cross-border transfer question that most policies leave out.
The failure logbook — the cohort’s consolidated record of every way the assistant misled somebody during the week. Participants tend to forward it to their own teams before they have unpacked, which is as good a measure of usefulness as we have found.

title: Turning Data into Business Growth
text:
The week
Each day has a shape and a verb. Monday frames the problem, Tuesday gets the data into a state you can trust, Wednesday models it, Thursday communicates it, and Friday asks whether any of it would survive being challenged by someone who does not report to you.

 Monday 12 October · Frame

Strategy, value, and what AI actually changed


Where analytics value really comes from, the KPI tree, sizing the prize, and the new division of labour between you and the machine.

  Tuesday 13 October · Get

Getting data you can trust


SQL as the lingua franca, the laptop warehouse, Excel as a bridge rather than an engine, joins that lie, and data quality written as a contract.

  Wednesday 14 October · See & Model

Seeing, forecasting, segmenting


What is odd here, charts that survive a board room, forecasts with intervals, segments a marketer can act on, and the feature that leaks.

  Thursday 15 October · Publish

Unstructured data and the executive narrative


Five thousand reviews into five themes with volumes, classification you can validate, dashboards built for a decision, and the one-number brief.

  Friday 16 October · Guard

Proof, governance and the capstone


Correlation, contribution and cause; experiments that settle arguments; governance you can actually run; then you defend your case to a panel that does not work here.

title: Turning Data into Business Growth
text:
The daily rhythm
Every day runs to the same shape. That is partly so nobody spends the week guessing what happens next, and partly because a predictable timetable is what makes it possible to protect the parts of the day that are easiest to lose.



08:45


Doors open, and the setup desk is staffed for anyone still wrestling with their laptop




09:00


The daily one number. Each person writes one number they now believe about their business, with an interval around it. Fifteen minutes, every morning.




09:15


Session A (60 min) — a short input, then hands on keys within four minutes




10:15


Coffee




10:45


Session B (60 min)




11:45


Session C (60 min)




12:45


Lunch




13:45


Session D (60 min)




14:45

15:30

15:45


The lab (60 min) — one named artefact on the wall board, then capstone work




16:45

Five teaching blocks and a lab come to 345 minutes of contact time, which is precisely what is left between 09:15 and 16:45 once coffee, lunch and the afternoon break are taken out. The arithmetic is stated because it explains a design choice: nothing on this timetable assumes a session will be allowed to overrun. When a five-day programme falls behind, the casualty is almost never the input and almost always the part where the room stops and asks whether the result in front of it is actually true. That is the part we are here to build, so the schedule is drawn to make it hard to sacrifice.
Wednesday breaks the pattern once, on purpose. The 15:45 lab becomes the forecast market, because three o’clock on Wednesday is the energy trough of any five-day programme and the honest answer to that is not more slides.
Friday runs to a different clock: lunch moves to 12:30, teaching finishes at 14:30, and the afternoon belongs to the capstone — rehearsal at 14:30, defences from 15:30 in three parallel rooms, and a 17:30 close. It is worth knowing that before you book a flight home.

title: Turning Data into Business Growth
text:
Before you arrive
There are three things to do in advance. None of them takes long, and all three exist so that Monday morning starts with the work rather than with admin.

Three things, ten days out

A one-page problem charter. The business problem you would like to leave the week with an answer to. Each one is read individually by faculty, and it becomes your capstone, so it is worth choosing something you genuinely care about rather than something safe. There is a template on the capstone page, which also carries the full marking rubric — published before the programme starts rather than after it, because a rubric you can see on Monday changes how you work all week.
A twenty-minute data-triage diagnostic. This is not a test and it is not marked. It is how we stream the labs and pair people sensibly, so that nobody spends the week either bored or lost. Nobody sees anybody else’s score, and that includes you.
The setup clinic. A session staffed by a technician, plus a pre-built cloud workspace for anyone whose laptop their IT department has locked down. Everything you need to know is on Before Monday, and the earlier you tell us about a problem, the less of a problem it turns out to be.

title: Turning Data into Business Growth
text:
How the teaching works
Four mechanics do most of the work of this programme, and they are described in full on How this programme works. In brief:
The four-minute rule. No demonstration runs for longer than four minutes before the room does it themselves. Watching a fluent demonstration is enjoyable and teaches remarkably little, precisely because the friction has been removed — and the friction was where the learning lived. The rule puts it back.
Driver and Sceptic. You work in pairs, and the roles swap every day. The Driver is on the keyboard. The Sceptic may not touch it, and has to produce an objection before any result gets used. That second role sounds like a courtesy and turns out to be the harder seat, because an assistant is an excellent generator of answers and a poor auditor of the question it was handed. Somebody has to do the auditing, and this is the habit that installs it.
Salted data. The data room carries thirteen deliberate defects, unevenly distributed — a join key that silently duplicates rows, a feature that leaks the answer, a structural break a forecast will ignore, and ten more. Which defect sits in which file is not published until Friday, and some files are entirely clean, so the only habit that works is to check everything the same way. The point is not to catch anyone out. It is that being wrong in a classroom costs a moment of discomfort, and being wrong in a board paper costs considerably more — and the instinct that prevents the second is built by living through the first.
The failure logbook. Everyone keeps a record of what the assistant got wrong and which question caught it. On Friday the entries are consolidated into a single page and sent to the whole cohort.

title: Turning Data into Business Growth
text:
What you will be reading
You will read SQL and R. The assistant writes both fluently. Python appears once, so that you can recognise it in the wild and hold a useful conversation with your data science team, and it is available as a capstone option for the analytics leads in the room.
That is a deliberate narrowing, and the reasoning is worth stating rather than asserting. There are roughly fourteen hands-on hours in this week. Split across two languages, that falls below the threshold at which either becomes comfortable, and half-fluency in two languages is less useful than working fluency in one. What we are teaching is a reading skill — the ability to look at what an assistant produced and see what is wrong with it — and reading is language-specific in a way that concepts are not. So: one language, properly, and the concepts underneath it explained well enough to carry across.

A claim this programme does not make
Some of these tools are free. Not all of them are. An AI assistant seat, Power BI Pro and a Copilot licence all cost money, and rather than glossing over that we will tell you what each one costs and exactly what the free substitute gives up.
Some of them will need a conversation with your IT department, which is precisely what you would expect from a programme that spends a day on governance — tooling that touches company data ought to require permission.
And we cannot install software on a laptop we have never seen. That is why there is a setup clinic and a pre-built cloud workspace, rather than a promise that everything will simply work on the day.

title: Turning Data into Business Growth
text:
Track your week





About these materials
This site is the complete programme: every session, every lab, every dataset, and the slides. It stays online after the cohort ends, and it is version-controlled in the open, so you can see exactly what changed between one cohort and the next and why.
The structure — a page per session, a hex badge in the corner, everything given away for free — is owed to the open teaching materials movement in academic statistics, and particularly to the workshop format pioneered by university data-skills teams who published their courses openly rather than locking them inside a learning management system. We have rebuilt the pedagogy for a rather different room: people carrying P&L responsibility, an assistant that can write code faster than they can read it, and a Friday afternoon panel that does not care how elegant the model is.
