title: Competing on analytics
section: Three questions about a dashboard you know well
text:
Three questions about a dashboard you know well
Bring to mind the last dashboard your organisation commissioned, and hold three questions against it:

Which recurring decision does it exist to support?
Who makes that decision, how often, and what are their options?
What did they do differently after it was built?

These are harder questions than they look, and if the answers do not arrive immediately, that is worth knowing rather than worrying about. When we run this exercise with a room of experienced people, a few can answer all three straight away and most find at least one of them difficult. That pattern tells us something about the way dashboards get commissioned, rather than something about the people answering.
The reason is structural, and it is worth stating plainly before we go any further. A dashboard is nearly always specified by describing what it should show — revenue by region, margin by category, a trend line with last year behind it. It is only rarely specified by describing what somebody should do differently once they can see it. The first kind of specification is easy to write and easy to sign off. The second requires you to know whose job changes, and that is a harder conversation to start. The rest of this session is about the gap between the two.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Competing on analytics
text:
Four mechanisms, not one
It helps to be precise about how analytics turns into money, because “analytics creates value” is true and useless. There are four distinct routes, and they behave very differently in terms of how large the return is, how long it takes to arrive, and how much organisational effort it costs to capture.










#
Mechanism
What it looks like
Typical return
Typical spend




1
Better recurring decisions
Pricing, credit limits, replenishment, staffing, collections priority
Highest, compounding
Lowest


2
Faster cycle time
Month-end close from 12 days to 4; a pricing review from quarterly to weekly
High
Medium


3
New products or revenue
Usage-based pricing, a data product sold to suppliers, risk-based premiums
High but slow
Medium


4
Visibility
“Now we can see it” — reporting, dashboards, single version of truth
Real but modest, and it decays
Highest



Read the last two columns together and the tension in this table becomes visible: the mechanism with the highest return tends to attract the least spending, and the mechanism with the most modest return tends to attract the most. That is not a comment on anybody’s competence. As we will see in a moment, there are three quite rational reasons why budgets flow the way they do. But it does mean that returns are frequently reported as though the money had gone into mechanism 1 when in practice it went into mechanism 4.
Mechanism 4 is genuinely worth something, and it is worth saying so clearly. You cannot manage what you cannot see, and the first credible dashboard in an organisation that has never had one does change behaviour — people look at it, they are surprised by something, and they act. The difficulty is that the effect decays. Six months later the dashboard is open in a browser tab that nobody reads, because seeing a number does not by itself tell anybody what to do about it. The visibility was consumed; the decision was never redesigned.

The test that separates 1 from 4
There is a quick way to tell which mechanism an initiative really belongs to. Try to fill in four blanks: name the decision, name the decision-maker, name the frequency, name the alternative action.
“Depot managers reorder every Tuesday. Today they order to a fixed weeks-of-cover number. With this, they order to a forecast with a service-level target, and the ones with a stockout risk above 15% get flagged for expediting.”
That sentence is mechanism 1, and you can see why: there is an owner, a cadence, a description of what happens today, and a specific alternative. Somebody’s Tuesday changes.
If you cannot fill in all four blanks, the initiative is very likely mechanism 4 — which is not a reason to abandon it, but is a good reason to price the business case as visibility rather than as decision improvement, and to say so before somebody else does.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Competing on analytics
section: Why the spending goes where it does
text:
Why the spending goes where it does
Three forces push budget towards visibility. Each of them is entirely rational from where the decision is being taken, which is exactly why the pattern is so persistent.
Visibility is easier to specify. “I want to see revenue by region by month” is a complete requirement — a competent team can build it and both sides can agree when it is finished. “I want depot managers to order better” is not a requirement at all; it is a change programme involving forty people who did not ask to be involved. Faced with a deadline, the specifiable thing wins.
Visibility is easier to buy. There is a vendor for it, a demo you can sit through, and a licence cost that fits neatly on a budget line. Improving a recurring decision means changing how somebody already does their job, and there is no product that does that part for you. Procurement processes are much better suited to the first than the second.
Visibility does not create a loser. This is the one that decides most outcomes. When you improve a recurring decision, you are displacing somebody’s current judgement — and that somebody is usually experienced, respected, and right often enough to have a real case for their method. They may also be right that the model does not see what they see. Programmes that stall rarely stall on the mathematics; they stall here. It is worth recognising this early, because it is an organisational question wearing technical clothing, and treating it as a technical question is what makes it intractable.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Competing on analytics
text:
The analytics value chain
It is useful to see the whole path from raw data to money, because it makes clear where the value actually appears — and every stage before that point is cost.





flowchart LR
  A[Ingest] --> B[Model]
  B --> C[Analyse]
  C --> D[Decide]
  D --> E[Act]
  E --> F[Measure]
  F -->|learn| C
  style A fill:#EEF3FA,stroke:#2E3A6E
  style B fill:#EEF3FA,stroke:#2E3A6E
  style C fill:#E4F1FB,stroke:#16549B
  style D fill:#D9EEF6,stroke:#00699B
  style E fill:#D6F0EA,stroke:#00695C,stroke-width:3px
  style F fill:#F6EFE0,stroke:#8A6D2F


 Value appears at ‘act’. Everything before it is investment. 



Two observations about this chain matter considerably more than the diagram itself.
The chain tends to break at “decide” rather than at “analyse”. Most organisations are better at producing analysis than at consuming it, and when a stalled programme is examined closely the model is rarely the problem. Far more often the output arrived on a Thursday for a decision that gets made on Mondays; or it arrived with somebody who has no authority to change what happens next; or it arrived in a format that would have needed forty minutes of interpretation, and the recipient had four. None of those are analytical failures. They are all failures of fit between an output and a decision, and they are all fixable once you are looking for them.
The loop from “measure” back to “analyse” is what compounds. McKinsey’s work on scaling analytics keeps returning to the same finding: the distance between the leading firms and everybody else is widening rather than narrowing. The mechanism behind that is the feedback loop. A firm that measures what happened after each decision, and feeds it back into the next analysis, learns something from every cycle. A firm that does not is running a series of unrelated projects, each starting from the same standing start. Over three years the difference between those two is very large, and it comes from a habit rather than from a technology.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Competing on analytics
text:
Four sectors, the same structure
The mechanism is identical across industries; only the nouns change. It is worth reading all four of these, including the ones outside your sector, because the shared shape is easier to see when the specifics are unfamiliar.

FMCGBankingSupply chainHR


Decision: weekly replenishment quantity per SKU per depot. Decision-maker: depot manager, every Tuesday, 40 SKUs. Today: fixed weeks-of-cover, adjusted by feel. With analytics: forecast plus service-level target, with expedite flags. Value driver: stockouts fall, which protects revenue, and obsolescence falls, which protects margin — and they improve together rather than trading off against each other. That combination is why replenishment has been the highest-return analytics use case in consumer goods for thirty years: you are not choosing between service and working capital, you are buying better information about which SKUs need which.


Decision: which of 12,000 customers gets a retention call this month, and what is offered. Decision-maker: retention team lead, monthly, capacity for 600 calls. Today: highest balance first. With analytics: highest expected value at risk first — probability of leaving, multiplied by value if they do, multiplied by probability the call works. Value driver: that third term is the one most models omit. A customer who is certain to leave and cannot be talked out of it is worth nothing to call, however large their balance; a customer who was never going to leave is worth nothing to call either. The calls worth making are the ones where the conversation changes the outcome, and ranking by balance alone finds those only by accident.


Decision: which supplier gets the next tranche of volume, and which gets a conversation. Decision-maker: category manager, quarterly. Today: price per unit, and relationship. With analytics: landed cost including the cost of lateness — expediting, stockouts, and the working capital tied up in safety stock that exists only because a supplier is unreliable. Value driver: once lateness is priced, the cheapest supplier on a unit basis is frequently the most expensive one in total. That is not a rhetorical flourish; it is what happens when a cost that sits in three other departments’ budgets is finally added to the one being negotiated.


Decision: where to spend a fixed retention budget across seven departments. Decision-maker: CHRO with the exec committee, annually. Today: wherever attrition looks highest. With analytics: where attrition is highest among people who are expensive to replace and whose leaving is preventable. Those are three separate questions — how many leave, what it costs when they do, and whether anything you can afford would have changed their mind — and the department that tops one list is very often not the department that tops the others. Spending against the first list alone is the most common way a retention budget gets used up without moving anything.




Core lab · 20 minutes
Working in your pair.


Each of you names one analytics initiative currently live in your organisation.


Classify it into one of the four mechanisms. Argue if you disagree.


Fill in the four blanks: decision, decision-maker, frequency, alternative action.


If you cannot fill in all four, write the sentence that would have to become true for you to be able to.


Sceptic: name the person whose current judgement this initiative displaces, and what they will say about it.


Spend real time on that last item. In our experience it is the question that most reliably predicts whether an initiative ever reaches daily use, and it is far cheaper to answer in week one than in month six.


Stretch · if you finish early
Take the same initiative and write the version of it that would be mechanism 1 rather than mechanism 4. Same data, same team, same budget. Usually the change is not analytical at all: it is a change in who receives the output and when, so that it lands with a person who has both the authority and the occasion to act on it.
Then find another table and ask them to break your answer.


Ask the assistant, then argue with it
Paste your initiative into the assistant with this prompt:

I am going to describe an analytics initiative. Do not tell me it is a good idea. Instead: (1) classify it as decision-improving, cycle-time, new-revenue or visibility; (2) name the specific recurring decision it changes, or say clearly that it does not change one; (3) name whose existing judgement it displaces; (4) give me the three assumptions that, if wrong, make it worthless. Be blunt.
The initiative is: …

Then read what comes back with the Sceptic’s eye. It will be articulate and it will often be useful. What it will also do is accept your framing of the problem more or less uncritically — if you have described the wrong initiative, you will get an excellent critique of the wrong initiative. That is the failure mode this whole programme is built around, and it is worth naming now: an assistant is an excellent generator and a poor auditor of the question it was handed.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Competing on analytics
text:
Takeaways

Analytics creates value in four ways. Most spend goes to the weakest one and gets reported as though it went to the strongest.
The test is four blanks: decision, decision-maker, frequency, alternative action.
The value chain breaks at decide, not at analyse.
Every use case that improves a recurring decision displaces somebody’s judgement. Name that person on day one, not in month six.


Next: 1.2 The KPI tree →
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Sizing the prize
section: The number you have to make up
text:
The number you have to make up
Every analytics business case contains at least one invented number, and there is no honourable way around it. You are estimating the value of a decision that has not been improved yet, in a business that has not yet behaved differently. The evidence you would need does not exist, because generating it is the thing you are asking to be funded to do.
What separates a credible case from an incredible one is therefore not whether it contains an estimate. It is where the estimate sits. The common instinct is to bury it — to build a model with fourteen tabs so that the invented figure appears as a cell reference three sheets away from anything a reader will open. That instinct is understandable and it backfires, because it is the main reason finance functions distrust analytics business cases as a category.
The professional move is the opposite. Put the invented number on one line, in front, with its assumptions named and a range around it. A CFO has read a thousand business cases and is not fooled by the fourteen tabs; what they are looking for is whether the person in front of them knows which part of their own case is soft. Somebody who says “this is the number I cannot know, here is my range, and here is what would move it” is much easier to fund than somebody defending a point estimate to four decimal places.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Sizing the prize
text:
The one-line value hypothesis
The form is always the same, whatever the sector:

Value = Volume × Rate × Improvement × Unit economics

Read left to right, that is: how many opportunities are there in a year, what share of them currently go wrong, how much of that can you realistically fix, and what is one fixed instance worth. Four terms, four different kinds of evidence — and it is usually only the third that is a genuine guess.
Here is the same structure filled in four times. Read at least two, including one outside your sector, because the pattern is easier to see when the nouns are unfamiliar.

FMCG — availabilityBanking — retentionSupply chain — supplier consolidationHR — targeted retention



12 depots × 40 SKUs × 52 weeks = 24,960 depot-SKU-weeks a year. Stockout rate in Q1 2026 3.06% → 764 stockout weeks a year. Better replenishment removes one third of them → 255 weeks recovered. Average weekly revenue per depot-SKU ₦1.14m, gross margin 34%. Of the recovered demand, one third is genuinely lost sale rather than deferred to the following week.
Annual gross profit recovered ≈ 255 × ₦1.14m × 0.34 × 0.33 ≈ ₦32.5m

Walk the arithmetic once, slowly, because the shape of it is what transfers. The first line counts the opportunities: twelve depots each stocking forty lines, observed every week for a year, gives 24,960 chances for a line to be available or not. The second applies the observed failure rate to that count — 3.06% of 24,960 is about 764 depot-SKU-weeks in which something was out of stock. The third is a judgement about how much of that is fixable; the fourth converts a recovered week into gross profit; and the fifth accepts that a customer who could not buy today may simply buy tomorrow, so not all recovered demand is new money.
Five numbers, four of which come straight out of the data and one of which is invented. Notice which is which as you read, because a sceptic will.

The line that is doing all the work
“One third is genuinely lost sale.”
Nothing in the data supports that figure, and nothing could: the file records what was sold, not what somebody would have bought had the shelf not been empty. It is a judgement, and it happens to be the judgement the whole estimate rests on. At 15% the case is ₦14.8m; at 60% it is ₦59.1m. That is a four-fold range produced by one unmeasured assumption, while every other input stays exactly where it is.
This is precisely why a value hypothesis carries a range and names its driving assumption out loud. A single number in this position is not a forecast; it is a decision about which number to say in the meeting, and a sceptical listener will locate it in about eleven seconds. Naming it first is both more honest and, in practice, more persuasive.
You will meet this same assumption again on Thursday, as a named vector in 4.6’s starter file. Putting it in code is not a formality: it means anybody can change one line and watch the case move, which turns an argument about belief into an experiment about sensitivity.

And check the period. This case takes a stockout rate measured over a single quarter and uses it to build an annual figure. That may be entirely reasonable — or the quarter may have been unusually bad, or unusually good, or affected by a supplier problem that has since been resolved. Either way it is worth one sentence in the case saying which quarter the rate came from. A quarterly number wearing an annual label is among the most common arithmetic errors in a value case, and once it reaches a slide it is effectively invisible.



Base 12,000 customers, annual churn 10.6% → 1,224 leave. Retention capacity 600 calls a month = 7,200 contacts a year. Targeting today: highest balance. Targeting with a model: highest expected value at risk. Assume the model lifts the hit rate of those calls from 6% to 11% — i.e. of the customers called, the share who would have left and now stay. Average annual contribution per retained customer ₦180,000.
Value ≈ 7,200 × (0.11 − 0.06) × ₦180,000 ≈ ₦64.8m

Notice what the middle line is really claiming. The capacity is fixed at 600 calls a month whether or not anybody builds a model, so the value here does not come from calling more people. It comes from calling different people: the same 7,200 conversations, aimed at customers where the call actually changes the outcome. That is why the arithmetic uses the difference between two hit rates rather than the hit rate itself.
The fragile assumption is not the model’s accuracy, which is the thing everybody wants to argue about. It is the 6% baseline. Most banks have never measured it, because retention calls are not run against a control group, so nobody knows what share of those customers would have stayed anyway. If the true baseline is higher, the incremental value shrinks even if the model is excellent. Establishing that baseline is a Friday topic, and it is usually cheaper than the model.



Annual spend ₦44.6bn across 8 suppliers. One supplier is on time 98.5% of the time; the network average is 77.4%. Moving 15% of spend to the best supplier lifts network on-time by roughly 3 points. Each point of on-time is worth an estimated ₦65m in avoided expediting and safety stock — call it 0.15% of spend.
Value ≈ 3 × ₦65m ≈ ₦195m, plus the working capital release

The soft input here is the ₦65m per point. Nobody knows it precisely, and its provenance is usually a percentage of spend that somebody estimated once and that has been repeated ever since. Rather than defending it, put a range on it: at 0.07% to 0.22% of spend, one point of on-time is worth somewhere between ₦30m and ₦100m, and the case becomes ₦90m to ₦300m. That is a wide range, it is still an easy yes at every point inside it, and it is now honest — which means the discussion moves on to how you would narrow it rather than whether you believe it.



4,200 employees, attrition 18.6% → 783 leavers a year. Replacement cost averages 45% of annual pay; median pay ₦7.4m. Total attrition cost ≈ 783 × 0.45 × ₦7.4m ≈ ₦2.61bn. Suppose a third of attrition is preventable and targeted intervention prevents 15% of that third.
Value ≈ ₦2.61bn × 0.33 × 0.15 ≈ ₦129m

Two of those three fractions are guesses, and the case is stronger for saying so than for pretending otherwise. It is also worth noting what happens at the pessimistic end: even at a quarter of this estimate the value comfortably exceeds the cost of the programme, which is the fact the decision actually turns on. When the answer is the same across the whole range, the width of the range stops being a problem.
There is a quieter choice in the second line that is worth pausing over. Mean pay in this workforce is ₦11.66m and the median is ₦7.4m, because pay distributions are right-skewed: a small number of very senior salaries pull the average well above what a typical employee earns. Using the mean here would inflate the case by 58% — not because anybody intended to, but because mean() is the default in every tool you might reach for. Whether the people who actually leave look more like the mean employee or the median one is a question the data can answer, and it is worth ₦900m either way, so it deserves the ten minutes.




The three-assumption rule
Every value hypothesis gets exactly three assumptions listed underneath it, ranked by how much the answer moves if they turn out to be wrong.
Three, rather than seven. A list of seven assumptions feels rigorous and functions as camouflage: with everything declared, nothing is emphasised, and the reader cannot tell which one to worry about. Being held to three forces you to do the ranking yourself, and it changes the conversation from “do we believe this number?” — which has no productive answer — into “how would we find out about assumption one?”, which ends with somebody agreeing to go and do something specific.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Sizing the prize
text:
Ranges, not points
A point estimate invites a fight about the point. A range invites a discussion about the decision, which is the discussion you wanted.
The cheapest method that is genuinely useful is a three-point estimate: for each uncertain input, write a pessimistic, a central and an optimistic value, then combine them. You do not need a Monte Carlo simulation for a first pass — and if you ask an assistant for one it will produce a beautiful simulation that attaches false precision to inputs you invented five minutes earlier.
# Three-point value hypothesis, supply chain consolidation.
# Deliberately crude. The point is the width of the answer, not its centre.

spend            <- 4.1e9
share_moved      <- c(low = 0.08, mid = 0.15, high = 0.22)
points_gained    <- c(low = 1.5,  mid = 3.0,  high = 4.5)
value_per_point  <- c(low = 3e6,  mid = 6e6,  high = 10e6)

outer_range <- c(
  low  = points_gained["low"]  * value_per_point["low"],
  mid  = points_gained["mid"]  * value_per_point["mid"],
  high = points_gained["high"] * value_per_point["high"]
)

round(outer_range / 1e6, 1)   # ₦m:  low 4.5   mid 18.0   high 45.0
The inputs in that block are placeholders — a smaller, illustrative business rather than the one in the tab above — so read the structure rather than the figures. What it produces is a spread from four and a half million to forty-five million: a factor of ten, and an honest one, because the low case multiplies the pessimistic gain by the pessimistic value per point while the high case does the opposite. That is deliberately the widest defensible interval rather than a statistically careful one.
Then ask what decision the range is supposed to support. If the question is “should we spend three weeks building a supplier scorecard?”, the answer is yes at every point in the range, and the width is irrelevant. A wide range only becomes a problem when it straddles the threshold that decides the matter — and when it does, you have learned something more useful than a number. You have learned that the next step is not to build the thing, it is to spend a small amount of effort narrowing assumption one.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Sizing the prize
text:
The portfolio matrix



Value against feasibility. Size the bubbles by time-to-first-value, not by cost.


Two axes, and it is the second one that most portfolios get wrong.
Value is the hypothesis you have just written, expressed as a range.
Feasibility is not technical difficulty. In 2026 the technical difficulty of almost everything on a typical shortlist has collapsed, which means ranking by it tells you very little. What actually determines whether a use case can be delivered is a different set of questions:

Does the data exist, at the grain you need, for long enough to see a pattern?
Is there a named decision-maker who has agreed to change what they do?
Can you get access without a six-month data-sharing negotiation?
Is there a control group, or any other way to know afterwards whether it worked?

The fourth question disqualifies more use cases than any technical constraint, and it is rarely on anybody’s feasibility checklist. A project that cannot be evaluated will be judged on whether people liked it, which means it will be defunded the first time the budget tightens regardless of what it delivered.
Sequence rather than rank. It is tempting to treat the top-right quadrant as a to-do list in value order, but that ordering ignores what each project leaves behind. Your first project should usually be the one that builds the capability the next three depend on — the pipeline, the definitions, the access — which tends to be unglamorous and is rarely the highest-value item on the sheet. Teams that begin with their largest prize are attempting their hardest problem with their least developed plumbing, and when it goes badly the conclusion drawn is usually “analytics does not work here” rather than “we sequenced that badly”.

Core lab · 25 minutes


Write the one-line value hypothesis for the use case in your charter. Volume × rate × improvement × unit economics.


List exactly three assumptions, ranked by leverage.


Give the top assumption a low / mid / high and recompute. Report the range, not the midpoint.


Answer the four feasibility questions. Be honest about the fourth.


Place your use case and two others from your organisation on the matrix.


Sceptic: pick the assumption they ranked third and argue it is actually first.




Stretch
Take the use case you placed lowest on the matrix and find the version of it that moves right — same value, better feasibility. In practice this nearly always means one of three moves: narrowing the population, shortening the time horizon, or replacing a model with a rule that captures most of the same signal.
A rule that captures 60% of the value and ships in a fortnight beats a model that captures 90% and ships in April, because the rule starts compounding four months earlier and teaches you what the model would need to do. Say that out loud in your own organisation once and see how the conversation changes.


Copilot check
Give the assistant your value hypothesis and this instruction:

Here is a value hypothesis for an analytics use case. Do not improve it. Instead: (1) identify every number in it that is an assumption rather than a measurement; (2) for each, tell me what evidence would be needed to replace it, and roughly what that evidence would cost to obtain; (3) tell me which single assumption, if wrong by a factor of two, changes the decision; (4) give me the strongest argument a sceptical CFO would make against the whole case.

The fourth request is the one that earns its keep. An assistant asked to critique produces something quite different from the same assistant asked to help, and the difference lies entirely in how you framed the request. That framing is a skill in its own right, and it will be worth more to you this week than any syntax you pick up.

title: Sizing the prize
text:
Takeaways

Every analytics business case contains an invented number. Put it on one line, in front, with a range.
Exactly three assumptions, ranked by leverage.
Feasibility is about data, decision ownership, access and measurability — not about technical difficulty.
Sequence by what capability the next three use cases need. Do not start with the biggest prize.

title: Where the data lives
text:
One page, five boxes
Data estates look bewilderingly different from the outside, mostly because every vendor gives its box a different name. Underneath, they are the same five stages in every organisation and every sector, and once you can see the five, the product names stop mattering.





flowchart LR
  S["<b>Sources</b><br/>ERP · CRM · core banking<br/>POS · WMS · HR system<br/>spreadsheets · APIs"]
  L["<b>Landing</b><br/>raw copies<br/>files, as they arrived"]
  W["<b>Warehouse</b><br/>modelled, conformed<br/>facts and dimensions"]
  M["<b>Marts & models</b><br/>per function<br/>the numbers people quote"]
  C["<b>Consumption</b><br/>dashboards · reports<br/>notebooks · Excel"]
  S --> L --> W --> M --> C
  style S fill:#EEF3FA,stroke:#2E3A6E
  style L fill:#E9EEF7,stroke:#2E3A6E
  style W fill:#E4F1FB,stroke:#16549B,stroke-width:2px
  style M fill:#D9EEF6,stroke:#00699B
  style C fill:#D6F0EA,stroke:#00695C


 Five boxes. Every estate. The vendor names are noise. 



Reading left to right: systems that record what happened; a raw copy of what they sent; one modelled, agreed version; function-specific cuts of that version; and finally the places where people actually look. Three things about this picture are worth more than the picture itself.
The warehouse box is where the arguments happen. It is the only box where somebody has to decide what a customer is — whether a lapsed account is still one, whether two records with the same phone number are one person, whether a franchise counts. The source systems disagree with each other because each was built for its own purpose; the consumption layer simply assumes an answer; the warehouse is the one place that has to commit to a definition in writing. Where an organisation has no warehouse box, that commitment does not disappear. It gets made separately, and usually silently, inside each individual report — which is why two dashboards built by careful people can disagree without either of them containing a mistake.
Landing exists so that you can rebuild. It holds raw copies, unmodified, kept exactly as they arrived. For long stretches it looks like pure cost, since nobody queries it and it only grows. Its value appears on the day a definition changes and somebody asks for three years of history restated on the new basis. If you kept the raw copies, that is a re-run. If you only kept the modelled output, it is an archaeology project with an uncertain ending.
Many organisations have all five boxes several times over. Finance built a stack; marketing built one; the digital team built one. Each is internally coherent and none quite reconciles with the others. This is worth understanding rather than deploring, because the cause is structural: the warehouse box is the expensive, slow one, and every function has had to keep moving. The useful question is not “who allowed this?” but “which of these is going to become the agreed one, and what would it take?”
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Where the data lives
text:
The grain question
If you take one sentence from this session, take this one, and learn to ask for it by name:

One row per _____ per _____ per _____.

That sentence is called the grain of a table, and it says what a single row represents. Fill in the blanks for any table and a whole class of mistakes becomes impossible, because you now know what you are adding up when you total a column.







Table
Grain




fmcg_sell_out.csv
One row per depot per SKU per week


bank_customers.csv
One row per customer, as at the snapshot date


supply_chain_pos.csv
One row per purchase order line


b2b_funnel.csv
One row per lead


ab_test_checkout.csv
One row per user, per experiment



Now read that table a second time, more slowly. Two of those grains contain a decision that somebody made on your behalf, and both decisions have consequences.
bank_customers.csv is “as at the snapshot date”, which is a polite way of saying it has no history. Every customer appears once, described as they are today. That is perfectly usable for reporting the current book — and it makes it impossible to ask what a customer looked like three months before they left, which is exactly the question a churn model is built from. A customer table with no history is a very common shape and an expensive one, and it is worth finding out on Monday whether yours has history or only a snapshot, because the answer determines what you can promise.
ab_test_checkout.csv is one row per user per experiment. Read literally, that allows the same user to appear twice — once in each of two experiments running at the same time. If that happened, the two experiments are influencing each other’s results, and nothing in the file records it. This is not a flaw in the file so much as a limit on what the file can tell you, and it is the kind of limit that only becomes visible when you say the grain out loud.

Grain, said differently
If nobody can state the grain of a table in one sentence, then no total computed from that table can be relied on — not because the arithmetic is wrong, but because nobody knows what is being added up.
This makes a good question to carry into a meeting where you have thirty seconds and a number you have never seen before. “Where did this come from?” gets you a system name and tells you very little, because everybody has an answer to it. “One row per what?” is harder to answer from memory, and the quality of the pause tells you a great deal about how carefully the number was built.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Where the data lives
text:
Star schemas, without the jargon
Warehouses are usually organised in a shape called a star schema, and behind the name there is one idea: separate the things that happen from the things that exist.

Facts are things that happen. Each has a date, one or more quantities, and references to the things involved. They are long and thin, and there are millions of them. A sale. A purchase order. A call. A payment.
Dimensions are things that exist. They describe. They are short and wide, and there are thousands of them at most. A customer. A product. A depot. A supplier. A date.

The name comes from the picture: one fact table in the middle, dimensions around it, joined in like the points of a star.





flowchart TD
  D1["dim_depot<br/><i>depot_code · region · state</i>"]
  D2["dim_product<br/><i>sku · category · pack · cost</i>"]
  D3["dim_date<br/><i>week · month · quarter · year</i>"]
  F["<b>fact_sell_out</b><br/><i>one row per depot per SKU per week</i><br/>units · price · revenue · promo flags"]
  D1 --> F
  D2 --> F
  D3 --> F
  style F fill:#D9EEF6,stroke:#00699B,stroke-width:3px
  style D1 fill:#EEF3FA,stroke:#2E3A6E
  style D2 fill:#EEF3FA,stroke:#2E3A6E
  style D3 fill:#F6EFE0,stroke:#8A6D2F


 The distributor’s star. One fact, three dimensions, one date table. 



Why this matters commercially rather than aesthetically: the shape is what makes a Power BI model fast, and — more importantly — what makes it consistent. When every measure is defined once against the fact table and every filter comes from a dimension, two people slicing the same number in different ways get answers that reconcile, because they are using the same definition with different filters applied. When measures are instead defined inside individual reports, each report carries its own quiet variant of the definition, and reconciling them becomes somebody’s monthly job.
The date dimension deserves a sentence of its own. Build a real date table: one row per day, carrying week, month, quarter, fiscal period, holiday flags and, in Nigeria, the public holidays that move from year to year. It feels like clerical work and it is probably the highest-leverage twenty minutes in the entire model, because it is what turns “the same period last year” from an argument into a click — and it is what stops a fiscal calendar being re-implemented, slightly differently, in four separate reports.

Open the dimension and count
Open fmcg_depots.csv. It is the smallest file in the course — one row per depot, a dozen columns — and it is exactly the kind of table that gets waved through, because there is visibly not much in it to go wrong.
Two minutes, now, before you go to coffee:

How many depots does the business have? Count them from this file.
How many rows does this file have?
If those two numbers are not the same, what would you expect to happen when you join it to something?

Whatever you find, leave it exactly as it is today. Write it in your failure logbook and do not fix it. It has somewhere to be tomorrow afternoon in 2.4, and a defect that bites you in front of your own table is worth about ten that somebody pointed out to you.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Where the data lives
section: Where the data physically is — a legal question
text:
Where the data physically is — a legal question
Three questions that your IT function can usually answer within a day, and that most executives have never had reason to ask:

Which of our systems store personal data outside Nigeria? In most organisations that will include the CRM, the HR system and email, and it may include the core platform. The answer is rarely a surprise once somebody looks; it is just that nobody has looked.
What is the lawful basis for that transfer under the NDPA 2023? There is a correct answer for each system, and there may not yet be a documented one — which is a normal place to start from, and a much better one than assuming the question does not arise.
If we put customer data into an AI assistant, where does it go, and is that transfer covered? This is the question that determines what your team is actually permitted to do with the tools taught this week.

We are not answering these today — Friday is given over to them. But it is worth asking this week, because the answers take time to obtain and they constrain what your capstone can be.
There is a practical consequence, and it is the reason this appears on Day 1 rather than Day 5: there is a version of every technique in this programme that runs entirely on your own laptop, with no data leaving it. Local models, local query engines, local everything. That version is somewhat slower and, in places, slightly less capable. For a bank’s customer records, that is usually the right trade — and knowing the option exists changes what you are able to say yes to when somebody asks whether the data can be analysed at all.

Core lab · 20 minutes


Draw your estate. Five boxes. Name the actual systems in each. One page, by hand.


Circle the box where your organisation argues about definitions.


Name the three tables your capstone needs, and write the grain of each as a sentence.


For each, note: does it have history, or only a current snapshot?


Write down the one question about data residency you will ask your IT function this week.




Stretch
Draw the star schema your capstone needs: one fact table, its grain, and the dimensions it joins to.
Then pick the dimension in your own organisation that you would least like to bet on — the one most likely to have gained an extra row along the way, through a duplicate, a rename recorded as a new entry, or two entities that were merged in the business but never merged in the system. Write down how you would check whether that has happened, in one query.
crumbs: Day 1 — Strategy, value and what AI actually changed

title: Where the data lives
text:
Takeaways

Five boxes: sources, landing, warehouse, marts, consumption. Vendor names are noise.
“One row per what?” is the highest-yield question available to a non-technical executive.
Facts happen; dimensions exist. Build a real date table.
Where the data physically sits is a legal question, and there is always a local-only version of the work.

title: SQL as the lingua franca
section: Why SQL, and why writing it is no longer the point
text:
Why SQL, and why writing it is no longer the point
SQL is the one language that every data platform you will ever buy has in common. Your warehouse speaks it. Power BI generates it underneath the visuals. Your core banking extract is defined in it. Your data team argues about business rules in it. It has outlived four generations of tooling around it and it will comfortably outlive the current one — so the ability to read it is a durable skill in a field where most skills are not.
What has changed is that it has become readable in an afternoon. The expensive part of learning SQL was never the vocabulary; it was the blank page — knowing which of six constructions to reach for and in what order, which took months of practice. That part is now handled for you, on request, in seconds.
So this session inverts the usual teaching order. You will not learn to compose queries. You will learn to read, predict and audit them. The test at the end is not “can you write this?” but “can you say what this query will do to the data before you run it, and be right?” That skill is what lets you supervise work you did not do — which, for most people in this room, is the actual job.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: SQL as the lingua franca
text:
The six verbs
Every analytical SQL query in existence is some arrangement of six ideas. Learn the ideas and the syntax stops being the obstacle.



Verb
The idea
SQL
The one-word version




1
Pick rows
WHERE
filter


2
Pick columns
SELECT
choose


3
Make new columns
SELECT ... AS
derive


4
Collapse to groups
GROUP BY
summarise


5
Put in order
ORDER BY
arrange


6
Bring tables together
JOIN
combine



Five of those six are safe, in a specific sense: if you get them wrong, you generally get an obviously wrong answer or an error. The sixth behaves differently. A join can quietly change how many rows you have, and every total computed afterwards changes with it — with no error, no warning and a result that still looks entirely plausible. That is why it has a session to itself this afternoon.
The same six ideas exist in R’s tidyverse and in Python’s pandas, with different spellings. Learn them once as ideas and you can read all three, which matters because your organisation almost certainly contains all three.

SQLR (tidyverse)Python (pandas)


SELECT
  depot_code,                                    -- choose
  SUM(units_sold)  AS units,                     -- summarise
  SUM(revenue_ngn) AS revenue,                   -- summarise
  SUM(revenue_ngn) / SUM(units_sold) AS asp      -- derive
FROM 'fmcg_sell_out.csv'
WHERE week_starting >= DATE '2025-01-01'         -- filter
  AND on_promotion = 0
GROUP BY depot_code                              -- summarise, by what
ORDER BY revenue DESC;                           -- arrange


library(tidyverse)

read_csv("data/fmcg_sell_out.csv") |>
  filter(week_starting >= as.Date("2025-01-01"),   # filter
         on_promotion == 0) |>
  group_by(depot_code) |>                          # summarise, by what
  summarise(units   = sum(units_sold,  na.rm = TRUE),
            revenue = sum(revenue_ngn, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(asp = revenue / units) |>                 # derive
  arrange(desc(revenue))                           # arrange


import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("data/fmcg_sell_out.csv", parse_dates=["week_starting"])

(df[(df.week_starting >= "2025-01-01") & (df.on_promotion == 0)]
   .groupby("depot_code")
   .agg(units=("units_sold", "sum"), revenue=("revenue_ngn", "sum"))
   .assign(asp=lambda d: d.revenue / d.units)
   .sort_values("revenue", ascending=False))



Read the three side by side and follow one verb through all of them — the filter, say. Same idea, three spellings, and none of the differences is conceptual. Once that is visible, the “which language should we standardise on?” debate becomes a good deal less consequential than it usually feels to the people having it. What matters is that everybody can read the answer, and the ideas above are the part that transfers.

The na.rm = TRUE in the R version is a decision, not a default
That argument tells R to ignore missing values when it adds the column up. It is typed so routinely that it hardly registers as a choice — but it is one.
In this dataset, 789 rows have a missing units_sold, because a stockout was recorded as “unknown” rather than as zero. Dropping those rows removes the worst trading weeks from any average you compute, which pushes the answer upward in a way nothing on screen will indicate. SQL’s SUM does exactly the same thing, and without even a flag to remind you it happened.
Neither behaviour is wrong, and neither is a bug. Both simply require a decision from you: is missing here the same as zero? In this dataset the two are close — the depot sold nothing because it had nothing to sell — so treating the blanks as zeroes is defensible, and worth writing down. In a survey dataset the two are emphatically different, and treating a non-response as a zero would be a serious error. The code cannot tell the difference between those cases, and neither can the assistant that wrote it. You can, because you know where the data came from.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: SQL as the lingua franca
text:
Reading a query out loud
Here is the discipline, and it is worth practising deliberately for a week until it becomes automatic: before you run anything, say what it does in English, in the order the database will actually do it.
Take this one:
SELECT p.category,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.sku)              AS skus,
       SUM(s.revenue_ngn)                 AS revenue,
       AVG(s.discount_pct)                AS avg_discount
FROM 'fmcg_sell_out.csv' s
JOIN 'fmcg_products.csv' p USING (sku)
WHERE s.on_promotion = 1
GROUP BY p.category
HAVING SUM(s.revenue_ngn) > 1e9
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
Out loud, in execution order:

Take the sell-out rows. Attach product attributes by SKU. Keep only the promotional weeks. Collapse to one row per category. Count distinct SKUs, total the revenue, average the discount. Then throw away any category whose total is under a billion naira. Sort by revenue.

Notice that the reading order is not the writing order: the database starts with the tables and the filters, does the grouping next, and only then applies HAVING and the sort. Once you read queries in that order, two things in this one stand out — and neither is a question of syntax.
AVG(s.discount_pct) is an unweighted average of week-rows. Every row counts equally, regardless of how much money went through it. Take a category with two SKUs on promotion in a week: one sells ₦100m at a 5% discount, the other sells ₦2m at a 40% discount. AVG reports 22.5%, because it averages 5 and 40. The discount you actually paid is (100 × 5 + 2 × 40) ÷ 102, which is about 5.7% — the small SKU had a deep discount and almost none of the volume. If the question is “what discount are we actually paying?”, the answer is SUM(units*price*discount)/SUM(units*price) rather than AVG. This is among the most common quiet errors in commercial SQL, and it is invisible in the output, because a wrong average looks exactly like a right one.
HAVING filters after grouping; WHERE filters before. In this query, WHERE decides which rows go into each category total and HAVING decides which category totals survive. Move the condition from one to the other and you are asking a different question — the first would drop individual weeks below a billion naira, which is not what anybody meant. Assistants generally place these correctly. Humans reading assistants’ output frequently do not notice which one was used, and the two produce results that are equally plausible on the page.

The read-aloud test
If a query cannot be said in English in under twenty seconds, it is doing too much at once to be reviewed reliably.
The fix is to break it into named steps using a CTE — WITH step_one AS (...), step_two AS (...) — where each step is named for what it produces. A CTE, or common table expression, is simply a temporary named result you can build the next step on top of. The database does not care either way; the person reviewing the query in six months does, and so do you in six months.
You can ask for this directly: “rewrite this as a sequence of named CTEs, one per logical step, with a comment on each saying what it produces and what its grain is.” What comes back is something you can audit a step at a time, which is a different kind of artefact from something you can only run and hope.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: SQL as the lingua franca
section: Window functions — the one advanced thing worth knowing
text:
Window functions — the one advanced thing worth knowing
There is exactly one piece of so-called advanced SQL that repays the effort immediately in commercial work: the ability to calculate something per group without collapsing the rows away.
The ordinary GROUP BY gives you one row per depot and loses the detail underneath. Often that is not what you want — you want to keep every SKU line and, beside it, that SKU’s share of its depot’s total. That is what a window function does.
-- Each SKU's share of its depot's revenue, and its rank within the depot.
SELECT
  depot_code,
  sku,
  SUM(revenue_ngn) AS revenue,
  SUM(revenue_ngn) / SUM(SUM(revenue_ngn)) OVER (PARTITION BY depot_code) AS share,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY depot_code ORDER BY SUM(revenue_ngn) DESC)    AS rank_in_depot
FROM 'fmcg_sell_out.csv'
GROUP BY depot_code, sku
QUALIFY rank_in_depot <= 5
ORDER BY depot_code, rank_in_depot;
The phrase to hold on to is OVER (PARTITION BY ...), which says: do this calculation separately within each depot, but keep all the rows. The word “partition” here means nothing more sinister than “group, for the purposes of this one calculation”. That single construction is how you get shares, ranks, running totals, moving averages, period-on-period changes and “compared with the same week last year” — which between them account for most of what a commercial dashboard actually contains.
You will not be asked to write this from memory. You will be asked to read it and say what it produces, which, having read the paragraph above, you can now do.

Core lab · 30 minutes
Driver and Sceptic. Swap roles from yesterday.


Ask the assistant: “top 5 SKUs by revenue in each depot for 2025, from fmcg_sell_out.csv, DuckDB SQL.” Do not run it yet.


Sceptic reads it aloud in English before it runs. Predict the number of rows.


Run it. Were you right? If not, why not?


Now ask for “average discount by category”. Read it. Is it weighted? Fix it.


Ask the assistant to rewrite your fixed query as named CTEs with grain comments.


Add today’s failure logbook entry.


Predicting the row count before running is the part that feels artificial and is the part that teaches. A prediction you got wrong is a precise piece of information about which part of the query you misread.


Stretch
Commission — and then audit — a query that answers this: which SKU–depot combinations have both above-median revenue and above-median stockout rate? Those are the lines where poor availability is costing real money rather than notional money, and it is precisely the shortlist a supply planner could act on next week.
Then the harder version: express it as a single query using window functions rather than two queries and a join. Ask the assistant for it, then explain to your Sceptic why the result is correct. If you cannot explain it, you have a query you can run but not defend, which is the thing this session exists to prevent.


Copilot check
Three failure modes turn up in assistant-written SQL often enough to be worth watching for, in rough order of frequency:

Column names that do not exist. Where you have not supplied a schema, one gets inferred, and the inference is plausible rather than correct. Pasting the column list takes ten seconds and removes most of the problem.
AVG where you needed a weighted average. The request is answered literally, and “average discount” literally means the average of the discount column.
Dialect drift. QUALIFY works in DuckDB and Snowflake but not in PostgreSQL, and EXTRACT syntax varies between engines. Naming the dialect in the prompt — “DuckDB SQL” — settles it.

And one more that is not a failure of the machine at all: it will happily aggregate a table that has never been deduplicated, because it has no way of knowing whether the rows in front of it are the rows that should be there. You will have a way of knowing from about 2pm today.

title: SQL as the lingua franca
text:
Takeaways

Six ideas: filter, choose, derive, summarise, arrange, combine. Five are safe.
Read queries aloud in execution order before running them.
AVG is rarely the average you meant in a commercial context.
Ask for named CTEs with grain comments. It is the difference between code you can audit and code you can only trust.

title: Excel as the bridge
text:
The honest position
Excel is not the problem. Excel is often in the wrong position in the chain.
In 2026 the natural place for a spreadsheet is at the two ends of the work: it is where data arrives from other systems, and it is where the board reads the result. What has moved away is the middle — the transformation, the joining, the recalculation every month — not because a spreadsheet cannot do those things, but because they are now done faster, more reproducibly and far more auditably somewhere else.
That is a demotion from engine to interface, and it is worth being precise about it, because the version of this argument that circulates online — “stop using Excel” — is both wrong and useless to anybody actually running a finance function. Nobody is going to stop, they should not stop, and an analytics team that insists on it will simply be routed around.

What Excel is still the best tool in the world for

Small, structured, judgement-heavy modelling. A three-scenario business case that a CFO wants to poke at live in a meeting: change a growth rate, watch the answer move, argue about it. Nothing else comes close, because the model and its interface are the same object.
The last mile of a number. Somebody senior wants to see it, sort it, filter it and put it in a paper. Give them a spreadsheet and let them work the way they work.
Being the universal interchange format. Every system exports to it and every person can open it, which is a genuine and underrated property.
Ad-hoc arithmetic under time pressure. Twenty numbers, four minutes, one answer.

Insisting that these move into code is how analytics teams acquire a reputation for being difficult to work with, and it is usually wrong on the merits as well.


Where it starts to cost more than it saves

As a database. Once a workbook becomes the source of a fact rather than a view of one, there is no lineage, no version history, and no controlled definition — the number exists because the file says so.
As a pipeline. Fourteen sequential sheets, each referencing the last, with a refresh order that has to be performed by hand in a particular sequence that one person knows. This is among the most common operational risks in mid-sized companies, and it tends to come to light at the least convenient moment, when that person is unavailable.
At scale. Not primarily because of the row limit, but because a 400,000-row workbook cannot be reviewed by a colleague, tested automatically, or compared with last month’s version to see what changed.
For anything that must be reproducible. A spreadsheet cannot tell you what differs between this month’s version and last month’s. Every other tool in this stack can, and that is often the whole reason to move a process.
Where a single-cell edit can silently change a total. The issue is not that people are careless — they are usually careful. It is that the tool offers no way to notice, so care is the only defence available.

title: Excel as the bridge
section: Power Query is the bridge, and it is under-used
text:
Power Query is the bridge, and it is under-used
Many long-standing Excel users have never opened Power Query, which is a pity, because it is the best on-ramp from spreadsheet thinking to pipeline thinking that exists — and it ships inside the product they already have and already pay for.
What it gives you that formulas do not:

Steps, in order, named. Every transformation appears as a listed step that you can inspect, rename, reorder or delete, and the list is the recipe. That is a pipeline, whether or not anybody uses the word.
Refresh. Point it at a folder or a database and next month’s file flows through the same steps, in the same order, without anybody repeating the work by hand.
It does not touch the source. The raw file stays exactly as it arrived, which means a mistake in step three is always recoverable.

The mental model transfers precisely. A Power Query step list is a sequence of CTEs, and somebody comfortable with Remove Columns → Filter Rows → Group By → Merge Queries already understands SELECT / WHERE / GROUP BY / JOIN. They have simply never been told that the thing they do on Thursday afternoons has a second name and a job title attached to it.

The four-step demo
Data → Get Data → From File → From Folder. Point it at the data/ folder. Two workbooks are waiting there: board_pack.xlsx, which arrives with three sheets and two title rows above the header, and regional_report.xlsx, which was laid out for reading rather than computing.

Combine — it stacks every CSV in the folder into one table.
Filter Rows — drop the weeks you do not want.
Group By — depot and SKU, sum the units.
Merge Queries — attach the depot dimension.

Four steps, no formulas written, and the whole thing refreshable next month. Then look at the formula bar: Power Query has been writing M code the entire time. You have been reading a pipeline without anybody telling you that is what it was.
Keep one number in view as you go: the row count at each step. Write it down before step 4 and again afterwards. Attaching attributes from a dimension is supposed to describe the rows you already have — so if the count moves, what would that imply about the dimension? Hold the question, and your two numbers, until 2.4.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: Excel as the bridge
section: Crossing the boundary in both directions
text:
Crossing the boundary in both directions
Excel in. Read the workbook where it sits. No export step, no “save as CSV”, and no opportunity for somebody to have opened it, changed a cell and saved it on the way past.
INSTALL excel; LOAD excel;

SELECT * FROM read_xlsx('data/board_pack.xlsx', sheet = 'Sales', header = true);
library(readxl)
sales <- read_excel("data/board_pack.xlsx", sheet = "Sales")

# The sheet with the merged cells and the title rows above the header
sales <- read_excel("data/board_pack.xlsx", sheet = "Sales", skip = 4)
The skip = 4 in the second call is doing something worth understanding rather than copying: it tells the reader that the first four lines of the sheet are decoration — a title, a subtitle, a note, a blank — and that the real header row comes after them. Getting that number wrong is the single most common reason a read “works” but produces a table whose column names are ...1, ...2, ...3.
Excel out. Write a formatted workbook from your pipeline, so that the last mile is a spreadsheet even though the arithmetic never was.
library(openxlsx)

wb <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb, "Depot summary")
writeDataTable(wb, "Depot summary", depot_summary)
freezePane(wb, "Depot summary", firstRow = TRUE)
setColWidths(wb, "Depot summary", cols = 1:6, widths = "auto")
saveWorkbook(wb, "outputs/depot_summary.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)
That pattern — pipeline in code, delivery in Excel — is the right answer for most organisations most of the time. It is also a far easier internal sell than asking a finance team to change how they work, because from their side nothing changes except that the numbers now arrive already correct and can be traced back to a source.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: Excel as the bridge
text:
The unmerge-and-unpivot problem
Here is the most common real-world Excel-to-analysis task, and one that assistants happen to be genuinely excellent at. Somebody sends you a workbook that was laid out for reading rather than for computing: merged cells, a title row, months running across the top as columns, blank rows separating regions, and a total row somewhere in the middle.
The shape you need is one row per observation — one line for each region, depot and month, with the value beside it. The shape you have is a report. Converting between the two is called reshaping, or unpivoting, and it is four verbs.
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)

# regional_report.xlsx: two title rows, an italic draft warning, a blank row,
# then the header. Months across the top. The region written once and left blank
# for every subsequent depot. A total row in the middle. Currency stored as TEXT
# with a naira sign and thousands separators.
raw <- read_excel("data/regional_report.xlsx", skip = 4)

tidy <- raw |>
  fill(region, .direction = "down") |>               # unmerge merged cells FIRST
  filter(!is.na(depot), region != "Total") |>        # then kill the total row
  pivot_longer(cols = matches("^(Jan|Feb|Mar|Apr|May|Jun|Jul|Aug|Sep|Oct|Nov|Dec)$"),
               names_to = "month", values_to = "revenue") |>
  mutate(revenue = parse_number(as.character(revenue)))  # strip ₦ and commas

# The reconciliation. Do this every single time.
stopifnot(abs(sum(tidy$revenue, na.rm = TRUE) -
              parse_number(as.character(total_row))) < 1)
Take the four verbs in turn. fill() copies the region name downwards into the blank cells beneath it, which is what a merged cell actually looks like once it has been read into a table — the value is present in the first row of the merge and missing in the rest. filter() then removes the total row and any empty lines. pivot_longer() turns the twelve month columns into two columns, one holding the month name and one holding the value, which is what “one row per observation” requires. And parse_number() converts text like ₦1,240,000 into a number, because a currency symbol and thousands separators make a column text as far as any reader is concerned.
Of those, fill() doing the work of unmerging is the trick that saves people the most time, and almost nobody discovers it unaided.
The order matters more than it looks. Fill before you filter. If you filter first, you delete the very rows that were about to carry each region label downwards, and the remaining labels then attach themselves to whichever depots happen to follow — quietly, with no error, and with every total still adding up to something plausible. It is the same class of problem as a join that changes your row count, wearing a spreadsheet’s clothes.

Core lab · 25 minutes


Open Power Query. Point it at the data/ folder. Combine, filter, group, merge. Note the row count at every step.


Now do the identical four steps in SQL. Compare the two step lists side by side.


Take a real report-shaped workbook — yours, or the one on the shared drive — and get it to one row per observation.


Write the result back out as a formatted workbook.


Sceptic: find one number in the finished workbook and trace it all the way back to a raw row. If you cannot, the pipeline is not finished.


That last step is the one to protect if you run short of time. A pipeline you cannot trace backwards is one you will have to defend on trust, and trust is exactly what this week is trying to replace with evidence.


Stretch
Think of the workbook in your organisation that is quietly doing the job of a database — the one that is the source of a number rather than a view of it, and that one person refreshes in a particular order each month.
Write down three things: what happens if that person is unavailable for a fortnight; what the pipeline version would look like expressed as four named steps; and what it would take to get there, in people and weeks. Bring it to the Day 30 clinic.
Most cohorts turn up several of these, and at least one usually feeds a regulatory return. They are not signs of a badly run function — they are what happens when a capable person solves a real problem with the tool they had — but they are worth converting before somebody’s annual leave converts them for you.


Copilot check
Assistants are very good at the unmerge-and-unpivot problem, often better than a person, because it is pattern-matching against a shape they have seen an enormous number of times. Hand one a description of the layout and it will produce the reshaping code faster than you could type the file path.
What they cannot know is whether the total row you just deleted was actually a total, or a region legitimately called “Total Nigeria”. Both look identical from inside the file, and a rule written to drop the first will happily drop the second.
So the rule for this session: after any reshaping, check that the sum of the tidy table equals the sum you started with. One line, every time, and it catches both the row you should not have dropped and the one you should have.
sum(tidy$revenue, na.rm = TRUE) == sum(raw_total, na.rm = TRUE)

title: Excel as the bridge
text:
Takeaways

Excel is where data arrives and where the board reads it. It is no longer where the work happens.
Power Query is a pipeline. Learn it and you have already learned the mental model.
Pipeline in code, delivery in Excel, is the right answer for most organisations.
After every reshape, check the total still reconciles.

title: Data quality as a contract
text:
From cleaning to testing
Most organisations approach data quality as a clean-up: somebody is given a fortnight, works through a table, fixes what they find, and the table is declared clean. It is a perfectly sensible response to the problem as it appears, and it usually works — for about six weeks. Then the table is dirty again, because nothing in the process prevented new defects arriving; it only removed the ones that had already arrived.
The alternative is to treat quality as a contract: a written set of conditions the data must satisfy, expressed once, checked automatically every time the data moves, and producing a result that is either pass or fail. The word “contract” is doing real work there. A contract is agreed in advance, it is specific, and both sides can tell whether it has been honoured. “The data should be clean” is none of those things; “every purchase order has a receipt date on or after its order date” is all three.
The shift, then, is from cleaning to testing — from an activity that consumes somebody’s time repeatedly to an asset that keeps working after they have moved on. It has three consequences worth spelling out.
It is cheap after the first time. Writing the rule takes ten minutes; running it takes milliseconds and happens automatically. The cost is paid once and the benefit accrues every month afterwards, which is an unusually good shape for anything in this field.
It moves the argument to the right place. “The data is bad” is a complaint, and the person receiving it can only really respond by feeling got at. “Rule 7 failed: 126 purchase orders have a receipt date before their order date” is something else entirely — a ticket, with a count, a definition and an owner. Nobody has to be defensive about a number.
It makes trust legible. A dashboard with a green quality badge beside it is a different object from one without. That matters most for the executive who has been given a wrong number before, and has since been quietly discounting everything that arrives from the same source. A badge does not argue with them; it gives them somewhere to look.

Types are not the point
Most automated data checking stops at types and nulls: is this column really a date, is it populated, is the identifier a string of the right length. Those checks are worth having and they are almost never the ones that matter, for a simple reason — the defects that cost money are all type-valid.
received_date < po_date is two perfectly good dates in perfectly good columns. A duplicated dimension row is a perfectly good row. A churn definition that disagrees with finance’s is two perfectly good flags.
Every one of those passes a schema check comfortably, because a schema describes the shape of the data and says nothing about whether it can be true.
The rules worth writing are therefore business rules that cannot be false — statements about the world that hold whatever the data happens to say, so that a violation is necessarily a defect rather than a surprise. Receipts follow orders. Percentages sum to one hundred. A customer cannot churn twice. Units sold cannot be negative. Every transaction belongs to a depot that exists. Nobody is 126 years old.
Those come from the business rather than from the schema, which is why the person writing them has to understand the business. It is also why this is not a task you can hand downwards: the rules are only as good as the domain knowledge behind them.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: Data quality as a contract
section: Six rules for the course data
text:
Six rules for the course data
Below is a suite written against the course data. Read it as a worked example rather than as a template — the interesting part is the shape of the rules, not the syntax.
Each rule is expressed the same way: a sentence describing what must be true, and a query that counts the rows where it is not. Zero failures means pass. Anything above zero means the rule caught something, and the count tells you how big the something is.
Note also that this suite is written expecting failures. A suite where everything passes on the first run has usually not been written honestly — it has been written to describe the data rather than to interrogate it.

SQLR (pointblank)Python (pointblank)


-- A quality report as one query. Each row is a rule; failures > 0 is a fail.

WITH r1 AS (  -- Rule 1: the fact table is at its stated grain
  SELECT 'fact grain is unique (depot x sku x week)' AS rule,
         COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT (week_starting, depot_code, sku)) AS failures
  FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv'
), r2 AS (    -- Rule 2: the depot dimension has one row per depot
  SELECT 'depot dimension key is unique',
         (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM 'data/fmcg_depots.csv')
       - (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT depot_code) FROM 'data/fmcg_depots.csv')
), r3 AS (    -- Rule 3: every fact row has a valid depot
  SELECT 'every sale maps to a known depot',
         COUNT(*)
  FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv' s
  LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT depot_code FROM 'data/fmcg_depots.csv') d
    USING (depot_code)
  WHERE d.depot_code IS NULL
), r4 AS (    -- Rule 4: units are never negative
  SELECT 'units_sold is never negative',
         COUNT(*) FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv' WHERE units_sold < 0
), r5 AS (    -- Rule 5: receipts follow orders
  SELECT 'goods are received after they are ordered',
         COUNT(*) FROM 'data/supply_chain_pos.csv'
         WHERE CAST(received_date AS DATE) < CAST(po_date AS DATE)
), r6 AS (    -- Rule 6: discount only ever appears on promotional weeks
  SELECT 'discount implies on_promotion',
         COUNT(*) FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv'
         WHERE discount_pct > 0 AND on_promotion = 0
)
SELECT * FROM r1 UNION ALL SELECT * FROM r2 UNION ALL SELECT * FROM r3
UNION ALL SELECT * FROM r4 UNION ALL SELECT * FROM r5 UNION ALL SELECT * FROM r6;
The first two rules deserve a second look, because they use the same trick. Counting all the rows and subtracting the count of distinct combinations gives you exactly the number of surplus rows: if the two counts agree, every combination appears once and the difference is zero. It is the cheapest uniqueness test there is, and it works on any set of columns you care to name.


library(pointblank)
library(tidyverse)

sales  <- read_csv("data/fmcg_sell_out.csv")
depots <- read_csv("data/fmcg_depots.csv")
pos    <- read_csv("data/supply_chain_pos.csv")

agent <- create_agent(
    tbl = sales,
    tbl_name = "fmcg_sell_out",
    label = "TDBG data contract — sell-out"
  ) |>
  rows_distinct(columns = vars(week_starting, depot_code, sku),
                label = "Grain: one row per depot per SKU per week") |>
  col_vals_gte(units_sold, value = 0, na_pass = TRUE,
               label = "Units sold is never negative") |>
  col_vals_in_set(depot_code, set = unique(depots$depot_code),
                  label = "Every sale maps to a known depot") |>
  col_vals_between(discount_pct, 0, 0.5,
                   label = "Discount is between 0% and 50%") |>
  col_vals_expr(expr = ~ !(discount_pct > 0 & on_promotion == 0),
                label = "A discount implies a promotion") |>
  interrogate()

agent                          # renders a readable pass/fail report
export_report(agent, filename = "outputs/quality_sell_out.html")
pointblank is worth knowing about specifically because of the last two lines. The interrogate() call runs every rule you have attached to the agent, and printing the agent renders a coloured pass/fail table rather than a console dump. The label on each rule is what appears in that table, so writing the labels as plain English sentences is what makes the output readable by somebody who will never see the code.


import pointblank as pb
import polars as pl

sales = pl.read_csv("data/fmcg_sell_out.csv")

validation = (
    pb.Validate(data=sales, tbl_name="fmcg_sell_out",
                label="TDBG data contract — sell-out")
    .rows_distinct(columns_subset=["week_starting", "depot_code", "sku"])
    .col_vals_ge(columns="units_sold", value=0, na_pass=True)
    .col_vals_between(columns="discount_pct", left=0, right=0.5)
    .interrogate()
)

validation                      # the same report, in Python
The Python library is a direct port of the R one, so the vocabulary transfers unchanged. If your organisation has both languages in use — most do — the same contract can be maintained in either without anybody having to relearn the idea.





What fails, and what each failure means










Rule
Failures
What it means




Fact grain is unique
214
An ETL job was re-run. Every total is overstated.


Depot dimension key is unique
1
The Abuja rename. Every join to it fans out.


Every sale maps to a known depot
0
Referential integrity is fine.


Units never negative
0
But see below — the nulls are the problem here, not negatives.


Receipts follow orders
126
A timezone bug in the WMS export. Mean lead time is understated.


Discount implies promotion
0
This one passes, and it should — that is what a control looks like.



Two of those counts repay a moment of arithmetic, because the interesting thing about a failure count is rarely the count itself.
214 surplus rows out of 55,474 is about four-tenths of one per cent, which sounds negligible and is not, because the duplicated rows are not a random sample of the file. They are whatever the re-run happened to cover, so their effect concentrates wherever that was. Subtract them and the table holds 55,260 genuine depot–SKU–week combinations, which is the number every subsequent total should be built on.
126 impossible receipt dates out of 9,000 purchase orders is 1.4% of the file. Again the share matters less than the shape: those rows do not simply add noise to the lead-time distribution, they add a negative tail that cannot exist, and a negative tail pulls the mean down. The 1.4% is small; its direction is not.
Note the overall shape of the result: three rules fail and three pass. A suite where nothing fails has not been written honestly, and a suite where everything fails will be switched off by Thursday. Both failure modes are common, and the second is more dangerous, because a switched-off suite looks exactly like a suite that has nothing to report.
Two rules are not in the suite above and should be. Write them:

units_sold is null only when stockout_flag = 1. All 789 nulls are stockouts, against 10 rows that record a genuine zero. So the rule passes — and that is the useful outcome, because it is what licenses the decision you are about to make in the pipeline: treating those nulls as zero. Without the rule you would be guessing; with it you have evidence, and the evidence is in the report where a reviewer can see it. A passing rule that authorises a judgement call is quietly one of the most valuable things a suite can contain.
Row count per week is stable. A step change in rows per period is the signature of a silent grain change, of the kind 2.4 described. It is the cheapest early warning there is.
