title: Data quality as a contract
text:
Where the suite runs
A contract only does its work if it runs somewhere it cannot be skipped. There are three places to put it, and they differ far more in effect than in effort.

In the notebook, by hand. Better than nothing, and it is how everybody starts. The difficulty is that it depends on somebody remembering, which works well for a few weeks and then stops.
In the pipeline, before the analysis step. The checks run every time the pipeline runs, and the pipeline stops if the contract fails. Nobody has to remember anything. This is the right default, and it is what tomorrow’s lab builds.
On the source extract, as a gate. The check runs where the data is produced, and a failure is raised against the team that produced it, with a rule number and a row count attached. This is the version that actually improves the data over time, because it puts the cost of a defect back where the defect was created rather than leaving it with the person who found it three systems downstream.

Level 3 is an organisational move rather than a technical one. The code is the same code; the difference is that somebody senior has said “we are not accepting this extract until rule 7 passes”, and has meant it. That is a decision for the person reading this page rather than for the analyst, and it is worth recognising it as the substantive one.

The severity column
Not every failure should stop a pipeline, and treating them all alike is how good suites get abandoned. Give every rule a severity when you write it:

Fatal — the analysis is invalid and there is no sensible way to proceed. Stop. (Grain is not unique: every total is wrong.)
Warn — the analysis proceeds, with a caveat printed on the output so that the reader sees it too. (126 impossible lead times, 1.4% of rows, excluded and noted.)
Note — logged and trended rather than acted on. (Null rate on units_sold was 1.2% last month and is 1.4% now.) The value here is the trend: a rate that drifts upward month after month is telling you something even while every individual month looks acceptable.

Without severity, a team faces a choice between stopping the pipeline constantly and turning the checks off altogether. Both happen. The second happens quietly, and it is usually discovered months later by somebody wondering why the report has stopped complaining.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: Data quality as a contract
section: The report a non-technical stakeholder reads
text:
The report a non-technical stakeholder reads
The output of a quality suite should be a single page: a green or red badge at the top, the date and time it ran, the number of rows checked, and one line per rule with its label, its severity and its failure count. Not a log file, and not a screenshot of a console.
That page then goes next to the dashboard, where the people relying on the numbers will see it without going looking. The effect on the conversation is out of proportion to the effort. “Do I trust this?” is an unanswerable question and slightly awkward to ask. “Which rule failed, and who owns it?” is a specific question with a specific answer, and it can be asked without implying anything about anybody.

Core lab · 20 minutes


Run the six-rule suite. Confirm you get 214, 1 and 126.


Add the two missing rules: nulls-versus-stockouts, and rows-per-week stability.


Write three rules that are specific to your business. Not types — business rules that cannot be false.


Assign a severity to each of your rules.


Export the report as HTML and read it as if you were the person who has to sign the number.


Sceptic: find a defect the suite would not catch. There is always one.


The third item is the one to spend your time on. The first two you can copy; the three rules that are true of your business and of nobody else’s are the ones that will still be catching things next year, and they are the ones only you can write.


Stretch
Try to write a rule that catches the review-corpus problem — a filter applied at extraction time that removed part of the population before the file was ever created.
You will find that you can only get close, and only by accident: the flag the filter was built on happens to have survived in the export, so a rule comparing the low-star share between the two groups would fire. Write it, and then notice what it depends on. Remove that one column and no rule in any suite can find the filter, because the information about what was removed is not present in what remains.
That is a limitation worth stating carefully, because it bounds everything else in this session:
A quality suite validates what arrived. It cannot validate what was removed before it left.
Which is the strongest argument in the programme for a habit that is procedural rather than technical: ask for the extraction query, not just the extract. The query tells you what was excluded. The extract, by construction, cannot.


Copilot check
Writing quality rules is one of the tasks assistants are genuinely excellent at, and it is worth using them for it properly. Give the column list and ask:

Here are the columns and types of a table, and here is what one row represents. Propose twelve data quality rules as business rules that cannot be false — not type checks. For each, give me the rule in English, the SQL that counts violations, and a severity of fatal, warn or note.

You will get twelve good rules in thirty seconds. In practice perhaps eight are worth keeping, two are things you would not have thought of, and the rest are near-duplicates or too generic. That is an excellent return on thirty seconds, and it is a far better use of an assistant than asking it to find problems in data it cannot see.
What it cannot know is anything that is true only of your business: that a negative quantity is a legitimate return in your operation, that your fiscal year starts in April, that account numbers beginning 07 are dormant by convention and have been since a migration in 2019. Those rules come from you, and they are the ones that catch the expensive things.
crumbs: Day 2 — Getting data you can trust

title: Data quality as a contract
text:
Takeaways

Quality is a contract, not a clean-up. Write rules once; run them forever.
Type checks catch almost nothing that matters. Write business rules that cannot be false.
Every rule gets a severity, or the suite gets switched off.
Push the gate upstream to the extract. That is an organisational decision, and it is yours.
A suite validates what arrived. Ask for the extraction query to find out what did not.

title: What is odd here?
section: The question is not “what is the average?”
text:
The question is not “what is the average?”
There are two quite different things people mean when they say they are analysing data, and keeping them apart is most of this session.
The first is checking an idea you already have. You suspect the Lagos depots are carrying the network, so you go and see whether the numbers agree. That is confirmatory analysis, and it asks “is this true?” It is valuable, it is what most reporting consists of, and it has one structural limitation: it can only ever inspect the thing you already suspected. Anything you did not think to suspect passes underneath it untouched.
The second is going and looking with no particular hypothesis, on the assumption that the data will contain something you did not expect. That is exploratory data analysis, usually shortened to EDA, and its question is “what is odd here?” John Tukey, the statistician who gave the field its name and most of its tools in the 1970s, described its purpose about as well as anyone has since: it exists to force you to notice what you were not expecting.
Both are necessary and they run in that order: explore first, so that you discover what the data actually contains; confirm second, so that you test the idea you have arrived at. Trouble arrives when an organisation does only the second, because a confirmatory analysis built on a file nobody has looked at is a careful answer to a question about a world that may not exist.
There is a reason this has become more valuable rather than less. An assistant will produce a mean, a median, a correlation and a chart of anything you point it at, in seconds, and it will usually get the arithmetic right. What it cannot do is be surprised. Surprise requires an expectation, and an expectation requires having spent years in a business — which is something you have and it does not. As the mechanical part of analysis gets cheaper, the scarce input becomes the person who looks at a number and thinks that cannot be right.

title: What is odd here?
text:
Five things, in this order
The order matters. Each step catches a class of problem that would otherwise contaminate every step after it, so working the list in sequence saves you from discovering at step five that step one had already invalidated the exercise.

1 · The shape of the file
Before any statistic at all, establish the basic facts of the object in front of you. How many rows, covering what period, at what grain — that is, what one row represents — and with what missing. In DuckDB there is a single command that does most of this for you.
SUMMARIZE SELECT * FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv';
SUMMARIZE returns one row per column, with its type, its minimum and maximum, its count of nulls and its count of distinct values. It repays the second it takes, provided you know what you are reading it for. Four things are worth looking for specifically.
Null counts that differ wildly between columns. If one column is largely blank and its neighbours are complete, something happened to that column in particular, and finding out what is usually more informative than filling the gaps.
A distinct count of 1. A column with exactly one value in it is a constant, and a constant column in a transactional file is nearly always the residue of something upstream — a flag that stopped being populated, a filter applied at extraction, a default never overwritten.
A distinct count equal to the row count on something that should repeat. If depot_code has as many distinct values as there are rows, it is not a depot code any more: it has been concatenated with something, or the grain is not what you were told.
Minimum or maximum values that cannot be true. Negative quantities, dates in 1900, percentages above one hundred. These are the cheapest defects to find, and none of the four requires any knowledge of the business — they are available to you in the first minute with a file you have never seen before.


2 · The calendar
Almost every disaster on this list turns out, on inspection, to be a calendar problem. Time is the dimension people are least careful with, partly because everybody feels they already understand it.
SELECT EXTRACT(year FROM week_starting) AS yr,
       COUNT(DISTINCT week_starting)    AS weeks,
       COUNT(*)                         AS rows,
       ROUND(SUM(revenue_ngn)/1e9, 2)   AS revenue_bn
FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
The query does one thing worth noticing: alongside the revenue it counts the periods. That second column is the one almost nobody asks for, and it is the one that saves you.


What this shows, and why your first chart of the week is wrong





Year
Weeks
Revenue
Revenue per week




2024
53
₦16.44bn
₦310m


2025
52
₦23.48bn
₦452m


2026
13
₦7.13bn
₦549m



The fourth column is not in the file; it is the third divided by the second, and it is where the interesting part lives. ₦16.44bn spread over 53 weeks is about ₦310m a week. ₦23.48bn over 52 weeks is about ₦452m a week. ₦7.13bn over 13 weeks is about ₦549m a week.
Now consider what happens without that fourth column. Ask an assistant for “revenue by year” and you will get three bars, correctly computed and correctly labelled. The third bar is ₦7.13bn against ₦23.48bn, which is 70% below the year before, and the deck more or less writes itself: the business has collapsed. Somebody will commission a recovery plan, and everyone in the room will have behaved reasonably.
2026 has thirteen weeks in it. The file simply stops partway through the year. Measured per week, 2026 is the strongest period in the file — not a collapse at all, but the best trading the business has done.
A second calendar problem sits behind the first, and it is subtler because both years look complete. 2024 has fifty-three Mondays and 2025 has fifty-two. Weekly data indexed on Monday therefore gives 2024 one extra week for free. So even the “clean” 2024-to-2025 comparison — the one that produces the +42.8% headline everybody quotes, being ₦23.48bn against ₦16.44bn — is comparing fifty-three weeks against fifty-two. Put both years on the same footing, ₦310m a week against ₦452m a week, and the growth is +45.6%. The headline was understating the business, which is the direction nobody thinks to check.
Neither of these is a subtle statistical point, and neither reflects badly on anyone caught by them. They survive review precisely because everything downstream is correct: the query is right, the chart is right, the arithmetic is right. Only the comparison is wrong, and comparisons are not what a reviewer’s eye is trained on.
Always count the periods before you compare them. One extra column, and it costs nothing.




3 · The distribution, not the average
An average is a one-number summary of a shape you have not looked at. Sometimes the shape is such that the average describes it well. Frequently it is not, and there is no way to tell which case you are in without looking.



Weekly units per depot-SKU. The mean sits 17% above the median, dragged there by a long right tail.


Two words are worth fixing before we go on, because the rest of the session leans on them. The mean is the total divided by the number of observations — what most people say when they say “average”. The median is the middle value: line every observation up in order and take the one in the centre, so that half are above and half below. When a distribution is symmetrical the two are near enough identical. When it is not, the gap between them is itself a finding, and in the figure above the mean sits 17% above the median.
Four things a distribution tells you that a mean cannot.
Is it symmetric? Most business quantities are not. Revenue, order size, customer tenure, account balance and supplier lead time are all right-skewed — many ordinary cases bunched at the low end, and a thin tail of very large ones stretching away to the right. The tail pulls the mean upwards, so the mean ends up above the median and above the typical case. Quote a mean revenue per customer in a retail bank and you will overstate the customer you are actually likely to meet by a wide margin, without having made a single arithmetic error.
Is it bimodal? Two humps mean two populations have been mixed together and described as one — almost always two products, two channels, two periods either side of a change, or one definition that quietly became another. The mean lands in the valley between the humps, describing a case that barely occurs.
Where is the mass? “There is a long tail” is a description; it becomes a fact when you attach a number to it. A tail holding 40% of revenue and a tail holding 4% look similar on a chart and are entirely different businesses.
Are there impossible values? Negative lead times. Ages over 120. Discounts over 100%. These sit in the extremes of the distribution, which is exactly where a mean hides them and a plot exposes them.


4 · Missingness, as a pattern
Blank cells feel like an absence of data. They are usually the opposite: something happened, and the blank is the record of it. The useful question is therefore never “how much is missing?” but “what do the missing rows have in common?”
The way to answer it is to split the file into the rows where the value is present and the rows where it is not, and then compare the two groups on everything else you know about them.
library(tidyverse)

sales <- read_csv("data/fmcg_sell_out.csv")

sales |>
  mutate(is_missing = is.na(units_sold)) |>
  group_by(is_missing) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            stockout_rate = mean(stockout_flag),
            promo_rate    = mean(on_promotion))
Read the output as a comparison between two rows. If values went missing for reasons unrelated to the business — a flaky export, a truncated file, a network drop — then the missing rows would look like a random sample of the file, and the stockout and promotion rates would come back roughly equal in both. They do not. Essentially every row with a missing units_sold is also flagged as a stockout.
Once you see that, the interpretation follows on its own. “Missing” here does not mean we do not know what was sold; it means nothing was sold, because there was nothing on the shelf. The two readings lead to opposite handling. Treat those rows as unknown and drop them, as most default cleaning code does, and you delete precisely the weeks when the business could not serve its customers — the weeks you most needed to see, and whose removal makes availability look better than it was.
This is the distinction between data missing at random, which is annoying but survivable because what remains is still representative, and data missing for a reason, which biases everything downstream in a direction you can usually predict once you know the reason. The words are worth having: they are what a statistician will use when you ask whether it is safe to drop the blanks.


5 · Time, plotted
Plot every important series against time before you model it, summarise it or quote it. Not a summary of the series — the series itself, one point per period, in order.



Weekly units by region, each indexed to its own first 26 weeks. Something happens in the North in November 2025.


Each line in that chart is set to 100 in its own first 26 weeks, so that regions of very different sizes can be compared on how much they have changed rather than on how big they are. Three of them wander along in the ordinary way. Two step down together, on one specific week, and stay down.
That is a level shift, or structural break: the series does not drift to a new level over a quarter, it moves in a single week and then carries on with the same shape from a different starting point. Here it begins in the week of 3 November 2025, and weekly volume in the affected regions drops 29% in a single week without recovering.
In the course file the cause is a distributor re-segmentation. In your own business, a shape like this is a lost customer, a depot closure, a competitor opening, a change in policy or pricing, or — very often — a systems migration that changed what got recorded rather than what happened. The last of those is worth watching for, because it produces exactly the same picture while nothing in the real world has moved at all.
This belongs in the exploratory list rather than the modelling one because no forecasting tool will tell you about it. Fit a model across a break and it will average the two regimes and predict a level that neither the past nor the future ever occupies — confident, well-formed, and wrong in the same direction every week. Session 3.3 takes that up in detail. What matters here is that the break is found by eye, in twenty seconds, before any model exists.

The one habit from this session
Plot it before you model it. Plot it before you summarise it. Plot it before you send it.
Twenty seconds each time, and often less. Between them, those twenty seconds catch the partial year, the structural break, the two populations wearing one name, the impossible value and the outlier that turns out to be a data entry error rather than a customer.
Those are five of the most expensive mistakes available in commercial analysis, and the thing they have in common is that no summary statistic reveals any of them. Each one is a property of the shape of the data, and a summary is what you get when you throw the shape away.

title: What is odd here?
section: The four questions applied to a new dataset
text:
The four questions applied to a new dataset
Reading about a checklist is not the same as running one, so take a file you have not opened yet — supply_chain_pos.csv, the purchase order history — and work the list on it: what shape is it, what cannot be true, what does the distribution look like, and how many real-world things are in it.
-- shape
SUMMARIZE SELECT * FROM 'data/supply_chain_pos.csv';

-- the impossible value check
SELECT COUNT(*) AS receipts_before_orders
FROM 'data/supply_chain_pos.csv'
WHERE CAST(received_date AS DATE) < CAST(po_date AS DATE);

-- the distribution of the thing you care about
SELECT supplier_id,
       COUNT(*)                       AS orders,
       ROUND(AVG(actual_lead_days),1) AS mean_lead,
       MEDIAN(actual_lead_days)       AS median_lead,
       MAX(actual_lead_days)          AS worst_lead
FROM 'data/supply_chain_pos.csv'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY mean_lead;

-- the entity count
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT supplier_id) AS supplier_ids FROM 'data/supply_chain_pos.csv';
Notice the third query in particular. It asks for the mean and the median of the same column side by side, which costs nothing extra and turns a table of averages into a table that tells you about shape. Try to predict what you will see before you run it, then open the panel.


Three findings in four queries



126 receipts precede their orders (1.4% of rows). Goods appear to have arrived before they were ordered, which cannot have happened; the cause is a timezone bug in the export. Those rows carry a negative lead time, negative lead times do not exist, and so the mean lead time computed from this file is pulled below the truth by a tail that describes nothing real.
Mean lead time exceeds median for every supplier, sometimes substantially — the right-skew from step three, showing up in an operational measure. Most orders arrive roughly when they should and a few are catastrophically late, and the late ones drag the mean up. The planning implication is the useful part: set your safety stock to the mean and you are by construction late on every order in the upper tail, which is exactly where stockouts come from. Plan to a percentile instead — a lead time you beat the great majority of the time is a number you can promise against.
Nine supplier IDs. The business has eight suppliers; the ninth identifier is the rename from 2.4 still sitting in the file. No summary statistic would have told you, because a count of distinct identifiers only means something to somebody who knows how many suppliers there are supposed to be.

Four queries. Three findings. About ninety seconds, and none of it required a model.



Core lab · 30 minutes


Work the five-step list on bank_customers.csv. Shape, calendar (there isn’t one — note that), distributions, missingness, entity counts.


Find the variable that is bimodal. Explain the two populations.


Find the two columns that measure nearly the same thing and disagree.


Plot avg_balance_ngn. Then plot its logarithm. Note which one you can actually read, and why that is a property of the data rather than of the chart.


Now do all five steps on your own capstone data, or on its shape if you cannot bring it.


Failure logbook: what did the assistant summarise without looking?


The second item is the one people abandon first, so it is worth saying that the difficulty is the point: two humps are easy to see and hard to explain, and naming the two populations correctly requires thinking about how the business works rather than about the column. Take your guess to your table and argue about it.


Stretch
Write a reusable EDA report — one script that takes any CSV and produces: row count, grain candidates, per-column nulls and distinct counts, distributions for every numeric column, a time plot for every date column, and a list of every value that violates a basic plausibility rule.
Ask the assistant to write it. It will do a good job, because this is exactly the kind of task assistants are strongest at: well specified, repetitive, and entirely determined by the input rather than by any knowledge of your business. Then use it on every dataset for the rest of the week, and on everything that lands on your desk afterwards.
Of everything built during the programme, this is the artefact people report still using a year later. It costs an hour once, and it changes what happens in the first ten minutes with every new file you are ever sent.


Copilot check
Ask: “Summarise this dataset for me.”
You will get a competent paragraph containing means, ranges and a note about missing values. It will be accurate, and there will be nothing in it you can point at and call wrong.
It will also not tell you that 2026 is a single quarter, that the northern regions broke in November, that missingness is concentrated on stockouts, or that there are nine identifiers for eight suppliers. That is less a failure of the model than a consequence of the question: none of those four is a property of the summary, they are all properties of the shape, and a summary is what you get by discarding the shape.
Then ask the better question: “What in this dataset would surprise a domain expert? Give me five specific things to check, as queries.”
Same file, same assistant, an entirely different quality of answer — because the second prompt asks for candidate oddities rather than a description, and checking a candidate takes seconds. The distance between those two answers is the whole session.

title: What is odd here?
text:
Takeaways

The question is “what is odd here?”, not “what is the average?”
Count the periods before you compare them.
Look at the distribution. Business quantities are right-skewed and the mean misleads.
Missingness is a pattern. Ask what the missing rows have in common.
Plot the series against time before you model it.


Next: 3.2 Charts that survive a board room →

title: Forecasting with intervals
section: A forecast without an interval is a wish
text:
A forecast without an interval is a wish
Almost every forecast that reaches a management meeting arrives as one number. Next quarter’s revenue will be ₦2.4bn. It is precise, it fits in a cell, and it is the shape the meeting expects. It is also, on its own, close to useless for planning — and the reason is worth working through rather than asserting, because it is the foundation of everything else here.
Consider a planner deciding how much stock to hold. Told only that the forecast is ₦2.4bn, they know what somebody expects and nothing at all about how wrong that expectation might be. Should they cover ₦2.5bn of demand? ₦3bn? The single number cannot say, so in practice they add a margin based on how burnt they were last time — a decision made with information nobody wrote down.
Now give them the same forecast expressed differently: ₦2.4bn, with an 80% interval running from ₦1.9bn to ₦2.9bn. That is ₦500m of downside and ₦500m of upside around the central figure, and it changes the conversation completely. The planner now knows the shortfall they must survive, the upside they should be equipped to serve, and the width of everybody’s ignorance. A range half that wide would justify a leaner inventory position; a range twice as wide would tell them the forecast is not, on its own, a sound basis for the decision at all.
Which is why the sentence worth carrying out of this session is this one:

The interval is the forecast. The central line is a convenience.

Organisations that forecast without intervals do not eliminate uncertainty. They relocate it. The uncertainty that went unstated in the forecast reappears three months later in the variance report, where it has become an argument about whose fault the gap was — and by then nobody can distinguish a plan that was wrong from a plan that was right about a range the outcome happened to land at the edge of.

What an 80% interval promises
An interval attached to a forecast is called a prediction interval, and the promise it makes is narrower than most people assume. Here is the whole of it, in one sentence:
“If we produced a hundred forecasts like this one, we would expect the actual outcome to fall inside the stated range about eighty times.”
Eighty times inside, twenty times outside — one in five. That is the claim, and it is a claim about the procedure rather than about this particular quarter. Note carefully what it does not say.

It does not say the central line is likely. It is not, and this surprises people. On a continuous quantity, almost every specific value is unlikely; the central line is simply the value with the most probability packed around it.
It does not say the true value is equally likely anywhere in the range. Outcomes near the middle are more likely than outcomes near the edges, which is why “we came in at the bottom of the range” is a different kind of result from “we came in at the middle”.
It does not cover events the model has never seen. A currency devaluation, a regulatory change, a port closure, a competitor exiting the market. The interval is calculated from how much the series has varied in the past, so intervals are conditional on the future resembling the past — and saying that out loud is precisely what separates a forecast from a promise.

That last point is the one to say in the meeting, in those words. It is also why the 95% interval is usually the wrong one to show: widening from 80% to 95% buys a range so broad that it stops constraining any decision, and it still does not cover the things that actually go wrong, because those are the ones with no precedent in the data. An 80% interval is narrow enough to plan against and honest about being beaten one time in five.

title: Forecasting with intervals
Forecasting with intervals
text:
Fit several. Never one.
The most common forecasting error in business is not choosing the wrong model. It is fitting one model and believing it, with nothing to compare it against.
The remedy is to fit several at once, including some that are deliberately unsophisticated, and let them compete on evidence. Modern forecasting packages make this almost free — the block below fits five in a single statement.
fit <- weekly |>
  model(
    naive    = NAIVE(units),                          # last value. The benchmark.
    seasonal = SNAIVE(units ~ lag("year")),           # same week last year
    ets      = ETS(units),                            # exponential smoothing
    arima    = ARIMA(units),
    ensemble = combination_model(ETS(units), ARIMA(units))
  )

fc <- fit |> forecast(h = "13 weeks")

fc |>
  autoplot(weekly |> filter(week_starting >= as.Date("2025-01-01")), level = c(80)) +
  labs(title = "Thirteen-week unit forecast, five models, 80% intervals",
       subtitle = "If the naive benchmark is competitive, the sophisticated model is not earning its keep")
Five names, in plain language, because knowing what each one assumes is more useful than knowing how it is implemented:

NAIVE predicts that next week will equal this week. No parameters, no judgement; it carries the last observation forward.
SNAIVE — seasonal naive — predicts that this week will equal the same week last year. On a series with a strong annual pattern this is a surprisingly strong rule.
ETS stands for error, trend, season: exponential smoothing, which estimates level, trend and seasonal pattern as weighted averages where recent observations count for more.
ARIMA is the other classical family, modelling the series in terms of its own recent values and its own recent errors.
combination_model averages two forecasts. Averaging several reasonable models is one of the most reliable free improvements available, because their errors are partly independent and averaging cancels some of them.

Now look at what happens when this is done honestly against data the models were not shown.



Thirteen weeks ahead, backtested on the last thirteen weeks of the shipped file. Two rules: plain seasonal naive, and the same rule with a drift term. The drift term is 4.6 times worse.


Sit with that figure for a moment longer than is comfortable, because it is not the figure a forecasting session usually shows. Sessions like this one normally end with a chart in which the clever model tracks the outcome closely. This one does the opposite, and it is more useful for it.
Start with what went right. The interval behaves exactly as an interval should. The band widens as the horizon lengthens, which is correct — the further ahead you look, the less you know — and it covers 85% of the held-out weeks. Eighty-five per cent of thirteen weeks is eleven of them: eleven weeks inside the 80% band and two outside, against an expectation of about ten or eleven inside. The interval was honest.
Now what went wrong. The central line is wrong all quarter, running 7.2% high in every single week — not high on average with weeks either side, but high every week. That persistence is the diagnostic. Errors that scatter around zero are noise; errors that all point the same way are a missing ingredient.
And the “improvement” made it worse. The refinement was to add a drift term: instead of predicting that this week equals the same week last year, predict that it equals the same week last year adjusted upwards for the growth seen recently. That is a reasonable thing to try, and it is what most analysts would try next. It made the forecast 4.6 times worse than the plain rule it was built on — its average error was four and a half times the simpler rule’s.
The reason is instructive. The drift term compares the last 26 weeks against the same 26 weeks a year earlier, and that comparison runs straight across the November 2025 northern break. The recent period contains the reduced volumes; the year-earlier period does not. The rule cannot distinguish a business that is growing from a business that lost a chunk of demand at a point in time, so it reads a level shift as a growth rate and projects it forward for thirteen weeks.
Three things follow, and between them they are the session.

The benchmark beat the model. Publish that. It is the most useful result available in forecasting and the one people are most reluctant to report, because it feels like arriving at a review having done nothing. It is the opposite: it is the finding that stops an organisation buying complexity that does not pay.
A wide interval rescued a wrong central line. Published as a point estimate, this would have had the business plan a quarter around a number it never once achieved. Published with its interval, nobody was misled about how much was known.
The break is upstream of all of it. No forecasting tool finds it. You find it in 3.1, by plotting the series and asking what is odd here.


Always fit the naive benchmark
NAIVE predicts that next week equals this week. SNAIVE predicts that this week equals the same week last year. Neither of them took any skill, any data science, or any budget.
That is the entire point. They give you a floor. If a sophisticated model cannot beat both of them on data it has never seen, whatever it is doing is not worth the licence fee, the maintenance or the meeting — and you have found that out in ten seconds rather than after two quarters of quiet under-performance.
So report the benchmark alongside your model, every time, on its own row of the table. It is the single most credibility-building line in a forecasting presentation, because it shows the audience that you went looking for evidence against your own work before they had to.
For anybody commissioning a forecast rather than building one, this becomes one pleasant question: “How does this compare with just assuming next quarter looks like the same quarter last year?” If the answer is a number, you are in good hands. If nobody has checked, the check takes an afternoon and is worth having before the forecast is used.

title: Forecasting with intervals
section: Backtesting: the only evidence that counts
text:
Backtesting: the only evidence that counts
How well a model fits the data it was built on tells you almost nothing about how well it will forecast, and it is worth being concrete about why. A model with enough flexibility can be made to pass very close to every point in the history it was shown. That is not skill; it is memory.
The measure of a forecast is its performance on periods it has never seen, and the only way to obtain that measure honestly is to hide some of your own data from the model, forecast the hidden period, and compare. Doing that once is called a holdout. Doing it repeatedly, at many different cut-off points in the history, is called backtesting, or rolling-origin cross-validation, and it is the version that gives you an answer you can rely on.
# Rolling origin, properly: refit at many cut-offs, forecast 13 weeks from each,
# and average the error across all of them. One holdout is one draw; this is
# the distribution.
folds <- weekly |>
  tsibble::stretch_tsibble(.init = 78, .step = 13)   # grow the training window

accuracy_table <- folds |>
  model(naive  = NAIVE(units),
        snaive = SNAIVE(units ~ lag("year")),
        ets    = ETS(units),
        arima  = ARIMA(units)) |>
  forecast(h = 13) |>
  accuracy(weekly)

accuracy_table |>
  select(.model, MAE, RMSE, MAPE, MASE) |>
  arrange(MASE)
stretch_tsibble(.init = 78, .step = 13) does the work, and it is easier to picture than to read. It takes the first 78 weeks as a training set, fits every model to just that, and forecasts the next 13 weeks. Then it extends the training window by 13 weeks and does it again, and again, until it runs out of history. Each pass produces a forecast made with no knowledge of the period it is scored against — exactly the position you are in when you forecast next quarter.
Why the repetition? Because a single holdout is a sample of size one: it tells you how one model did on one quarter, and quarters differ — one with a promotion in it, one containing a break, one unusually quiet. Roll the origin forward and you get the same comparison at every cut-off in your history. That is the difference between “our model beat naive” and “our model beats naive”: one is an anecdote, the other is a property.

Which error measure to read
The table above reports four measures, and choosing between them matters more than it looks.
Read MASE, not MAPE. MAPE — mean absolute percentage error — is the measure everybody quotes, and it is badly behaved in exactly the situations commercial data produces. It takes each week’s error as a percentage of that week’s actual value, which creates three problems. It is undefined when the actual is zero. It explodes when the actual is merely small: miss by 5 units on a week that sold 10 and you have a 50% error, but miss by the same 5 units on a week that sold 2 and MAPE records 250%. And it penalises over- and under-forecasting asymmetrically, because a forecast can be more than 100% above the actual but never more than 100% below it. For a business with stockout weeks and slow-moving SKUs, all three are live rather than theoretical.
MASE — mean absolute scaled error — avoids all of that by dividing your average error by the error a simple naive rule would have made on the training data. That denominator is what makes the measure comparable across series of wildly different sizes: a MASE of 0.8 means the same thing on a series measured in units and a series measured in billions of naira.
The half people get wrong when they explain it is which errors are being compared. Read it as: below 1, your out-of-sample error is smaller than the naive rule’s in-sample error — a demanding bar. Above 1, it is not. That is not quite the same statement as “we beat naive on the holdout”, because the two sides of the ratio come from different periods, and over a long horizon the two comparisons can genuinely disagree. Which is why the accuracy table reports the benchmarks on their own rows: you can read both comparisons directly rather than infer one from the other.

title: Forecasting with intervals
Forecasting with intervals
section: Judgemental adjustment, and when it is legitimate
text:
Judgemental adjustment, and when it is legitimate
Planners override forecasts. Analysts often treat this as interference, and they are often wrong to, because the planner frequently knows things the history cannot contain: the promotion agreed for week 6, the new listing that starts in week 9, the customer who gave notice last Thursday. Refusing overrides on principle throws away real information. The question is not whether to allow them but how to keep them useful, and two rules do most of the work.
Log every override: who made it, when, how much they moved the number, and why. Then, a quarter later, measure them — what the forecast said, what the override said, what actually happened. In organisations that do this, roughly half of overrides improve accuracy and half degrade it, and the split is strikingly consistent by individual: some people reliably add information and others reliably add noise. That is enormously useful management information, it costs almost nothing to collect, and hardly anybody collects it.
Override the level, not the interval. Adjusting the central case on the basis of something you know is legitimate judgement. Narrowing the range because you feel confident is almost always overconfidence, and it removes exactly the protection that made the forecast safe to plan against. If new information genuinely reduces uncertainty — the promotion is now signed rather than proposed — say so explicitly, and let somebody else agree the range should narrow.

Core lab · 25 minutes


Build the total-network weekly series. Decompose it. Read the remainder panel.


Fit five models including both naive benchmarks. Backtest on a 13-week holdout, rank by MASE, and say how many models beat naive.


Now the northern series. Fit it ignoring the break, then handle the break one of the three ways. Report both intervals and how much narrower the honest one is.


Prepare your forecast market entry: one depot, quarter ahead, 80% interval.


The second item has a specific answer and it is worth writing it down rather than glancing at it, because “how many models beat naive?” is the question you will be asking of other people’s forecasts for the rest of your career, and the number is often smaller than expected.


Stretch
Forecast at the SKU–depot level rather than the total, then add the individual forecasts together. Compare that sum with a direct forecast of the total.
They will not match, and the reason repays understanding: aggregating forecasts is not the same as forecasting an aggregate. Individual series are noisier than their total, and their errors are correlated rather than independent, so the two routes to a national number arrive at different places. This is the hierarchical forecasting reconciliation problem, and it is precisely the problem your S&OP process has every month when the sum of the regional plans does not equal the national plan — usually resolved by somebody adjusting a spreadsheet until the numbers tie.
There is a formal solution rather than a manual one (fable’s reconcile() with min_trace), which finds the adjustments that keep the hierarchy consistent while disturbing the individual forecasts as little as possible. For anyone who runs a planning cycle, it is a genuine competitive advantage and almost nobody uses it.


Copilot check
Ask an assistant to “forecast this time series” and you will get a fitted model, a chart and a number, quickly and competently, and the code will usually be correct. What is missing is not technique but scepticism, in four consistent places.

A naive benchmark. Without one you have no idea whether the model added anything at all over assuming next week looks like last week.
A backtest. It will typically report how well the model fits the data it was trained on, which as we have seen is close to meaningless as evidence about the future.
The break. It will not notice one unless it can run code and plot the series — in which case it often will. Ask for it explicitly rather than hoping.
The caveat. It will rarely volunteer that the interval is conditional on the future resembling the past, which is the sentence that keeps the forecast honest in the meeting.

None of that is a defect in the assistant so much as a consequence of the request. “Forecast this series” asks for a forecast, and it obligingly produces one. Ask for the evidence as well and it will produce that too:

Forecast this weekly series 13 weeks ahead. Requirements: fit NAIVE and SNAIVE benchmarks alongside ETS and ARIMA; evaluate with rolling-origin cross-validation on a 13-week horizon and report MASE; check for structural breaks and tell me if you find one; produce 80% intervals; and state in one sentence what the interval assumes.

That prompt is worth keeping. Every requirement in it is something this session argued for, which means you have both the checklist and the reasons behind it — and the reasons are what let you adapt it when the next request is not a weekly series thirteen weeks ahead.

title: Forecasting with intervals
text:
Takeaways

The interval is the forecast. The central line is a convenience.
Always fit the naive benchmarks. Report MASE, not MAPE.
Backtest on periods the model has never seen, repeatedly.
Handle breaks explicitly. Fitting across one produces persistent, one-directional error.
Intervals are conditional on the future resembling the past. Say so out loud.

title: Propensity and the leak
section: Build it first, and let it be too good
text:
Build it first, and let it be too good
A propensity model is simply a model that estimates, for each customer, the probability that something will happen — that they will leave, buy, default or respond. It produces a number between 0 and 1 for every row, and the whole commercial value of it lies in what you do with that ranking afterwards.
Build one now, before reading further. It matters that you see the result before you see the explanation.
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

bank <- read_csv("data/bank_customers.csv") |>
  mutate(churned = factor(churned_90d, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("yes", "no")))

set.seed(2026)
split <- initial_split(bank, prop = 0.75, strata = churned)
train <- training(split); test <- testing(split)

rec <- recipe(churned ~ tenure_months + age + products_held + avg_balance_ngn +
                digital_engagement_score + txns_last_90d + complaints_last_12m +
                salary_domiciled + nps_last_survey + segment +
                closure_form_started,                 # <- everything available
              data = train) |>
  step_log(avg_balance_ngn, base = 10) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>
  add_model(logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm")) |>
  fit(train)

augment(fit, test) |> roc_auc(churned, .pred_yes)
#> 0.984
The number at the bottom is the AUC, or area under the ROC curve. In plain terms it answers one question: if you pick a customer who churned and a customer who did not, entirely at random, how often does the model give the churner the higher score? An AUC of 0.5 means the model is doing no better than a coin, and 1.0 means it never gets that comparison wrong.
0.984, then, means the model wins that comparison roughly ninety-eight times in a hundred. In a churn context that is extraordinary. Most production churn models in retail banking live between 0.70 and 0.80, and a team that moved from 0.74 to 0.79 would reasonably regard it as a good quarter’s work.
Which is the moment to slow down rather than to write the email. A result that far outside the normal range is telling you something, and the something is usually about the data rather than the modelling.

title: Propensity and the leak
section: Before anything else, run the leakage test
text:
Before anything else, run the leakage test

The only leakage test you need
Take the list of features, go down it one at a time, and ask a single question of each:

Would I have known this at the moment I needed to act?

Note what the question is not. It is not “is this correlated with the outcome” — you hope everything is. It is not “is this statistically significant”. It is a question about time: at the moment you would score the customer and decide whether to call them, does this value exist yet, in the system, in the form the model saw it?
Going down the column list one at a time takes about two minutes, and it is the highest return on two minutes anywhere in this course.








Feature
Known at scoring time?




tenure_months
Yes


age, segment, branch_state
Yes


products_held, avg_balance_ngn
Yes


digital_engagement_score, txns_last_90d
Yes


complaints_last_12m
Yes


salary_domiciled
Yes


nps_last_survey
Yes, if the survey predates the scoring date — check


closure_form_started
No. The form is filled the week they leave.



The last row is the one that matters. A closure form is not a predictor of leaving; it is part of the act of leaving. Its presence in the training table is not evidence of carelessness by whoever built the extract — they were asked for the customer record and they supplied it, complete. The column belongs in the warehouse. It simply does not belong in a model that has to run before the customer has decided anything.
This is what target leakage means: information about the outcome has leaked backwards into the features, so the model is partly being told the answer rather than predicting it.
Drop the column and refit.
rec_clean <- rec |> step_rm(closure_form_started)
# ... refit ...
#> roc_auc 0.766
The AUC falls from 0.984 to 0.766 — from a result nobody in retail banking achieves to a result that is entirely ordinary. And the ordinary one is the real one. A model at 0.766 is useful, deployable, and roughly what the published literature on retail churn would lead you to expect. Nothing has been lost by removing the column, because the performance it was providing was never available at the moment you needed it.
Now do the thing that almost nobody does, and that turns this from an anecdote into a discipline. Simulate production. At the moment of scoring, nobody has started a closure form yet — so set that column to zero for everybody, re-score the held-out customers, and see what the leaked model would actually have done in service.
test_prod <- test |> mutate(closure_form_started = 0)
augment(fit, test_prod) |> roc_auc(churned, .pred_yes)
#> 0.768
augment(fit, test_prod) |> summarise(mean_predicted = mean(.pred_yes))
#> 0.009      <- against a true base rate of 0.106

What actually breaks is not what you expect
Look carefully at the first of those two numbers, because it is the counter-intuitive one. The leaked model’s ranking survives: AUC 0.768 in simulated production, essentially the same as the clean model’s 0.766. The order it puts customers in is still broadly right. If all you ever do with the scores is sort them and call the top 600, you might run this model for a year and never notice anything was wrong.
What collapses is calibration — the correspondence between a predicted probability and the real-world frequency it claims to describe. The model learned, quite correctly given its training data, that almost nobody churns unless a closure form has been started. Strip the form away and every predicted probability falls to the floor. Mean predicted risk comes out at 0.9% against a true base rate of 10.6%, so the model is understating the risk in the book by better than a factor of ten.
That is invisible until somebody multiplies the probability by something else — and sooner or later somebody always does. Expected value at risk, provisioning, a retention budget, an economic threshold: every one of those is a probability multiplied by a naira figure, and every one of them is now out by an order of magnitude while the model still looks fine on the metric everybody checks.
The general point is worth carrying away from the specific example. Discrimination and calibration are different properties of a model, and leakage can destroy one while leaving the other intact. If your model feeds a ranking, discrimination is what you need. If it feeds an arithmetic decision, calibration is what you need — and it is the one nobody reports.


Leakage does not announce itself as an error
It announces itself as success, and that is precisely what makes it so durable.
An error that produces a bad result gets investigated. Nobody investigates a result that exceeded expectations — there is no meeting scheduled for “the model worked better than we hoped”, and the natural response to 0.98 is congratulation rather than suspicion. That is not a failing of individual reviewers; it is how review processes are built, and it is why leakage survives them so reliably.
The habit worth installing, in yourself and in your team, is a small reversal of that instinct: an unexpectedly good result is a bug report until proven otherwise. It costs an hour when you are right and saves a deployment when you are not.
Four forms of leakage turn up often enough in real organisations to be worth recognising by shape:

Post-outcome fields. Closure forms, exit interviews, cancellation reason codes, write-off flags. These are populated because the outcome happened, which is exactly the direction of causation you are trying to model.
Updated-in-place fields. A customer_status column that gets overwritten each time it changes. Your historical training data then contains today’s status rather than the status as at the training date, and today’s status knows how the story ended.
Aggregates computed over the whole period, including the future. An “average spend” figure that silently includes the months after the customer churned — during which they spent nothing — is a very effective churn predictor and a completely useless one.
The identifier that encodes the answer. Account numbers issued in blocks, where a prefix happens to correspond to a closure batch. This sounds far-fetched until it happens to you.

title: Propensity and the leak
text:
Evaluate in business terms
AUC is a technical summary, and it belongs in the appendix. It is not a business case, and it is not the number you present, because nobody in the room can convert it into a decision.
Lift is the number that can be converted. If your retention team has capacity to call 600 customers a month, the only question that matters is: how many more churners do I reach in the top 600 by score than I would by calling 600 people at random?
scored <- augment(fit_clean, test) |>
  arrange(desc(.pred_yes)) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number(),
         decile = ntile(rank, 10),
         churner = churned == "yes")

base_rate <- mean(scored$churner)

scored |>
  group_by(decile) |>
  summarise(customers = n(),
            churners  = sum(churner),
            rate      = mean(churner),
            lift      = mean(churner) / base_rate)
That block sorts everybody by score, cuts the sorted list into ten equal groups, and reports the churn rate in each. Dividing each group’s rate by the overall base rate gives the lift: a lift of 1.0 means the group is no better than random, and a lift of 3.0 means you are finding three times as many churners there as chance would give you.



Cumulative gains. Contact the top three deciles and you reach roughly 66% of the churners.


The right-hand panel is the cumulative gains curve, which answers the same question cumulatively: work down the ranked list and, at each point, what share of all the churners have you covered? Reaching roughly 66% of the churners in the top three deciles means that contacting 30% of the book finds two thirds of the people who were going to leave.
The top decile has a churn rate around 3.0 times the base rate. Translated out of the jargon: calling the top 10% by score finds three times as many at-risk customers as calling 10% at random. That sentence is what goes in the memo, because a reader can act on it without knowing what a model is. The AUC stays in the appendix, where somebody technical can check it.

title: Propensity and the leak
text:
Choosing the threshold
At some point the ranking has to become a rule: call this customer, do not call that one. The threshold that gets used by default is 0.5 — call anybody the model thinks is more likely than not to leave — and it is worth being clear that this number has no business content whatsoever. It is a mathematical midpoint, inherited from the way classification is taught, and it survives because nothing in the tooling prompts anybody to change it.
A defensible threshold comes from three things instead:

Capacity. Six hundred calls a month is six hundred calls a month. If capacity is the binding constraint, the threshold is simply “the top 600 by score” and the probability attached to the 600th customer is incidental.
Economics. What a call costs, fully loaded, against what a successful save is worth.
Asymmetry. Missing a valuable churner costs far more than making an unnecessary call, and the ratio between those two is usually large.

# Threshold from economics rather than from convention.
cost_of_call        <- 2500          # ₦, fully loaded
value_of_save       <- 180000        # ₦, annual contribution
prob_call_works     <- 0.30          # measure this. Do not assume it.

# Call is worth it when:  p(churn) * value * effectiveness > cost
threshold <- cost_of_call / (value_of_save * prob_call_works)
round(threshold, 4)
#> 0.0463   -> call anyone above a 4.6% churn probability
The arithmetic is worth doing by hand once, because it is the kind of calculation a board can follow. A call costs ₦2,500. A save is worth ₦180,000 of annual contribution, but only 30% of calls actually save anybody, so the expected return on a call to a customer who is certain to leave is 180,000 × 0.30 = ₦54,000. Dividing the ₦2,500 cost by that ₦54,000 expected benefit gives 0.0463 — meaning the call breaks even at a churn probability of about 4.6%, and is profitable above it. Not 50%, and not by a small margin: an order of magnitude lower.

And now notice that the threshold does not bind
Apply that 4.6% cut-off to the book and something awkward emerges. 64% of the book scores above 4.6% — roughly 7,700 customers, against a stated capacity of 600 calls a month. The economic threshold selects nearly thirteen times more people than anyone can ring.
So the economic threshold is not really the cut-off. Capacity is. What the 4.6% figure actually tells you is how much capacity is costing you: every customer sitting between the 600th-ranked name and the 4.6% line is somebody it would have been profitable to call and you could not. Multiply that gap by the expected value per call and you have a costed business case for a larger retention team — which is a considerably more interesting number than the threshold, and one almost nobody computes because the threshold question feels like where the analysis ends.
Two rules follow, and they are worth settling before the argument starts:

When capacity binds, rank and take the top N. The probability is a sorting key and nothing more.
When capacity does not bind, the economic threshold is the cut-off — and you should be asking why you have idle retention capacity in the first place.

Work out which case you are in before you argue about where the line goes.


Three numbers, three different things
Deciding who to call actually requires three quantities, and it is easy to build only the first:

Probability of the event — will they leave?
Value at stake — does it matter to us if they do?
Probability the intervention works — can we do anything about it?

Most propensity models compute the first and are then deployed as though they had computed all three. The consequence is specific and predictable: a customer who is certain to leave and cannot be persuaded scores at the very top of a probability-ranked list, and is precisely the person least worth spending a call on. A naive high-probability-first targeting rule fills the call list with exactly those people, which is one reason retention programmes so often report disappointing effectiveness against a model that was working perfectly well.
Rank by the product of the three, not by the probability alone. The third term is the hardest to obtain, because it has to be measured with a holdout rather than assumed — which is Friday’s subject, in 5.2.

title: Propensity and the leak
text:
The survivorship trap next door
Leakage is about time. Its close relative is about membership: which rows made it into the file at all. Open b2b_funnel.csv and try to find what drives a win.
funnel <- read_csv("data/b2b_funnel.csv")

funnel |>
  filter(!is.na(sales_touchpoints)) |>
  summarise(cor = cor(sales_touchpoints, closed_won))
More touchpoints, more wins. The correlation is clear, and the conclusion looks obvious: tell the sales team to do more touchpoints. Before you do, work out what had to be true for a row to appear in that calculation at all.


Why that conclusion is worthless


sales_touchpoints is blank on 86% of rows. It was back-filled from the CRM only for opportunities that reached SQL stage.
The filter() in that first block therefore did more than drop some missing values. It restricted the analysis to a population defined by having already qualified. Of course those opportunities convert more often — qualification is what the filter selected on.
The question to ask of every dataset is this: what had to be true for a row to exist in this file? If the answer involves having already succeeded partway through the process, then every conclusion you draw is a conclusion about survivors.
funnel |>
  group_by(has_touchpoints = !is.na(sales_touchpoints)) |>
  summarise(n = n(), win_rate = mean(closed_won))
The win rate among rows with touchpoints recorded is 31%. Among rows without them it is 0% — not low, but exactly zero — because a lead that never reached SQL stage could not be won at all.
So the correlation is real, and it is real within a population defined by having already qualified. Both of those statements are true simultaneously, and that is what makes survivorship harder to spot than an ordinary error: nothing in the arithmetic is wrong, no assumption has been violated, and no diagnostic will flag it.
The question that finds it is not a statistical one. It is: what had to be true for a row to have this column filled in?



Core lab · 20 minutes


Build the churn model with everything. Record the AUC.


Run the leakage test on every column, refit clean, and note the size of the drop.


Build the decile lift table, and compute your threshold from capacity and economics rather than from 0.5.


Rank by probability × value × effectiveness and compare the top 600 to the probability-only top 600. How many names differ?


That final comparison is the one worth reporting back to the room. The two lists usually overlap much less than people expect, and the difference between them is the difference between a model that ranks risk and a model that ranks opportunity.


Stretch
Run the same exercise on hr_attrition.csv and find both traps:

the post-outcome column (exit_interview_booked, correlation 0.88 with the outcome), and
the strong, legitimate-looking predictor that is a proxy for a protected characteristic.

The second is the harder and more consequential of the two, because it does not fail any technical test at all — the feature is genuinely predictive, genuinely available at scoring time, and genuinely improves the model.
Then write the two-sentence answer you would give a risk officer who asks whether you would deploy it. Bring that answer to 5.4. We will read some of them out.


Copilot check
An assistant will build this model competently and will not detect the leak. That is not a weakness in the model; it is a boundary. Detecting the leak requires knowing when a business process fills a field, which is knowledge about how your operations run rather than knowledge about the shape of your data — and nothing in the file records it.
What it will do, if you supply that missing piece:

Here are the columns in my training data and a one-line description of what each one means and when it is populated in the business process. Identify any feature that could only be known after the outcome occurred, or that is a proxy for a protected characteristic. Explain your reasoning for each flag.

The load-bearing phrase there is “and when it is populated in the business process”. Supply it and the assistant becomes genuinely good at this, often catching columns a person would skim past. Withhold it and no amount of prompting will help, because the information simply is not present.
That generalises well beyond leakage: an assistant’s usefulness on any given task is roughly proportional to how much of the surrounding business context you were willing to type.

title: Propensity and the leak
text:
Takeaways

An unexpectedly good result is a bug report until proven otherwise.
The leakage test is one question about time: would I have known this in time?
Report lift and gains, not AUC. Lift is a sentence a board understands.
The threshold comes from capacity and economics. It is never 0.5.
Rank by probability × value × effectiveness.
Ask what had to be true for a row to exist in the file.

title: Text as data
section: Most of what you know about your customers is text
text:
Most of what you know about your customers is text
Some of what your organisation knows about its customers sits in structured tables. A much larger share of it is in sentences somebody typed: call-centre notes, the free-text box at the bottom of a branch survey, app store reviews, WhatsApp complaints, relationship manager comments, exit interview transcripts, supplier emails, and the “any other comments” field that has been quietly filling up for years and has never been read end to end.
For most of the history of corporate analytics, reading all of that was economically impossible — five thousand reviews at two minutes each is more than a fortnight of somebody’s working life — so the sensible thing was to keep the part that was already a number and let the words go. That was a reasonable trade at the time, and it is worth being precise about what it cost. A star rating tells you that somebody is unhappy, and roughly how unhappy. The words tell you what to fix. Only one of those two can be turned into a work item on a Monday morning.
The cost of reading text at scale has now collapsed. What has not changed is that the answer you get out is only as good as the corpus you were handed and the care you took over the counting — and the last section of this session, about who filtered the file before it reached you, matters more than everything before it.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: Text as data
text:
The classical pipeline still matters
Before reaching for a language model, it is worth running the version of this analysis that has existed for thirty years. It is not a courtesy to tradition. It costs nothing, it runs in seconds on a laptop, every step of it can be explained to an auditor line by line, and it answers the question outright more often than people expect.
The pipeline has four steps, and each has a plain meaning underneath a technical name.
Tokenise → remove stop words → count → compare.
To tokenise is to cut the text into individual words, so that a review becomes a list rather than a sentence; each word is then called a token. Stop words are the words that appear in nearly every sentence and so distinguish nothing between them — “the”, “and”, “is”, “of” — and the conventional list of them is called a stop-word list. What is left is a table you can count.

R (tidytext)Python


library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)

reviews <- read_csv("data/customer_reviews.csv")

words <- reviews |>
  unnest_tokens(word, review_text) |>          # one row per word
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") |>        # drop "the", "and", "is"
  filter(!str_detect(word, "^[0-9]+$"))        # drop bare numbers

words |> count(word, sort = TRUE) |> head(20)


import pandas as pd, re
from collections import Counter

STOP = set("""the a an and or but is are was were be been being to of in on for with
at by from as it its this that i we you they he she my our your their not no so if
then than have has had do does did will would can could been just about""".split())

reviews = pd.read_csv("data/customer_reviews.csv")
tokens = (reviews.review_text.str.lower()
                 .str.findall(r"[a-z']+")
                 .explode()
                 .dropna())
tokens = tokens[~tokens.isin(STOP)]
print(Counter(tokens).most_common(20))



Both versions do the same three things — one row per word, drop the words that carry no signal, count what remains — and both give you a first frequency table.

The move that turns word counts into a finding
That first table is nearly always a disappointment, and it is worth expecting that rather than concluding you have done something wrong. “Account”, “app” and “bank” will sit at the top of it — as they will for every bank, in every market, in every quarter. Frequency in a single corpus mostly measures what the corpus is about, which you already knew.
The move that rescues the analysis is to stop counting one pile of text and start comparing two. Three comparisons do most of the work:

the words that appear in one-star reviews and not in five-star reviews;
the words that were rare last quarter and are common now;
the words that appear on WhatsApp and never appear in the branch survey.

Each turns a description into a difference, and a difference is something somebody can act on. Here is the first:
library(tidylo)

# What distinguishes detractors from promoters?
words |>
  filter(star_rating != 3) |>                                    # drop the middle FIRST
  mutate(sentiment_group = if_else(star_rating <= 2,
                                   "detractor", "promoter")) |>
  count(sentiment_group, word) |>
  bind_log_odds(sentiment_group, word, n) |>                     # weighted, prior-smoothed
  filter(sentiment_group == "detractor", n > 25) |>
  slice_max(log_odds_weighted, n = 15)
Read that block in English. Set the three-star reviews aside, because they are neither a complaint nor a compliment and including them only blurs the contrast. Split what remains into detractors and promoters, count how often each group uses each word, then score every word by how much more characteristic it is of detractors — taking the fifteen highest, restricted to words used at least twenty-five times so the list is not dominated by one person’s unusual vocabulary.
Frequency describes the corpus. Difference describes the problem. That one substitution is most of the value in classical text analysis.

Do not compute the raw log-odds by hand
The obvious way to score a word is to divide its detractor count by its promoter count and take the logarithm — in code, log((detractor + 1) / (promoter + 1)). That is a perfectly natural thing to write, and it is biased in a direction that is easy to miss.
The arithmetic shows why. Detractors are 26% of this corpus and promoters are 60%, so there are roughly 60 ÷ 26 ≈ 2.3 promoter reviews for every detractor review. A word used at exactly the same rate by both groups will therefore still turn up about 2.3 times more often in the promoter pile, purely because that pile is bigger. Rank by the raw ratio and you are ranking group size as much as meaning.
bind_log_odds() implements the weighted log-odds ratio with an informative Dirichlet prior (Monroe, Colaresi and Quinn, 2008). The log-odds ratio part asks how much more likely a word is in one group than the other, on a scale where “twice as likely” and “half as likely” sit the same distance either side of zero. The informative prior part pulls the estimate for a rare word back towards what the corpus as a whole does, so a word seen four times cannot leap over a word seen four hundred times on the strength of a coincidence. Together they normalise for group size and keep noise off the top of the list.
One function instead of one arithmetic expression, and the ranking becomes about the words rather than about the sample.

title: Text as data
section: Why the word cloud is usually the wrong deliverable
text:
Why the word cloud is usually the wrong deliverable
Word clouds are popular for understandable reasons. They are immediate, they photograph well on a slide, and they make it obvious that a lot of text was involved. None of those are bad things to want from a chart.
The difficulty is what a word cloud does with the numbers it was given. It encodes quantity as font size, and people compare type sizes poorly — far less accurately than they compare lengths along a common baseline, which is what a bar chart offers. It encodes position as nothing at all, so the most readable channel on the page is spent packing words into a pleasing shape. Long words look larger than short ones at identical frequency, and with no axis, scale or ordering a reader cannot tell whether “delayed” appeared 400 times or 40.
Two settings do earn one: as a first look for yourself, when you have never seen a corpus, and as decoration on a slide whose point is “there is a great deal of text here”. Neither is a decision paper.
What to send instead: the five themes, their volumes, their trend, and one verbatim quote each. That is a business case — it names what is wrong, says how much of it there is, says whether it is getting worse, and lets a reader hear a customer say it in their own words. A word cloud is a picture.



Five themes with volumes you can act on, and movement you cannot — every quarter-on-quarter interval crosses zero.


The right-hand panel is doing something honest and slightly uncomfortable. Each theme’s share moved between quarters, and each movement carries an interval showing the range of values consistent with the data. Every one of those intervals includes zero — meaning that for every theme, “no change at all” remains a perfectly good explanation. The volumes on the left are solid enough to plan against; the movements on the right are not yet distinguishable from noise, and presenting them as a trend is the most common way a text analysis loses credibility on the second reading.

title: Text as data
section: The multilingual problem, which is not optional here
text:
The multilingual problem, which is not optional here
About one review in twelve in this corpus — 8.6% — is in Nigerian Pidgin. On 4,938 reviews that is roughly 425 of them, which is more than enough to move a theme ranking.
"dem debit me two times, e never reverse"
"network no dey work for my area"
"customer care no pick my call at all"
An English stop-word list does nothing useful with these sentences: it does not recognise “dey” or “dem” as function words, so they survive into the frequency table as though they were content. An English sentiment lexicon — a dictionary that assigns a positive or negative score to each word — reads “e never reverse”, finds no word it holds an opinion about, and scores a clear complaint as neutral. The same happens with code-switching, where a writer moves between languages inside a single sentence, which is entirely normal in everyday Nigerian writing and completely outside what a single-language lexicon is built for.
The consequence is not random error, and that is what makes it serious. A classical pipeline systematically under-counts complaints from the segment most likely to write in Pidgin — and in most Nigerian consumer businesses that is not a random slice of the customer base. The themes that group cares about are quietly shifted down the ranking, and nothing in the output signals that it happened.
This is a real, quantifiable bias with a commercial consequence, and it is the strongest argument for the language-model approach in 4.2 — which handles Pidgin, code-switching and mid-sentence language changes without any additional work.
Whichever route you take, note it in your method section. “9% of the corpus is in Nigerian Pidgin and was handled by the classifier rather than by the lexicon” is the kind of sentence that makes a technical reviewer trust the rest of your paper, because it shows you knew the limitation was there rather than hoping nobody would ask.
