title: Text as data
text:
The filter
Now the part that matters more than any of the above, and the part that no amount of skill with the previous sections will save you from.
reviews |> summarise(n = n(),
                     mean_stars = mean(star_rating),
                     detractors = mean(star_rating <= 2))
#> 4,938   3.52   0.260
A mean of 3.52 stars, 26% detractors. Both figures are arithmetically correct, and both describe a population somebody else defined before the file reached you. That is not a criticism of whoever produced the extract: extracts are always scoped, usually for a good operational reason, and the person scoping one is answering the question they were asked rather than the question you are about to ask. The habit worth building is to look for the scope before quoting the numbers.


Look at the column nobody looks at


customer_still_active.
Cross-tabulate it against the star rating:
SELECT customer_still_active, star_rating, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM 'data/customer_reviews.csv'
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2;
Among customers who are still active, one- and two-star reviews are 30% of the file. Among customers who have left, they are 8%. Side by side, that is odd: the departed group looks close to four times less likely to be angry than the group who stayed, when the expectation runs firmly the other way. Sixty-eight such reviews survive where several hundred should be.
Somebody built a “voice of the active customer” report and filtered out most low-star reviews from customers who had already gone — a defensible thing to do for that report’s purpose. Carried into this analysis, it means sentiment reads several points better than reality, the top complaint themes are under-weighted exactly where they were most severe, and every conclusion drawn from this file is a conclusion about the people who stayed.

And you were lucky
Notice what made that cross-tabulation possible. The column the filter was built on was left in the export. A tidier extract would have dropped it — the report only needed active customers, so the flag was redundant — and there would then have been nothing in the file to compare against. No data quality rule would have caught it, because every row present is valid. No amount of reading the review text would have caught it, because the missing reviews are missing. Next quarter’s extract may well be tidier.
So the defence cannot be analytical. It is procedural, and it fits in one sentence:

Ask for the extraction query, not the extract.

Then read the WHERE clause. That takes about ten seconds, it requires no tooling, and it is the single most valuable habit on Day 4.




The most dangerous sentence in an analytics review
“Here is what the data says.”
The honest version is “here is what the data that reached me says”, and the gap between the two is where most avoidable analytical embarrassment lives. It is not a gap about skill: somebody can run every technique in this session flawlessly and still be describing a population they never chose.
Every extract has a WHERE clause. Somebody chose it, usually for a sound operational reason that had nothing to do with your question, and usually months before your question existed. Asking what it was costs one email and is never resented.


Core lab · 30 minutes


Tokenise the corpus. Count. Note how uninformative raw frequency is.


Build the detractor-versus-promoter log-odds table. Now you have a finding.


Do it again with bigrams, keeping negations. Compare what you learn.


Isolate the Pidgin reviews. Run your English pipeline on them. Quantify how badly it does.


Find the filter. Cross-tabulate the two columns that reveal it and quantify the distortion.


Then answer the harder question: if that column had not been left in by accident, how would you have found out? Write the sentence you would send to whoever produced the extract.


Write the one-sentence caveat that must accompany every number from this corpus.


The sixth item is the one to spend real time on. The first five teach a technique; that one teaches the habit that survives after you have forgotten the technique.


Stretch
Bring your own text — call notes, survey free-text, complaint logs, anything you can lawfully use — and run the same pipeline.
Then, before you look at any output, write down the WHERE clause you think was on the extract, and go and check with whoever produced it. Comparing your guess against the real clause is the exercise, and being wrong is the interesting outcome rather than the embarrassing one. In most cohorts at least one person finds that a population they have been reporting on for years is narrower than they believed.


Copilot check
Assistants write text-processing code excellently, and there is no reason to type the boilerplate above by hand. Two things are worth checking every time:

The default stop-word list will delete your negations. Not because the assistant erred, but because it used the standard list, and the standard list treats “not”, “no”, “never” and “without” as noise. Say otherwise explicitly in the prompt.
It will offer you a word cloud. That is the most common output associated with this task in everything it has read, so it is a reasonable prediction of what people usually want. Ask instead for “the terms most over-represented in one-star reviews relative to five-star reviews, with counts and a log-odds ratio.”

And the thing it cannot do, for the same reason it could not detect Wednesday’s leak: it cannot tell you what the extraction filter was. That information is not in the file, in the text, or anywhere the assistant can reach. Only a person can ask that question, of another person.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: Text as data
text:
Takeaways

Text is data, and most of what your organisation knows about customers is in it.
Frequency describes the corpus; difference describes the problem.
Keep negations. Use bigrams.
A word cloud is a picture. Five themes with volumes, trend and verbatims is a business case.
Ask for the extraction query, not the extract.

title: Dashboards that get used
text:
Why most dashboards are abandoned
On Monday, in 1.1, we separated the four mechanisms by which analytics turns into money, and observed that the one attracting the most spending — visibility — returns the least, and that its return decays. This session is where that argument stops being a framework and becomes a set of design choices you make on a Tuesday afternoon. A dashboard is the archetypal visibility product. It can also be a mechanism-1 product, improving a recurring decision, and almost nothing about the technology determines which of the two you end up with. What determines it is the order in which you make the decisions about what goes on the screen.
The familiar story runs like this. Somebody asks for “a dashboard of our KPIs”. Six weeks later there are twenty-eight tiles, four filter panes and a page of definitions nobody reads. Usage peaks in week two, when everyone looks out of curiosity, and settles down to the person who built it.
That is not a failure of craft, and the tiles are usually well made. It is a consequence of building forwards from the data available rather than backwards from a decision somebody makes — and building forwards is the natural thing to do, because the data is the part you can see at the start of the project and the decision is not. Somebody asks for the KPIs; you have the KPIs; you put them on a screen. Every individual step is reasonable. It is only at the end that you notice nobody’s Tuesday changed.
There is one question that separates the two kinds of dashboard, and you can ask it in any meeting without sounding difficult:

“What does the user do differently when this number is red?”

If the answer is “they investigate”, you have an exploration tool. That is a legitimate thing to build — investigation is real work and it needs support — but it should be resourced and named as exploration, with a small audience of analysts, rather than presented as a management instrument and then judged as though it were one.
If the answer is “they escalate to the depot manager and authorise expediting”, you have a decision-support dashboard. That sentence names an actor, an action and an authority, and every design choice on the rest of this page follows from it.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: Dashboards that get used
text:
Design backwards, in five steps
The sequence below is deliberately the reverse of the usual one. Nothing about the data appears until step four.
1 · Name the decision. “Which SKU–depot lines get expedited this week?” One sentence, in the language the business already uses, phrased as a choice rather than as a topic. “Supply chain performance” is a topic; the sentence above is a decision.
2 · Name the user and the moment. “The supply planner, Tuesday morning, 20 minutes, before the replenishment run.” The moment matters as much as the person. A number that arrives after the replenishment run has gone out is not information, it is history — and this is the point at which the value chain from Monday most often breaks, not at the analysis.
3 · Name the actions available. Expedite, substitute, accept the stockout, delist. Four options. That is the decision space, and the dashboard exists to choose among exactly those four. Writing them down is often the moment somebody in the room realises two of the supposed options are not actually available to this user, which is worth finding out in week one.
4 · Work out the minimum information that discriminates between those actions. Now, and only now, think about data. The test for including a number is not “is it relevant” — almost everything is relevant — but “would a different value of this number lead to a different choice among the four?” Usually three or four numbers survive that test. Forecast demand, current cover, supplier lead time, margin at risk.
5 · Design the screen around those four numbers. Everything else is a drill-down, not a tile.

The four-numbers rule
If a dashboard carries more than about six top-level numbers, the user has to decide what to look at before they can decide anything else. That second decision is unpaid, it recurs every time they open the screen, and it is what quietly turns a daily habit into a monthly one.
Four numbers, one screen, no scrolling. Everything else lives one click down — not deleted, just demoted, which is usually enough to satisfy the person who wanted it there.
The instinct to add “just one more useful metric” is well-intentioned and it is how every twenty-eight-tile dashboard was built: nobody ever added twenty-eight tiles, they added one, on twenty-eight separate occasions, each time for a good reason. The defence is to agree the number of top-level tiles before the first one is built, so that adding a metric means a conversation about which to demote rather than an unopposed addition.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: Dashboards that get used
text:
The layout that works



One decision, four numbers, an exception list, and a quality badge. Everything else is a click down.


Reading order matters, because eyes go top-left first and then rightwards, and whatever occupies that corner is what the screen appears to be about.

Top-left: the decision, written as a sentence. “Which lines to expedite this week.” Yes, in words, on the dashboard itself. It costs one line of space and it does two things: it tells a new user what the screen is for without a training session, and it survives the departure of the person who commissioned it, which a shared understanding in somebody’s head does not.
Top row: the four numbers, each with its comparison — versus last week, versus target, versus the same week last year. A number without a comparison is not information: an availability figure tells the planner nothing until they can see it against the target it is measured to, and against where it stood a week ago.
Middle: the exception list. The actual lines needing action, sorted by value at risk, with the recommended action as a column. This is what the user came for. It is also what most dashboards bury below the charts, because charts feel like the deliverable and a list feels like an appendix — when in fact the list is the only part anybody acts on.
Right or bottom: the trend, for context only.
Corner: the data quality badge and the refresh timestamp. From 2.5. It changes the conversation from “do I trust this?” to “rule 7 failed, who owns it?” — which is the difference between a meeting that stalls and a meeting that assigns something.

Filters: default them to the user’s own scope. A supply planner should open the dashboard already filtered to their own depots, with the ability to widen it if they want to. Every filter somebody has to set before they see anything is a small tax on opening the screen at all, and those taxes compound.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: Dashboards that get used
text:
Define measures once
This is the technical decision on the page with the largest organisational consequence, and it is usually taken by accident.
Measures — revenue, margin, availability, churn — should be defined once, in the model, against the fact table, with every report referencing that one definition rather than restating it. The alternative, which is what happens when nobody decides, is that each report contains its own version of the calculation, written by whoever built it, on the day they built it.
The form this takes depends on your tooling but the principle does not change. In a semantic model it is a DAX measure. In a warehouse it is a metrics layer or a governed view. In a Quarto dashboard it is one function in one file that every page calls.
# One definition, used everywhere. Not copied into four scripts.
availability <- function(df) {
  df |>
    summarise(availability = 1 - mean(stockout_flag),
              .by = c(depot_code, week_starting))
}
The consequence of getting this wrong is specific and recognisable: two reports, both correct, both showing something called “availability”, disagreeing by two points — and a forty-minute meeting that ends with the discovery that one of them excludes delisted SKUs. Nobody made a mistake. Two people made two reasonable choices, months apart, without a shared definition to consult. The cost is not really the two points; it is that everything else on both screens is now treated with suspicion, and rebuilding that confidence takes considerably longer than fixing the measure.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: Dashboards that get used
section: Power BI, Quarto dashboards, or a page you host
text:
Power BI, Quarto dashboards, or a page you host
Three delivery routes. Choose by who reads it and how often, not by preference or by what the team already knows.

Power BIQuarto dashboardA hosted page


Choose it when the audience already lives in it, needs row-level security, needs to slice interactively, or when IT will only support what they have licensed.
Do this:

Star schema in the model. Facts and dimensions, as in 1.5. Do not import one wide flat table — it is slower and it makes consistent measures impossible.
Import mode unless you have a genuine real-time need. DirectQuery is slower than people expect and pushes load onto the source.
A real date table, marked as the date table.
Measures in one folder, named consistently, with descriptions filled in.

Be honest about: Pro licences cost money per user per month, and “everyone can see it” usually means “everyone with a licence”. That distinction is worth establishing before you promise a readership.


Choose it when the audience is small, the content is more narrative than interactive, and you want it reproducible and version-controlled.
---
title: "Weekly availability"
format:
  dashboard:
    orientation: rows
---

## Row {height=20%}

::: {.valuebox icon="box-seam" color="primary"}
Availability this week

`r scales::percent(current_availability, 0.1)`
:::

## Row {height=55%}

### Column {width=60%}
Exception list — lines to expedite

### Column {width=40%}
Twelve-week trend
Advantages: free, a plain HTML file you can email or host anywhere, regenerates from the same source as your report — which is 4.4’s subject — and diffable in Git.
Limits: it is static. Filters need a live back end, which is a different kind of project with a different cost.


Choose it when you need something clickable in front of an executive within the hour, or when the thing is genuinely a one-off exploration.
Generate a self-contained HTML page from your analysis and share the link. It is the fastest route from a result to something a senior person can interact with, and it is the right answer considerably more often than the weight of tooling around the enterprise platforms would suggest.
Be honest about: if it is not regenerated from the pipeline, it goes stale — and a stale dashboard is worse than no dashboard, because people trust it. An absent number prompts a question; a wrong one that looks current does not.




The dashboard that made the wrong number famous
Suppose you build a regional revenue dashboard on the joined table from 2.4 without first checking the depot dimension for duplicates. The screen will show North Central as the second-largest region — permanently, refreshing every night, on a display in the corridor.
What makes this different from the same error in a one-off analysis is repetition. A wrong number in a slide is seen once and challenged or forgotten. A wrong number on a dashboard is seen every day by everyone, and familiarity does the rest of the work: people plan against it, budget from it, and cite it in papers that cite each other. The error becomes institutional, and when somebody eventually finds it the correction does not land as a small fix. It lands as a reason to doubt every other number on the same screen, most of which were fine.
That is why the quality badge belongs on the dashboard, and why the pipeline gate belongs before the publish step rather than after it. A dashboard that refuses to refresh when a rule fails is a mild inconvenience for a morning. A dashboard that refreshes confidently with a broken join is a year of decisions.


Core lab · 30 minutes


Write the decision sentence for your capstone dashboard. One line.


Name the user, the moment, and the four actions available to them.


List the minimum information that discriminates between those actions. Stop at four.


Sketch the screen on paper before you build anything. Two minutes.


Build it — Power BI or a Quarto dashboard, your choice.


Put the quality badge and the refresh timestamp on it.


Sceptic: sit down at it cold and try to make the decision in three minutes. Report what was missing and what was noise.


The cold-user test in the last item is the whole lab, and everything before it is preparation. Three minutes is not an arbitrary limit — it is roughly what the real user will give the screen before falling back on what they did last week. Note both halves of what you find: what was missing is a gap to fill, and what was noise is a tile to demote, and the second list is usually longer and harder to act on.


Stretch
Take an existing dashboard from your organisation — ideally one you suspect nobody uses — and do the archaeology:

What decision was it built for? Ask the person who commissioned it.
Who opens it now, and how often? Most platforms will tell you.
How many of its tiles have ever changed anybody’s action?

Then rebuild it as one screen with four numbers and an exception list, and show both to the intended user.
In most cohorts somebody does this and finds the dashboard has three users, one of whom is the person who built it. That is a genuinely useful thing to discover, and it is worth saying that it reflects how the thing was specified rather than how well it was made. Almost every organisation has several of these, and finding one is the beginning of reclaiming the effort that maintains it.


Copilot check
Assistants build dashboard code well. They make dashboard scope decisions badly, and they do it in a consistent direction: they add tiles.
Ask for “a sales dashboard” and you will get twelve visuals, because twelve visuals is what a sales dashboard looks like in the material it learned from. It is not making a judgement about your business and losing; it is reproducing a convention faithfully, and the convention is the thing this session is arguing with.
The prompt that fixes it:

I need a dashboard for exactly one decision: [decision]. The user is [role], at [moment], with [time available], choosing between [actions]. Give me the minimum set of numbers that discriminates between those actions — no more than four — and tell me what you deliberately left out and why.

That last clause changes the answer completely. Asking for the omissions and the reasoning behind them turns the task from “produce a dashboard” into “defend a selection”, and a model asked to justify what it left out is far more disciplined than one asked to be concise. The same trick is worth keeping for any request where the temptation is to include everything.

title: Dashboards that get used
text:
Takeaways

Design backwards from a named decision, a named user and a named moment.
Four numbers, one screen. Everything else is a click down.
Every number needs a comparison.
The exception list is what the user came for. Do not bury it.
Define measures once, in the model.
Put the quality badge and the timestamp on the screen.

title: The executive narrative
section: The interruption is the design constraint
text:
The interruption is the design constraint
You will be interrupted, and it is worth designing for that rather than hoping against it.
Consider what is happening on the other side of the table. The senior person you are presenting to has read your first line, formed a provisional view, and is now either testing that view or deciding whether this item needs any more of their morning. That is not rudeness and it is not impatience; it is how somebody with thirty items on a list gets through the list. If your argument builds carefully from context, through method, to a conclusion on slide fourteen, the conclusion is very likely never to be reached — not because it was wrong, but because the meeting moved on while it was still being justified.
So the structure is inverted, always:

The answer. One sentence. The number and what to do about it.
The confidence. The interval, and the one assumption it rests on.
The ask. What you need from the person in the room.
Everything else, in descending order of importance, to be reached only if nobody interrupts.

That order feels wrong to almost everybody the first few times, and there is a good reason for the discomfort. Anyone trained in a technical discipline has been taught to earn a conclusion before stating it, and putting the answer first can feel like asserting rather than arguing. The resolution is that you are not skipping the argument — you are reordering it, so that the part your audience most needs arrives while they are still listening, and the justification is available in full the moment anybody asks for it. Journalists call this the inverted pyramid and have used it for a century, for the same reason: readers stop at unpredictable points, and a story should be useful wherever it is abandoned.

The one-number brief
Two pages. It is the deliverable for the Day 4 lab and the core of the capstone.
Page 1, in this order:

The number. Availability in Q1 was 96.9%, and closing the gap to 97.5% is worth ₦17.9m of gross profit a year.
The interval and the assumption. Between ₦8.1m and ₦32.5m. The range is driven almost entirely by one judgement: how much of the recovered volume is genuinely lost sale rather than demand deferred to the following week. I have assumed a third, with a plausible range of 15% to 60%.
The ask. Approval to change the reorder policy at three depots for one quarter, with the other nine as a comparison group. No new spend. Decision needed by 30 October.
What happens if we do nothing. The 97.5% target has not been met in any quarter of the series — Q1 2026 is the best of the nine at 96.9%, and the gap has never closed on its own.
One chart. The one that makes the case. Not four.

Page 2: the method, in the order a sceptic will attack it — data and its grain, what was excluded and why, the assumption most likely to be wrong, and how you will know afterwards whether it worked.

The line that used to be on this page
For several drafts, the “what happens if we do nothing” line above read: “The gap has widened for three consecutive quarters.”
It is a good sentence. It creates urgency, it sounds like the kind of thing a supply chain director says, and it is false in this dataset — the relevant stretch of quarterly availability runs 96.5, 96.5, 96.2, 96.9, so the most recent quarter is the best one rather than the worst. A widening gap would need the series to be falling; this one rose.
Nobody typed it dishonestly. It is what the argument wanted to be true, written at the point in the drafting where the shape of the case was clear and the chart had not yet been made. That sequence — conclusion first, verification later, verification quietly skipped — is how almost every wrong number in a board pack gets there, and it happens to people who would never knowingly misstate anything.
It is also why the “what happens if we do nothing” line is the one a sceptic should attack first. Look back at page 1 and notice the asymmetry: the number, the interval and the assumption all came out of a calculation somebody could re-run, whereas the do-nothing line is usually a piece of narrative that nobody has ever computed. It is the only claim on the page with no arithmetic behind it, which makes it both the easiest to get wrong and the least likely to be checked.

That is it. Two pages. Anything longer is an appendix, and appendices are welcome.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: The executive narrative
text:
Say the uncertainty out loud
The instinct under pressure is to project confidence. It is understandable — you are being asked to justify a recommendation, and hedging feels like weakening it — but it is exactly wrong, and it is expensive.
Consider two answers to “how sure are you?”:

A. “Very confident. The model has been thoroughly validated.”
B. “The central estimate is ₦17.9m a year. My range is ₦8.1m to ₦32.5m. That width is almost entirely one assumption — how much stockout demand is genuinely lost rather than deferred. I have used a third; the range spans 15% to 60%. Pin that down to within five points either side and the range narrows to roughly ₦15m–₦21m. It would cost about two weeks of point-of-sale analysis to find out.”

A is what an anxious person says, and everybody in the room recognises it as such. It cannot be checked, which means it also cannot be defended: the first time the number turns out to be wrong, there is no account of why it was wrong, and the cost is not that one estimate but every future estimate you present.
B does five things at once. It gives the decision-maker the figure they need in order to decide. It demonstrates that you know precisely where your ignorance is, which is a stronger signal of competence than confidence ever is. It makes the next step obvious. It is impossible to catch out, because every weakness has already been named by you. And — the part people underuse — it prices the cost of certainty, so that somebody senior can make an informed decision about whether to buy two more weeks of analysis or to proceed on the estimate they have.
Notice as well how tightly that range is tied to the one assumption. The mid estimate of ₦17.9m assumes a third of stockout demand is genuinely lost. The low end assumes 15% — which is a little under half of a third — and ₦8.1m is a little under half of ₦17.9m. The high end assumes 60%, which is about 1.8 times a third, and ₦32.5m is about 1.8 times ₦17.9m. The value moves in direct proportion to that single judgement, which is exactly why naming it is more useful than quoting the range on its own: a listener who disagrees with you about lost sales can convert their own view into a number without asking you to redo anything.
B is what a professional sounds like. It is also, not coincidentally, harder to produce, because it requires you to have actually done the work in 3.3 and 1.3.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: The executive narrative
text:
The hostile question
Somebody in the room does not want your conclusion to be true. This is normal, it is often useful, and it is rarely personal — the most common reason is that your conclusion implies work or risk for their function. There are four recognisable kinds of hostile question and each has a correct response, which is worth knowing in advance because none of them is the response instinct suggests.
1 · The data attack. “Where did this number come from? I don’t recognise it.”
Correct response: name the source, the grain, the period and the exclusions, in one breath. “Sell-out from the WMS, one row per depot per SKU per week, January 2024 to March 2026, deduplicated — there were 214 duplicate grains from an ETL re-run — with stockout weeks counted as zero rather than dropped. This quarter’s figure is Q1 2026, 6,240 depot-SKU-weeks.”
Two things happen when you can say that fluently. The attack ends, because you have demonstrated that you know the data better than the person asking. And, more usefully, the person asking now knows that if their figure differs from yours, the difference is locatable — a different period, a different exclusion, a different grain — which turns a disagreement into a reconciliation. This is why Tuesday exists.
2 · The method attack. “Isn’t this just correlation?”
Correct response: agree, precisely, and say what you would need. “Yes. This is an association, not a causal estimate. To claim causation I would need the three-depot pilot with a comparison group, which is what I am asking for.”
Never defend a causal claim you cannot support. It is the one move from which there is no recovery, because the room will remember it. Concede the exact point — not more than the exact point — and reframe the concession as the reason for your ask, which is what it genuinely is. The whole apparatus behind this answer is Friday morning.
3 · The relevance attack. “So what?”
Correct response: the decision, the owner, the money, the date. Four items, one sentence. If you cannot assemble that sentence, the difficulty is not presentational and no amount of rewriting will fix it — the work has not yet been attached to a decision, which is the subject of 1.1 and worth going back to.
4 · The authority attack. “That’s not what the sales team says.”
Correct response: “Then one of us has a definition problem, and it is worth ten minutes to find out which. My definition of availability is X and it excludes Y. What is theirs?”
Almost always it is the definition — see 1.2 — and naming that immediately does two things at once. It turns a confrontation into a joint investigation, in which you and the sales team are now on the same side of a shared puzzle. And it removes the question of who is right, which was never going to be settled in that meeting anyway. It also, incidentally, makes you look considerably better than winning the argument would have.

The answer that costs you everything
“I’d have to check.”
It is honest, and once per meeting it is entirely fine — better than the alternative, and senior people generally respect it. Twice in the same meeting and the room quietly reclassifies the whole item as not yet ready, however good the analysis behind it.
The fix is not to bluff, which fails worse and fails permanently. The fix is preparation, and it is a specific exercise rather than a general intention: before any presentation, write down the five questions you most hope nobody asks, and answer them on paper.
The reason this works is that the questions you hope to avoid are not random. They are the places where you already know the evidence is thinnest — an assumption you could not check, a period you excluded for a reason you are not sure survives scrutiny, a definition you inherited without verifying. Your discomfort is a reliable detector, and it is pointing at the real content of the meeting.
Do this once and you will never present the same way again.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: The executive narrative
section: Structure for the memo, and the one for the meeting
text:
Structure for the memo, and the one for the meeting
They are different documents for different situations, and people routinely write one and use it as the other.









The memo
The meeting




Read
Alone, quickly, possibly on a phone
Together, aloud, with interruption


Structure
Answer, confidence, ask, evidence
Answer, then respond to whatever they raise


Charts
One, embedded
One per point, large, no legends


Length
Two pages
Eight minutes, planned for five


Prepare
The document
The five questions



The difference that matters is in the last row. For a memo, the artefact is the preparation: you write it, you edit it, and what you hand over is the thing you worked on. For a meeting, the artefact you prepare is almost never the thing that gets used — you prepare answers, and the sequence in which they are needed is chosen by somebody else.
One pattern is worth trying, and it works better than its awkwardness suggests: send the memo 24 hours ahead, then run the meeting as questions only. No presentation at all. It requires nerve, because the first thirty seconds are silent and it will feel as though nothing is happening. It produces better decisions, because everybody has actually read the document and the time is spent on the genuine disagreement rather than on exposition that half the room did not need.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: The executive narrative
section: Where the assistant helps, and where it cannot
text:
Where the assistant helps, and where it cannot
It helps with: structure, tightening, generating the hostile questions, rewriting for a specific audience, and turning a two-page memo into eight slides without losing the argument.
It cannot: know what your CFO cares about, know that the Head of Supply Chain has a history with this depot, or decide what the recommendation should be. Those depend on information that exists only in the room, and no amount of prompting will conjure it.
Two prompts worth keeping:

Here is a two-page analytical memo. Act as the CFO it is addressed to. You are sceptical, short of time, and you have been given optimistic analytics numbers before. Give me the five questions you would ask, in the order you would ask them, and tell me which one you think the author is least prepared for.

and:

Rewrite this memo’s opening so that the first sentence contains the number, the action and the deadline. Then tell me what got lost, so I can decide whether to put it back.

The second one matters more than it looks. Compression always loses something — that is what compression is — and the usual failure of an edited draft is not that it is too short but that a caveat disappeared without anybody noticing. Asking the assistant to name what it dropped turns an invisible loss into an explicit choice, and keeps the choice with you.

Core lab · 20 minutes


Write your one-number brief. Page 1 only. Ten minutes, hard stop.


Write the five questions you most hope nobody asks. Answer them, briefly.


Present page 1 to your Sceptic in ninety seconds. They interrupt at will.


Sceptic: use all four attack types, in any order.


Rewrite the opening sentence so it contains number, action and deadline.


The ten-minute limit on the first item is doing something deliberate. A brief written in ten minutes contains only what you actually believe; the fourth and fifth drafts are where hedging creeps back in.


Stretch
Write the version of your brief for a different audience: the same finding, addressed to the operations manager who has to implement it rather than to the CFO who has to fund it.
Then note what changes. The number stays — it must — but the framing, the ask and very likely the chart all move. The CFO needs the value and the risk; the operations manager needs to know what changes on their Tuesday, who has agreed to it, and what happens when it goes wrong at the depot with the oldest system.
Most of us have exactly one register and use it on everybody, usually the one that suited the job we were good at before this one. It is the most common reason a technically excellent finding does not travel beyond the function that produced it.
crumbs: Day 4 — Unstructured data and the executive narrative

title: The executive narrative
text:
Takeaways

Answer, confidence, ask, evidence. In that order, because you will be interrupted.
Say the range and name the assumption that drives its width. It increases credibility.
Four hostile question types, four correct responses. Concede the exact point; never defend a causal claim you cannot support.
Write the five questions you hope nobody asks, and answer them. That is the preparation.
Send the memo ahead and run the meeting as questions.

title: Correlation, contribution, cause
section: Three claims, and only one of them justifies spending money
text:
Three claims, and only one of them justifies spending money
Three quite different statements can be made about the same pair of columns, and in a slide they look almost identical. It is worth separating them slowly, because the whole of Friday morning rests on the distinction.
The first is a statement about what tends to happen together. Customers who use the app a lot tend to stay; customers who use it rarely tend to leave. That is an observation about a pattern in data you already have, and it can be checked by anybody with the same file.
The second is a statement about what a model did. A model has scored a particular customer as high-risk, and you can take that single score apart and say which pieces of information pushed it up and which pushed it down. This is a fact about the model’s arithmetic, not about the customer’s life.
The third is a statement about what would happen if you intervened. If we persuaded this customer to use the app more, would they be less likely to leave? That is a claim about a world that does not yet exist, and nothing in a historical dataset can settle it on its own.
Those three are correlation, contribution and cause. Only the third justifies spending money on change, and only the third requires evidence you cannot get by looking harder at the data you already have.









Claim
What it says
Evidence needed
What you may do with it




Correlation
X and Y move together
Observational data
Predict. Target. Segment.


Contribution
X pushed this prediction up
A model, plus SHAP or similar
Explain a model’s output. Debug a model.


Cause
Changing X changes Y
Experiment, or a strong quasi-experimental design
Decide to spend money



A great many analytics presentations make claim three using evidence for claim one, and the room rarely notices, because nothing announces the change. The chart does not move; only the verb does. “Digital engagement drives retention” is a causal sentence resting on a correlational chart, and the slide before it said “is associated with”. That is the whole mechanism by which a bank comes to spend ₦400m pushing customers into an app in the hope of retaining them — not through anybody’s dishonesty, but through a series of small, natural paraphrases, each of which sounds like the last.

The sentence discipline
Watch the verbs. Each of these makes a different claim, and only some of them are usually supported by what is on the page:

“is associated with” — correlation. Honest.
“predicts” — correlation, used for targeting. Honest.
“contributes to the model’s prediction” — contribution. Honest and narrow.
“drives”, “causes”, “leads to”, “improves” — causal. Needs an experiment.

Almost the whole session is contained in that list, and it makes a practical test you can apply to somebody else’s memo in thirty seconds as well as to your own. If a sentence uses a verb from the last line, either the design that supports it is described somewhere in the document, or the verb needs to change. Both are acceptable outcomes. Only leaving it unexamined is not.

title: Correlation, contribution, cause
section: The classic confounder, using the marketing data
text:
The classic confounder, using the marketing data
library(tidyverse)
mkt <- read_csv("data/marketing_spend.csv")

mkt |>
  group_by(channel) |>
  summarise(cor = cor(spend_ngn, conversions),
            cost_per_conversion = sum(spend_ngn) / sum(conversions))
Run that and every channel shows a strong positive correlation between what was spent and how many conversions arrived. Weeks with heavy spend are weeks with many conversions, in search, in display, in every line of the file. The obvious conclusion, and the one that will be reached in the meeting if nobody intervenes, is: spend more.
Before reading on, it is worth asking what else could produce that pattern.


Why that is not what the data says


Spend and conversions both respond to seasonal demand. When demand is high, the marketing team spends more and more people convert — and neither of those facts caused the other.
# The confounder is visible the moment you look
mkt |>
  mutate(week = lubridate::week(week_starting)) |>
  group_by(week) |>
  summarise(spend = sum(spend_ngn), conv = sum(conversions)) |>
  ggplot(aes(week)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = scale(spend)), colour = "#16549B") +
  geom_line(aes(y = scale(conv)),  colour = "#C4A060") +
  labs(title = "Spend and conversions move together — because demand moves both")
A variable that causes both of the things you are comparing is called a confounder, and seasonal demand is the textbook example: it raises conversions directly, and it raises spend because the marketing team quite sensibly puts money behind the periods when people are buying. The correlation between spend and conversions is then perfectly real and almost entirely uninformative about the next naira.
Worse, the genuine response to spend diminishes as you spend more: doubling the budget does not double conversions, because the easiest customers are reached first. So the naive correlation overstates the return on the next naira in two directions at once — it credits spend with demand it did not create, and it assumes the next naira works as well as the average one.
The chain that makes this expensive:

Correlation observed: high spend weeks have high conversions.
Causal language used: “search drives conversions.”
Budget decision made: increase search spend 40%.
Conversions rise — because it was Q4.
The decision is validated by the outcome, and repeated next year.

Nothing in that chain is stupid. Everything in it is wrong. Notice in particular that step 4 supplies apparently confirming evidence, which is what makes the loop self-sustaining: the result you predicted did arrive, so the belief is strengthened, and the same decision is made with more confidence next year. Only step 5 is preventable, and only by having designed a comparison at step 3 — holding some of the budget flat somewhere, so that “what would have happened anyway” is a thing you measured rather than a thing you assumed.

title: Correlation, contribution, cause
text:
What SHAP actually is
This is the part of the day that most changes what people do on Monday, and it is worth building up from the plain idea before the acronym arrives.
Suppose a model gives a particular customer a churn score. You would like to know why it gave that customer that score. The natural way to find out is to ask how the score would change if one piece of information about them were different — if their app usage were typical instead of very low, say — and to do that for every piece of information the model used, in a way that makes the pieces add up to the score. That is exactly what SHAP values are: a decomposition of one single prediction into a contribution from each feature. The name comes from Shapley values, an idea borrowed from co-operative game theory about how to divide credit fairly among players who contributed jointly to a result.
Take a real row from the file in front of you. Customer C100306 scores 57% against a base rate of 10.6% — a little over five times the average risk in the book. Decomposing that prediction, the largest single push comes from digital_engagement_score = 9.9 — near the floor of the distribution — the next from products_held = 1, then tenure_months = 34 and a low balance. In plain terms: this customer barely uses the digital channel, holds a single product, is a few years in, and does not keep much money with the bank.
(Those four are the largest contributions from a logistic model fitted on the clean columns. Run it yourself; the numbers are in the file, not in this page.)
One technical caveat is worth carrying, because it is the most common way this gets misquoted. The contributions add up in whatever space the model does its arithmetic in, and for a classifier that is normally log-odds rather than probability. Log-odds is simply a rescaling of probability that runs from minus infinity to plus infinity instead of from 0 to 1, which is what lets the model add things up without ever producing a probability of 120%. The consequence for you is practical: a contribution of a given size in log-odds does not translate into a fixed number of percentage points, because the same push matters much more near a probability of 50% than near 2%. Attributing “six percentage points” to a feature requires an explainer configured for probability output, and even then the decomposition stops being cleanly additive. Unless you have done that work, say “the largest contribution” and not “worth six points”.
So SHAP is a genuinely useful and precisely defined thing. It answers: why did the model say this about this customer? — and that is a question worth being able to answer, both for debugging a model and for giving a retention caller something concrete to open with.
It does not answer: what should we change?



A feature-importance ranking answers “why did the model say this?” well, and “what should we change?” not at all. Only the second question justifies a budget.



Say this out loud once and it will stay with you
A SHAP value is a contribution to a prediction, not a causal driver.
It tells you what the model used. It does not tell you what the world does.
The distinction is easy to state and genuinely hard to hold on to under the pressure of a slide titled “top drivers of churn”, so here are the three ways the misreading goes wrong in practice. Each has cost somebody real money.
One — the feature is a symptom. complaints_last_12m contributes heavily to the churn prediction, because people who are about to leave complain first. Read causally, that says “reduce complaints and churn will fall”. But the cheapest way to reduce the feature is to make complaints harder to log, and a team measured on it will find that route without anybody intending fraud. Complaints would fall, churn would not, the model would quietly get worse because its best signal had been switched off, and nobody would be able to explain why.
Two — correlated features share credit arbitrarily. txns_last_90d and digital_engagement_score measure nearly the same underlying thing: how active this customer is. When two features carry the same information, the model can lean on either, and SHAP has to split the credit between them somehow. How it splits depends on the fitting procedure rather than on the world. Refit with a different algorithm and the two can swap places in the ranking while the model’s predictions barely change. A “top drivers” chart that reorders when you change the model is not describing reality; it is describing the model, and it is worth checking whether it does, which is one of the lab tasks below.
Three — the intervention is not in the data. This is the deepest of the three. The model has never seen a customer whose engagement was changed by anything. It has only seen customers who differ from one another — and a customer who was always highly engaged is not the same kind of person as one who was pushed into the app by a campaign. Those are two different populations, and the difference between them is precisely the causal question. No amount of historical data answers it, because the observation that would answer it was never made.

title: Correlation, contribution, cause
text:
What you may legitimately say
The gap between these two paragraphs is narrower than it looks and matters more than almost anything else on the page.
Legitimate:

“The model relies most heavily on complaints, digital engagement and tenure. Customers flagged high-risk typically show a recent complaint and falling app usage. This gives us a targeting rule and a conversation opener for the retention call.”

Not legitimate:

“Complaints are the biggest driver of churn. Reducing complaints by 20% would cut churn by 8%.”

The first describes who to call and what to raise with them, which is worth real money and is fully supported by what you have. The second promises a return on an intervention: it will be put in a business case, somebody will be given a budget and a target against it, and the only kind of evidence that supports it is an experiment. Read the two again and notice how little separates them on the page — one is a statement about the model’s inputs, the other about the world’s mechanics — and how completely they differ in what they license.

title: Correlation, contribution, cause
text:
The bridge to causal work
If you want the causal claim, there are three routes, in descending order of strength.

Randomise. 5.2. The strongest, and usually cheaper than people expect, because the comparison group costs nothing but the discipline of holding it back.
Find a natural experiment. 5.3. Weaker, and sometimes the only route available, because the change already happened and nobody was going to randomise a regulation.
Assume a causal structure and defend it. Write down the causal diagram you are assuming, state what you have adjusted for, and be explicit that the whole claim rests on there being no important confounder you failed to measure. This is a legitimate scientific move, used routinely in epidemiology and economics, and it is far more honest than a SHAP chart presented as a list of drivers. What it costs you is exposure: you have to put the diagram on the wall and let people attack it, and some of the attacks will land.


The causal diagram, in ninety seconds
Before any causal claim, sketch the boxes and arrows. It takes a minute on a whiteboard and it is the cheapest way to find out whether your analysis is answering the question you think it is. There are four kinds of thing to draw, and the difference between them decides what you should and should not control for.

Treatment → Outcome. The effect you are claiming. One arrow.
Confounders → both. Anything that causes the treatment and the outcome, like the seasonal demand above. These must be adjusted for, because otherwise their influence is credited to your treatment.
Mediators. Things that sit on the path between treatment and outcome — part of how the effect happens. These must not be adjusted for. Control for a mediator and you erase the very effect you are trying to measure, because you have held constant the mechanism through which it works.
Colliders. Things that treatment and outcome both cause. Conditioning on one of these manufactures an association out of nothing, and it produces the most spectacular spurious findings in the literature.

The collider is the one nobody draws, so it is worth taking slowly, and you have already met a live example. On Wednesday, sales_touchpoints was recorded only for leads that reached SQL — and reaching SQL is caused by two separate things: how hard the sales team worked the lead, and how good the lead was to begin with. A thing with two causes pointing into it is a collider. Filtering your analysis to the rows where touchpoints are populated is conditioning on that collider, and here is why it bites: among leads that got through, a lead that was worked lightly must have been strong, and a weak lead must have been worked hard, because otherwise it would not be in the file at all. Effort and quality now appear negatively related, and that relationship was created by the filter.
Note precisely how strong that claim is, because it is stronger than the one people usually make. “Survivorship” says your sample is unrepresentative of the population. A collider says the correlation itself was manufactured by the act of filtering — it was not there, you made it, and collecting more data on the surviving rows will not make it go away.
The mediator error is the more common one in commercial work, and it looks completely reasonable while you are making it: measuring the effect of a retention call on churn while controlling for “customer contacted us afterwards”. Being contacted afterwards is part of how the call works, so controlling for it subtracts the effect from itself.
Draw it on the whiteboard. If nobody can attack your diagram, either it is right or nobody understood it, and it is worth finding out which.


Core lab · 30 minutes


Take the marketing data. Compute the naive spend-conversion correlation by channel.


Show that seasonality drives both. Quantify how much of the correlation survives once you condition on the season.


Fit the churn model from 3.5 and compute SHAP values.


Write two sentences from the same chart: one legitimate targeting claim, one illegitimate causal claim.


Refit with a different algorithm. Does the “top drivers” ranking change? Report by how much.


Draw the causal diagram for your capstone’s central claim. Name the confounder you cannot measure.


The last item is the one to protect if the clock beats you. Every observational causal claim has a confounder somebody could name, and naming yours before the panel does is the difference between a limitation you have accounted for and one you have been caught by.


Stretch
Go back through your capstone brief and audit every verb.
Circle every sentence that makes a causal claim. For each one, write down what evidence you actually have, and then either downgrade the verb to match the evidence or specify the design that would support the verb you wanted.
Most people find between two and five, and the discovery is nearly always the same: the causal verbs crept in during the rewrite that made the memo read well, not during the analysis. It is the most uncomfortable twenty minutes of the programme, and it is the one that most improves the Friday defence — because the panel will do this to you anyway, and it is a great deal better to have done it to yourself first.


Copilot check
Assistants use causal language freely, because the writing they learned from does. Ask why churn is happening and you will get “the main drivers are…” — a causal framing built on correlational evidence, delivered fluently and with no signal at all that a line has been crossed. It is not being careless; it is reproducing the register of the millions of business documents that make exactly the same move.
They are, however, good at catching it when asked directly, which is the useful asymmetry here:

Here is a paragraph from an analytics memo. For each sentence, classify the claim as correlational, contributional or causal. For every causal claim, state what study design would be required to support it, and rewrite the sentence to match the evidence I actually have, which is: [describe your data].

Run your capstone through that prompt tonight. It is the cheapest possible rehearsal for the panel, and the rewritten sentences are usually good enough to keep.

title: Correlation, contribution, cause
text:
Takeaways

Three claims, three evidence standards. Only causal claims justify spending money on change.
Watch the verbs. “Drives”, “causes” and “improves” need an experiment.
A SHAP value is a contribution to a prediction, not a causal driver.
Correlated features share SHAP credit arbitrarily. If the ranking moves when the model changes, it is not describing the world.
If you must make a causal claim from observational data, draw the diagram and let people attack it.

title: When you cannot randomise
section: Most of the time, you cannot randomise
text:
Most of the time, you cannot randomise
Session 5.2 made the case for experiments, and the case is a good one. It is also, for a large share of the questions you will actually be asked, unavailable — and not because anybody was careless.
The price change went live everywhere at once, because a staggered price is a customer relations problem. The competitor entered the market on their own timetable. The regulation changed. The depot closed. The system migration happened on a Tuesday and could not have happened on half a Tuesday. Nobody was going to randomise any of those, and yet somebody will still ask what effect it had — often at the point where the answer determines a budget.
The useful news is that this situation has its own toolkit, developed largely in economics and epidemiology, where randomising is frequently impossible or unethical. The methods give you weaker claims than an experiment, they rest on assumptions you have to state out loud, and — this is the part that surprises people — being explicit about both is what makes you credible. A stated assumption invites a specific challenge, which you can then answer. An unstated one leaves the whole estimate vulnerable to a general suspicion you cannot address.

title: When you cannot randomise
text:
Before-and-after is not evidence
Start with what almost everybody reaches for first, because it is the most natural thing in the world to reach for:

“We changed the reorder policy in November. Availability improved. The policy worked.”

The sentence has a comforting shape and it is very hard to argue with in a meeting. But consider what else happened between November and now. The season turned. The promotion calendar moved. A supplier’s performance changed. The exchange rate moved, which changed landed cost, which changed what got ordered. A competitor repriced. And — the one people forget — a group of people started paying closer attention because they knew a change was being watched, which on its own often improves an operational metric for a while.
A before-and-after comparison attributes every one of those to your change. It does not apportion them, and it does not flag them. It quietly credits your policy with the whole of the movement. That is why it is worth being blunt about the status of this design: it is not a weak causal design that could be strengthened with more data. It is not a causal design at all, because it contains no mechanism for separating your change from everything else that happened at the same time.

title: When you cannot randomise
text:
Difference-in-differences
The fix is to find a comparison group that did not get the change, and the idea is exactly what its name says: compare the change in the treated group with the change in the untreated group over the same period.
The reasoning is worth walking through in words before any notation. The treated group’s before-and-after movement contains two things mixed together: the effect of the intervention, and the effect of everything else that happened over those weeks. The control group’s movement contains only the second, because they had no intervention. So if you are willing to believe that “everything else” affected both groups by the same amount, you can subtract the control group’s movement from the treated group’s, and what remains is the intervention.





flowchart LR
  A["Treated<br/>before"] -->|"observed change<br/>= treatment + everything else"| B["Treated<br/>after"]
  C["Control<br/>before"] -->|"observed change<br/>= everything else"| D["Control<br/>after"]
  B -.->|"difference of the<br/>two differences<br/>= the effect"| D
  style B fill:#D6F0EA,stroke:#00695C,stroke-width:2px
  style D fill:#EEF3FA,stroke:#2E3A6E


 The counterfactual is what the treated group would have done had it followed the control group’s path. 



An invented example makes the arithmetic concrete. Suppose the treated depots averaged 500 units a week before the change and 380 after — a fall of 120. Over the same weeks the control depots went from 400 to 440 — a rise of 40. Before-and-after would report the treated group’s fall of 120 as the effect. Difference-in-differences says the control group’s rise of 40 is what “everything else” was doing, so absent the intervention the treated group would have risen by 40 too, to 540. The estimated effect is 380 minus 540, or −160 units — larger than the naive figure, because the intervention had to overcome a favourable background trend before it could produce a fall at all. Two differences, subtracted: hence difference-in-differences, often written DiD, and you will meet it under that name in any economics paper on policy evaluation.
Note what that example also shows: the naive figure can be too small as easily as too large. It is not a conservative estimate. It is an arbitrary one.
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)

weekly <- arrow::read_parquet("outputs/fmcg_weekly.parquet")
#  no pipeline output yet?  arrow::read_parquet("outputs/fmcg_weekly.parquet")
#  ships as a reference build - use it and come to the floor at the break.

# Four northern depots were re-segmented on 2025-11-03; the other eight were not.
did <- weekly |>
  mutate(treated = region %in% c("North West", "North Central"),
         post    = week_starting >= as.Date("2025-11-03")) |>
  group_by(depot_code, week_starting, treated, post) |>
  summarise(units = mean(units_sold, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Three decisions, and all three matter more than the arithmetic:
#   1. keep the weekly panel - do not collapse to four numbers per depot
#   2. model the LOG, because the effect is multiplicative
#   3. cluster the standard errors on the unit of treatment
feols(log(units) ~ treated:post | depot_code + week_starting,
      data = did, cluster = ~depot_code)
The treated:post term is the estimate you want: the extra movement in the treated depots after the change, over and above whatever the treated depots and that week were doing generally. The | depot_code + week_starting part handles those two “generally”s — it allows every depot its own level and every week its own level, so that a depot which is simply larger than the others, or a week in which everybody sold more, cannot be mistaken for an effect. Because the outcome is modelled in logs, the coefficient reads as a proportional change: exponentiate it and subtract one to express it as a percentage.

Three specification choices that decide whether you find anything
Here is something worth knowing before it happens to you. Run the naive version of this analysis — collapse each depot to one number per period, model units in levels rather than logs, use ordinary standard errors — and you get an estimate whose confidence interval contains zero. The honest reading of that output is that there was no detectable effect, and a careful person would report exactly that.
Run the version above and you recover −37%, with the interval nowhere near zero.
The two analyses use the same data and the same intervention date. The difference is not statistics in any deep sense; it is three modelling decisions, each of which can be argued for in advance of seeing any result.
Do not collapse the panel. Averaging each depot down to four numbers — treated or not, before or after — discards nearly all the information you collected. The week-by-week series tells you how variable a depot ordinarily is, which is the yardstick against which any change has to be judged. Throw that away and you have no yardstick, so the interval widens until it swallows everything.
Model the log if the effect is multiplicative. A re-segmentation that moves a share of demand elsewhere takes a proportion of each depot’s volume, not a fixed number of units — a big depot loses more units than a small one for the same underlying effect. Modelling in levels asks the data to find one common number of units, which fits nobody. And parallel trends in levels and parallel trends in logs are genuinely different assumptions that cannot generally both hold, so pick the one that matches how the world works, decide before you look, and say which you picked.
Cluster on the unit of treatment. Consecutive weeks within a single depot are not independent observations — they share a manager, a catchment and a stock position, so if one week is high the next is likely to be high too. Standard errors calculated as though every week were independent are therefore too small. Clustering on depot tells the calculation to treat each depot, rather than each week, as the unit that supplies genuinely new information.
Do that on this dataset, though, and you will find the clustered standard error is only about 10% wider than the unclustered one — which is worth pausing on, because the received wisdom is that clustering inflates standard errors severalfold. It does when there is strong correlation within clusters. Here the week-to-week noise inside a depot is close to independent once the depot’s own level is accounted for, so there is little for the correction to find.
The lesson is not “clustering doesn’t matter”. It is that you cluster because the design says the errors might be correlated, not because you expect a particular answer — and then you report whatever comes out. A specification chosen after seeing which one gave the more convenient interval is not a specification; it is a preference wearing one.
And then the constraint nobody can fix by being cleverer: there are four treated depots. The cluster-robust machinery assumes you have enough clusters for its approximations to hold, and four is not enough, however many weeks each of them contributes. The binding limitation on this design is the number of things that got treated, not the amount of data — which makes it a design conversation to have before the next rollout, not an analysis conversation to have after it.


The assumption, and how to check it
Everything above rests on one thing, and it is worth naming plainly before naming it technically: you are assuming that if the intervention had never happened, the two groups would have carried on moving up and down together. Not that they would sit at the same level — northern depots can be larger or smaller than the rest — but that they would move in step, so that the control group’s path is a fair stand-in for the path the treated group would have taken.
That assumption is called parallel trends, and it is the whole design. If it fails, the number you compute is not an effect; it is the divergence the two groups were going to show anyway.
You cannot test it directly, and it is worth being honest about why: it is a claim about a world that did not happen, and no data exists from a world that did not happen. What you can test is its observable implication. If the two groups really do move together absent an intervention, they should have been moving together in the weeks before the intervention, when neither had received it.
weekly |>
  mutate(grp = if_else(region %in% c("North West", "North Central"),
                       "North (treated)", "Rest (control)")) |>
  filter(week_starting < as.Date("2025-11-03")) |>
  group_by(grp, week_starting) |>
  summarise(units = mean(units_sold, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(week_starting, units, colour = grp)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Pre-period trends. If these diverge, the design fails.")
Plot it. Every time. The two lines will not lie on top of one another, and they are not meant to; what you are looking at is whether the slopes match and whether the wobbles happen at the same time in both. If the pre-period trends visibly diverge, difference-in-differences is simply not available to you on this data, and no amount of added controls repairs it — worth being firm about, because the instinct when the plot looks wrong is to start adding covariates until it looks better.
Putting the pre-trend plot on the page beside the estimate is the single strongest credibility move available in observational causal work. It costs four lines of code, and it shows the audience the assumption rather than asking them to take your word that it holds.

title: When you cannot randomise
section: Synthetic control, when there is no obvious comparison
text:
Synthetic control, when there is no obvious comparison
Sometimes only one unit was treated — one depot, one region, one market — and no single other unit is a plausible comparison for it. The largest depot has no twin; the capital city behaves like nowhere else.
The idea behind synthetic control is to build the comparison rather than to find it. Instead of picking one control unit, you take a weighted blend of several untreated units, choosing the weights so that the blend tracks the treated unit as closely as possible in the period before the intervention. If a mixture of 40% of one depot, 35% of another and 25% of a third reproduces the treated depot’s history convincingly, then that mixture is a defensible stand-in for what the treated depot would have done next. The blend becomes your counterfactual, and the gap that opens up after the intervention date is your estimate.
# Conceptually: find weights over control depots that best reproduce
# the treated depot's pre-period series, then project forward.
library(tidysynth)

# The donor pool must contain only UNTREATED units. DP04, DP09 and DP12 were
# re-segmented at the same time as DP05; leaving them in biases the estimate
# towards zero, because the "control" would have moved too.
donors <- panel_data |> filter(!depot_code %in% c("DP04", "DP09", "DP12"))

synth <- donors |>
  synthetic_control(outcome = units, unit = depot_code, time = week,
                    i_unit = "DP05", i_time = as.Date("2025-11-03")) |>
  generate_predictor(mean_units = mean(units)) |>
  generate_weights() |>
  generate_control()

synth |> plot_trends()      # treated vs synthetic
synth |> plot_differences() # the estimated effect over time
synth |> plot_placebos()    # the inference: run it on untreated units
The comment about the donor pool is the part that most often goes wrong in practice, and it goes wrong quietly. Every unit you allow into the blend must be genuinely untreated. Include one that got the same change at the same time and your “control” moves along with the treated unit, which pulls the estimated gap towards zero and makes a real effect look like nothing.
The plot_placebos() step is where the inference lives, and it is a lovely piece of reasoning. With one treated unit there is no conventional standard error to compute, so instead you run the entire procedure again pretending, in turn, that each untreated unit was the treated one. Each of those runs produces a gap you know is pure noise, because nothing happened to that unit. If your real treated unit’s gap sits comfortably among the placebo gaps, you have found noise; if it stands well outside them, you have found something. In effect you build your own null distribution out of units where you know the answer is zero.

title: When you cannot randomise
text:
Interrupted time series
Sometimes there is genuinely no comparison group at all — a regulation that applied to everybody on the same day, a national price change, a system that was switched over everywhere at once. You can still do better than before-and-after, by building the counterfactual out of the history of the series itself.
Fit a model to the pre-intervention period, forecast forward as though nothing had happened, and then compare what actually occurred with that forecast and its interval. The gap between the two is your estimate; the width of the forecast interval is your uncertainty, and it widens honestly as you look further past the intervention date, which is exactly as it should be.
library(fable); library(tsibble)

pre <- series |> filter(week < intervention_date)
counterfactual <- pre |> model(ARIMA(units)) |> forecast(h = "13 weeks")

# The effect is actual minus counterfactual; the uncertainty is the
# forecast interval, and it widens with the horizon - honestly.
This is 3.3 put to a causal purpose, and it inherits every caveat from that session. It is the weakest of the three designs, for a reason that is easy to state and impossible to fix: it assumes the only thing that changed at the intervention date was the intervention. In a real economy, with a promotional calendar, a currency and a competitor, that is rarely true, and the further you forecast the less true it gets.

title: When you cannot randomise
text:
Ranking the claims honestly
The point of this table is not to shame the lower rows: a well-executed interrupted time series presented with its assumption on the page is far more useful than a randomised experiment nobody ran. What it gives you is the sentence you are entitled to say once you have chosen a design, and the assumption you must be prepared to defend when somebody asks.








Design
The claim you may make
The assumption




Randomised experiment
“X caused a Y% change, 95% CI [a, b]”
Randomisation worked (check SRM)


Difference-in-differences
“Consistent with X causing Y, assuming parallel trends, which held for N weeks before”
Parallel trends, in the scale you modelled


Synthetic control
“X is associated with a Y-point divergence from a matched synthetic comparison; placebo tests put it in the top k of m”
The donor pool spans the treated unit


Interrupted time series
“Outcomes after X were outside the 80% interval projected from history”
Nothing else changed at that date


Before-and-after
—
This is not a causal design




The sentence that makes you credible

“This is not a randomised result. It is a difference-in-differences estimate against the eight comparison depots, in logs, with standard errors clustered on the depot. It rests on the assumption that the two groups would have moved together — and that held for the twenty-six weeks before the change, which is the plot on the left. My estimate is a 37% reduction in northern weekly volume, interval 36% to 38%. The honest limitation is that only four depots were treated, so the real interval is wider than that arithmetic suggests — cluster-robust inference with four clusters is not reliable however many weeks you have. If we want a stronger claim, the next rollout phase should be randomised, which costs nothing extra.”

Six sentences, and each is doing a specific job: refusing a claim you are not entitled to, giving the specification so somebody could reproduce it, stating the assumption and pointing at the evidence for it, giving the estimate with its interval, conceding the limitation a well-briefed sceptic would have raised — in more detail than they would have managed — and converting the whole thing into a cheap, specific next step.
Nobody in the room can attack it, and the reason is not rhetorical skill. It is that every attackable thing has already been conceded, by you, in your own words, with the remedy attached. What is left for the sceptic to do is agree with the next step, which is what you wanted anyway.


Core lab · 20 minutes


Plot the pre-period trends for northern versus other depots. Are they parallel? Say how you decided.


Run the difference-in-differences the naive way — collapsed, in levels, unclustered — then again on the weekly panel, in logs, clustered on depot. Report both intervals and explain the gap without using the word “significant”.


For your capstone: which design is available to you? Write the honest claim sentence for that design.


Sceptic: name the thing that changed at the same time as the intervention and is not accounted for. There is always one.


The second item bans the word “significant” on purpose. It does a lot of hiding, and being denied it forces you to say what actually differed between the two analyses — which is what you would need to say to a panel anyway.


Stretch
Run a placebo test on the difference-in-differences: pretend the intervention happened thirteen weeks earlier than it did, on the same groups, and re-estimate using only the data from before the real intervention date.
You should find nothing, and finding nothing is the result you want. If you find an effect at a date when, by construction, nothing happened, your design is picking up a divergence that was already under way — which means the estimate at the real date is picking up some of it too, and is not trustworthy.
Placebo tests are cheap, they take four lines, and almost nobody in a commercial setting runs them. Running one and reporting that it came back null is disproportionately persuasive, precisely because it is evidence you went looking for a reason to disbelieve your own result.


Copilot check
Assistants write difference-in-differences code correctly and quickly. What they will not do unprompted is any of the four things that decide whether the estimate means anything:

plot the pre-trends,
mention that the estimate is meaningless if the pre-trends diverge,
suggest a placebo test,
or tell you that something else changed at the same date.

This is less a defect of reasoning than of framing: you asked for an estimate, and an estimate is what you were given. The prompt that fixes it asks for the scepticism explicitly:

Estimate the effect of an intervention on [date] on [group] using difference-in-differences against [comparison]. Requirements: first plot and assess pre-period parallel trends and tell me honestly whether the design is valid; then estimate with a confidence interval; then run a placebo test at a date thirteen weeks earlier; then list three things that could have changed at the same time as the intervention and how I would check each.

The last clause is the one it cannot fully answer, and it is worth knowing that in advance rather than discovering it in front of a panel. It will generate entirely plausible candidates — seasonality, a competitor move, a systems change — with no way of knowing which of them actually happened in your business in that particular November. Supplying that is your half of the work: the division of labour from 1.4, applied to the hardest problem in the programme.

title: When you cannot randomise
text:
Takeaways

Before-and-after is not a causal design.
Difference-in-differences needs a comparison group and rests on parallel trends. Plot the pre-trends and show them.
Synthetic control builds a comparison when no single unit will do. Placebo tests are the inference.
Interrupted time series is the weakest option and assumes nothing else changed.
State the design, the assumption, the evidence for it, the estimate, the interval, and the route to a stronger claim. Six sentences.
