title: The operating model
section: What an operating model actually is
text:
What an operating model actually is
“Operating model” is one of those phrases that can mean almost anything, so it is worth pinning down before choosing between versions of it. For analytics, it is the set of standing answers to six questions — standing, in the sense that they are decided once and then apply to every piece of work, rather than being renegotiated each time somebody asks for a number.

Where do the analysts sit? In one central team, in the business units, or in some arrangement of both.
Who owns a definition? When “revenue” or “active customer” or “availability” needs a precise meaning, who decides, and what happens to somebody who wants a different one.
How does work get chosen? What the queue is, who sets its order, and how something urgent overtakes something important.
How does something get into production? What has to be true before a number, a table or a model is allowed to be relied upon by other people — tests, review, documentation, an owner.
Who is accountable for the output being used? Not for producing it. For it changing a decision.
How is value checked afterwards? What is recorded when something ships, and who looks back.

Most organisations have explicit answers to the first and third of those, vague answers to the second and fourth, and no answer at all to the fifth and sixth. That distribution is the reason analytics functions can look busy, well-staffed and productive while the business quietly struggles to name a decision that changed. The rest of this session is about the questions in the second half of the list, because the first half is where attention naturally goes and the second half is where the value is.

title: The operating model
section: Three shapes, and the honest trade
text:
Three shapes, and the honest trade
The first question — where the analysts sit — has three standard answers. None of them is right in general; each buys something and pays for it somewhere else, and the table is an attempt to be honest about the payment.










Centralised
Federated
Hub and spoke




Analysts sit
In one team
In the business units
Both


Standards
Strong
Weak
Set centrally, applied locally


Business context
Weak
Strong
Adequate, if rotation happens


Speed
Slow — queue
Fast
Fast for the spokes


Duplication
Low
High
Medium


Fails by
Becoming a ticket queue nobody uses
Producing five incompatible versions of “revenue”
Hub becoming a policeman



Read the last row first, because how a model fails tells you more than how it is meant to work.
A centralised function fails by becoming a ticket queue. The standards are excellent, the code is clean, and the turnaround is six weeks — so the commercial teams stop asking, build their own spreadsheets, and the central team ends up producing high-quality analysis of questions nobody is waiting for. Nobody decided this; it is what happens when the cost of asking exceeds the value of waiting.
A federated function fails by fragmentation. Every unit moves quickly and produces its own numbers, and then one Thursday three of them present revenue figures for the same quarter that do not agree, and the meeting spends its time on reconciliation instead of on the decision. The analysts were all competent. They were answering slightly different questions with slightly different filters, and no mechanism existed to notice.
Hub and spoke fails by the hub becoming a policeman: a body that reviews, approves and says no, without producing anything the spokes want. Once that happens the spokes route around it, and you have a federated model with an extra approval step.
Most organisations should be hub and spoke, and most say they are while actually running one of the other two — usually without anyone intending to mislead, because the org chart genuinely shows a hub and some spokes.
The test is not the chart. It is two questions:

Does the hub set the definitions, own the pipeline standards and hold the model register — or does it just take requests? A hub that takes requests is a central team with a friendlier name, and you are centralised.
Do the spokes have anybody who can read a query? If the people in the business units can only consume finished outputs, they cannot check anything, cannot ask a second question without raising a ticket, and cannot be a spoke. You are centralised with extra steps.

The good version is recognisable by a specific behaviour: someone in a business unit writes their own analysis using tables and definitions the hub maintains, the hub reviews it because reviewing is genuinely useful rather than because approval is required, and neither party thinks of the other as an obstacle. When that is happening, the arrangement is working regardless of what the chart says.

title: The operating model
text:
Who to hire first
The instinct is to hire a data scientist, and it is understandable — it is the role with the clearest identity and the most obvious connection to the thing you want. It is usually the wrong first hire, and the failure it produces is specific enough to describe.
A capable data scientist joins a mid-sized organisation with no reliable tables. There is nothing trustworthy to model on, so they spend their first months assembling extracts by hand, discover that the extracts disagree with the finance system, spend more months reconciling, and eventually build something impressive on a dataset only they can reproduce. Eighteen months in, they leave — not because anybody treated them badly, but because they were hired to do one job and spent their time doing a different and less interesting one. The organisation concludes that data science does not work here.
The right first hire is nearly always an analytics engineer: somebody who builds pipelines, models data properly, writes tests, and produces tables that other people can rely on without checking. It is an unglamorous role, it is in short supply, and it is the thing that makes every subsequent hire productive, because everyone who comes afterwards starts from data they can trust rather than from data they have to rebuild.








Order
Role
Why




1
Analytics engineer
Trustworthy tables. Everything else depends on this.


2
Business analyst embedded in a function
Knows the decision. Reads code. Translates.


3
Data scientist
Now has clean data and a real question


4
Platform / infrastructure
When scale genuinely demands it, not before



The second row is the one most often skipped, and it is the one that decides whether anything gets used. A business analyst embedded in a function sits close enough to the decision to know what it actually turns on, and is technical enough to read what the hub produced and say “this does not answer the question we ask on a Tuesday”. Without that person, requirements arrive as requests for charts, and charts are what you get.
And then the role nobody budgets for and every organisation needs: somebody whose job is to make the output get used. Change management, under another name. In most organisations this is the binding constraint on value — not the modelling, not the infrastructure — and it is typically filled by an enthusiastic volunteer doing it alongside their real job until they burn out. If you can fund only one thing beyond the analytics engineer, consider funding this instead of the next technical role.

On buying versus building
The cost of building analytics capability has collapsed over the past few years. The cost of maintaining it has not moved at all, and the gap between those two facts is where a lot of plans go wrong.
Every model you deploy is a permanent commitment. It needs monitoring, because the world it learned from moves. It needs retraining, and then revalidating, which is a different and larger job than training it the first time. It needs documentation that stays current. And it needs somebody who can explain it when the person who built it has left, which they will. A reasonable planning assumption is to budget roughly as much for the second year of a model’s life as for the first — and then to ask, of every model somebody proposes, whether a rule would capture most of the value.
A rule that gets 60% of the benefit, that a depot manager can be told in one sentence, and that anybody can check by hand is frequently the better decision. It is also a decision that people who have just learned to build models find very hard to make, and there is no shame in that: it is hard to argue for the less sophisticated option immediately after acquiring the sophisticated one. Making the comparison explicit — what does the model add over the rule, and what does that increment cost to keep alive for three years — turns it from a matter of taste into a matter of arithmetic.

title: The operating model
section: Three mechanisms that turn pilots into a portfolio
text:
Three mechanisms that turn pilots into a portfolio
Here is the difference between an organisation with an analytics portfolio and one with a graveyard of pilots, and it is not talent and it is not budget. It is three mechanisms, each of which is cheap, dull, and almost never in place.
1 · A model register with a retirement date. One row per model in production: what it is, who owns it, what decision it feeds, when it was last validated, and the date by which it must be revalidated or switched off. Without it, models accumulate. Nobody removes anything, because removing something requires knowing what depends on it, and after a few years no one does. Eventually one of them fails in a way that reaches the board, and the question asked will be “who owned this?” — a question the register answers in five seconds and its absence cannot answer at all.
2 · A decision log. For every analytics-supported decision: what was decided, on what evidence, what was expected to happen, and — the line everybody omits — what actually happened. That last column is the whole point. Six months of an honest decision log is the most valuable management asset the function will ever produce, because it is the only thing that closes the loop back to 1.1 and tells you whether the analytics is working. It also transforms the annual budget conversation, which otherwise turns on anecdotes and whoever remembers the good quarter.
Keep it short enough that people fill it in. Five fields, one screen, filled in at the moment of the decision and revisited once, on a date set at the time.
3 · A quarterly portfolio review that kills things. Not a status update in which each initiative is reported as amber and continues. A review at which at least one thing is stopped, with the stopping treated as a normal outcome rather than as a failure attributable to a person. An analytics portfolio that has never stopped anything is not being managed; it is being accumulated, and its capacity is being consumed by work that nobody would start today.
The reason to name the killing explicitly is that stopping things is socially expensive. Somebody built it, somebody sponsored it, and in most organisations the path of least resistance is to let it continue at low intensity forever. Making “we stopped one” an expected output of the review is what makes it possible for an individual to propose stopping their own project without it reading as an admission.

title: The operating model
section: The 90-day plan that goes in your capstone
text:
The 90-day plan that goes in your capstone
Three milestones, in an order chosen so that the first one requires nobody’s permission — which matters more than it sounds, because a plan whose first step needs a committee is a plan that starts in month three.

The shape that gets funded
Days 1–14 · Prove the pipeline. Raw extract to tested table, running, with the quality contract. No new spend, no new headcount, no permissions. Deliverable: the pipeline runs and one number is defensible.
Days 15–45 · Prove the decision changes. One person, one recurring decision, using the output. Not a rollout — one person. Deliverable: they used it, and you can say what they did differently.
Days 46–90 · Prove the value, with a comparison. The randomised or quasi-experimental design from 5.2 or 5.3. Deliverable: a number with an interval, and the honest statement of what design produced it.
Each stage is deliberately a proof of something different, and the order is not arbitrary. It proves the plumbing before the decision, and the decision before the value, because a plan that tries to prove value first has to assume the other two and will be attacked on both.
At Day 90 you either have evidence and a case for scaling, or you have learned cheaply that the value hypothesis was wrong — which is also a success, and is the outcome you should say out loud when you present the plan rather than leaving it to be discovered. Saying it disarms the reviewer whose real objection is “what if it doesn’t work”, because you have already told them what happens in that case and how little it costs.

title: The operating model
section: The thing that will actually stop you
text:
The thing that will actually stop you
It is worth being direct about this, because plans of the kind above are usually derailed by something that appears nowhere in them. It is not the technology, which is adequate. It is not the data, which is imperfect everywhere and has never on its own stopped anything. It is not skills, which can be bought or taught.
It is the person whose judgement your initiative displaces — the topic of 1.1 and section 6 of your charter.
The depot manager who has ordered by feel for eleven years and is usually right. The relationship manager who knows which customers to call and why. The category buyer whose supplier relationship is not in any system. Each of them is experienced, respected, and correct often enough to have a genuine case — which is exactly what makes this hard, and why treating it as resistance to be overcome tends to fail. They are not obstacles to the analysis; in most cases they are holding information the analysis does not have.
Three things work, in ascending order of how uncomfortable they are and roughly ascending order of effectiveness:

Make them the author. Bring them the model as a draft rather than as a decision, and ask what it gets wrong. They will tell you, in detail, and they will be right about some of it. Their corrections improve the model, and the model becomes something they helped build rather than something being done to them. This costs two meetings and is the single highest-return move available.
Show the override log. Let them override the model. Log every override with its reason, and measure afterwards which ones improved the outcome. In many organisations roughly half of overrides turn out to be improvements — which is a genuinely useful finding, because it says the model needs the human, the human needs the model, and the conversation is no longer about replacement. It also identifies precisely where the model is weak, which is information you could not have got any other way.
Change what they are measured on, rather than what they are told to do. This is the one that requires seniority, and it is the one that actually settles the matter. If the depot manager is still measured on stock cover while the dashboard optimises for service level and obsolescence, then following the dashboard makes their numbers worse. No amount of training, communication or executive sponsorship will fix that, and they are entirely right to ignore it. Fix the measure and the behaviour follows without an argument.

title: The operating model
text:
Takeaways

Hub and spoke, in practice as well as on the chart. The test is who owns definitions.
Hire the analytics engineer first. Trustworthy tables come before clever models.
Budget the second year as heavily as the first. Ask whether a rule would do.
Model register with retirement dates. Decision log with outcomes. A quarterly review that kills things.
The binding constraint is the person whose judgement you are displacing. Make them the author.

title: Before Monday — setup
text:
This page is longer than a setup page usually is, because it tries to explain what each piece of software is and why the week needs it, rather than simply listing commands to paste. If you have never installed a programming toolchain before, that context is the difference between following instructions and understanding what you are doing — and the second is much less unnerving when something goes wrong.
If you have done all this before, the tables and the code blocks are the whole story and you can skim the prose in between.

title: Before Monday — setup
text:
The three tiers
You do not need everything on this page. Work out which tier you are in, and install that.










Tier 1 · Essential
Tier 2 · Recommended
Tier 3 · If you are going deeper




Query engine
DuckDB
DuckDB
+ Parquet workflow

—

+ Python


Reporting
—
Quarto
+ LaTeX (TinyTeX)


Delivery
Excel (you have it)

Quarto dashboards


Assistant
Any assistant, in a browser
+ Positron Assistant
+ a local model


Version control
—
Git
+ a GitHub account



Tier 2 is the programme’s actual requirement, and we would rather say so here than discover it together on Wednesday morning.
Tier 1 will carry you comfortably through Monday and Tuesday. Monday’s strategy work needs no tooling at all, and every Day 2 exercise — the SQL session, the laptop warehouse, joins, the quality contract — has a browser-and-DuckDB path through it that genuinely works.
From Wednesday the honest position changes. Forecasting with intervals, segmentation, propensity and leakage, and Thursday’s reproducible reporting all assume that R and Quarto are sitting in front of you. There is a DuckDB-only route through the arithmetic, and people have taken it successfully, but you will spend the second half of the week reading somebody else’s output rather than producing your own. Thursday’s lab, whose entire point is a document that regenerates itself when the data changes, does not really exist without Quarto.
So the recommendation is simple: install Tier 2 before you arrive. If your IT department will not permit it, that is a common and entirely reasonable situation rather than a failure on your part, and it is exactly what the pre-built cloud workspace exists for. Ask for it at the setup clinic rather than arriving on Wednesday and hoping.
Tier 3 is for the analytics leads in the room and is genuinely optional. Nothing in the assessed work depends on it.

Why we are telling you this
A programme that spends a full day on governance should not open by implying there is a free lunch.
Some of this stack costs nothing at all. Some of it does cost money, and some of it needs permission from your IT department — which is precisely what you would expect of tooling that touches company data. We would rather you arrived on Monday already knowing which is which than discovered it in week three, when you try to share a dashboard with a colleague and find that sharing is the part that is licensed.
Nothing in the assessed work requires you to spend money. Where a paid tool appears, the free substitute is named and we will say what it gives up.

title: Before Monday — setup
text:
Installing
Everything below follows the same shape: what the thing is, why the week needs it, the command, what a successful result looks like, and what to do if it does not appear.

DuckDB — everybody, ten minutes
What it is. A database engine that runs entirely inside a single file on your own laptop. There is no server to install, no account to create, and nothing leaves your machine. Think of it as a spreadsheet engine that has no row limit and speaks the same language as your warehouse.
Why the week needs it. It is the one genuinely non-negotiable install, because it is what lets you query the course data directly. In most corporate environments it installs without administrator rights, since it is a single executable rather than a system-wide package — which is exactly why we chose it for a room full of managed laptops.
Use whichever of these matches your operating system:
# macOS
brew install duckdb

# Windows
winget install DuckDB.cli

# Or download the single binary from duckdb.org/docs/installation
Then check that it works:
duckdb -c "SELECT 'ready' AS status, version() AS duckdb"
What success looks like. A small table printed in your terminal with two columns — status showing ready, and duckdb showing a version string. The exact version does not matter; the fact that it printed anything at all means the install worked.
If it does not work. The usual message is some variant of “command not found”, which almost always means the installer worked but your terminal does not yet know where to look. Closing the terminal and opening a fresh one resolves it most of the time, because the new window picks up the updated path. If it persists, download the single binary from the address above, put it somewhere you can find, and bring the error message to the clinic.
And this is the friendliest thing in the whole stack, for anyone who would rather not spend the week in a terminal:
duckdb -ui
That opens a notebook in your browser — tables down one side, queries and results and charts in the middle. Nothing is uploaded anywhere; the browser is just the interface to the engine running on your own machine. Several people in every cohort do most of the week here, and they are not at a disadvantage.


R and an IDE — Tier 2
What it is. R is a programming language built for working with data; an IDE is the application you write and run it in. You need both, in that order, because the IDE is the front door and R is the engine behind it.
Why the week needs it. From Wednesday onwards, forecasting, segmentation and reproducible reporting all run in R. You will not be writing it from scratch — the assistant does that — but it needs to be installed for you to run and inspect what it writes.

R from cloud.r-project.org — take the latest release.
An IDE: Positron (R and Python in one place, with an AI assistant panel) or RStudio Desktop. Either is fine and neither will hold you back. Positron is where the tooling is heading; RStudio is what most people recognise from a screenshot.
Packages. R ships small and gains its capabilities from add-on packages, so this step downloads the specific ones the week uses. Run it once. It takes fifteen to thirty minutes, mostly unattended — start it before Sunday and do something else.

install.packages(c(
  # core. dplyr and lubridate come with tidyverse, but the sessions call them
  # by name, so they are listed by name -- an install list that relies on you
  # knowing what is inside a metapackage is not a list, it is a quiz.
  "tidyverse", "dplyr", "lubridate", "arrow", "duckdb", "DBI", "janitor",
  "scales", "glue",
  # quality
  "pointblank",
  # modelling
  "tidymodels", "fable", "tsibble", "feasts", "pwr", "mclust",
  # causal inference (Friday)
  "fixest", "tidysynth",
  # text (Thursday)
  "tidytext", "tidylo", "irr",
  # reporting
  "quarto", "knitr", "rmarkdown", "openxlsx", "readxl",
  # assistants
  "ellmer", "mall"
))
What success looks like. A great deal of scrolling text, ending without the word ERROR. Warnings are common and usually harmless; errors are the ones to note. The definitive check is the script at the foot of this page, which loads every package by name and tells you which, if any, are missing.
If it does not work. Package installation is the step most likely to go wrong, and it usually goes wrong for one of three reasons: a corporate proxy blocking the download, a missing system library on macOS or Linux, or simply running out of patience and stopping it early. All three are quick for a technician to diagnose and slow to guess at alone. Copy the last twenty lines of output and bring them to the clinic — that text is genuinely all we need.


Quarto — Tier 2
What it is. A publishing tool that turns a document containing both prose and code into a finished report, dashboard or slide deck, running the code as it goes.
Why the week needs it. It is what makes Thursday’s central claim possible: a two-page brief in which every number is computed from the data rather than typed in by hand, so that when the data changes the document changes with it. This very website is built with it.
Download from quarto.org, then check it:
quarto check
What success looks like. A list of checks, each marked with a tick, covering the Quarto installation itself and the R and Python setups it can see. Do not be alarmed if the Python line reports a problem and the R line does not; Quarto reports on everything it looks for, and you only need the parts the week uses.
For PDF output, add the small LaTeX distribution — LaTeX is the typesetting engine that turns a document into a properly laid out PDF, and TinyTeX is a compact version of it that downloads what it needs on demand:
quarto install tinytex
If it does not work. quarto: command not found after a successful install is the same path problem described under DuckDB, and the same fix applies — open a new terminal window. If quarto check reports that it cannot find R, it is usually because R was installed after Quarto; reinstalling Quarto, or simply restarting the machine, resolves it.


Power BI Desktop — Tier 2, Windows only
What it is. Microsoft’s dashboard authoring tool, and the one most likely to be already standard in your organisation.
Why the week needs it. Thursday’s dashboard session is built around designing backwards from a decision, and it helps to practise that in the tool your colleagues will actually open. The principles transfer to any tool; the muscle memory does not.
It is free from the Microsoft Store. On macOS it does not exist — the options are a Windows virtual machine, a remote desktop your organisation provides, or the Power BI web service for viewing only. If you are on a Mac and Power BI matters to you, tell us before Monday and we will pair you appropriately for 4.3. This is a common situation and it is easily handled with a little notice.


An AI assistant — everybody
What it is. The conversational assistant that will write most of the code you run this week, while you read it, question it and correct it.
Why the week needs it. It is the subject of the programme as much as it is a tool for it. Any competent assistant works, and the method transfers unchanged between them. In class we all use the same one, so that everybody is looking at the same screen and the floor staff can help without having to learn your particular setup first.
Check your organisation’s policy before Monday. Some of you will find that a hosted assistant is not permitted for company data. That is frequently a correct policy rather than an obstructive one, and it is exactly the reason the local option below exists — so please do check rather than assume, and tell us what you find.


A local model — Tier 3, and the answer to most policy problems
What it is. A language model that runs entirely on your own laptop, with no network connection and no data leaving the machine.
Why it is here. It is what makes the Thursday classification session available to people whose data genuinely cannot go anywhere. It is slower than a hosted assistant and slightly less accurate, and neither of those matters much for the work we do with it.
# Install a local model runner, then:
ollama pull llama3.2
ollama run llama3.2 "Reply with the single word: ready"
What success looks like. The first command downloads a few gigabytes and shows a progress bar; the second prints a short reply. If the reply is the single word you asked for, everything is working. If it is a chatty sentence containing that word, everything is also working — models vary in how literally they take an instruction, which is itself a small lesson for the week.
If it does not work. The most common causes are disk space and memory: the model needs roughly 8 GB of each. A download that stalls partway usually restarts cleanly if you run the pull command again.
Nothing leaves your laptop. It works offline. It is free. It is worth setting up even if you are fairly sure you will not need it — see 4.2 for where it earns its place.

title: Before Monday — setup
text:
The data
The course datasets live in the same public repository as this site. Cloning it copies the whole thing to your machine, data included:
git clone https://github.com/bongoadi/turning-data-into-business-growth.git
cd turning-data-into-business-growth
duckdb -c "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM 'data/fmcg_sell_out.csv'"
# 55474
What success looks like. The count printed by the last command matches the number in the comment beneath it. That single line confirms three things at once: the clone worked, DuckDB works, and the file you have is the file we shipped.
No Git? Download the repository as a ZIP from the same address and unzip it anywhere convenient. The data/ folder, plus outputs/, is all you actually need — Git is a convenience here rather than a requirement.

title: Before Monday — setup
text:
The setup clinic
Thursday 8 October, 16:00–18:00, online. A technician, plus faculty.
The clinic exists so that installation problems are solved by somebody whose job that is, rather than by you at midnight. Come if any of the following is true — and there is no threshold of seriousness to clear first:


Your laptop is managed by your IT department and you cannot install software.


The package installation failed and you do not know why.


You are on macOS and need Power BI.


Your organisation blocks AI assistants.


You would rather someone did it with you than read instructions.


That last one is a perfectly good reason on its own, and it is the reason several people give every cohort.
The cloud workspace fallback. If none of this can be resolved on your own machine, we will provision you a pre-built environment that runs in a browser, with everything already installed and the data already loaded. It is a little slower than working locally, and you cannot use it with your own confidential data — but you will not lose a single session, and everything you learn in it applies directly to your own data once you are back at your desk.
Do ask for it early. Provisioning a whole cohort’s environments on Sunday night is a very different task from provisioning three on a Tuesday.

title: Before Monday — setup
section: Bring, or do not bring, your own data
text:
Bring, or do not bring, your own data
Every session in the week works perfectly well with the course datasets. Several people in each cohort deliberately work only with those and get more out of the week for it — the planted defects are the teaching material, and your own data, whatever else is wrong with it, does not have its problems arranged quite so conveniently for learning.
If you do want to work with your own data, four suggestions:


Check what you are permitted to take out of your systems, and get it in writing.


Prefer shape over content: column names, types, row counts, date range, grain. That is enough for most of the week, and it carries no risk.


If you bring real data, keep it on your own machine, do not put it in a hosted assistant, and read 5.4 before you arrive rather than after.


Three tables is the right number. Not thirty.


The third of those is the one people most often wish they had followed. Reading the governance session in advance takes twenty minutes and occasionally changes what somebody decides to bring.

title: Before Monday — setup
text:
The pre-work
Ten days before: your one-page problem charter. There is a template on the capstone page. It is read individually by faculty and it becomes your capstone, so it repays a little thought.
Ten days before: the twenty-minute data-triage diagnostic. It is not a test. It is used to stream the labs and pair people well, so that nobody spends the week either stranded or idle. Nobody sees anybody’s score, including you.
Before Sunday: run the installation check below, and tell us if anything fails. Two quick confirmations first:
duckdb -c "SELECT 'duckdb ok'"
quarto check
Then the R check. This one deliberately loads every package the week actually calls, rather than the three obvious ones, because the failure it is designed to catch is not “R is broken”. It is a single missing package surfacing at 09:20 on Thursday, on conference wifi, across a room full of laptops at once.
Rscript -e '
pkgs <- c("tidyverse","dplyr","lubridate","arrow","duckdb","DBI","janitor","scales","glue",
          "pointblank","tidymodels","fable","tsibble","feasts","pwr","mclust",
          "fixest","tidysynth","tidytext","tidylo","irr",
          "quarto","knitr","rmarkdown","openxlsx","readxl","ellmer","mall")
missing <- pkgs[!sapply(pkgs, requireNamespace, quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing)) {
  cat("MISSING:", paste(missing, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  cat("Run: install.packages(c(\"", paste(missing, collapse = "\",\""), "\"))\n", sep = "")
} else cat("R ok - all", length(pkgs), "packages present\n")
'
What success looks like. A single line beginning R ok. If instead you get a line beginning MISSING:, the script has already written out the exact command that fixes it — copy that second line, run it, and run the check again.
Bring the output either way to the clinic. “It said MISSING: tidylo, irr” is a thirty-second fix on the Thursday before the programme. The same words on the Thursday morning of the programme are considerably less convenient, and that is the entire reason this check exists.

Stuck? Please just ask — that is what these are for. execedsales@lbs.edu.ng · +234 (0) 802 501 4624 · or come to the clinic on Thursday 8 October.
